question_text:
Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**STATION S**

**Presenting Situation:** A 37-year old man presents for the first time to this primary care physician’s office to get a refill for his pain medication. He had a knee injury several years ago and has not been pain free since then.

You have already met this patient today and completed a pain assessment. You needed to step outside the exam room (reason is not relevant) and you are re-entering to complete the interview as described below.

**Setting**: Primary Care Clinic

**Your Tasks:**

1. Read the medical chart (initially unavailable), and screen and assess the patient for risk of prescription drug abuse. It is not necessary to give advice, refer the patient, or perform a physical examination. The focus is abuse of prescription drugs, not the injury per se.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**MEDICAL CHART**

**Patient:** Charles White, Age 37

**CC:** Chronic knee pain due to an old football injury. Requests a refill of Percocet.

**HPI:**

* Fifteen years ago, patient injured right knee. States pain has never completely gone away. No recent re-injury.

**SH:**

* Married, 2 children
* Insurance adjuster, recently transferred, needs a new physician.

**Vital Signs:**

Height: \_\_\_\_\_\_

Weight: \_\_\_\_\_\_

Temperature: 101.7 degrees oral

Pulse: 97 per minute

Blood Pressure: 135/84

Respiratory Rate: 22

BMI: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

Allergies: Penicillin Medications

**PMH: (Information you received from earlier in the interview with the patient):**

While playing collegiate football, patient sustained an extensive, "career ending injury." Patient underwent four surgeries to restore mobility to the knee and then, what patient calls an ‘agonizing 18 months’ of physical therapy to restore partial use. He has not had any physical therapy since. Two years after the surgery he had steroidal injections and imaging of his knee. He tried acupuncture a year ago without much effect He still walks with a cane and experiences significant periods of pain which requires medication if he is to have any productivity that day. Without medication he states he is unable to work, socialize, or even concentrate for long periods.

He has tried Advil (600 mg every 4 hrs, about 12/day), which didn’t help. When he feels well he walks as much as he can with his cane for exercise and tries to be active with his children. He is currently taking Percocet (10mg/325mg [2 tablets 3x a day]) and has for the past 4 years.

**Pain Assessment done earlier in the interview:** Today, he stated the pain in his knee is moderate. He only has enough Percocet medication for three more days and he is afraid the pain will be severe if he runs out.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Charles White

**Presenting Situation:** The patient is a 37-year old man who recently moved to Chicago from Houston. He needs a new physician to prescribe him Percocet (a narcotic pain medication) for constant pain he has due to an old injury sustained 15 years ago from playing college football. He takes Percocet 3 times a day and has enough medication for three more days. For the patient this medication is a necessity; he cannot do without it. The patient knows it might be a crutch. The purpose and goal of this visit is only to get more Percocet prescribed. He feels that having to be evaluated is a demeaning waste of time.

* **Opening statement:** I was just transferred by my employer to Chicago and need a new physician to prescribe my pain medication. It took me a long time to find you and get an appointment, so I am almost out of pills. I only have 3 more days left.
* **Appearance and dress:** Wear casual business clothes. You need to look like you are in some pain. Have a cane by your chair (will be provided).
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:** Look uncomfortable. Act irritated at times, especially if there is any resistance to getting the Percocet. If the clinician starts giving you too much advice, you can be unhappy or not ready to hear it.

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset**: 15 years ago, I injured my right knee when I played college football. I was a running back. Once when I was tackled, my knee was injured and that was the end of my career. I had 4 operations and 18 months of physical therapy which was agonizing for me. My knee was never the same again and I walk with a cane. Also, the pain never went away completely.

**Location and quality**:

* The pain is in my right knee and sometimes goes up and down my leg.
* The pain feels manageable when I am on medication, even though it still hurts

**Characteristics/Intensity**:

* I’ve had pain for 15 years with a small decrease after the surgeries and physical therapy.
* I would describe my pain as moderate (3-4/10 on pain scale) when on the pain medicine.
* When I take Percocet (if have already revealed the name; if not say pain medicine), my pain is: 3-4 (1-10 pain scale). Without Percocet: 8 (1-10 pain scale).

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**: If I’m not on Percocet, it hurts all the time no matter what I do. Only the Percocet helps.

**Medications/Treatments**

* **Percocet**
* Dose:
  + I take 2 pills, 3 times a day. I take the Percocet in the morning, after work and in the evening. The pills are 10 mg/325 mg tablets.
  + If asked about a starting dose: I started with 1 pill three times a day, but now I take 2 pills three times a day.
  + I’ve been on the Percocet for the past 4 years.
  + How does the Percocet affect you?
    - It really helps. The pain never totally goes away, but at least I can work and function. I can concentrate better. It makes my life manageable and the only way I can live a halfway normal life.
    - Occasionally, I wake up in the morning with a sharp pain, but it subsides after I take Percocet.
  + Side effects:
    - I get constipated sometimes and could use a prescription for that.
    - I sometimes feel sleepy, but not often. I make sure I don’t drive. But I usually don’t have trouble with that
  + If asked why was the change made to Percocet: My doctor put me on the Percocet. It has fewer side effects (than the morphine – nausea and dizziness, sometimes).
  + Significance**:** Without the Percocet, I can’t do anything. I can’t concentrate enough to work and my knee hurts with any movement. I just need a new prescription for Percocet to manage my life.
* **Other treatments**
  + I had physical therapy for 18 agonizing months after my surgery
  + Two years after my surgery (13 years ago), I had steroids put in my knee with a needle
  + Six years ago, I tried Advil so I could get off prescription pain medicine. It didn’t help at all. I took 600mg tablets 4 times a day for about 1 week.
  + A year ago, I tried acupuncture. It only helped for a day and I never went back for more treatments.

**Other:** If asked about your knee: I can bend my knee a little bit, but not all the way

**Past Medical History**:

**Childhood and adult illnesses**: Own history. Last physical was a year ago.

**Hospitalizations and surgeries:** Only for my knee injury. The injury required four separate operations.

**Allergies:**

* Penicillin. Found that out when I was a kid. I broke out in a rash.
* I have seasonal allergies. I take Chlortrimeton occasionally for sinus congestion.

**Medications:**

* Morphine (only if asked):
  + I was given morphine immediately after my surgery while I was in the hospital. This was given to me intravenously.
  + Once I was home, I took the long acting release pill. I continued to take it until 4 years ago (total time on morphine pills was 11 years). ow my
  + If asked about the dose: I took 30 mg twice a day for the first four weeks after I got home. My dose was then lowered to 15 mg twice per day. Also, I started physical therapy about this time.
  + Side effects: I had some nausea and bad constipation. Sometimes I got dizzy and felt out of it. The dizziness lasted about 2 weeks. I was nauseous a few times a day the whole time I was on the morphine. It was mostly in the afternoon and evenings. I did my best to deal with it.
* Over-the-counter drugs:
  + Allergy medicine (Chlortrimeton) in the spring and fall
* **Other Specific pain medication information:**
  + **Have you ever taken more than the prescribed amount**? Yes, but just twice
    - Once after they reduced my prescription for long-acting morphine. I think I took 3-4 pills over the course of a week.
    - And 2 years ago when I had a particularly bad pain spell. I took an extra 3- 4 pills over the course of a week. Then my doctor increased the Percocet from one to two pills and it has been better.
  + **Have you ever tried to stop taking the pain medication?** Yes, only once
* I tried was 6 years ago. I wanted to try to stop because I didn’t like taking pain meds all the time. It didn’t last long. I wasn’t able to do anything normal, I didn’t feel well and I wasn’t able to sleep. I never made it more than a week.

**Life Style Behavioral Risks**:

* **Diet:** Own history. 3 cups of coffee a day.
* **Exercise:** My only exercise is walking, with a cane.
* **Sleep**: Sometimes I have trouble sleeping. The pain sometimes keeps me awake or wakes me up in the middle of the night and then I have trouble getting back to sleep. The pain that wakes me up is quite sharp and then I can’t get comfortable, no matter the position. But usually the Percocet helps that.
* **Stress**: Things seem really stressful right now--from moving, new job responsibilities, new schools for the kids, the pain in my knee, lack of sleep, tenseness in the relationship with my wife. My wife and I are getting short with each other because of all the changes in our lives.
* **Tobacco**: Don’t smoke; never have.
* **Alcohol:** I drink 1-2 beers maybe once a month, when my pain is bad after work or before bed. I know I shouldn’t drink, so it is only when the pain is worse and I don’t want to take more medication than I should. I did have a beer last night to help with all the stress I’ve been under.
* **Prescription drug use behavior:**
* I have had a few early refills (2, I think) because my pain was really bad. Last time, my doctor warned me that he would discontinue the medication if I did it again (about 2 years ago). He increased my dosage of Percocet so now I’m okay.
  + I have never over-sedated myself (put to sleep or knocked out)
  + I have never felt intoxicated
  + I have never gotten prescriptions from friends or more than one doctor at a time
* **Illegal drug use:** none
* **Sexual history:**
* **Current:** I’ve had a monogamous relationship with my wife for the past 10 years since my marriage.
* **Number of partners:**  Own history.
* **Birth Control:** Own history.
* **Sexually transmitted diseases:** Neither one of us have had a sexual illness
* **Sexual issues**: It hasn’t been great because of the stress of moving, my pain and medications. My desire for sex and ability to "perform" have decreased.
* **Legal Issues:** I have never had legal problems or been arrested due to drug or alcohol use or anything else.

**Psychological History:**

* **Age:** 37 (Sept 10, 1974)
* **Marital/Parental status**: I've been married for ten years. We have two children (a boy 8 yrs. and a girl 6 yrs.).
* **Occupation**: I’m an insurance adjuster for a national insurance company. I just moved to the Midwest from Houston about one month ago when I was transferred to a regional branch.
* **Where do you live?** Chicago.
* **Mental Health**:
  + **Depression:** I feel down sometimes because I’ve had pain for such a long time and I’ve taken meds for so long. The depression never lasts for more than a day or two. My wife and kids help pull me out of it.
  + **Treatment:** I’ve never had treatment for depression or felt I needed it.
  + **Suicidal thoughts:** No. I’ve never thought about hurting myself.
  + **History of preadolescent sexual abuse:** None

**Family History**:

* **Mother:** 68; alive and well
  + If asked about alcohol of drug abuse: My mother doesn’t drink or use illegal drugs
* **Father:** 69; alive and well
  + If asked about alcohol of drug abuse: My father drinks socially, but isn’t an alcoholic. Doesn’t use illegal drugs.
* **Siblings:** None
* **Family Health:** No family history of any health problems.

**MONITORING QUESTIONS:**

**Urine Screening:** If asked if you’d be willing to have urine drug screening: I suppose so if I have to in order to get the Percocet but I’m not happy about it. Can I get a temporary prescription until I come back for the next appointment?

**Records from Texas Physician:** If asked about getting records from your doctor in Texas: Go ahead, but that will take so long, won’t it? I really need the medication now. Please, can I have a temporary prescription?

**Signing an Agreement**: If asked to sign an agreement (one doctor, one pharmacy, no early refills, etc.): I think it’s demeaning, but if I have to, I will.

**Other Pain Management Options**: If asked to consider other pain management options: (Be reluctant) I’ve tried a lot of things, but they never help or not for long. I’ve tried things like acupuncture and physical therapy. My doctor in Texas understood that all of it just didn’t work as well as the medications.

Summary: TimeLine for Treatment

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**STATION HR**

**Presenting Situation:** Patient was seen by you in the clinic 1 week ago. Prior to that visit, his normal physician had very recently retired. As of today, he has enough of his medication for one more week. As part of your initial assessment of the patient, you asked him to submit a urine sample for analysis.

**Setting:** Primary Care Clinic

**Your Tasks:**

1. Read the medical chart
2. Give the patient the results of his urine drug screening
3. Discuss the next steps in pain management

Note: The focus is abuse of prescription drugs, NOT the injury per se.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**MEDICAL CHART**

**Patient:** Robert Jameson, Age 39

**CC:** Severe hip pain due to a motorcycle accident 5 years ago. Patient was seen in the clinic 1 week ago. He returns today for his second visit to get the results of his urine test, and he wants a refilled prescription for long acting morphine and short acting Vicodin. His previous physician retired very recently.

**HPI:** See notes from previous physician below.

**SH:**

* Divorced; 2 children, living with their mother in another state
* On SSI for disability; was in the construction and roofing business

**Vital Signs:**

Height \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Weight \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Temperature: 98.6 degrees oral

Pulse: 95 per minute

Blood Pressure: 120/80

Respiratory Rate: 15

BMI: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Tobacco: About a pack a day

Allergies: None

Medications: Long acting controlled-release morphine sulfate, 30 mg 2x/day; Vicodin 10 mg 325 2x/day; Zoloft 50 mg once/day at bedtime.

**Notes in previous physician’s chart**:

Five years ago, the patient had dislocated his right hip due to a motorcycle accident. The femoral head was dislodged from the socket. It was a posterior dislocation treated by surgical realignment and traction. The protective cartilage on the bone was also disturbed in the accident. He went through three months of what he described as “extremely painful” physical therapy. He was prescribed controlled-release morphine sulfate 100 mg, twice daily for pain after the surgery. His pain and functioning improved after physical therapy, so the morphine was reduced to 30 mg twice daily from 100 mg. Vicodin (10mg/325mg 2x/day) was added three months ago when he reported episodic extreme pain (8-9 on a numeric pain scale).

The patient has been in recovery from heroin addiction for fifteen years. Four and ¾ years ago, he was prescribed Zoloft 50 mg once/day at bedtime for extreme depression during rehabilitation from the hip surgery. He had one overdose (attempted suicide?) while addicted to heroin, which he said was accidental. Sixteen years ago the patient forged a prescription, which was before treatment for heroin use. Three months ago, he had two early refills. One refill was given at an Emergency Room visit. The other was given at a follow-up clinic visit at which time Vicodin was prescribed in addition and the patient signed a new agreement with the physician indicating one physician, one pharmacy, no early refills. Notation: if the patient breaks the agreement, he will no longer be prescribed narcotic medications.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Robert Jameson

**Presenting Situation:** This is a one week follow-up appointment for this 39-year old man with severe pain due to a hip injury from a motorcycle accident five years ago. He returns today to get the results of his urine drug test that was taken at his last visit. The patient’s goal is get a refill of his prescriptions for morphine and Vicodin. His regular physician has recently retired. He would see his regular physician for prescription refills and have him check his pain levels. His very last visit with his physician was about 1 month ago. Today, he is seeing the same health care provider as he did one week ago. The patient will be told that his urine is positive for his prescribed medication of morphine, negative for his prescribed Vicodin and positive for marijuana.

* **Opening statement:** I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week.
* **Appearance and dress:** Dress casually. Jeans are okay. Be neat and clean. Bring a cane for extra support on your right side when walking.
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:**
  + You are pleasant, but slightly nervous.
  + You are as cooperative as possible so you will get the prescription refilled.
  + If challenged about your current or past drug use behavior, be apologetic and use excuses why you used drugs in the past. For example, if you are told that marijuana was found in your urine, say: it helps you sleep, apologize and say you won’t smoke again if you get your pain medication.
  + You are in a moderate amount of pain

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset:**  My hip pain started five years ago because of a motorcycle accident I was involved in.

**Location:** The pain is in my right hip and sometimes goes down my back or right leg. Also sometimes my left hip hurts. I suppose it’s because I’m over compensating with more use of my left leg and hip.

**Duration:** The pain is constant and gets a lot worse when I don’t take the pain medicine.

**Characteristics/Intensity**:

* For some reason about 3 months ago, the pain became worse and was a 6-8 (1-10 pain scale). The pain was severe then. When I started taking the Vicodin plus the morphine about 3 months ago, the pain was less and usually a 3-4 (1-10 pain scale).
* Right now the pain varies between a 3 and 4 (1-10 pain scale). I would describe my pain as moderate.

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**:

* Standing and walking makes it worse.
* If I sit too long it makes it worse, especially when I first move to get up.
* It was worse when I tried to work, that is why I am on SSI (SSI is Supplemental Security Income, a program to provide benefits/money to the disabled).
* Only the pain medicine (morphine and Vicodin) seems to make it better and keep the pain in check so I can function.

**Treatments tried/results**:

* After the motorcycle accident, my doctor gave me controlled-release morphine sulfate 100 mg. I took it two times a day and it helped a lot. A few months later (3 or 4 months), my dose was lowered to 30 mg two times a day because my hip was somewhat better (less pain).
* A few months ago, I started getting really extreme pain at times. On the pain scale, it was about an 8-10, especially at night. My doctor prescribed Vicodin too. Now I am no longer getting such extreme pain.
* Tylenol has never helped. Aspirin and Advil cause stomach problems for me so I don’t take them.

**Consequences/Impact:**

* Without medication:
  + I cannot live a normal life. I can’t do any of my normal activities without difficulty.
  + I can’t sleep well
  + My appetite is less.
  + I get somewhat depressed. That is why I take the Zoloft.

**Other:**

* If asked how well you have been functioning since your last visit 1 week ago: I’m managing okay as long as I take my pain medicine.
* If asked what you think is going on/or why you needed the additional pain medication: I don’t know. I think I just got used to the 30 mg morphine and so needed the Vicodin in addition.
* Heroin addiction:
  + If asked about illegal drug use, deny at first. If asked again, say the following:
    - I’ve been in recovery from using heroin for fifteen years. (I used 10 bags/day. I spent about $60/day). I started using heroin 20 years ago and used for 5 years.
    - I have worked so hard to recover from heroin. I was very motivated to do treatment after the birth of my children. (Note to SP: you are afraid you might go back to using again to relieve your pain. Also, you are afraid this clinician won’t give you a refill because you are a recovering heroin addict).

**Pertinent negatives:**

* + I’ve had no withdrawal symptoms, but I’m afraid I will get them if I don’t get my prescriptions filled. (Note to SP: withdrawal symptoms may include the following: agitation, worse mood, irritability, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle aches, goose bumps, runny nose, runny eyes, enlarged pupil, diarrhea, yawning, or not able to sleep).
* If asked about changes/new stresses in your life: No except that I can’t work, which means I get quite bored and feel guilty about it and I would like to have more money especially to help my children

**Past Medical History:**

* **Childhood and adult illnesses:** Own history. Last physical was 6 months ago.
* **Hospitalizations and surgeries:** I was in the hospital 3 times
  + After my motorcycle accident, I was in the hospital for hip surgery (5 years ago).

Motorcycle accident info: A car side swiped me and the bike spun out of control and I fell on my right hip. My hip has never been the same. It also sometimes affects the muscles in my lower back area.

* + I was in the hospital once about 16 years because I accidently overdosed. This was before I recovered from using heroin. I accidently took too much heroin and some other pills. I’m not even sure what they were.
  + When I went through heroin withdrawal 15 years ago I was in the hospital for 5 days
* **Allergies:** None
* **Medications:**
  + **Prescription medications:**
    - Long acting controlled-release morphine sulfate, 30 mg, two times a day
    - Vicodin 10 mg/325mg two times a day
    - Zoloft 50 mg once/day at bedtime (for depression).
  + **Side effects:**
    - I’ve gotten used to most of the side effects. I get constipated and drowsy from the Vicodin.
    - The drowsiness spikes after I take the medicine. After that I’m okay.
    - I don’t feel sleepy when driving.
  + **Stopping use of pain medication:** I’ve been on the pain medicine since my hip injury. I haven’t tried to stop because it is pretty effective. If I stop, I’m afraid that the pain would be too great.

**Life Style Behavioral Risks:**

* **Diet:** Not very good. I can’t afford much. I eat a lot of junk food because it’s cheaper. I drink about 3 cups of coffee a day.
* **Exercise:** I try to walk a few times a week when my hip isn’t hurting too much. I try some of the exercises the PT suggested if my hip isn’t hurting too much.
* **Sleep:** I do have some trouble sleeping, probably a few nights a week. Sometimes I just can’t get comfortable because of my hip and sometimes I wake up because of the pain. It has been better since the Vicodin.
* **Stress:** I never seem to have enough money since I’m not working. I would like to do more for my children. It is very stressful. I sometimes do odd jobs for my friends. I tried getting up on a roof again recently, but it was just too painful.
* **Tobacco:** I smoke about a pack a day. Have since I was a teen.
* **Alcohol**: I don’t drink now because my Dad is an alcoholic. I did drink when I was younger and even when I was on heroin, but not anymore.
* **Prescription drug use behavior:**
  + I have not over sedated myself on my medication.
  + I felt intoxicated (lightheaded and super happy) a few times when I was first taking morphine. But never after the dose was reduced.
  + I‘ve increased my dose on my own twice when the pain was really bad, but not since I’ve had Vicodin. And I signed an agreement (with my doctor) 3 months ago saying I wouldn’t (this was the same time Vicodin was prescribed). (Note to SP: the agreement is that he will use one physician, one pharmacy to get his prescriptions; no early refills. If the patient breaks the agreement, he will no longer be prescribed narcotic medications).
  + I’ve had two early refills, both just before I got the Vicodin prescription. I increased the dose when the pain was worse. Once I went to the emergency room and once I saw my doctor. When I saw my doctor, last time, he warned me that he would discontinue the medication if I did it again. And he added the Vicodin, which has helped.
  + I only have one week left on my prescriptions for morphine and Vicodin. I’m not out yet so I’m not feeling any withdrawal symptoms ((Note to SP: withdrawal symptoms may include the following: agitation, worse mood, irritability, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle aches, goose bumps, runny nose, runny eyes, enlarged pupil, diarrhea, yawning, or not able to sleep).
* **Illegal drug use**:
  + **Heroin**
    - First deny any use. But if asked again, admit to using. See “other” section above. I used heroin for about 5 years, but have been recovering for 15 years.
  + **Marijuana**:
    - I smoked a little marijuana after I recovered from using heroin, but I quit.
    - If asked about current use: do not admit to using marijuana unless told it was found in the urine test:
      * I must have used it right before my urine test. I smoked some to help with the pain, especially to help me sleep. I really don’t want to go back to using heroin and I’m afraid I will if the pain is too great. I also didn’t want to take more of my pain medications without permission.
      * If asked additional questions about marijuana use the following as appropriate:
* I’ve actually smoked a few times because of the pain. I don’t have very good health coverage through Medicare. I have easy access to marijuana from old friends. Now that I have the Vicodin, I don’t need to use the marijuana very often. I’ll stop if you continue to give me the morphine and the Vicodin.”
* I’ve used marijuana ever since my accident. I’ve used it off and on to relax or for sleep at night. I’ve used it rarely since my doctor prescribed Vicodin.
* The last time I used marijuana was several nights ago before bed.
  + - If asked why only marijuana showed up in the urine/told Vicodin was not found in urine test/asked if selling Vicodin/giving Vicodin to someone else:
      * + Oh no, sometimes the marijuana works even better than the Vicodin and I sometimes take it if I have it on hand. But if you renew my prescriptions, I promise not to use the marijuana anymore and I will always take the Vicodin.
        + Note to SP: real reason for no Vicodin in urine is he is selling to friends. He needs money, the marijuana is working. Can tell the truth only if pressured to do so
* **Attempts to stop** using illegal drugs:
  + Of course I stopped using heroin with the help of drug rehab.
  + Only give marijuana information if discussed marijuana in urine: I haven’t tried stopping marijuana completely. I think marijuana isn’t as harmful, but I will stop if you tell me to, as long as my other pain medications work
* **Sexual history:**
* **Current:** Since my divorce, I’ve slept with a lot of women, which I’m not proud of.
* **Number of partners:** ballpark 20 or 30. I’m not really sure.
* **Birth control:** I always use a condom. I’m not with anyone right now.
* **Sexually transmitted diseases:**
  + I’ve been tested for HIV and I don’t have it. The last time I was tested was 2 months ago. I haven’t been with anyone for about 4 months.
  + I’ve had my share of STDs when I was on heroin, but not since.
* **Legal issues:**
  + I was arrested a few times for possession of heroin and forging checks. That was when I was using heroin. I spent a few days in jail, but that eventually got me into treatment. I had small children and I was afraid my wife would leave me. I’ve had no arrests in the last fifteen years.
  + Also, I was arrested once for forging a Vicodin prescription 16 years ago.

**Psychological History:**

* **Age:** 39 (July 15, 1973)
* **Marital/Parental status:** I’ve been divorced for 7 years. I live alone and am not involved with anyone right now. I have 2 children; A boy, 17 and a girl 16. They live with their mother in Iowa.
* **Occupation:**  Until my accident, I worked for a construction and roofing company. But now I’m considered permanently disabled and can’t do that work anymore. I still do a few minor odd jobs for friends.
* **Where do you live?** In Chicago.
* **Mental Health:**
* **Depression:** I was diagnosed with depression after my hip treatment and rehabilitation.
* **Treatment:** I take Zoloft which has helped a lot.
* **Suicidal thoughts:** I accidently took an overdose once during the ups and downs of heroin use, but it really was an accident. I didn’t realize how much heroin and other substances I had taken. So it was an overdose.
* **History of preadolescent sexual abuse:**  I was sexually abused when I was a child by my aunt. It went on for 3years
* **Support systems:** a few friends

**Family History:**

* **Mother**: My mother died of an overdose of sleeping pills when she was 55 years old. I don’t know what pills she took. I don’t know if it was a suicide or accident. My mother was often very depressed.
* **Father:** Age 65 and is an alcoholic. I stay away from him. I haven’t seen him in years.
* **Siblings:** I have 1 sister who won’t have anything to do with me because of my past use of heroin.
* **Family Health:** No family history of any other health problems except my mother’s depression.

**Other Treatment Options**:

* If asked: “what else have you tried to control the pain?”
  + I haven’t tried anything. I can’t afford the cost. And besides I’m afraid it would be too painful without the medicine.”
* **Be willing to try an alternative medication** such as Suboxone instead of morphine?
  + I don’t know much about it, but I’d like to know more.
* **Be referred to an addiction specialist or a detox program?**

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a surgical resident. You are about to meet with a patient who has just returned to the hospital room following an operation that you performed with the attending.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 30-55 years old with Crohn’s disease on the surgery service. You have just done a partial small bowel resection (for strictures) which was unexpectedly complicated, and required a loop ileostomy rather than the expected end-to-end anastomosis. During pre-operative planning, you and your attending had told the patient there was a small chance of this happening but you did not expect it.

The patient has not been easy to care for from the outset. You have met them a couple of times before, and the patient has chastised you for running even 15 minutes late. The patient has a reputation around the office for being “difficult,” and the secretary has complained to you about the number of calls from this patient about relatively minor concerns. The two times that you’ve seen the patient in clinic, they brought a long list of issues for you to deal with, including many that had nothing to do with the Crohn’s disease and the upcoming surgery, but were more primary care type of concerns.

**Student Tasks:**

Give the news about the ileostomy to the patient. You enter the hospital room to tell your patient this news, knowing the patient will be unhappy.

You are a patient in a hospital room. You just returned from the post-surgery recovery area, having undergone a small bowel surgery (“partial small bowel resection”) for Crohn’s disease-related strictures a few hours ago. You have recently come out of anesthesia but are fully awake. You have a good handle on what these terms mean. Although weak from surgery and in pain, you will be livid and respond with anger. You cannot believe how your doctor “lied to me.” He/she “promised me that I wouldn’t need a bag.” You have called the office many times in recent weeks to go over the plan and to ask questions and your understanding was that it was highly unlikely that “I’d end up with a bag.” Your doctor only called back a few times, otherwise you always had to speak with the nurse, and you wonder if all of your concerns were made clear.

You don’t know how you will function. You feel that your social life will be ruined. You just began dating again after a messy divorce three years ago. He takes Vicodin 3 times a day and has enough medication for three more days. For the patient this medication is a necessity; he cannot do without it. The patient knows it might be a crutch. The purpose and goal of this visit is only to get more Vicodin prescribed. He feels that having to be evaluated is a demeaning waste of time.

* **Opening statement:** I was just transferred by my employer to Chicago and need a new physician to prescribe my pain medication. It took me a long time to find you and get an appointment, so I am almost out of pills. I only have 3 more days left.

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset**: 5 years ago, I injured my right shoulder and top part of my humerus (bone runs from shoulder to elbow) in a bicycle accident. I had one operation where they pinned the bones together. After that, I had 3 months of physical therapy which was very painful for me. My shoulder was never the same again. My shoulder is very stiff and I can’t move it like I used to. Also, the pain never went away completely.

**Location and quality**:

* The pain is in my right shoulder and sometimes goes up and down my arm.
* The pain feels manageable when I am on medication, even though it still hurts

* I’ve had pain for 5 years which got a little better after the surgery and physical therapy.

* When I take Vicodin (if have already revealed the name; if not say pain medicine), my pain is: 3-4 (1-10 pain scale). Without Vicodin: 8 (1-10 pain scale).

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**: If I’m not on Vicodin, it hurts all the time no matter what I do. Only the Vicodin helps.   + I take 2 pills, 3 times a day. I take the Vicodin in the morning, after work and in the evening. The pills are 10 mg/325 mg tablets.

  + Significance**:** Without the Vicodin, I can’t do anything. I can’t concentrate enough to work and my shoulder hurts with any movement. I just need a new prescription for Vicodin to manage my life.

  + After surgery, I had a sling for 4 weeks and I had physical therapy for 3 very painful months
  + Two years after my surgery (3 years ago), I had steroids put in my shoulder with a needle. It reduced the pain for about a month and then it was back.

**Other:** If asked about your shoulder: I use my right arm as long as I am careful not to jar my shoulder. It is still painful when I get dressed and put on my shirt and jacket.

**Childhood and adult illnesses**: Own history. Last physical was a year ago.

  + If asked about the dose: I took 30 mg twice a day for the first four weeks after I got home. My dose was then lowered to 15 mg twice per day. Also, I started physical therapy about this time.

# I. Rattlesnake bite (Crotalinae envenomation) simulation

# IV. Environment

a. Simulation Environment Setup: Simulation lab Emergency Department room, medication area (Pyxis or second area), audio-visual control room, debrief room/area

V. Actors

ii. Physician(s): One to three participant physicians. Multiple configurations are possible. The Course Director may choose a primary or may have learners work in groups.

# Appendix D

Participant Information Card

This is a patient with a history of mild intermittent asthma who presents with a snake bite. The patient told triage: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” Their main complaint is increasing pain in the arm and they noticed some mild wheezing upon arrival (the patient stated it was: “like my asthma is acting up”)

# Appendix B

Moulage & Standardized Patient Support

The standardized patient (SP) has a history of mild intermittent asthma and presents with a snake bite. The complaint will be: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (If asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”

During the scenario, the SP will complain of increasing pain in the arm, nose bleed, and wheezing “like my asthma is acting up”.

The standardized patient should be coached on which pathway the instructor plans to use to avoid adding any unnecessary symptoms or complaints that may confuse the clinical picture.

If available, the instructor may utilize an earpiece so that they can communicate with the standardized patient during the scenario to help address and concerns that arise.

Since endotracheal intubation is not a part of this scenario, if the participants discuss this with the patient, the patient should tell them, “ I don’t want a tube in my throat and I’m starting to feel a little better”

# a. Scenario Background

i. Chief complaint (given freely): “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (if asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”   
ii. Past Medical History (if asked): Asthma, mild intermittent   
iii. Allergies: None   
iv. Medications: albuterol rescue inhaler prn dyspnea (uses 1-2 times a month)   
v. Immunizations: “No idea”   
vi. Family and Social history: no family diseases, social alcohol (1 drink a week), no tobacco or illegal dugs   
vii. Review of systems: Mild chest tightness with dyspnea (“I think my asthma is back”)

# b. Scenario Initial State

i. Patient Habitus and Presentation: the patient gives history of being bitten by a snake. “I think it was a rattlesnake” and complains of worsening swelling and pain in the hand.   
ii. Physiology: T 37.2, HR 120bpm, BP 140/80 R 22 SPO2 98%. Narrow complex rhythm with tachycardia on monitor.   
iii. Focused exam:

1. General: Reveals a patient in moderate distress (pain) and anxious

b. Skin: Normal color and turgor, no diaphoresis or rash

c. Hand: Right hand is swollen and discolored with fang marks and edema, patient is wearing a ring and a watch.

e. Lungs: Tachypnea and expiratory wheezing

h. Nose and IV site: coagulopathy can be represented by adding simulated blood to area surrounding IV site and nose

# c. Scenario Branch Points

ii. Scenario B: The patient is experiencing moderate pain at the bite site, mild expiratory wheezing, and some bleeding for the nose. If participants do not recognize envenomation, contact poison control or administer antivenom, the patient will become hypotensive and delirious.

1. Changes in Patient Condition: The patient’s condition will deteriorate over the course of the scenario. They will become increasingly somnolent and delirious.

**CASE 3B**
Robert Goodman,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Robert Goodman is a 45 year old laborer who works for a moving company. Over the last month he has experienced some vague, minor chest pains on exertion, especially while at work when he is lifting. One of Robert’s coworkers recently had cardiac problems and was a smoker. His physician recommended that he quit smoking and he did so. He discussed the issue with Robert several times.

Robert is now concerned that there may be some connection between his current symptoms and his smoking. He approached this friend, who gave Robert his leftover patches. Robert tried them a month ago for a few days but used them incorrectly.

Robert is now blaming his inability to quit on the patch. However, Robert smokes about two or three packs a day but started on the lowest level of the patch. That’s what his friend gave him. In addition, Robert took the patch off two or three times a day to smoke. He kept a pack of cigarettes in the moving van, “just in case”. Robert never read the package instructions and did not make any behavioral changes.

The chest pains persisted for about a week, so Robert is now in the office for a follow up visit after having the usual battery of cardiac diagnostic tests (all of which are negative). The subsequent visit revealed that the chest pains were a result of gastritis and reflux which have responded to antacids (Zantac). However, Robert does not like taking medicines, and this incident has brought the concept of quitting to the forefront of Robert’s thinking. He is now motivated to quit, but this prior “attempt” has left him somewhat disheartened. He does not understand why the patches worked for his friend and not for him.

**Your role is to play a smoker who is** <u>**definitely interested in quitting**</u>**. However, he has come to believe that his recent failure to do so is the fault of the patches he used. He does not understand that he used them incorrectly. He also does not understand that the quitter must actively participate in the quit (make behavioral changes) to be successful. He is mistakenly waiting for the patches to “cure” him.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

Robert is scared that he is going to have a heart attack at any moment even though all the tests came back negative. There is a long history of cardiac problems in Robert’s family, all of whom were smokers. His father reminded him of this in a recent conversation.

During the office visit he is anxious, stating many times that he really wants to quit now. However, in spite of his anxiety, he is motivated to quit smoking, but not at all confident that he will be able to do so.

When the student asks why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work.”**

**“What do I do now?”**

<u>**Your Smoking History**</u>

You began smoking while in the service at age 18. You have been smoking ever since and now smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy you are at work. On slow days you smoke more since you have a lot of time on your hands. You have never tried to quit before, other than the attempt last month.

During that attempt you experienced significant withdrawal in spite of wearing the patch. You were very irritable, anxious, restless, and impatient. After three days you returned to your regular pattern of smoking.

<u>**Family Smoking/Medical History**</u>

Both sets of grandparents smoked as well as both parents. Father has quit but mother still smokes about a pack a day.

Paternal grandmother had two heart attacks at age 57 and died at 58 as a result.

Maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 55. He was bedridden for eight years as a result and died at age 63.

Father had triple bypass at age 54.

Mother has had a long history of angina starting in her mid-forties.

<u>**Drug/Alcohol use**</u>

You drink a few beers a week on Friday or Saturday night. You have cut back considerably on your drinking in recent years.  **“ I just can’t do it anymore!”**

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

If the student asks you about family cardiac history, review the above information with him or her. Otherwise, don’t bring this up.

If the student asks you what you did the last time you tried to quit, just say,

**“I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work.”**

If the student questions you further as in, **“Which patch did you use?”** or “**Describe to me how you used the patch,”** you may explain exactly what you did:

**“I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me.”**

**“I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”**

**“They didn’t work at all. I still wanted to smoke even though I had the patch on.”**

**“But I want you to know I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.”**

As you explain all this become increasingly anxious. Ask the student,

**“Why can’t you cure me? Can’t you just give me a pill or something?”**

If the student asks you to set a quit date,

**"It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday."**

**"Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready."**

If the student asks you what kind of changes you made in your routines or behavior, ask,

**“What do you mean? Don’t you just put the patch on and forget about it?”**

If the student asks you when you most need a cigarette,

**"In the morning when I wake up, during breaks at work, and after meals."**

If the student asks you what you could do besides smoking at those times,

**“What do you mean?”**

If they give examples of other behaviors (chewing gum, etc.),

**"That's interesting. My buddy who quit is always carrying around those pretzel sticks. I never really asked him about them, but that would probably help.  I also like gum."**

**"I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals."**

If the student suggests that you go to a group cessation program, say,

**“I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do?”**

If the student <u>**does not**</u> ask you any questions about how you used the patch or what you did, just continue with the “What am I supposed to do? I really want to quit” line of questioning until he or she does.

# Station 3 – Shared Decision Making

Scenario:

You are a third year student rotating through a longitudinal ambulatory rotation. You are seeing a patient, Joanna Mills, for the second time. Ms. Mills is a 45-year old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. When you saw her for the first time last week, she had not been receiving medical care or medication refills for 6 months due to the loss of her medical insurance. Last week, she came to clinic to re-establish care and receive refills of her medications for diabetes mellitus. Last week, you agreed to refill her medications and ordered blood work. Ms. Mills has come in to clinic today to discuss the lab results with you.

You discussed this with your attending preceptor prior to seeing Ms. Mills. Your attending physician instructs you to discuss the results with Ms. Mills and encourages you to engage in shared decision making with your patient.
private_patient_context:
**Station 3 – Shared Decision Making**

**Training Materials:**

# 3. <u>Scenario for Standardized Patient</u>

You are Joanna Mills, a 45-year old woman. Last week, you came to a new hospital-based clinic to establish a primary care doctor and get refills of your medications, since you ran out of medications for diabetes mellitus. You haven’t been to see a doctor in over six months, and you’ve been rationing your medications during that time, but you ran out of medications last week.  The medical student whom you met last week gave you a one month supply of your medications (metformin and glyburide) but asked you to get blood work done so that s/he could “get a sense of how well controlled your diabetes was” and to make changes in medications, if necessary. You went to the laboratory last week after your visit and are now here for your scheduled follow up visit to go over the results of the blood test. You feel fine and have refilled your medications and do not have any new problems to report to the medical student today; but you are curious to learn about the results of your blood tests and hope to hear that your diabetes is well controlled.

<u>Medical History:</u>

You were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years ago by your primary care doctor at the time, Dr. Alvarez. You were not surprised when you received this diagnosis because you have a strong family history of diabetes. You know that the A1C blood test shows whether or not your diabetes is controlled, and you also know that anything less than 7 is good and anything higher than 7 means that the sugars are too high. You remember that when you were first diagnosed with diabetes, your A1C was 7.6. The doctor had you on Metformin first, but the following year, she added glyburide because the A1C was not at goal. Your doctor slowly increased the doses of these medications; and as of one year ago, had you at your current dose of metformin and glyburide.

You have not had any complications related to diabetes mellitus, and you have been taking your medications as prescribed. However, 6 months ago, you lost your job and your medical insurance. You could not afford to continue seeing your primary care doctor so you stopped going at that time. The doctor gave you last refills of your medications and encouraged you to come to the hospital-based clinic since they had a sliding scale fee service for patients. Six months ago at your last visit with Dr. Alvarez, you also had a blood test. You received a letter from Dr. Alvarez stating that your A1C was 8.8 and that you needed to follow up on this, but you were unable to see her or any other doctor until now.

You have been busy for the past few months so you did not come to the hospital clinic.

You have admittedly stretched out your remaining pills, sometimes skipping doses to make the prescription last a little longer. Last week, you were completely without medications; and you were scared about your sugars getting too high, so you came to the clinic.

<u>Family History:</u>

As noted above, you were not surprised when you were diagnosed with diabetes four years ago. Both of your parents suffered from it, and you know that it is an illness that can run in the family. However, you were still frightened when you were first given the diagnosis. You have seen both of your parents suffer from medical problems related to diabetes. Your father had high blood pressure and kidney problems, which his doctor said was due to diabetes. He passed away suddenly from a heart attack when he was 66 years old. Your mother, who is now 64, is alive but has many medical problems. Prior to her recent stroke 3 months ago, she had very poorly controlled high blood pressure and diabetes.  She has been in and out of the hospital several times a year for the past few years, either for chest pain or “fluid in the lungs” or skin infections and infected foot ulcers.

Besides diabetes, you do not have any other medical problems.

<u>Social History:</u>

You were laid off from your job as a clothing buyer for a large department store. Since then, you have been looking for a new job and have been trying to keep your spirits up. You were busy caring for your mother in another state for the past few months because she had a recent stroke. Between your mother’s illness and your search for a job, the past six months have been extraordinarily stressful for you; and you have not really had time to take care of yourself. But you have always wanted to stay in good health to avoid illness, and you know that it’s important to focus on your health right now.  You have been without health insurance since losing your job as you could not afford COBRA and you postponed looking into applying for Obama care in hopes that you would soon have a new job.  You have been unable to afford to refill your medications, and therefore, rationing the pills until you ran out of them last week.

You do not have any history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

You are divorced and have a 20 year-old daughter, who is in college and no longer living at home

<u>Emotional Tone:</u>

You are very concerned about your health condition although it has been difficult for you to focus on your own health for the past six months, between your economic hardship and your mother’s acute illness. When you had insurance, you were always good about following up with your primary care doctor and taking all of your medications. Even though you have had diabetes for four years, you were told that you could be “in control” of your illness and maybe avoid complications of diabetes. You have been happy to take your pills, as long as it meant controlling your illness and avoiding complications of the disease.  You know that you have not taken your pills as prescribed, mostly because of financial concerns and the cost of medications.  You are very reluctant to start insulin. You know that being on insulin means needing to prick yourself several times a day to check your blood sugar and give yourself the insulin shots and you hate the thought of pricking yourself so frequently with needles.  Also, you know that the diabetic supplies (insulin and more lancets and paper strips for frequent sugar checks) are expensive and another cost that you feel would be really hard to absorb now.

**Your role is to portray a patient who is very concerned about your health. You want to know how to keep yourself healthy. Yet, you are upset and worried when you learn that your diabetes is not well controlled.  You are reluctant to start insulin therapy because you dislike the thought of using the needles to give yourself medication and the extra cost of medications and supplies feels like a financial burden that you feel unable to take at this time. In addition, although you know it is not rational you feel that using insulin means you are more likely to develop the complications you saw your parents go through because they were on insulin.  However, you normally always follow your doctor’s advice and are unsure about going against his advice by not starting insulin.**

<u>Scenario:</u> 

The student will enter the clinic room, where you are waiting to be seen. You are seated next to the desk, appearing comfortable but a little anxious. You met this student last week and are happy to see the same person again.

The student may ask, “I wanted to talk to you about your blood test results that we did last week. Do you know what an A1C test signifies?”

**“Yes, I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that the doctors took to show whether the diabetes was controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7.”**

The student will inform you that your A1C level was elevated, at 11.

You are surprised and concerned.

**“Oh no, that’s really high isn’t it?”**

The student should inform you that this A1C is very elevated and indicates that the diabetes is very poorly controlled at this time. You are upset and very worried by this news.

**“It’s never been so high like this. You know I was worried about my sugars but I never thought it could get up to this level.” What does this mean I have to do now?”**

The student should describe treatment options. Since you are on high doses of your current medications, there is no way to simply go up on the current dose of medications. The student will recommend starting insulin therapy as a way to rapidly bring down the A1C level and control the diabetes.

You interrupt the student when s/he mentions insulin and get visibly upset.

**“Wait, insulin? Oh, I don’t want to do that.”**

The student should ask you why you do not want to start insulin. S/He should give you a chance to state what your concerns are. You state many reasons why you don’t want to start insulin therapy now. After you give each reason, you should give the student a chance to discuss it with you.

**“I know that there are a lot of reasons why my sugars got uncontrolled like this. I wasn’t doing all the things that I know I should have been doing about my health. I wasn’t eating right, I wasn’t consistently taking my pills every day. I wasn’t really focusing on my health. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order.”**

**“I know that when you start insulin, you have to check your sugars many times throughout the day. And those extra supplies, those strips and lancets, they all cost a lot of money that I don’t think I’d be able to afford right now.”**

**“To tell you the truth, I’m really afraid of pricking myself with a needle to give myself insulin.  I don’t think that I could do that. I hate needles and the thought of giving myself shots every day is really scary to me.”**

**“I am so afraid of insulin.  I know it isn’t rational but I feel like insulin means I have diabetes with a capital D.  Do you know what I mean – it seems more serious.  I saw my dad go through so much, and now my mom with her stroke.  They were both on insulin.”**

The student should respond to all of your concerns and reasons for not wanting to start insulin. If he does not acknowledge or validate your concerns then you should remain resistant to starting insulin.

The student should ask you about what your desires regarding the management of your illness are. S/He might ask, “Ms. Mills, can you tell me a little bit about how diabetes is affecting your life, and what you are hoping to do to manage your illness? What would you like to see for yourself regarding your diabetes?

**“I really don’t want to be sick from diabetes like my mother was. I know all about the complications, the foot ulcers, the amputations, dialysis, strokes… I’m just really scared about my diabetes being out of control because I never want to go through what she’s been going though with her health. I want to be healthy for my daughter and for myself. So I want to do what you think is best. I’ve always listened to doctors in the past. But right now, I am just really scared of this insulin for a lot of reasons too. I am just hoping for a way that I can get back into good health again without going down the insulin road.”**

The student should try to engage you in deciding what the best treatment for your diabetes is. If he only recommends insulin and says that nothing else will work right now, but you don’t feel that he/she acknowledges the reasons why you do not want to start insulin, you will be more resistant to starting insulin now. However, if the student shares information with you about insulin treatment that addresses your concerns, you might consider changing your mind. Here are some examples of effective statements:

“The insulin that I would recommend starting you on is a once daily insulin that works slowly over 24 hours. You do not have to give yourself multiple injections of insulin each day. Rather, you could give yourself one injection a day.”

“The benefit of starting insulin is that it is more likely to successfully bring your A1C level down to signify good control of your diabetes. The better we control your diabetes, the less likely it is that you would ever get the complications of diabetes (such as kidney problems or eye problems.)

“One concern that I have in continuing with oral medicines rather than insulin, is that the oral medications do not bring down the A1C level as effectively as insulin does. I can tell that it is really important for you to get in control of your diabetes, and I think that this is the most successful way that we can do it.”

“Insulin is one part of the plan that we can create to control your diabetes. You are right that diet and exercise and taking your medications every day are equally important in controlling your diabetes. I think that we can work together on each of these issues, and perhaps insulin can be a component of this plan.”

If you feel that the student has engaged you as a partner in making the decision and has given you a chance to address your beliefs and concerns about your illness, then you should agree to work with the student to come up with a plan together; and you can agree to try the insulin.

**“Okay, I see what you are saying. I think that if you feel the insulin may really help me get my diabetes under control and keep me healthy, then I will try it for a while and see how my sugars improve.”**

If you feel that the student has not given you a chance to speak about your concerns and has not enlisted you as a partner in decision making, but rather unilaterally recommended insulin without building a consensus with you, then you should not agree to start insulin. You are calmer at the end but are very resolute about not starting insulin today.

**“You know, I don’t think I am able to get over my fear of starting insulin right now. I’d really rather try getting back on my pills every day and see how I do for a while before I switch my medicines.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a radiology-oncology prelimary resident rotating on the inpatient medicine service.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 35-75 years old with hypertension, epigastric pain, and mild shortness of breath. The patient has been otherwise healthy.

The patient came to the ED yesterday afternoon. The original ED plan was to discharge the patient home with a working diagnosis of “dyspepsia” and outpatient follow-up, but after 3 hours the patient complained of increased pain. The ED doctors changed the plan to bring the patient into the hospital on “observation status.”

You examined the patient at 9 pm last night, shortly after the patient arrived on the floor. The patient was in modest discomfort.

It is now about 10 hours after the surgery and you have returned for another overnight shift. The patient is back in a hospital room, now on the surgery service. You are no longer directly involved in the patient's care.

**Student Tasks:**

Explain to the patient why there was a delay in diagnosing the perforated duodenal ulcer and getting to surgery.

**Episode:** Disclosure of Error
**Workshop:** Advanced Communcation Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are a patient in a hospital room.

Here is the timeline of your story:

* 2 days ago you began to have some discomfort, a little pain, in your belly.
* Yesterday at 3 pm you went to the hospital emergency room and waited 3 hours to be seen.
* While being examined you had blood tests done and they told you that if the blood tests were normal, you could go home with an appointment to see a doctor in the clinic.
* While waiting for the results, the pain got a little worse. A doctor examined you again, said he thought you were OK, but agreed to “watch you for a while” so they admitted you to the hospital where you met more doctors.
* At about 10 pm they sent you for an Xray of your belly.
* You tried to sleep, but the pain in your belly kept you awake.
* About 6 am, the pain got much worse. You called the nurse.
* A doctor came back to see you at 6:30 am and said that the Xray showed a problem in the belly that might require surgery.
* At 10am you were taken to the operating room.

Now it is evening, and you are recovering from surgery. The surgeon told you that you had an ulcer, which had caused a small hole in your bowel, and that this was repaired with surgery. You need to be in the hospital for a few more days, get IVs and antibiotics, and not eat for a few days. The good news is that the surgeons expect you will recover completely.

You are relieved that you will be OK, but thinking back, you wonder about the sudden concern of the doctors this morning and the emergency surgery. You had an Xray at 10 pm and got worse for hours after it was done, but the doctor only told you the Xray was bad in the morning. Why did it take more than 8 hours to find out that you needed emergency surgery?

Background: You do not see doctors regularly, and you felt perfectly healthy until this belly pain started. You did go to the medical clinic at the hospital last year, and received some medicines for your blood pressure and cholesterol. You did not come back to see the doctor, but your medicine is running out and they told you that you could not get more refills without another visit to the clinic. All these doctors, nurses, and tests at the hospital are a little scary. Fill in other details that come up as you see fit.

A doctor is coming to your room to talk to you. This is one of the many doctors you have seen, and is the one who told you about the Xray results early this morning. Your character does not yet know this, but the doctor’s task is to disclose to you that an error was made (this doctor did not check the Xray results which is what accounted for the delay). Ideally the doctor will address your emotions, apologize, and take responsibility, in which case your initial emotions will give way to gratitude that everything is ok and appreciation for the doctor’s honesty. If the doctor is evasive, defensive, makes excuses, or takes any approach that seems inappropriate to your character, you can prolong your confusion and anger, and retreat to a withdrawn affect rather than having an outburst of emotion.

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a medicine intern in the primary care clinic. This patient has been coming to the clinic for 5 years for treatment of their hypertension, but you have not personally met the patient before.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 50-60 years old and was diagnosed with pancreatic carcinoma 7 months ago. The patient has received 2 different chemotherapy drugs over 6 months and neither worked. The patient received the most recent chemotherapy 3 weeks ago, but the cancer has continued to spread. The patient's oncologist has said there are no other treatment options for the cancer. You have read a report from the oncologist that states the patient knows the full extent of the disease and that no further cancer specific treatment is available.

**Student Tasks:**

Take a palliative care history from a patient who has been told there are no more cancer treatments available.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 50-60
**Episode:** Palliative Care
**Workshop:** Advanced Communication Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are following up in your primary care office today but are meeting a new doctor.

You began to experience pain in your stomach and back and began to lose some weight about 8 months ago. After a couple of weeks you went to the doctor who sent you for blood work and X rays. The testing led to a diagnosis of cancer of the pancreas and you began treatment for it with chemotherapy 6 months ago. Two months into therapy, repeat scans showed that the cancer continued to grow so you were switched to another regimen. That therapy has not halted the spread of the cancer and your cancer doctor told you last week that there are no other treatments she can offer. Since the chemotherapy made you feel very sick, you are accepting of her advice. The main focus of your treatment now is on keeping you comfortable. You are fatigued, have lost your hair and 40 lbs. The oncologist sent you back to your primary care doctor to manage your symptoms and other medical problems and that is why you are here today.

At the moment you are taking lisinopril 40 mg for your high blood pressure (you have been on this medicine for over 10 years), oxycodone 5 mg as needed about twice a day for pain, and ondansetron (“Zofran") 4 mg once or twice a week for nausea. Your symptoms are well controlled and you know you could take more medicine if you were more uncomfortable. You have also begun to experience some light headedness when you stand up quickly. You sleep “okay,” but not great. You do not eat as much because your appetite has decreased.\*

You worked as a teacher of theater at your local college and had been able to continue with some sick days. You found it challenging to go to work and the end of the school year was a relief. You have good health insurance through work. You are happily married and you are worried\*\* about how your spouse will manage financially without the dual income. However, you know “it will be okay,” as your spouse is employed as a manager of the local grocery store and is able to take time off to care for you as needed. You have 2 adult children who are working and living independently. They know you are ill and are very sad about your declining health. Both are willing and able to help at home. You do have life insurance that will help some. Your home is paid for.

You are also pondering the question of why you are terminally ill so early in your life. You pray and meditate and that provides some comfort. On the other hand you have been doing practical things like making out a will and thinking about who will make health care decisions if you cannot. You are an active Roman Catholic who is very involved in the local church. You have also decided that you want to die a natural death when the time comes avoiding resuscitation, breathing and feeding tubes and your partner knows this.

You have used some of your family’s home remedies of taking bitter melon juice, but do not have other cultural beliefs about treating cancer. You have heard of hospice and are interested in having their support since you wish to remain at home to the extent that is possible. Your goals for the next few months are to spend time with your family and be spiritually ready for your death if there is no miracle.

You are not a smoker, do not drink alcohol, nor do you use drugs like marijuana. There is no family history of cancer.

\* If the student focuses too much on your cancer treatments and medical symptoms, gently redirect them and let them know that you fully understand your treatment status (“I’m done with chemo… I know there are no more options… I’m here to talk about next steps.”)

\*\* Ideally the student will provide a natural opening for you to express your emotions. Suitable windows could be inquiries about your family, mental health, or existential concerns, or more direct questions about your emotions. “Worry” about your partner’s well-being is your primary emotional concern, and thinking about this may make your character cry. If the student recognizes your emotion and demonstrates empathy, you should be able to collect yourself and move forward with the conversation. If the student is not effective in handling your emotion, the conversation will stall as you find it difficult to move beyond your worry, which could then escalate to other emotions (fear, isolation, etc.).

**Standardized Patient Role: Sample Patient Case 3**

**Andrea Sands**

The following is the typical order for this patient encounter.

Student should introduce himself/herself as a first-year medical student and offer to shake hands. He/she may ask how you wish to be addressed (Ms., Miss, Mrs., first name).

**Chief Complaint:** (Why you came to see the doctor today.) Feel tired and weak all the time.

**History of Present Illness:** (Explanation of the chief complaint—LOCATES mnemonic. Questions in parentheses below will likely be asked. Responses for the SP are provided.)

**L**OCATION: (Where is the pain?) Low back. (Does the pain radiate [move around, do you feel it anywhere else]?) Some radiation.

Standardized Patient Training Materials

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting on bed in gown.

**Props**: Tissue, water bottle, glycerin and water in spray bottle for patient forehead sweat.

**Opening Statement**: "I can't seem to get rid of this cough."

**Presentation/Affect**: You are holding a tissue and cough deeply for duration of encounter.

**Current Condition**:

You are B. Radcliffe and are 55 years old. You really feel sick. You are weak. You noted a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then you have felt intermittent chills but nothing like you did 4 days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days. You are coughing now but this only started about 3 days ago, and seems to be getting worse. The cough is a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm but only with great effort. Your chest also hurts on the right side, down low, (on side of body, below breast) when you cough or if you take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when you breathe in (and has increased from a 2 to 3 out of 10 on the pain scale). You feel like you have a fever, but not checked it and your throat hurts from the coughing. Yesterday, you vomited (looked like the chicken broth soup you ate if asked) once after a coughing spell but it was mostly mucous (no nausea). You have had some shortness of breath with activity (going up the stairs), none at rest. You have not had any nasal congestion, runny nose or sinus pressure. You have not had any wheezing. At baseline you do not have a cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheezing. You have taken Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally (3-4 times each day according to package directions) since it started but nothing seems to help. The coughing is waking you up at night and you have tried using extra pillows to prop yourself up.

You volunteer regularly at the Nashville Rescue Mission in downtown Nashville, TN. Even though you didn't feel well, you went in on your regularly scheduled days (three and four days ago). You have been exposed to a lot of people in the shelter and have been pushing yourself to be there helping when you really felt like being in bed. A number of people in the shelter seem to be coughing/sneezing.

**Social History:**

You are a native of Baltimore and work as an accountant for the State of Tennessee government. You have been married 28 years and have 2 children, a daughter, Amy (27), and son, David (25). David is stationed overseas in Germany and Amy lives in Nashville and has two sons, Todd (now 10) and Adam (now 7) and is currently going through a divorce. Because the divorce is not amiable, your grandsons have been staying with you for the past few months. The younger one is in the first year of grade school and the older one is in fourth grade. You live in an older frame house. You do not use drugs or tobacco currently.

You occasionally have a glass of wine in the evenings. You have environmental allergies in the spring.

**Past Medical History:**

You are generally healthy. You work at a desk five days a week. You work around the house and yard on the weekends. You have never been hospitalized nor had any surgeries. You only see a doctor when sick and you haven't seen a doctor in years (to save money). You always remember to get a flu shot every year.

You've never had the pneumococcal vaccine. No medications or medical conditions. You used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day (you started in high school), but quit for the third time two weeks ago because your grandchildren are living with you now. You are currently using the patch for help. Your grandson Todd has also had a sore throat last week that was diagnosed as strep throat and treated with penicillin for 7 days. His symptoms included a very sore throat and fever but no cough. He's feeling better now. If asked, "Have you ever been exposed to tuberculosis (TB)?" respond, "Not that I know of." If asked if you've had a TB test, respond, "Yes, but it has been a number of years since my last one...."

**Family History:**

* Father: had high blood pressure and smoked. Died at age 80 - 10 years ago (of old age)
* Mother: seems to be healthy but may have high cholesterol and maybe arthritis. Age 78
* Maternal grandmother: died when you were a child. Was in a nursing home and never really knew her history.
* Maternal grandfather and paternal grandparents: Died before you were born.
* Son: No known medical conditions
* Daughter: No known medical conditions

**Embedded Concern:**

As the student transitions from taking the history to begin the physical exam, say:

*"I'm really worried that I might have lung cancer."*

If asked why you think you might have lung cancer and smoking has not been disclosed say:

*"I've known some folks that had lung cancer and coughed a lot and that's why I'm worried"*

If it looks like the student will leave without offering their treatment plan (i.e. "I'm going to go check with my attending....") you need to ask (around the 2 minute warning):

*"So what do you think is going on?"*

**Physical Exam:**

When the learner listens to your chest, cough vigorously (breathing deeply causes the cough)

During lung exam when they ask you to take a deep breath, cough 2 times and hold your side.
