**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Presentation to the Student:
private_patient_context:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Information for the SP:

You are a 45-year-old patient, who has diabetes. You do not take your insulin regularly, and have had poorly controlled diabetes for years. You take your insulin only when you remember, but it is difficult to remember to take it every day since you do not feel different or badly when you do not take your insulin. You have been frustrated lately because you like to play basketball with your 10 year old son, and haven’t been able to play basketball because you have developed an ulcer on your right foot (as a result of poorly controlled diabetes).

Medical history: diabetes, diagnosed 4 years ago

Medications: Lantus insulin daily 20 units at night (you are taking this only a few times weekly) and Lisinopril 10 mg daily (blood pressure medicine you were told to take because of the diabetes)

Allergies: none

Social history: you do not smoke, drink alcohol or use any drugs

Family history: father with diabetes

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to be able to play basketball with your son again, and you want to get rid of the foot ulcer. You really love your son and you love to play basketball.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with insulin can lead to complications like your foot ulcer, but you will need the doctor to help you make that connection and to describe other possible complications. You cannot play basketball with your foot ulcer. You are also not taking your blood pressure medication as prescribed, and this could also result in complications.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It is easy to “forget” to take your medications. At night you are very tired and sleepy from your day, so you tend to fall asleep while watching TV, and don’t take any medications before you fall asleep. Also, since you don’t “feel” your high sugars or blood pressure, there are no symptoms/reminders for you to take your medications. You like to think of yourself as “young and healthy,” and taking medications interferes with this way of looking at yourself.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid you might not be able to keep playing basketball with your son. Once the doctor describes possible complications from nonadherence with diabetes, you are afraid of those.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Your son, and ability to continue playing basketball with him; improved health.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Maybe you could take the medication at a different time of the day, or at least before you fall asleep watching TV. Maybe you could challenge your thoughts that people who take medications are not young or healthy. You could try using reminders, pill boxes, etc. You could test your sugars regularly to remind yourself of possible complications (since you don’t “feel” the high sugar levels).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You love your son and love to play basketball with him. You fear other complications like an amputation.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe put a picture of your son or a basketball on the pill bottle.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You exercise even when you are tired, so you believe you could take medications even if you are tired at night.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the links between noncompliance and complications. Perhaps your son could help you to remember to take your medications.
* Ask for a decision: You will take your insulin and blood pressure medications.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will get a pill box. You will ask your son to agree not to play basketball with you unless you have taken your medications.

**EXAMINEE INSTRUCTIONS**

**Case Name:** Case #1

1. **Opening Scenario**

* Patient name: Jenny Donlon
* Sex: Female

* Chief complaint: Mania

* Temperature: 98°F
* Blood Pressure: 135/87 mmHg
* Pulse: 95 bpm

1. **Case:**

Jenny Donlon is a 50-year-old female working as a middle-school teacher brought in to local emergency psychiatry services via police after her husband, Bobby Donlon, called community crisis sevices for bizarre behavior. When you had asked Jenny what brought her here, she stated that she was brought here by her family for "coming out as a lesbian, because they think that's related to mental health issues." She states how she found her "inner zen" and have plans to start a new spiritual and pure life with her new girlfriend. She was perseverative on how her family does not approve of her lifestyle, and how she is being held against her will. You had asked her multiple clarifying questions, but she is discharge-focused and repeats how she has no mental health issues and just wants to go home, particularly to “meet with my girlfriend, and probably future wife." She tells you that her outpatient psychiatrist cleared her of any psychiatric illnesses and told her to discontinue her medication, which she did several months ago.

When you asked if you can contact a family member or her girlfriend, she tells you that her girlfriend is Robyn Fenty (Rihanna), and her “true” family is Sean Carter (Jay-Z), and she calls these people her "advocates." You again ask about other family members, specifically her husband. She adamantly denies that Bobby is her husband, and that "I must leave him, because I'm lesbian. I'm planning to start a whole new life with Robyn."

**You are now preparing to go back to see the patient after you’ve completed your initial intake and called collateral. You would like to commit the patient for the following reasons:**

* **Pt has demonstrated risky behavior during episodes of mania (i.e., excessive spending, reckless traveling) that can lead to imminent risk of harm (e.g., financially, bodily, etc.) and further functional decline without treatment**
* **Husband has expressed that he is unable to keep his wife safe at home, thus there is no other safe alternative**

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**STATION LR**

**Presenting Situation:** A 40-year old woman presents to this primary care clinic for a follow-up visit. She was seen by you 1 week ago. Prior to that visit, she hadn’t seen her normal physician for 6 weeks. When you saw her a week ago, she had 2 weeks’ worth of the medication left. At her first visit, as part of your initial assessment, you asked her to submit a urine sample for analysis.


**Setting:** Primary Care Clinic

**Your Tasks:**

1. Read the medical chart
2. Give the patient the results of her urine drug screening
3. Discuss the next steps in her pain management

Note: The focus is abuse of prescription drugs, NOT the injury per se.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**Patient:** Julia Winters, Age 40

**CC:** Severe elbow pain from a work-related injury 15 months ago.

**HPI:** See notes from regular physician below

* Married, 3 children.
* Elementary school teacher

Height \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

BMI: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_

(Her regular physician left town on an extended leave). Patient sustained a fracture of the left elbow in a work-related accident 15 months ago. **Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Julia Winters

**Presenting Situation:** This is a follow-up visit for this 40-year old woman who had a work related injury 15 months ago which resulted in chronic severe left elbow pain. Six weeks ago she saw her regular physician to get a refill of her pain medication. The patient returned one week ago for another refill and was seen by a new health care provider who required a urine test (drug screen) be done. The patient is seeing the same health care provider for the 2nd time.

The patient’s goal is to get an increase in her prescription for MS-Contin.

* **Opening statement:** I would like to increase the morphine from twice to three times per day. Since the pain is still quite severe and interferes with my teaching work, I don’t think my prescription is helping the pain enough and it’s about to run out. I’m sometimes in terrible pain and can’t do all of my work duties. I can’t live a normal life like this.
* **Appearance and dress:**
  + Dress neatly like you would for teaching. Wear comfortable shoes as you stand often for your work.
  + Protect your left elbow against your side or across your stomach, or hold it occasionally with your right arm.
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:**
  + You are pleasant, but slightly annoyed in the beginning.
  + You are not happy that you needed to have another urine test.
  + You are in a lot of pain

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset:** I’m in terrible pain when I’m not on pain medication. With the medication, my pain is moderate, but still interferes with my work. It has been like this for the 15 months since I fell on the ice directly on my elbow. I’m a second grade teacher and I was supervising the kids on the playground during recess when I slipped and fell.

**Location**: The pain is in my left elbow. It hurts and sometimes the pain shoots down my arm.

**Duration**: It’s a constant pain. On days when I teach or when I do activities like grocery shop, it is worse.

**Characteristics/Intensity**:

* Right now when I’m on medication, the pain varies between 3-5 (1-10 pain scale).
* The pain is intense, if I try to do too much with my left arm. Otherwise, it’s usually a dull throb. But at times, suddenly I’ll get a sharp ache.

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**:

* Helping put coats on the elementary school children, supervising recess, correcting papers, dressing myself, washing and setting my hair, grocery shopping—anything requiring two arms—aggravates my elbow or I have to get someone else to help me.
* I’ve tried putting heat on my elbow. I’ve tried putting ice on my elbow. I’ve tried elevating my arm on a pillow. All of these things help somewhat, but the pain comes back shortly after I stop. I do the stretching exercises suggested by my PT, but I have to be very careful or it hurts, rather than helps.

**Treatments tried/results**:

* **Prescription medications:** MS-Contin (Note to SP: this is a long acting morphine)
  + Dose: 15 mg, two times a day
  + This medicine has helped to keep the pain at a moderate level and helped me be able to move by arm a little better.
  + I want to take the MS-Contin 3 times a day or possibly increase the dosage.
  + **Side effects:**
    - I have some constipation, but it is not often.
    - I get sleepy sometimes, but if I stay active I’m okay.
    - I’ve gotten used to most of the side effects.
    - I don’t feel sleepy when driving.
  + **Early refills:**
    - I had one early refill after I stopped the physical therapy.
    - If asked how managed without increase in dose or frequency: I used the heat and ice that the physical therapist told me to use.
  + **Stopping use of pain medication:** I’ve been on it since I hurt my elbow. I haven’t tried to stop because it is much better than being without. I would consider stopping my medication some day after my pain is in control and the elbow seems better, but that’s not happening yet.
  + **Signed agreements:**
    - You have signed an agreement with your physician that you will:
      * Use only him/her to refill your prescriptions
      * Use only one pharmacy
      * Not request for early refills
* Advil (200 mg) 4-5 times/day maybe 1-2 times week or more if the pain really bothers me. I’ve been doing this over the last eight months or so off and on. I don’t think the Advil helps very much though.
* I had physical therapy for 2 months after I left the hospital. I went 1- 2 times a week. They gave me exercises to do at home for stretching and strengthening. I used heat and ice to help with the pain.

**Significance:**

* I was off from work for several months and now I have to limit what I do. For example, I’m not taking my turn supervising recess. I feel guilty that my husband has to do more of the chores around home.
* I can’t do my normal activities without difficulty. I need the pain medicine just to function every day.
* I’m feeling a little depressed. I’m kind of discouraged that this is taking so long.

**Other:**

* If asked why you didn’t get your prescription filled at the last visit: I left the doctor’s office without realizing I didn’t get the prescription. Now I’m just about out of the pain medicine altogether. It’s been 6 weeks since I had the prescription filled.

**Past Medical History:**

* **Childhood and adult illnesses:** Own history. Last physical was 6 months ago.
* **Hospitalizations and surgeries:**
  + To have my three babies of course, and otherwise only for my elbow injury. I had surgery to fix the fracture of my left elbow. They put in a plate and a screw. I had physical therapy for 2 months afterwards. The plate and screw are still in there.
* **Allergies:** None
* **Medications:**
  + **Prescription medications:**
    - Morphine (see treatments in HPI)
    - If asked about other medications or asked about sleep (see sleep section): I’ve tried Flexeril to help me sleep at night. Now I’m out of my old prescription and I’m not sure of the dose, maybe 5 mg. My last physician prescribed this for me about 2 years ago for lower back pain (before I had this injury at work).

**Life Style Behavioral Risks:**

* **Diet:** The pain and medication seems to have decreased my appetite. I make my own lunch and try to eat healthy snacks. I drink about 2 cups of coffee a day and 2 to 3 diet cokes.
* **Exercise:** I do my PT exercises for my elbow. I try to walk 3-4 times/week for 30 min.

The child has been struggling in school as he is unable to sit still. Parents mentioned that the young man likes to arrange his clothes by color and becomes very upset if the order is altered.

You are expected to explain to the patient and his family what Tourette syndrome is as well as address the patient’s anxiety as it relates to having a poorly understood medical condition.

You are the resident in local psychiatry emergency services seeing Melanie Walker, a 60-year-old female with past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cerebrovascular accidents (recently 3 small strokes in the past year with mild residual left-sided weakness) brought in by her husband for progressively worsening delusions. **You are now preparing to go back to see the patient after you’ve staffed the case with your attending. The husband has left at this point. You would like to commit the patient for the following reasons:**

* **Pt is at imminent risk of harm to herself due to inability to care for self (not eating, not sleeping properly, not able to hold a job)**
* **Husband has expressed that he can no longer handle your behaviors at home, thus there is no other safe alternative**

Telemedicine- Sleep Problems

Patient Scenario

You are Lou Lewis, a 68-year-old who is contacting your family physician via a remote telemedicine hookup from your home computer. The nature of your consult is you have been having trouble sleeping for the past few weeks. You’re increasingly tired all day and so you emailed your physician the night before and they set up this telemedicine consult with you.

You live in the small town of Juntura, OR. Your family physician, Dr. Smith, is 1 hour away in Burns, OR. It is due to this remote location that your physician set you up with a telemedicine option in your home, which is accessible by logging into a secure web portal on your computer. You have satellite Internet connectivity that is excellent, allowing you to participate in the telemedicine program. You’ve used the technology to communicate with your family physician before and feel comfortable using the interface.

Last month you started having trouble sleeping. Usually you go to bed around 9 PM and fall asleep shortly thereafter. About a month ago you began to have trouble falling asleep. You often lie awake well past 10 PM and sometimes later. When you do finally fall asleep, you wake up frequently tossing and turning. You now feel tired most of the day as a result and have finally decided to talk to someone about it. You hope the doctor can help diagnose why you aren’t sleeping well and give you something that can help.

The student in this scenario will be asked to take a pertinent history from you and develop an action plan. The student is filling in for your regular physician, Dr. Smith. You like your new doctor and appreciate the use of technology to prevent you from having to always drive in to clinic. The student has never met you before.

Your opening statement will be: “I’ve been having trouble sleeping and now I feel tired all day. I’m hoping you can help me figure out what’s going on.”

History of current illness

Last month you started having trouble sleeping. Usually you go to bed around 9 PM and fall asleep shortly thereafter. About a month ago you began to have trouble falling asleep. You often lie awake well past 10 PM and sometimes later. When you do finally fall asleep, you wake up frequently tossing and turning. You’ve tried everything to make falling to sleep easier. You don’t watch TV in bed, you don’t drink alcohol immediately before you go to bed and you’ve tried reading as a way to help you fall asleep. Nothing has worked. You now feel tired most of the day as a result and have finally decided to talk to someone about it. Besides the trouble sleeping, you have no health issues.

Social history

You live alone and have been widowed for just over a year now. Your late partner and you moved to Juntura 5 years ago after they retired from a job as a schoolteacher and you retired as an office manager for a trucking company. You moved to Juntura from LaGrande, OR because you both wanted to live in a small town for your retirement. Your partner died unexpectedly last year from a respiratory infection. The two of you were very close and had planned on living many more years together. You have gone through many stages of grieving and, though you have accepted they are gone now, you do not really feel like you will ever be “over it.” You have one son who lives in Boise with his wife and they have a 5-year-old daughter. You are close with your son and his family but do not see them as often as you would like. You Skype weekly and see each other about twice a year. As you moved to Juntura and the town is quite small, you really don’t have a strong support network in town. Sometimes you volunteer at the local school but have done so less since your partner died. Sometimes you feel very lonely and think about selling the house and moving closer to Boise, but the housing market is bad and you don’t want to burden your son. Sometimes you feel stuck.

Before your partner passed away, you only drank occasionally. Since they passed, you drink 3 glasses of wine a week, though never more. You have never smoked cigarettes or used any recreational drugs. You do not take any medicines regularly.

Family history

Your mother and father both died of natural causes in their early 90s. Your father and your mother had no health conditions. You have no siblings. There is no other history of illness in your family.

Your affect and behavior:

* + - You do not think your trouble sleeping is connected to being depressed. If the student asks if you feel depressed say, “I don’t know. I just thought I was having trouble sleeping.”
    - If the student suggests you are depressed, you will initially disagree and ask how they know. You will only accept that you could be depressed if the student explains the results of the depression-screening tool that you completed before the visit. If the student does this, you will ask them to explain the test and the results.
    - You do not have any thoughts of suicide or self-harm (only reveal this if asked by the student)

    - Your demeanor is downbeat. You do not smile easily, and your voice lacks energy.
    - You will answer the student’s questions and not hold back information.
    - If the student asks you to come in for a clinic visit you will be hesitant. You are on a fixed income and gas is expensive, so you would rather not make the hour drive to Burns if you don’t have to. If the student is persistent and makes a good case as to why you should come in, you will ultimately agree to do so.
    - At the beginning of the encounter, place the camera so that it is angled at the top of your head so the student can only see the top of your head. If the student does not ask you to adjust your camera after the first minute of the encounter, ask the student if they can see you okay. If they still don’t ask you to adjust your camera, do it yourself and give them feedback at the end of the encounter that they should help make sure the patient is fully visible when doing a telemedicine encounter.

Screening Tests

Before meeting with the doctor, the medial assistant had you fill out two screening forms on your computer. If the student asks you about them, just say you can’t really remember what you answered but you think the assistant said doctor can get the results somewhere in the telemedicine room (the student will have to download them to view). Allergies: Penicillin – caused hives

Family history: Mother has diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, and dementia Father had a CVA at age 59.

The trainee will step out of the room at the examiner’s instructions. At this point, move to the exam table, sit in a cross-legged position, and with the examiner’s help place the pelvic model at the end of the exam table. Cover your lap and model with a paper drape.

If asked if you would like to try inserting the speculum yourself, rather than having the trainee insert it: No, you’d rather just get on with it and let them do their thing.

If asked if you would feel more comfortable with your feet in a different position other than in the footrests (stirrups): That’s OK. It doesn’t really make a difference to you what position you’re in. It’s tough no matter what.

**General Guidelines during exam:**

From the start of the exam, you should adjust your level of anxiety based on how sensitive or gentle the trainee is. For example, if the trainee is abrupt, not talking through all the steps, or not recognizing your baseline anxiety, you should have increased anxiety. If on the other hand the trainee is calm, professional, gentle, sensitive, then you should act visibly more relaxed.

Within seconds after speculum is placed, you should become very nervous, whispering to yourself “Oh no, Oh no, Oh no” (or something similar), legs start to tremble. Then say, “I don’t know if I can do this. Is there anything I should be doing?”

If the trainee tries any stress reduction techniques (any of the below or other similar interventions), state that you feel a little better, but are still really nervous – is there anything else you can try to bring down the stress level? After a second stress reduction technique, state that you’re feeling better, and it’s OK to go ahead with the exam.

Examples of Stress Reduction Techniques:

* Trainee asks you to take a few deep breaths
* Uses any MENTAL grounding technique (e.g., orients you by telling you where you are, what day it is, etc.)
* Uses any PHYSICAL grounding technique (e.g., asks you to make a fist and squeeze, hold the table, feel your hands, etc.)

If the trainee acts sensitive to your words even though they do not suggest any relaxing techniques whatsoever, give permission to proceed with the exam.

The only exception is if the trainee tries to force the continuation of the exam or acts especially insensitive, then you should say angrily, “I’m done! I can’t go through with this!” and the exam should be terminated.

When the trainee is done with the exam, the trainee should instruct you to sit up and get dressed before finishing the encounter (if they do not, ask if you can get your clothes on before finishing the visit). The trainee will then step out of the room.

When the trainee is out, move from the examining table back to the chair. The faculty examiner will let them know when you are ready.

**At the end of the exam:**

If asked what you are planning to do right after this appointment:

You anticipated this might be hard with your therapist, and agreed that you would give her a call if needed. You think you will do just that.

If asked if you have any questions or if there’s anything you need right now:

No, you think you’re OK.

Appendix B:  *SP Training Notes*

**Patient Name:** Robin Samuels

Setting: Outpatient/ Ambulatory Urgi-Center

Chief Complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

**Patient Profile**

SP recruitment profile: 20-40 years old, adaptable to any sex, race and age

Appearance: well-groomed, hospital gown

Moulage: petechiae, lower extremities

Affect: Pleasant and cooperative, normally a high energy person

Employment: Full time kindergarten teacher in Elmhurst, NY. You love your job and cannot think of any other job that you would want to have.

Education: You graduated high school and college – you were working on your masters but couldn’t keep up with it between your children, work and getting sick so often…. You decided to hold off on it for a few years until your children are a bit older.

Lifestyle: You lead a simple yet busy life, particularly as you balance working full time at a school and taking care of your three young children. They are involved in many after school activities and you love taking them to all of them. Your husband works in his own business (restaurant) and so is not around that much – weekends and evenings are his busy times and so you must do most of the child care.

Relationships: You have been married to your high school sweetheart for 15 years. You have a strong relationship. You have never been unfaithful to him, nor do you believe he has to you.

Habits: Smoking: you never smoked

Coffee/Caffeine: you drink a coffee in the morning – and 1-2 teas in the afternoon. In the summer you drink ice tea. You occasionally have a coke – but not often

Alcohol/Drugs: You have a glass of wine only on the weekends if you go out to dinner. No drugs.

Nutrition: You try to eat a well-balanced and healthy diet.

Exercise: no formal exercise program. Walks the dog ½ mile a day every morning and evening.

Sleep: you get a well-rested full night’s sleep normally.

Religion: You are protestant and attend service regularly

**Case information**:

Chief complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

Response to “tell me more”: “I started not to feel right three days ago. At first just a bit under-the weather – tired, a bit achy and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early and tried to sleep it off. However, I wasn’t any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I like I am underwater. My right ear hurts inside – like a pressure. I took some decongestant but yesterday my temperature popped up to 102 and when I was blowing my nose all this thick yellow to greenish stuff was coming out. Just feels like a typical sinus infection – I don’t want it to go into my lungs and now I am not short of breath at all and I don’t feel it in my lungs, so I want to get some antibiotics before it spreads there!

Additional concerns/agenda: none

History of Present Illness: You went to a Northwell GoHealth Urgent Care center for what seems like a fairly typical sinus infection. You get sinus and ear infections 2-3 times a year. Sometimes it even goes into pneumonia. You have had pneumonia three times in the last 10 years – and that is with the pneumonia vaccine.

Other than this infection you consider yourself healthy. The history of bronchiectasis is relatively recent (last bout of pneumonia was last year, at which time your primary doctor said you also had this). You cough up every day with thick and light-yellow phlegm but occurs usually once in the morning when you first wake up. You have a bout of coughing, bring up this phlegm and then go about your day. You have only noticed shortness of breath when you exert yourself, like running up the stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED: You have had many sinus and ear infections since you were about 18 years old. You have even had pneumonia so many times that you have some permanent lung damage from it [bronchiectasis]. You attribute this to your job as a kindergarten teacher because as a kid, you were always very healthy, rarely got colds and didn’t even have tubes in your ears.

ONLY IF ASKED - Are you short of breath? Not more than I usually am. My bronchiectasis is mild and generally only get short of breath if I am exerting myself, likely walking up a couple of flights of stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you coughing more? My cough is generally mild but daily. It is not worse than it has been.

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have chest pain? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have cough up blood? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Is your nasal discharge bloody? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Have you had weight loss? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you bringing up more phlegm than usual? no

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any kidney problems? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any rashes? Lately you notice these little red dots on your legs and arms where you were holding some groceries. They don’t itch, they don’t hurt, they don’t seem to be getting worse and they fade. You weren’t that concerned about them. during the PE if the student is examining it – say “isn’t that weird – it is so flat you can’t feel it.

Impact on Life: “if I get my antibiotics I do fine and there is no impact. If I don’t get my antibiotics, then I get sick really fast.”

Concern: “you are concerned that if you don’t get antibiotics quickly you will get really sick”

Explanatory model: “You are constantly exposed to sniffly, sick kids at work.”

Review of systems: Do not volunteer these symptoms – only disclose them if asked

Pertinent Positives:

* With the bronchiectasis you have a chronic cough with mucous production – there has been no change in this with this infection.
* You have chronic diarrhea – with watery stools daily – no hx of gi infections like salmonella, campylobacter or giardia. You attribute this to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
* Lately you seem to be bruising a bit more easily- you seem to get them out of nowhere – they are mostly on your legs, but you also noticed them on your arm where you were holding a bag of milk.

Pertinent Negatives:

* No weight loss
* No history of cancers or lymphomas
* No history of lymph nodes being enlarged

Past medical history: Early bronchiectasis.

You did NOT have a lot of infections during your childhood. You began having recurrent sinusitis that started in your late teems – around 17 or 18. It often goes into your chest and you develop bronchitis – about once a year. You have even had pneumonia 3 x in the last 10 years – last year it was “pretty bad”. You recently have been worked up and told you have bronchiectasis.

Medications: no prescription, over the counter or herbal medications.

Allergies : denies medication, environmental or food allergies

Vaccinations: Flu shot yearly in November

Received all childhood vaccines

Pneumonia vaccine several years ago at PMD – “was supposed to help with my sinus issues and prevent me from having pneumonia again, but apparently it didn’t work out too well”

Sexual hx: Your husband is your one and only lifetime partner.

Family hx: Mother. Alive-age 76. High blood pressure, high cholesterol

Father. Alive-age 77. Gout

Physical Exam

General: You are well groomed, in a gown on the exam table. You can perform all required physical exam maneuvers without difficulty. You breathe comfortably throughout the exam without exertional dyspnea.

Vital Signs:

HEENT: If student performs otoscopic exam, hand them the ear PE finding card

Skin: Moulage will be applied to your lower legs. It will be a diffuse small scattered erythematous macule. As the student examines your rash, say “isn’t that weird, it’s so flat that you can’t even feel it!”

Lungs You will have SimScope patches placed on your front and back lung fields (rhonchi in lower fields)

Heart You will have SimScope patches placed over your heart (normal)

Abdomen: You will have a SimScope patch on your belly (normal)

Extremities: If student examines the nailbeds, hand them the finger PE finding card

**TOBACCO DEPENDENCE**

<u>**SCENARIO:**</u>

You are working in a busy primary care clinic and are about to see a 32-year-old who complains of cough for the past two months. She was seen at an urgent care center two weeks ago and again last week. The urgent care physician reported that the evaluation was normal and did not identify another cause of the cough.

A previous course of treatment did not help. The urgent care note advises follow up with the primary care physician.
private_patient_context:
## <u>**STATION**</u> 

**Tobacco Dependence**

# 1. <u>**INSTRUCTIONS FOR PATIENT:**</u>

You have experienced daily cough for about 2 months. You went to an urgent care two weeks ago and got a “Z-Pack” and an inhaler which did not help. They also did a chest x-ray and pulmonary function test and TB skin test. They “didn’t find anything.”  You think worry that your smoking might be causing the cough but you have tried to quit in the past and have not been able to. You are thinking about trying to quit, but you are doubtful about your chances of success.

## 1.1. ***Symptoms***

Daily morning cough for the past 2-3 months.  You have a cough in the morning with a little bit of gray mucous. Aside from the mild cough, <u>***you have no other symptoms***</u>.

Physical exam is normal.

## 1.2. ***Other history***

No history of asthma or allergy as a child.

No heartburn or reflux symptoms.

No wheezing.

No sick contacts.

No medications except Benadryl as needed.

No nasal congestion. No fever.

No regular exercise.

Allergies: Rash from Penicillin.

Family History: Your father’s mother (a smoker) had a heart attack at age 60.

Your parents are alive and in their 70s.

Three grandparents are alive in their 90s. One died of lung cancer two years ago (she did not smoke). No history of asthma or allergy in the family.

Social History

You are married with two kids. You are a teacher. You were born in US and never traveled outside US. No illegal drug use. No incarceration.

Smoking History (give details as prompted by the physician)

1. You smoke a pack of cigarettes a day since age 15.  You smoke Salem Lights. You switched from the regular Salem’s 8 years ago. You smoke after meals, with your coffee which you take on the back porch as your morning, afternoon, and evening ritual (while you grade papers), in your car when you drive, and during your lunch and planning period.
2. You have tried to quit a total of four times over the years.   You tried once with the patch (which you wore for two weeks) and once with the gum (you chewed only a few pieces when you had bad cravings). You still had cravings despite the medicines, and you didn’t like the taste of the gum, so you doubt the medicines work. Your longest quit attempt was two weeks.
3. Your spouse does not smoke and doesn’t let you smoke in the house. You can’t smoke at school. You do take a smoking break at lunch time, but you have to go out to your car or to a nearby coffee shop with an outdoor patio to smoke.
4. Your 70 year old father has smoked his whole life without health consequences.  Your grandfather still smokes a pipe at 94 years old.
5. You really enjoy smoking because it helps you relax and to concentrate and keep your weight down.

You should pay attention to the student’s behavior towards you if s/he explains the connection between your cough and the need for you to quit smoking. If they point out the connection between your smoking and your cough, and offer additional support, you are willing to try to quit and accept their offer of calling the quitline and using medications if they explain the fact that your symptoms suggest addiction, and offer you help to overcome the addiction with medications.  You doubt the NRT will work, but if they explain the need to take a high enough dose to eliminate withdrawal symptoms then you are willing to try any combination of medications other than the gum. Set a quit date if they suggest it. If they offer counseling, tell them that you are worried it will not fit with your schedule, but if they give you several alternatives that include the quitline or evening or weekend classes, tell them that you are willing to try counseling. If they get into too much blaming, you can get a little defensive. If they don’t offer you support when they suggest you quit, talk about how cigarettes help relieve your stress, and how you have had difficulty concentrating and headaches when you tried to quit before.

If the doctor gives you treatment recommendations that do not include quitting smoking, wait until the two minute warning or they say that they are done and then ask:

- “My partner thinks my cough is because I smoke, but my family all smoke and none of them cough. Do you think I should try to cut down?

**Transgender Health: A Standardized Patient Case for Advanced Clerkship Students**

**Appendix B: Michael**

**Activities and Time Required**

10 minute patient encounter followed by 5 minute post-encounter debriefing.

**Materials**

Prior to the encounter, the medical student will receive a folder labeled “Patient Chart” with a Date of Birth and the patient name “Cynthia Glenshaw” and instructions that the patient is here for an exam required to obtain life insurance (Appendix C). Student will either call the patient in from the hallway or greet the patient after reviewing the chart.

**Chief Complaint**

The patient is visiting the clinician to receive an exam required for obtaining life insurance.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

*Chief Complaint and Social History*

* Patient is at the doctor today for a documented note that has a complete history and exam required to obtain life insurance.
* Patient hasn’t been to the doctor for 5 years due to a number of transphobic interactions with previous doctors. Patient does not like or trust doctors, and does not want to be at the doctor today.
* Patient is in a long-term monogamous relationship with a cisgender woman. Patient and his partner recently got married and bought a condo, and the patient’s partner insists that they obtain life insurance.
* Patient does not smoke, drinks the occasional glass of wine, and does not use illicit or recreational drugs.
* Patient has no past medical history, surgical history, nor family history.

*Physician-Patient Introduction*

* The patient prefers the name “Michael” and the pronouns he/his. The ideal behavior is the student asks the patient what name/pronoun he prefers.
* The patient’s legal name is Cynthia as per the patient’s door chart for the case.
* If medical student initially uses the wrong name and/or pronouns, SP’s initial demeanor should be one of mild anger and frustration. The SP should become less angry and frustrated as the medical student makes efforts to establish the correct name and preferred pronouns. If the medical student misgenders the SP repeatedly and/or focuses the history-taking on inappropriate questions, the SP should gently refuse to answer questions and eventually ask for a different doctor.

*Medical history taking*

* During medical history, if medical student asks SP if they are on any other medications, the SP should ask what they mean by “medication” (e.g. define it, what drugs qualify as medications including those that are obtained over the counter, herbal, or in this case those purchased on the internet without a prescription). Following the response, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* During medical history, if medical student does not ask SP if he is on any other medications, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* The medical student should then inquire about where the patient obtains the needles and syringes and if he uses anyone else’s or shares his with other people. The patient endorses purchasing these on-line as well and using new needles and syringes every time he injects.

Pre-Brief Case 2

Author: Jenna Sizemore

Welcome to your discharge simulation!

You will perform a hospital discharge on a patient that has complex medical needs and has had an extended period of time being hospitalized very far away from their home.

You will be escorted to your patient’s hospital room when you arrive to the waiting area of our simulation center. In this scenario, you just started your first day of hospital service, so this will be your first time meeting the patient. A family member will be present that is planning to assist the patient home. The patient has an anticipated discharge date of the day of your simulation encounter.

During this encounter, your goal is to discuss the discharge plan with the patient and their family member. Please review and discuss their medication list, any anticipated follow ups, or other discharge needs that you can anticipate for the patient. Please answer the questions to the best of your ability. It is normal and expected that you may not know an answer that is asked, of which you can respond that you will find the answer for the patient.

After determining a discharge plan of care with the patient, you will leave the room and place discharge orders in the discharge navigator in a playground EMR environment.

A brief hospital summary follows.

Case 2:

Patient Name: Jo Smith, Adult patient

Hospital Service: Medicine 4

Admitting Diagnosis: Sepsis, MRSA bacteremia

Discharge Diagnosis: OUD, MRSA Aortic Valve Endocarditis s/p mechanical valve replacement, Mood Disorder, need for lifelong anticoagulation

Hospital Problem List:

Opioid Use disorder, severe, in early remission

MRSA Endocarditis and Bacteremia

Sepsis, resolved.

Aortic Mechanical Valve replacement

Coumadin therapy monitoring

Major Depressive Disorder

Generalized Anxiety Disorder

Brief Hospital Course: Adult patient admitted with *Methicillin-resistant staph aureus* with recent exposure to injected opioids was initially received as a transfer from a rural, critical access hospital several weeks ago. The patient was ultimately diagnosed with aortic valve endocarditis with embolic phenomenon, including CNS lesions. The patient received a successful mechanical valve replacement 5 weeks prior to discharge. After clearance from cardiac surgery, the patient was admitted to the multidisciplinary infusion service. Infectious disease and Psychiatry were consulted and have been actively following the patient. The patient completed a 6 week course of IV antibiotics, is currently in clinical remission for opioid use disorder, and is being discharged with lifelong anticoagulation needs. Laboratory monitoring remained stable for the last three weeks of hospitalization.

Activity/ambulation: Cleared for full activity without restrictions by CT surgery. No ambulatory restrictions.

DMC: Full capacity

Diet: Regular

**Child Neuro OSCE Case 5: Migraine headaches (Veronica)**

**Veronica Door Instructions**

A 16-year-old young lady and her parent come to clinic for follow-up. She had been referred six months prior for neurological evaluation as she had been having near daily headaches for three months. The headaches were associated to nausea, emesis, and vision changes. At the initial visit you diagnosed the patient as having migraines. Using over-the-counter medication did not have the desired effect. The headaches lasted several hours, or until the patient slept for two hours. The patient had missed several school days due to headaches. The rest of the patient’s medical history was unremarkable.

At the end of the last visit, a medication aimed at preventing headaches was prescribed. The medication had the desired effect until two weeks prior when the patient began experiencing frequent headaches again. Now she returns to discuss her plan of care.

Please speak with the patient and her parent regarding next steps in her care as well as answer any questions they may have.

# I. Rattlesnake bite (Crotalinae envenomation) simulation

# IV. Environment

Participant Information Card

This is a patient with a history of mild intermittent asthma who presents with a snake bite. The patient told triage: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” Their main complaint is increasing pain in the arm and they noticed some mild wheezing upon arrival (the patient stated it was: “like my asthma is acting up”)

# Appendix B

Moulage & Standardized Patient Support

The standardized patient (SP) has a history of mild intermittent asthma and presents with a snake bite. The complaint will be: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (If asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”

During the scenario, the SP will complain of increasing pain in the arm, nose bleed, and wheezing “like my asthma is acting up”.

The standardized patient should be coached on which pathway the instructor plans to use to avoid adding any unnecessary symptoms or complaints that may confuse the clinical picture.

If available, the instructor may utilize an earpiece so that they can communicate with the standardized patient during the scenario to help address and concerns that arise.

Since endotracheal intubation is not a part of this scenario, if the participants discuss this with the patient, the patient should tell them, “ I don’t want a tube in my throat and I’m starting to feel a little better”

# a. Scenario Background

i. Chief complaint (given freely): “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (if asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”   
ii. Past Medical History (if asked): Asthma, mild intermittent   
iii. Allergies: None   
iv. Medications: albuterol rescue inhaler prn dyspnea (uses 1-2 times a month)   
v. Immunizations: “No idea”   
vi. Family and Social history: no family diseases, social alcohol (1 drink a week), no tobacco or illegal dugs   
vii. Review of systems: Mild chest tightness with dyspnea (“I think my asthma is back”)

# b. Scenario Initial State

i. Patient Habitus and Presentation: the patient gives history of being bitten by a snake. “I think it was a rattlesnake” and complains of worsening swelling and pain in the hand.   
ii. Physiology: T 37.2, HR 120bpm, BP 140/80 R 22 SPO2 98%. Narrow complex rhythm with tachycardia on monitor.   
iii. Focused exam:

1. General: Reveals a patient in moderate distress (pain) and anxious

b. Skin: Normal color and turgor, no diaphoresis or rash

c. Hand: Right hand is swollen and discolored with fang marks and edema, patient is wearing a ring and a watch.

e. Lungs: Tachypnea and expiratory wheezing

h. Nose and IV site: coagulopathy can be represented by adding simulated blood to area surrounding IV site and nose

# c. Scenario Branch Points

iii. Scenario C: The patient is experiencing moderate pain at the bite site, mild expiratory wheezing, and some bleeding for the nose. In this scenario, the patient will develop anaphylaxis in response to antivenom administration. The patient’s wheezing will get worse and the patient will complain of itching and chest tightness. The patient’s symptoms will improve with treatment.

1. **Emergency Medicine Pre-Code Scenario: Theophylline Overdose**

6. **Case Narrative**
   1. **Scenario Background**
      1. Chief Complaint: A 55 year old patient presents to the ED with the complaint of 4 hours of severe nausea and vomiting accompanied by a new coarse tremor noted in the arms and legs bilaterally. Secondary complaints include palpitations, abdominal pain, and lightheadedness.
      2. History: A medical history of moderate to severe COPD controlled with a multi-drug regimen at home. The patient had some worsening of COPD over the last 48 hours and recognized this as a COPD exacerbation. The patient believed that 10 tablets of prednisone were taken at 8 hours and 1 hour before presentation (20 tablets total). Shortness of breath and wheezing completely resolved, but soon after the patient developed severe nausea, vomiting, and tremor.
      3. Extended History: The true story is that the patient accidentally took 20 theophylline tablets, not prednisone.
      4. Medications: The patient has a medication list in a pocket and will identify the medication that was taken as theophylline when asked by the medical learner.
      5. Allergies: NKDA
      6. Family and Social History: 100 pack year history of smoking cigarettes, quit within the last 5 years. No alcohol or illicit drug use. No family history of cardiac disease.
   2. **Scenario Initial State**
      1. Patient Habitus and Presentation: Sitting up in bed actively vomiting when the medical learner first arrives. Active coarse tremor visualized. No tachypnea is seen and the patient is not wheezing.
   3. **Scenario Branch Points**
      1. **Scenario A:** The patient is experiencing severe nausea and vomiting.
         1. **Changes in Patient Condition:** The patient will not deteriorate over the course of this scenario.

**Appendix B**

**Moulage & Standardized Patient / Manikin Support**

**Moulage** in this scenario included simulated sweat and vomit.

The **standardized patient** (SP) is a 55 year old patient with a history of COPD.

When learners enter the room the SP should be sitting up in bed actively vomiting. The SP should be in a patient gown. Sheet should be down covering the SP's feet but not legs.

* **Facial Expressions-** Pained.
* **Physical Movements-** Active process of retching and vomiting. Hands have a coarse tremor at rest and the shaking becomes much more noticeable as the SP tries to reach for the sheet to cover the legs. Make sure learners notice this shaking as it is a symptom.
* **Speech-** Short responses to questions. No full sentences. Speech is broken and labored due to nausea. No filler conversation. Once questions are answered, go back to focusing on nausea and stop focusing on the learners.
* **Key Talking Points to offer with minimal prompting**
  + I’ve been having a lot of trouble with my COPD lately.
  + I took 20 of my steroid pills.
  + The pills improved my breathing dramatically but now I am very nauseated, I have been vomiting for hours, and I have crampy abdominal pain.
  + I have never had this reaction to steroids before.
* **Key Talking Points to offer only when asked specifically**
  + The specific name of the medication that you took 20 tablets of is theophylline, or point to this medication on the medication list.
* **Important notes**
  + Learners may likely try to steer the SP toward a diagnosis of chest pain or a cardiac issue or focus on the pulmonary review of systems first; it is important to redirect the learner that the main concern is the vomiting, tremor, and palpitations.
  + When asked, breathing feels fine at this time.
  + Pain is abdominal, not in the chest.

**Appendix E: SP Training**

Title: Drug-Induced Acute Kidney Injury: A Standardized Patient Case for Clerkship Students

Issue: Swelling Ankles, Back Pain, & Decreased Urination

Patient name: Michelle Smith

Presenting Situation: Michelle Smith is a 55 year old individual whose family has brought her to their primary care doctor after they were “speaking nonsense”

**CASE SYNPOSIS**

You are Michelle Smith, a 55 year old individual who works in the kitchen of a local restaurant.

**WHY YOU ARE SEEING THE DOCTOR TODAY**

Your family brought you into your primary care provider today because you were confused, irritable, and had swollen ankles. Your family said you were mumbling incoherently and were talking about “being in the carwash” and were singing the song “When Johnny Comes Marching Home Again”. You are very tired and just want to sleep. When asked, you admit that you noticed that your feet and ankles have been swollen for two days; it was difficult to put shoes on to come in to the doctor’s office. You are wearing slippers. You also admit, when asked, that you have not been urinating very often during the past 2 days; you think it’s been at least 12 hours since you last urinated.

The cellulitis infection in your hand and arm for which you had been hospitalized for 3 days seems to be resolving. The visiting nurse has come out to your home every day since your discharge (the past 3 days) to administer your vancomycin twice daily. You probably got the initial infection at work while washing dirty dishes at work.

**OPENING**

**Note: Bolded information includes key points that should be shared with students and may not be ad-libbed.**

Your initial statement should relate to how you are feeling. It’s hard to predict what the student will say when s/he comes into the room, but you should respond appropriately to the student’s greeting or question. For example:

The student may ask: “What brings you to the office today?”

* You could respond: “My family brought me in. They said I was talking nonsense.”

The student may ask: “Hello. How are you feeling?”

* You could respond: “I’m really tired.”

NOTE: As a standardized patient, you should answer the student’s questions, but avoid volunteering more information than the student asks for.

**HOW YOU APPEAR DURING THE ENCOUNTER**

Physical description

* You should be reasonably neat and well groomed.
* As you are portraying a patient who is feeling quite poorly, you will wear loose fitting clothing and slippers.
* You should appear tired, with soft and slow speech and mentation.
* You should appear a bit confused.

Description of affect and behavior

* You should be a little confused.
* You should appear tired.
* You are concerned because you don’t know why your feet are so swollen.
* You don’t feel like eating; you have not been hungry.
* You are cooperative and answer questions the best that you can.

**REVIEW OF SYSTEMS**

Cardiovascular: You haven’t had any chest pain.

Pulmonary: You haven’t noticed any difficulty breathing or getting out of breath.

Gastrointestinal: You haven’t felt quite right on your stomach…not sick exactly, **just not hungry**.

Neurological: No weakness in your arms or legs. No difficulty walking. You are very tired. Your family told you that you were babbling about things that didn’t make any sense.

Musculoskeletal/External: **Your feet and ankles are swollen. The cellulitis infection in hand/arm is resolving – much less swollen and tender than it had been 6 days ago when you were admitted to the hospital for 3 days. Your back/neck/shoulder muscles are sore and tender radiating pain down into your neck (causing a headache) and down your arm. You couldn’t get comfortable in the hospital beds and have had ‘kink in your neck” that just won’t relax (4 out of 10 on pain scale).**

Genitourinary: A bit of mild flank pain (back below ribs) (a 1 out of 10 on a pain scale), if student palpates it. **You haven’t had any pain or burning when urinating. You haven’t noticed any blood in your urine, but you admit that you have not been urinating very much.**

**Medications:**

You normally take blood pressure pills at home. They had not given you blood pressure pills when you were in the hospital because your blood pressure was actually running on the low side, but you started taking them again when you got home.

* You were discharged with home health care providing **vancomycin** intravenously twice daily and are to continue this for a total of 14 days. You receive a dose of 1300 mg every 12 hours.
* Since returning home, you have resumed taking **Lisinopril 20** mg daily for blood pressure.
* Since returning home, you have resumed taking **Hydrochlorothiazide 25** mg daily for blood pressure
* Since returning home, you have been taking **ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours** for the “stiff back and kink in the neck” that you suspect you developed as a result of not sleeping well and not being able to get comfortable while in the hospital bed.

**You can show the table below which you normally keep up-to-date in your wallet.**

![DrugListCase3](data:image/jpeg;base64...)

**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY**

Your overall health has been pretty good, until you developed the infection just over a week ago. For the past 5 years you had taken medication for high blood pressure but that was the only medical condition you had.

You were hospitalized about a week ago for 3 days due to an infection in the tissues of your right hand that spread up your arm to your elbow. They called it “cellulitis”. You aren’t quite sure how you got the infection, but are guessing that you may have had a scratch that got infected when you were washing dirty dishes at work. You work in the kitchen of a local restaurant.

You were sent home from the hospital after 3 days of receiving vancomycin, with a visiting nurse stopping by your home twice daily to continue the two daily doses of the intravenous antibiotic. You are supposed to keep getting vancomycin intravenously for a total of 2 weeks – so you have another week to go until the antibiotic therapy is completed.

After you were discharged from the hospital, you resumed taking your normal blood pressure pills: lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. You also started taking ibuprofen 200 mg – 3 tablets every 6 hours for pain that you’ve had in your back/shoulder/neck. You suspect that you just slept wrong when you were in those hospital beds and now you have some really sore muscles.

You do not have any drug allergies that you know about.

**FAMILY HISTORY**

**Parents:** father died of a heart attack at age 68; mother died of a stroke at age 74

**Grandparents:** you never knew them, but heard that your grandmother had developed diabetes “late in life”

**Brothers/sisters:** 2 brothers ages 45 and 52, both in good health

**Children:** 2 teenager daughters, in good health

**PRESENT LIFE
Age:** 55
**Date of birth:** --/--/1959 (use your own birthday with the year listed)
**Occupation:** works in the kitchen of a restaurant
**Marital status:** married for 25 years; spouse age 59, in good health
**Life details**: you have 2 teenage daughters who live at home. You have a good relationship with your spouse. You have worked at the same restaurant for 15 years and typically work about 10 hours a day plus every other weekend.
**Health Insurance:** Commercial

**PERSONAL HABITS
Alcohol:** Not daily, but will sometimes have a cocktail after the restaurant closes at night
**Tobacco:** smoked as a teenager and throughout 20s (1/2 pack per day), but stopped more than 15 years ago
**Caffeine:** 3 cups per day
**Drugs (illicit):** no illicit drug use **Exercise:** no formal program. You intend to begin walking more.

**HOW YOU WILL RESPOND TO DIFFERENT INTERVIEWING QUESTIONS/STYLES**

1. **You are tired and just want to sleep**. **You are lying down on the examination table**. You are concerned mostly because your family was so worried that they brought you to the doctor’s office. You wait to be asked questions by the student and do not volunteer information.
2. If the student uses medical jargon, e.g. “renal”, “erysipelas”, etc. you should request clarification, e.g. “What does that mean?”
3. If the student asks if you have a fever, you can respond by saying, “No”.
4. If the student asks if you have any pain or burning when urinating, you can respond by saying, “No.
5. If the student asks if you have noticed any blood in your urine, you can respond by saying “No, I haven’t noticed any”.
6. You are used to being treated with respect by others. If the student acts condescending or uninterested in your comfort, you should respond by being less “friendly” – but should remain as cooperative as a tired person who is in a bit of discomfort and who has exhibited some mental status changes would.
7. If the student asks you what you think is going on, tell them, “**I am so sleepy. My family said that I was talking nonsense. Before my parents died, I remember when they got any sort of infection, it seemed to ‘go to their head’ – they just became all confused and said things that didn’t make any sense. I am worried that my infection has come back.”**

**ENDING THE ENCOUNTER**

Ordinarily, students will end encounters with a statement such as “Do you have any questions?” At this point, you should respond, “**What is wrong with me? Did my infection come back**?”

However, if the student has already given you an opportunity to express this concern regarding a serious condition or a resistant/persistent infection, you should respond with a statement like, “No, I don’t have any more questions at this time.”

In some cases, students will end the encounter abruptly. In this case, you should respond, “**What is wrong with me? Is my infection spreading or getting worse**? **Please don’t leave me alone worrying about this. Tell me what is going on**.” (If this issue has not been previously raised during the interview.)

**PHYSICAL EXAM**

* No chest pain
* Blood pressure is normal
* Regular heart rate and rhythm
* No difficulty breathing or getting out of breath
* Lungs clear to auscultation
* No weakness in arms or legs
* No difficulty walking
* Mild flank tenderness (back below ribs, 1 out of 10 on pain scale) upon palpation
* Head/Ears/Eyes/Nose/Throat are normal
* Abdominal exam is normal
* No swelling, tenderness or erythema in either calf
* Asterixis: The students may ask you to put your arms out in front of you and may push back on your wrists. If they do this, you should flap your wrists back and forth once they remove the pressure. The uncontrolled flapping does not need to be the same in both wrists. Students should note how long the flapping persists, the amplitude, and the frequency. You may wish to look at an example on youtube. This condition, called asterixis, is sometimes seen in patients with renal failure. It may be useful to view a patient depicting this condition: <http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sEnp2ss8VoA>.

**PHYSICAL EXAM 3x5 CARDS**

1. The infection site: is healing well without evidence of infection; the swelling and erythema are resolving. No pus or exudates. No evidence of infection noted near the PICC (peripherally inserted central catheter) line into which vancomycin is delivered.
2. Feet/Ankles: the ankles are swollen with 2+ pitting edema bilaterally. Radial and pedal pulses are palpable but distant.

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a medicine intern. You are talking to the patient’s adult child in a family meeting room.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is an 87-year-old man who was found by his adult child at home confused and poorly responsive. Aside from some curative skin cancer excisions and arthritis in the hips and knees, he had been doing well and living independently in a retirement community. He was admitted from the Emergency Department to the Medical Intensive Care Unit 3 days ago.

Currently, the patient is intubated and being treated for pneumonia with bacteremia and persistent rectal bleeding. The patient is obtunded and unable to participate in the discussion. Your team has witnessed a precipitous decline in the last 12 hours and sees the patient is actively dying with a time frame of hours. Any further intervention will not be helpful. Your team is recommending comfort care at this time.

You are about to have a face to face conversation with his adult child for the first time, as they had to travel out of town for work right after the patient was admitted. However the adult child is up to speed with the current condition, because they have been receiving updates from you and your team by phone. At the last phone conversation, the adult child was told they needed to come in to make important decisions about the goals of care.

**Student Tasks:**

Ensure that the adult child has a clear understanding of the father’s clinical situation and discuss goals of care. The patient is actively dying; your priority is to guide the adult child toward your team’s plan to focus on comfort as is appropriate in this situation.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 45-65 years old
**Episode:** Goals of Care
**Workshop:** Advanced Communcation Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are the adult child of the patient, your 87-year-old father, who is in the hospital. Your father is a widower and has been living independently in a retirement community for many years. You are an only child, and you live near your father and check in on him daily, which you’ve done for the last few years. You assist him with all transportation, finances, and medications, and your father has been able to walk with a walker and be independent in self-care. Your mother committed suicide when you were a teenager, but your father has rarely discussed her with you.

You found your father confused and sleepy when you checked in on him 3 days ago and brought him to the Emergency Department and they admitted him to the Medical Intensive Care Unit because he was very sick. You had to leave town for work the next day but have been speaking with the doctors in the hospital by phone every day, sometimes twice a day. They have explained things to you clearly and you have a good understanding of the medical details before today’s in-person meeting\* – he has a pneumonia, a blood infection, and is bleeding from his rectum. He is intubated and on a ventilator to support his breathing along with medicines to support his blood pressure. The rectal bleeding is thought to be from a new, large colon mass identified on CT scan but he has been too sick for a biopsy to be considered yet. More recently, his kidney function has worsened very quickly and significantly. And more importantly, the team told you within the last 12 hours that part of his colon has started to die due to lack of blood flow.\*\* He can’t go to surgery because he is too sick and unstable. Today, the team asked you to come in to see your father and discuss his care, expressing concern about any hope for recovery. You returned to town urgently and have come right to the hospital. You know that he is really sick, the sickest he has ever been – “he’s been a very strong guy until now but this is sounding really serious and scary.”

The doctor may ask you about advance directives, a living will, or durable power of attorney for health care, and should explain these terms to you in basic language. You should have a basic understanding about what these terms mean to move the conversation along.\*\*\* As far as you are aware your father didn’t have any advance directives, etc. He always spoke about “living every day to the fullest” but has mentioned a few times that he wouldn’t want to suffer like some other family members when his time to die approaches. You are shocked that all this has happened so quickly and don’t want him to die. Until this happened, your father was still enjoying playing cards, watching TV, and spending time with the family. You love having him in your life. However, as long as the doctors assure you that all has been done to try to help him recover, you would want him to die peacefully if it’s an inevitable path. You would look to the doctors to guide you toward the most compassionate and comfortable path for your father’s care. If not reassured when your concerns are expressed, you would continue to look for reassurance and clarification in the midst of distress and great concern.

\* Ideally the doctor will ask you about your understanding of the situation, and if they do, you can explain the background details that you had learned over the phone. This is important because it will allow the focus of the in-person meeting to be about the next-steps rather than the doctor providing a detailed explanation of a medical situation that you already understand.

\*\* This is a very important detail; the student should make it clear to you that this update suggests pending death.

\*\*\* Explanation - Advance directives are legal documents that allow you to spell out your decisions about end-of-life care ahead of time. They give you a way to tell your wishes to family, friends, and health care professionals and to avoid confusion later on when you may be unable to speak for yourself.

A living will tells which treatments you want if you are dying or permanently unconscious. You can accept or refuse medical care. You might want to include instructions on:

* The use of dialysis and breathing machines
* If you want to be resuscitated if your breathing or heartbeat stops (“DNR”)
* Tube feeding
* Organ or tissue donation

A durable power of attorney for health care is a document that names your health care proxy. Your proxy is someone you trust to make health decisions for you if you are unable to do so.
