# CASE 4

# Charlotte Day, Military Sexual Trauma

# Charlotte Day Military Sexual Trauma

LEARNER INFORMATION( to be shared with Learner prior to role –play)

Patient’s Name: Charlotte Day is a 22- to 30-year-old female.

Chief complaint: Ms. Day presents to a primary care clinic for her annual physical and pelvic/pap tests. She missed two previously scheduled appointments and was late to her appointment today. Her PHQ -2 was positive. Ms. Day reports increased problems/stress relating to her partner/husband.

Location: VA Physician’s Office

Learner Skill Set: Eliciting data in an objective and non-judgmental manner; accurate recording of symptoms; sensitivity; motivational interviewing (MI) skills; selfawareness
private_patient_context:
# MILITARY SEXUAL TRAUMA CHARLOTTE DAY STANDARDIZED PATIENT TRAINING MATERIAL

# PRESENTING SCENARIO

Ms. Day presents to a primary care clinic for annual physical and pelvic/pap tests. She missed two previously scheduled appointments and was late to her appointment today. Her PHQ -2 (depression screening test) was positive. Secondary complaint or psychosocial issues/subtext: Ms. Day reports increased problems/stress relating to her partner/husband.

# CHIEF COMPLAINT

“I’ve been trying to get pregnant for a year and my husband and I are starting to have problems about it. I’m here to make sure there is nothing wrong with me.”

# HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Ms. Day has felt depressed and down for the past few months and has had problems communicating with her spouse. They are trying to get pregnant for the first time and have been trying for about a year. The provider may ultimately refer patient to gynecologist for fertility evaluation, but the provider’s focus for this encounter is trying to understand how past trauma is affecting current functioning.

Ms. Day was sexually assaulted by her commanding officer two years ago during her military deployment in Afghanistan. Ms. Day was a Captain in the Marines. She worked closely with her commanding officer (CO) for several months, developing strategies to support the needs of Afghan women while assessing risk to soldiers involved with this work.

The attack occurred after two weeks of increasingly flirtatious comments and nonverbal indicators from her C.O. Ms. Day ignored the comments because they made her uncomfortable and she did not want to encourage what was an obviously inappropriate advance. The other staff was starting to notice, which increased her discomfort.

Charlotte got up in the middle of the night to use the rest room and when she returned her CO was in her room waiting for her. She initially resisted the attack but soon realized that resistance could lead to serious physical injury. He covered her mouth and used force to hold her down, while growling verbal threats against her career if she were to report what happened. The episode was utterly humiliating. He was there for only 20-25 minutes, but when he left she felt he had been there for hours.

□ The incident involved physical overpowering; there was no than additional brutality beyond the rape. Intimidation and the subtle power of a superior officer over a subordinate allowed the incident to happen. Her pride kept her from calling out or screaming. She is proud to be tough, stoic, and independent. She did not want him to see her fear.
□ Charlotte blames herself for this. She feels that she failed in some way and that she is somehow unworthy of respect. It is a male-dominated culture: The unspoken rule in the military is $\mathrm { C O } = \mathrm { G O D }$ . A commanding officer makes the rules. Marines are “trained to obey.” This CO was known to be a volatile, aggressive person and she didn’t want to do anything to provoke him.
□ The incident shattered her trust in the service. As a Marine you are trained to trust your CO as if they were a father figure who had your best interests at heart. The CO became the enemy, which is counter to all of her training. Her pride in being a Marine was shaken. Most service men/women never say they are ex-Marines when they return to civilian life. Charlotte identifies herself as an ex-Marine.

During the attack, Charlotte’s commanding officer threatened to ruin her military and even civilian career with bad evaluations and future references, if she were ever to come forward about the rape. Not only was she afraid of the CO’s reprisal; she was worried about being singled out from her work group, if she made the incident known. She knows of three peers (female) who reported similar situations and were further mistreated or left the service because of fear. Reporting an incident such as this is frowned upon by peers and other officers though most would not admit that. It’s commonly known that “perpetrators get promoted, victims get discharged.”

Ms. Day went back to work the day after the attack and told no one. He was in the office the next day as well and acted as though nothing ever happened but did not engage or flirt with Ms. Day again. Ms. Day was scared and depressed following the assault but did not report it. Her symptoms of trouble sleeping, trouble concentrating, and feeling blue resolved on their own about 3 months after the attack. (See Depression Screening for detailed information on symptoms.)

About two months after the rape, Charlotte was discharged from active duty. She came back to Dayton and served in the reserves (military police) for 6 months.

During this time, she began dating her future husband – her first serious relationship since the rape. Early on in their courtship, Charlotte had a brief recurrence of her symptoms, and her boyfriend (now husband) thought that he was not adequately pleasing her sexually or that perhaps she wasn’t interested in having a serious relationship.

He eventually expressed his concerns, and Ms. Day reluctantly shared her trauma experience with him and also informed him that he was her first sexual partner since the attack. This conversation led to increased understanding and opened up communication between them, which contributed to her healing process and improved their sexual relationship. Ms. Day and her husband were able to work through their relationship challenges together and have maintained a strong sexual and emotional bond, until the fertility issues started.

They became engaged after dating for only six months and have been married for about a year. Ms. Day had a brief recurrence of symptoms when she first became serious with her husband but has felt normal until now.

The transition from active duty to civilian life was hard for her. The freedom and lack of routine left her feeling adrift. It has been a challenge to take care of herself the way she knows she should. After all, why would a person put a lot of energy into self-care when you feel you are a bad or unworthy person? In the military there was no choice about schedule…you HAD to do things when you were told.

# TIMELINE:

today—Came in for PE/PAP
2 weeks ago—Last intercourse
3 weeks ago —Last period
2-3 months ago—Irritable, sleep issues, increased appetite (gained 10 lbs.), trouble concentrating, decreased motivation at work
Last year—Married (early in the year), got off the pill ASAP, wanted to start a family right away, has been “home” for about $1 \%$ years
6-months prior to marriage and 6 months after return from Afghanistan—Met “husband” at a bar when out with friends
2 years ago—Afghanistan, worked to build rapport with Afghan women. The assault occurred with little time left in country (meaning this assignment would soon be over).
3 years ago—OKINAWA
5 years ago—CAMP PENDELTON (http://www.marines.mil/Pages/ Default.aspx)
6 years ago—Enlisted, went through ROTC in college, and entered the Marines as a Second Lieutenant

# CURRENT SYMPTOMS

If asked any of the depression screening questions below:

How would you describe your mood? “I’m grumpy…..My husband says I’m a stick in the mud….I guess this tiredness is keeping me from wanting to do much.” OR “I’m upset more than usual. I’m worried something is wrong with me, because I’m not getting pregnant.”

Irritable: Patient has been more irritable than is normal for her. She finds herself snapping at her husband more than she used to, over simple things that really aren’t important.

Sleep: See above. Patient has had difficulty sleeping lately (falling and staying asleep).

Guilty: Regarding guilty feelings–with prompting —admit to feeling guilty about the fact that “there must be something wrong with me” that she relates to her inability to conceive. She feels bad for snapping at her husband more frequently. If the learner has been able to talk to Charlotte about the attack, she would admit to guilt feelings around the incident. This would be highly consistent with some common underlying themes MST survivors often face (“it’s my fault…I must have done something to deserve this”). She feels guilty that she didn’t fight harder against the attack or done more to seek help. She wonders if she encouraged him somehow and is concerned that he is still abusing women.

Concentration: She has mild difficulty concentrating. She often feels foggy and distracted. This makes it hard to work and hard to listen sometimes when others are talking to her.

Anhedonia: (Lack of interest in things that would normally bring you pleasure). Charlotte is not interested in being around people much…she does not feel like being social. This is unlike her. She hasn’t been very motivated to work much either and she is a bit concerned that she will be reprimanded. She has been late a couple of times but just has a hard time forcing herself to try harder.

Sadness: “I don’t know.”

Fatigue: Fatigue is not an issue for Ms. Day.

Appetite: You’ve been either hungrier or less hungry (10 pound gain or loss).

# PAST MEDICAL HISTORY

“I have a lot of stomach aches and headaches lately. I sometimes worry that I have a serious disease.”

Charlotte has a history of headaches and feels that her headache frequency has increased to a couple times per week. She also has GI upset more frequently now–a few times per month. She reports the pain associated with both headaches and GI has been increasing over the past year and is worried she might have a more serious disease. She does not realize that her past trauma is leading to relationship difficulties or somatization (GI upset, headaches).

ROS: Charlotte reports some instances of indigestion and diarrhea.

Hospitalizations/surgery: None.

Medications: Charlotte takes OTC medications (Advil, Tums, etc.) to treat uncomfortable symptoms.

# FAMILY HISTORY

Mom, Dad, and Charlotte’s two siblings (a brother and sister) are all in good health.

# SOCIAL HISTORY

Charlotte and her husband (an engineer) currently live in a condo. They have been married for about a year. The Days are financially comfortable but do not have a lot of excess cash flow.

Charlotte is a college graduate and currently works part time in human resources . Charlotte enjoys her H.R. job. (She helps employees with insurance benefits, education benefits, sick time, vacation time, career development.) Usually, she gets along well with others and enjoys socializing with her peers, but she has become more withdrawn lately. She also sometimes appears spacey at work and some of her peers have begun to take notice. She has been late to work a couple times, which is unusual behavior for Ms. Day.

# LIFESTYLE/HABITS

Smoking: Charlotte previously smoked one and a half packs of cigarettes a day, but quit about a year when they began trying to get pregnant. She had smoked for five years prior to quitting.

Alcohol: Charlotte drinks about 3 – 7 beers a week and has done so for about five years. She does not feel like she should Cut back, she has not been Annoyed at

others, she does not feel Guilty about her drinking or start the day with an Eyeopener. (CAGE)

Diet: Fast food is a frequent part of the Days’ diet. Charlotte has about two cups of coffee or soda a day. She exercises once or twice a week.

# SEXUAL HISTORY

Charlotte has had 4 life time partners (does NOT include the rape) including her husband. She is in a monogamous relationship with her husband. She has been on the pill, YASMIN, since college. (This pill is one of two that is FDA approved to treat acne.)

# REACTIONS TO SPECIFIC QUESTIONING

A victim of MST may have trouble trusting others and may be afraid of people trying to control them. They might also have strict boundaries that they don’t want people to cross. Due to these symptoms, there are certain pitfalls an interviewer might have when questioning Charlotte. Examples of things that the interviewer might do or say that would have a negative or positive affect are listed below.

# Learner Skills to which the Patient would respond positively

□ Acknowledging that psychological pain is very close to physical pain (validating) □ Allowing the emotion to open and then effectively moving to different areas Allowing the time to listen (This may be the $1 ^ { \mathrm { s t } }$ time this person has revealed incident to an authority. It is worth taking the time to listen.) □ Reflecting your understanding of the situation to the patient □ Encouraging self-reflection, self-change talk regarding the trauma □ Identifying changeable behaviors (don’t ding a patient for personality)

# Learner Behaviors to which the patient would respond negatively

□ Negative Questioning: “You aren’t’ feeling guilty are you?” □ Labeling: “Were you drinking at the time?” □ Assumptions: “Have you had many sexual partners while in service?” □ Minimizing: any indication to the patient that you think she is exaggerating.

Visit 1

The first interview is in the doctor's office for an urgent visit because of chest pain.

**(The expanded description of the** ***clinical, psychosocial, and presentation*** **information)**

***Why the patient is seeing the student doctor:*** You are in the doctor's office for an urgent visit today because you are having chest pain.

***Brief Summary of Case (*** *Limit to one paragraph):* You are scared, worried that you may be having a heart attack but putting on a brave front. The pain is under your breastbone toward your left side. The pain radiates into your neck and down your left arm about to your elbow. Today's pain started when you were moving some equipment in the barn. It is a heavy feeling (place fist on chest). The pain started about an hour ago. When it did not go away after 15 minutes, you asked your wife, Shirley, to take you to her new doctor. She wanted to call 911 but you would not let her. A similar pain has been occurring for the past few weeks. At first it was not very bad; you would stop what you were doing and the pain would go away in less than 10 minutes, but now it won't stop. On a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the worst (which is right now), yours is a "9," usually it has been 4-5.

If asked to describe your pain, it is pressure like a squeezing, tight feeling. You really want and need something for your pain.

You will be transferred to the hospital.

**TRAINING MATERIALS**

**Completion of sections I though VII will provide specific information used in training SP's**

I. **Patient Profile (A,B,C, and K are recruitment requirements)**

**A. Age**: late 40's

**B. Gender**: male

**C. Race**: same as rest of family

**D. Affect (Mannerisms, Behavior)**: scared because you are experiencing chest pains

**F. Occupation**: Farmer; grow tobacco and soybeans and get an average return on your crops (not a lot of money for 'wants'), but you like what you do. "It gives me a lot of satisfaction to look out over my fields in the late afternoon and see that I have done an honest day's work."

**G. Sexual History**: 1 partner, your wife; have always been faithful to her and are satisfied with your sexual relationship, intercourse one time per week. No history of partner or child abuse.

**H. Marital Status**: married to Shirley for 20 years; 2 children, Samantha 18, and Jeremy 16

**I. Habits**: smoke 1½ packs of cigarettes a day; drink 1-2 drinks (beer/liquor at home in evenings), CAGE: 0/4; eat fatty and fried foods; drink sweet tea; enjoy large portions of meat

**J. General Appearance**: clothes are simple "average farmer" look; wears a hat or cap; overweight (Body Mass Index around 30)

II. **History of Present Illness**

**Location**: Chest pain below the breastbone toward your left side. The pain started when you were moving equipment in the barn about an hour ago. The pain radiates into your neck and down your left arm.

(You have been having similar pains for the past several weeks. This is stronger and has lasted longer than the previous 10-15 episodes.)

**Quality**: This has been occurring for the past several weeks. At first it was not very bad, you would stop what you were doing and in a few minutes the pain would go away, but now the pain won't stop. It is a deep, dull ache, a heavy feeling (place fist on central chest), sometimes squeezing.

**Quantity/Severity**: on a scale of 1-10 with 10 being the worst, it is a "9," usually, it has been 4-5 in severity.

**Onset**: this time, about 1 hour ago

**Duration**: pain usually lasts about 10 minutes, this time it has not been relieved

**Frequency**: occurs off and on when you exert yourself. Initially, you were having one episode per week; the pain has occurred daily the past 3 days.

**Setting**: Working. Not at rest, while eating or while having sexual intercourse.

**Aggravating/Alleviating Factors**: pain is relieved with rest, is worse with exertion

**Associated Symptoms**: Slight shortness of breath and a feeling of weakness. Diaphoresis (sweating) and nausea. You have not experience these feelings before. You have not been light-headed or experienced palpitations, tachycardia, or syncope.

**Concerns:** Today you are worried about having a heart attack and dying. Previously, you thought that you were having indigestion. You are also worried about the cost of the office visit, hospitalization and physicians' fees.

**III. Past Medical History: Unremarkable**

1. **Prior Illnesses or Injury**: Few stitches from farm injuries. No fractures or other trauma.
2. **Past Hospitalizations**: None.
3. **Allergies and Immunizations**: Up to date on tetanus, 4 years ago.
4. **Current Medications**: Rare BC powder or advil (ibuprofen) for aches and pains, none in the past week.
5. **Other drugs**: No OTC products or illicit drugs. Tried marijuana as teenager.

**IV. ROS**

1. **General**: No symptoms
2. **HEENT**: No symptoms.
3. **Respiratory**: No cough or sputum production. No SOB but less work tolerance over the past 1-2 years.
4. **Cardiovascular**: No history of hypertension. See HPI.
5. **Gastrointestinal**: No issues, except for nausea with current pain.
6. **Genitourinary**: No symptoms. Sexual intercourse with Shirley once per week
7. **Musculoskeletal**: "Typical aches and pains of a farmer."
8. **Psychiatric**: Worried about dying, and who will take care of Shirley and the children.
9. **Hematologic**: No symptoms.
10. **Endocrinologic**: No history of diabetes. Never had a cholesterol panel.

**V. Family History**

Parents: father 62, deceased, suddenly died at farm 8 yrs ago (not sure of cause of death)

mother 70, deceased, pneumonia (died last year)

Siblings: sister 40's, probably healthy, lives in another town

**VI. Scenario Development**

**A. Describe** ***why the patient is seeing the physician***, including the ***specific opening statement***

Chief complaint: "I'm having some chest pain." You are here because of chest pain which is below your breastbone and radiates down your left arm and neck. It gets worse with exertion and has not gone away for the past hour.

**B. Describe the patient's** ***demeanor*** **at the beginning and throughout the encounter**

You appear anxious, this chest pain really has you scared.

**C. Describe the patient's** ***concerns regarding his/her understanding*** **of the presenting problem.**

You are very concerned about the seriousness of your problem. "Am I having a heart attack?" "Am I going to die?"

**D. Describe how the patient will** ***respond to different interviewing styles***

Problem focused interview. The physician is expected to be reassuring since the patient is scared.

"Is it my heart?" "Do you think its a bad one?"

**F. Describe the** ***challenges*** **the patient will present to the physician**

Initially anxious, you are somewhat reassured with the physician's interview and intervention in the office.

# Appendix B

Moulage & Standardized Patient Support

The standardized patient (SP) has a history of mild intermittent asthma and presents with a snake bite. The complaint will be: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (If asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”

During the scenario, the SP will complain of increasing pain in the arm, nose bleed, and wheezing “like my asthma is acting up”.

The standardized patient should be coached on which pathway the instructor plans to use to avoid adding any unnecessary symptoms or complaints that may confuse the clinical picture.

If available, the instructor may utilize an earpiece so that they can communicate with the standardized patient during the scenario to help address and concerns that arise.

Since endotracheal intubation is not a part of this scenario, if the participants discuss this with the patient, the patient should tell them, “ I don’t want a tube in my throat and I’m starting to feel a little better”

**Standardized Patient Case:**

**Acute Cholecystitis**

<u>**PROPS NEEDED:**</u>

One SP patient, ages 20 - 70, with their gallbladder still in place

Hospital gown for the patient

One White Bed Sheet

<u>**CASE SUMMARY:**</u>

The patient is between 20 - 70 year of age in good general physical health. The patient works in a bank in downtown Louisville in a low to medium pressure office job. The patient is clearly middle class, and dresses appropriately for employment in a bank. The patient has no history of previous gallbladder attacks and historically could eat anything they wanted to. The patient presents to the Norton's Hospital ER 3 hours after eating broccoli cheese soup and cheesecake for lunch, complaining of acute onset of right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the right shoulder. The patient walked to the hospital from their downtown bank office, vomiting once in the bushes on the way over.

<u>**PRESENTATION/EMOTIONAL TONE**</u>

As the patient you are dressed in a gown, lying on the bed, right side down. You are polite and perhaps a little embarrassed. You think you probably just have the stomach flu but your abdominal pain is really bad and so you came to the ER anyway. You are in PAIN but you try to be as cooperative as you can.

In response to the question: "Why are you here today?", you answer in these words:

**"My stomach hurts real bad!!"**

<u>**SUMMARY OF SCENARIO DEVELOPMENT**</u>

Speech/Demeanor: Speech is appropriate for a middle class bank worker with a college education. It is ok to have a sheepish grin or to smile through the pain occasionally. Eye contact should be appropriate for that of a middle class bank worker, meaning you are not afraid to make eye contact.

<u>**MEDICAL HISTORY OF THE PATIENT**</u>

<u>**History of Present Illness:**</u>

You felt well this morning. You got up, had your usual breakfast of cereal and milk, coffee, OJ. You showered, dressed, and went to the bank without any hesitation. You worked all morning and felt fine. You went to your favorite deli for lunch in the first floor of the bank building and had broccoli cheese soup and cheesecake for dessert. You went back to work but about 2 hours after lunch you started feeling bad with a little nausea and some upper abdominal pain. The pain never subsided but actually gradually continually worsened, localizing to the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. You can take one finger and point right to where it hurts. The pain worsened, began to throb, waxing and waning every 2 or 3 minutes. It never went away no matter what you did: loosen your belt, pass gas, burp, take TUMS, etc. Within a half hour the pain was the worst you ever felt, boring all the way to your back, and also causing your right shoulder to ache, too. You told your co-workers and they urged you to go to the ER right away. You decided to walk the 2 blocks to the Norton's ER. On the way, you vomited your lunch in the bushes, holding on to a street sign for balance. There is no fever, no chills, no diarrhea.

<u>**Description of the pain:**</u>

The pain is 3.5 inches to the right of midline right below your rib cage. It is a BORING, DULL, INTENSE pain. It is colicky, meaning that every 2 - 3 minutes or so it seems to get worse, then for 2 - 3 minutes it gets a little better. The pain makes it difficult to take a deep breath since moving the diaphragm down irritates the pain more. The pain seems to almost go straight through to the same location in your back. Also, your right shoulder is really aching, especially the lower part of the scapula. The pain is weird because it won't go away, and you have never had anything like this in your life. It did not get better when you vomited. You are still nauseated.

<u>**Radiation of the pain:**</u> The pain bores all the way to the back at the same location as the front PLUS the right shoulder (scapula) aches

<u>**Intensity:**</u> about an 8 or 9, but goes down to a 5 or 6 every 2 or 3 minutes.

<u>**Associated symptoms:**</u> nausea, anorexia, unable to take a deep breath, feels worse to lay on your back

<u>**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

- The PMH is basically negative for anything contributory

- Depending on age and gender, it is OK to mention minimal illnesses such as past pregnancies, past menopause or mild hypertension

- Please, no mention of heart disease, pneumonias, cancers, no smoking history, no major abdominal diseases, etc.

<u>**General Health**</u>: Generally healthy.

<u>**Past Surgical History**</u> - For previous scars, report past surgeries truthfully, e.g. hysterectomy, C-section, knee surgery, etc. However, for this SP it is best if you have no history of big abdominal or thoracic surgery.

<u>**Hospitalizations**</u> - Appropriate to history, e.g. childbirth or previous surgeries. Otherwise, none.

<u>**Current Medications**</u> - Appropriate to age. If age 50 or over, report one aspirin a day. If post-menopausal, report Premarin once a day. Birth control pills once a day are fine for younger female SPs. If mild hypertension was mentioned, report a blood pressure pill once a day. Otherwise, none.

<u>**Allergies**</u> - none.

<u>**Social History**</u> - No smoking or drinking should be reported. No recreational drugs either.

You may state your own personal marital status if you wish.

Education: 4 years of college.

<u>**Family History**</u> - Negative for cancer, heart disease, etc.

<u>**Review of Systems**</u> - All questions about problems with the head, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, teeth, neck, chest, breasts, arms, hands, legs, feet, liver, kidneys, urine, intestines, stomach, spleen, etc. are to be answered as "NO previous problems".

<u>**PHYSICAL EXAMINATION**</u>

<u>**Vitals:**</u> T = 100.3, P = 90's, RR = 16-20, BP = 140/80.

<u>**Ears**</u> - student does not have to look into ears, but if they do, that's OK

<u>**Eyes**</u> - student should check the eyes at least to see if the SP is jaundiced, meaning the sclera are yellow

<u>**Nose**</u> - student does not have to look into nose, but if they do, that's OK

Mouth - student does not have to look into mouth, but if they do, that's OK

<u>**Neck**</u> - student does not have to examine neck, but if they do, that's OK

<u>**Chest**</u> - student should listen to lungs in front or back in 3 different places on both sides

<u>**Heart**</u> - student should listen to your heart in front in at least 1 place

<u>**Back**</u> - student should punch the back lightly to see if this makes the pain worse, and this activity should only make the pain minimally worse

<u>**Abdomen**</u> - the student should ask you to lay on your back. It hurts to do so, so you should have pain while moving to the supine position. As soon as the exam is over you should roll over to the right side

- <u>Observation:</u> The student should observe your abdomen first.

- <u>Auscultation</u>: The student should then listen to the abdomen in 3 or 4 places. If they put the stethescope in the right upper quadrant and press down, you should wince a little, as this is a test to see whether or not the patient is faking it.

- <u>Palpation:</u> The student should press down on the abdomen in at least 4 places, starting away from the pain. The only place the pressing down hurts is in the right upper quadrant.

<u>- Rebound</u>: if the student presses down firmly and then releases quickly, they are testing for rebound tenderness. The only place this quick release should hurt is in the right upper quadrant.

<u>**GU/GYN**</u> - you should present a CARD to the student which states that the GU/GYN exam is normal

<u>**Rectal**</u> - you should present a CARD to the student which states that the Rectal exam is normal

<u>**Extremities**</u> - student does not have to do a thorough extremity exam, but if they do, that's OK. Student should briefly check arms, hands, feet and legs for gross tone, movement, sensation, and pulses.

**Case summary**

Name: Jonny Spencer

Chief complaint: pelvic examination for the purpose of cervical cancer screening

Profile: Jonny is a 45 year-old self-identified trans man who established primary care with you 3 weeks ago and returns by mutual agreement to discuss and possibly undergo a pelvic examination. His last Pap test was 20 years ago, and he admits that he has avoided gynecological care for years because of a history of incest and a “terrible experience” during his last pelvic examination.

**Standardized Patient Instructions**

Name:JONNY SPENCER

Setting: outpatient clinic

Dress: clean, casual clothes appropriate for a trans male in his 40s

Affect: cautious, nervous

**Background for appointment:** You are a 45 year-old self-identified trans man who established primary care with this trainee 3 weeks ago and now return by mutual agreement to discuss and possibly undergo a pelvic exam/Pap test. Last time you came to clinic you had a good experience with this trainee. You already addressed the rationale for and the process of the pelvic exam and agreed to come back to do it today.

**General guidelines:** You have been dreading the visit, which is part of the reason that you couldn’t go through with it a month ago. Your one and only prior Pap test was 20 years ago, and you’ve avoided gynecological care ever since because it was such a terrible experience. You’ve been seeing a therapist for the past year because of PTSD related to childhood incest, and she’s been working with you to get back on track with health screenings.

Purpose for the visit: You are here for your pelvic exam and Pap test. If the trainee asks for more details: You have no symptoms. You’re feeling pretty anxious, but you feel like things went well at the last visit, and that’s given you the confidence to be here today.

**Review of systems:**

If asked about your periods: You have not had a period since starting testosterone treatment.

If asked about vaginal discharge: You haven’t noticed anything like that.

If asked about other symptoms or diseases: No, I’ve never experienced anything like that.

If asked what happened during your last pelvic exam: You can’t remember all the details, because you think you blocked some of it out. You just remember experiencing searing pain when the doctor put something in your frontal pelvic opening. It seemed to go on and on. Afterwards you worried that something was wrong because you noticed blood staining your underwear for a few days. You never called the doctor to ask because you were afraid she hurt you during the exam and didn’t feel safe having any more contact.

If asked what you know about the reasons for doing a pelvic exam: You know it’s done to look for cancer and STDs.

If asked if you think it would be helpful to learn more about the pelvic exam: No, you heard the trainee loud and clear last time and you have no further questions.

If asked whether you have any concerns, say, “I’m just nervous that I will freak out or that this will be painful. I just don’t want to experience what happened last time.”

If the trainee asks whether you would be willing to try doing the pelvic exam today: “Yes, I think that would be okay.”

If asked if you would like to have a support person or a chaperone present during the exam:

Yes, you think that might be a good idea. You’d like to try to get it over with today and your partner couldn’t make it. It’s OK with you to have the medical assistant be the chaperone.

Past history:

If asked about any medical problems you've had: Except for the PTSD, you’ve always thought you were pretty healthy.

If asked about your medications: You do not use any prescription or over the counter medications.

If asked about drug allergies: You are not aware of any drug allergies.

Sexual history:

If asked about your current sexual activity:

You are not sexually active. You have zero libido these days, do not masturbate, and you have not been sexually active with your partner since the early days of your relationship 15 years ago.

If asked about prior sexual partners:

Before Ann, you had 2 girlfriends. You were infrequently sexually active with them also. Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in middle school. You have never had sexual contact with any other men.

If asked about use of barriers:

You’ve never used dental dams or Saran Wrap when you’ve been sexual with women. Condoms have never been an issue because you don’t use sex toys and aren’t sexual with men.

If asked about contraception use:

You’ve never used contraception because you haven’t needed it.

If asked about STD/HIV testing/treatment:

You were tested for everything a few years ago and all the tests were negative. There isn’t any need to test you again now because you aren’t sexual.

Information about safety and intimate partner violence:

If asked about any history of physical or sexual abuse/assault:

Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in grade school.

If asked if your current partner insults or talks down to you, screams or curses at you, makes you feel threatened or has ever made you feel unsafe or afraid, has ever physically hurt (pushed, grabbed, slapped, choked, or kicked) you:

No, Ann is very calm and supportive.

If asked if you’ve ever been coerced into having sex or pushed into doing things sexually you didn’t want to do:

No, Ann has a history of sexual abuse too, and sex has always been infrequent. In the past when you were more sexual together, it was always consensual and loving.

If asked if you or your partner own a gun or other weapon:

No.

If asked if you have ever attempted suicide:

No. You used to have suicidal thoughts, but not for a very long time. You never tried anything and don’t think you ever could.

If asked if you are having suicidal thoughts now:

You used to have suicidal thoughts, but that’s passed. The work you’ve been doing with your therapist has given you a lot of hope.

Information about coping and self-care:

If asked about support systems, safe places, personal strengths, how you’ve coped with hard things in the past and might use those skills to cope now:

Your partner is a huge support, and you have a lot of friends.

You see your therapist every week, and can call her if you need to between sessions.

You’ve developed a toolbox of coping strategies, including writing thoughts down so you can set them aside, playing the piano, and taking a walk.

Your personal history:

If asked about smoking: You smoked occasional cigarettes when you were a teenager.

If asked about alcohol use: You binged a lot in your 20s, but only have a few drinks weekly now.

If asked about drug use: You tried marijuana once or twice, but haven’t used any other drugs.

If asked about your job/school: You’re a tax accountant.

If asked about your living situation: You live with your partner and 2 cats.

Family history: Your father died suddenly when you were 10. There was no autopsy and you don’t know why.

**During the exam:**

The trainee will step out of the room at the examiner’s instructions. At this point, move to the exam table, sit in a cross-legged position, and with the examiner’s help place the pelvic model at the end of the exam table. Cover your lap and model with a paper drape.

If asked if you would like to try inserting the speculum yourself, rather than having the trainee insert it: No, you’d rather just get on with it and let them do their thing.

If asked if you would feel more comfortable with your feet in a different position other than in the footrests (stirrups): That’s OK. It doesn’t really make a difference to you what position you’re in. It’s tough no matter what.

**General Guidelines during exam:**

From the start of the exam, you should adjust your level of anxiety based on how sensitive or gentle the trainee is. For example, if the trainee is abrupt, not talking through all the steps, or not recognizing your baseline anxiety, you should have increased anxiety. If on the other hand the trainee is calm, professional, gentle, sensitive, then you should act visibly more relaxed.

Within seconds after speculum is placed, you should become very nervous, whispering to yourself “Oh no, Oh no, Oh no” (or something similar), legs start to tremble. Then say, “I don’t know if I can do this. Is there anything I should be doing?”

If the trainee tries any stress reduction techniques (any of the below or other similar interventions), state that you feel a little better, but are still really nervous – is there anything else you can try to bring down the stress level? After a second stress reduction technique, state that you’re feeling better, and it’s OK to go ahead with the exam.

Examples of Stress Reduction Techniques:

* Trainee asks you to take a few deep breaths
* Uses any MENTAL grounding technique (e.g., orients you by telling you where you are, what day it is, etc.)
* Uses any PHYSICAL grounding technique (e.g., asks you to make a fist and squeeze, hold the table, feel your hands, etc.)

If the trainee acts sensitive to your words even though they do not suggest any relaxing techniques whatsoever, give permission to proceed with the exam.

The only exception is if the trainee tries to force the continuation of the exam or acts especially insensitive, then you should say angrily, “I’m done! I can’t go through with this!” and the exam should be terminated.

When the trainee is done with the exam, the trainee should instruct you to sit up and get dressed before finishing the encounter (if they do not, ask if you can get your clothes on before finishing the visit). The trainee will then step out of the room.

When the trainee is out, move from the examining table back to the chair. The faculty examiner will let them know when you are ready.

**At the end of the exam:**

If asked what you are planning to do right after this appointment:

You anticipated this might be hard with your therapist, and agreed that you would give her a call if needed. You think you will do just that.

If asked if you have any questions or if there’s anything you need right now:

No, you think you’re OK.

private_patient_context:
**Context and Healing**

Standardized Patient Training Case

Standardized Patient Training Material

**Case synopsis:**

Janet Li is a middle-aged woman who has been suffering from headaches. She went to the Emergency Room one month ago, and is here for a follow up appointment.

**Case setting:**

You are in a suburban private practice clinic.

**How you appear during the encounter:**

General appearance:

* You are casually groomed
* You are dressed in comfortable clothing

General affect and behavior:

* You are relaxed, although somewhat shy
* You smile when the student enters the room
* You are respectful of your doctor

**How you respond during the interview:**

This case explores the context of the patient’s symptoms, and in particular, cultural and personal beliefs that shape the patient’s experience. In addition to giving the student an opportunity to conduct an interview, this case also gives the student an opportunity to recognize and respond effectively to several cultural and contextual c**ues,** both verbal and behavioral to help determine the information that is relevant to biomedical condition.

General communication traits:

You tend to give initial responses that are concise and (in your view) give the doctor the “right” answer. The student should be able to begin the interview with open-ended questions and other verbal or non-verbal cues to help you begin and continue your story. With prompting and encouragement, you are less reluctant and more willing to ‘open up’ and continue your story.

**Specific themes and cues:**

Biomedical theme: Headache, high blood pressure

Primary cue: Verbal

Behavior: Dispassionate retelling

Verbal: “I’ve been having headaches.” “I was told I had high blood pressure.” “The doctor gave me some medicine.”

When asked about your primary symptoms (headache, high blood pressure), you relay information about the onset, course, duration, and other details of your symptoms. Open-ended questions and fewer interruptions from the physician allow you to tell your story more freely. Closed-ended questions or interruptions cause you to be more concise and less descriptive.

Contextual Theme #1: Beliefs About Treatment

You are uncertain about the effectiveness of western medicine, including pills to relieve your headache symptoms, and you have also tried alternative therapy for your headache. (More detail is listed in the narrative.)

**Convey**: skepticism/uncertainty but not hostility

* **Non-verbal subtle**: Furrow brow and cock head to one side when recalling the story – as if you are recalling from a script (what the doctor told you to say)
* **Non-verbal obvious:** Shrug shoulder when mentioning “high blood pressure” (this would be on a second mentioning of it – not necessarily during the chief complaint.)
* **Verbal subtle:** Dispassionate retelling “I was *told* I have high blood pressure”, “That *other* doctor”, “No not any other *medicines*”
* **Verbal obvious:** “…but I’m not really sure that it helps” re: HCTZ

Students should ask you if you are taking any medications or have tried anything for the headache. When asked about this topic, you should respond with words that indicate no, but with a tone that indicates uncertainty. You may inflect the word medicines in such a way as to offer some doubt to the listener. If the student responds by inquiring further, such as, “What do you mean?” or “Are there other things you have tried,” you would go on to state you have tried an herbal medicine (as listed below). Your initial tone when sharing this information can imply that you think that the physician would not be interested in this, or that the physician might disapprove.

If the student does not pause, show interest or curiosity, or ask about this, you do not share anything about the herbal medicine.

Contextual Theme #2: Stressful environment

You have recently moved to the United States to care for your mother. (Your father passed away many years ago) There is strain on the relationship with your spouse (who wishes to return to China) causing stress.; you are discouraged and overwhelmed.

**Convey**: withdrawn, reserved, stillness, not agitated.

* **Non-verbal subtle**: Pauses, slow to respond
* **Non-verbal obvious:** overwhelmed. Slump, defeated, looking away shifting, withdrawing more.
* **Verbal subtle:** When discussing family or social history, be vague: “There’s a lot going on”
* **Verbal obvious:** “I am just feeling overwhelmed”

Partway during the interview, after you have shared some of the details of your symptoms, you should adopt a slightly overwhelmed/discouraged/withdrawn posture, shifting slightly away from the physician (turning slightly on the chair or table) and begin to look away. This behavior may be temporally related to questions about your family or environment (i.e. during the “Family History” or “Social History,” if the student is following a more structured approach to the interview). If asked about stress or “how are things at home?” you respond vaguely at first (“There’s a lot going on.”). Further inquiry and interest from the student will prompt you to talk about your circumstances (more detail in the case outline).

If the student ignores the behavior, or accepts your initial brief explanation, you do not share any more detail about the care of your mother or the stressful relationship with your spouse.

Contextual Theme #3: Fear of what symptoms mean

In this case, you are worried that your headaches may be a sign that you are developing Alzheimer’s disease. You need to appear more worried the longer this theme is unaddressed.

**Convey**: worry

* **Non-verbal subtle**: Avoiding eye contact, taking a moment to respond
* **Non-verbal obvious:** Wringing hands, rub thumb in hand
* **Verbal subtle:** Have trouble remembering medicine names. “Sorry, sometimes I think I am losing my memory like my mother-in-law. Anyway here is the name of the medication.”
* **Verbal obvious:** “My mother-in-law had a lot of headaches”

Throughout the interview, you exhibit worry about what your symptoms mean. You should adopt a largely blank or “flat” facial expression, as if you are obligated to go through the routine of this visit. To augment this affect, you rub your thumb of one hand against your fingers or palm, but not so vigorously that it is completely obvious.

In response to direct query, “You seem anxious,” or “What do you think might be going on?” **and if you feel genuine rapport** with interviewer (such as provided by ample waiting by the physician and to share your private thoughts about your symptoms), you share information about your spousal relatives who developed Alzheimer’s and frequently complained of headaches.

If the student does not address your worry or establish sufficient rapport, you keep thoughts about Alzheimer’s to yourself.

**Why you are seeing the doctor today:**

Opening Statement: “I’ve been having some headaches, and I went to the emergency room several weeks ago. They told me I should make an appointment to follow-up with you.”

Follow-up statement (in response to an open-ended question, such as “How have you been feeling?”, or “How have things been going?”): “I feel ok. I haven’t had any problems except some headaches.”

**Description of current problem:**

* About six months ago, you started to experience intermittent headaches.
* The headache first occurred six months ago when you were working out in the yard (you enjoy gardening, planting flowers, and trimming bushes outside your home) on a warm day.
* The headache was throbbing, over the top of your head (both sides), lasted about 20 minutes, was dull in intensity (3 out of 10) and seemed to resolve after going inside, sitting down, and resting on the sofa for about 20 minutes.
* The headaches have recurred, on average, about once every two weeks since then.
* They have occurred at various times, but mostly when you have been active, such as working outside, cleaning the house, or running errands.
* They have not changed, but do not seem to be getting any better.
* One of the headaches four weeks ago seemed stronger (8 out of 10) and lasted longer (about 1 hour), so you went to the emergency room. You went because you are stressed out by everything else in your life and even though you don’t traditionally subscribe to western medicine, you don’t need one more thing to worry about.
* The doctor in the emergency room talked with you and diagnosed ‘hypertension.’ You aren’t sure exactly what hypertension is, and you are skeptical that a pill would be effective for this problem. (When asked about which medicine you are taking, you will show a paper that has the name of pill on it, because you don’t know the name.)
* You took the medicine your doctor gave you for three days; however, you did not feel any better, and you had another headache on the third day after starting the medicine, so you stopped taking it.
* Since your visit to the ER 4 weeks ago, the headaches have not changed; you have had 2 more episodes of headache, similar to the ones you have been having.
* When you had the headache again (1 & 3 weeks ago), you decided you would try the medicine again for 1-2 days. It didn’t seem to make any difference in how you felt, so you didn’t take any more.
* (So, you have taken 3 pills (one each day for the first three days) then 2 pills (one each day for two days, after headache 3 weeks ago), then 2 pills (one each day for two days, after headache 1 week ago), over the last month.) You do not have to say each specific number, you can say, “I took it 3 weeks ago for the first 3 days like they said, but stopped because it didn’t seem to work. I tried again after the next couple of headaches for a few days but it didn’t work.”
* Associated symptoms: With the headache 3 weeks ago, you wondered if the vision in your right eye was a little blurry for about 30 minutes.
* You have been able to keep up with your regular activities, but you’ve cut back a little on gardening in recent weeks.
* You have not had these intermittent headaches before six months ago. You have only previously had headaches with acute illnesses, such as cold in the past (a few times in your life). The headaches you have now feel similar; it’s just that they seem to be recurring often.
* ***Contextual Theme #1: Beliefs about treatment****:*
  + You told your sister-in-law about your trip to the ER one month ago. She suggested a traditional (Chinese) medicine for the headaches. You first took it with the headache that you had 3 weeks ago.
  + You have tried some traditional Chinese medicine, Dong Quai – which is made in boiling water like tea – when you have the headache. It seems to help a little. It was recommended from your sister-in-law on your husband’s side of the family
  + You believe the natural medicine that these relatives take could help keep you healthy and strong, and as a result minimize the headaches.
  + You interpret “hypertension” as a similar condition related to imbalances in your body that might result in headaches.
  + You believe your doctor is sincere, but you are skeptical that an “artificial pill” will be effective, and probably will not be as effective as the natural medicine used by your spouse’s family members. And your experience this month seems to indicate that the “artificial pill” doesn’t make much of any difference.
* ***Contextual Theme #3: Fear of What Symptoms Mean:***
  + You believe that the headaches may be a sign or perhaps even a cause of dementia.
  + Several of your spouse’s (Chinese) aunts and uncles who complained of intermittent headaches also have dementia, and you have heard the word “Alzheimer’s” used to describe their condition.
  + You aren’t sure if they have been officially diagnosed with Alzheimer’s but you are a worried that the headaches you’ve been having may be sign that you are developing Alzheimer’s disease or possibly causing the disease.

**Review of systems/related symptoms:**

* General: No fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss/gain
* HEENT: No chronic runny nose, itchy/watery eyes, or other symptoms. No sore throat.
* Cardiovascular: No fast heart rate, dizziness, or chest pain.
* Pulmonary: No cough or shortness of breath.
* Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or change in bowel habits.
* Neurologic: No numbness or weakness anywhere.
* Musculoskeletal: No swelling or joint pain
* Psychiatric: No sadness, anxiety, feeling down or depressed; no suicidal ideation, thoughts of harm, hallucinations, or other symptoms. You are overwhelmed. If the doctor asks you can say, “No, not sadness.”

**Medical History:**

Overall health: You see yourself as generally healthy.

Medical history: You have been generally healthy, and you are not aware of any chronic medical problems. The only condition that you are aware of is:

1. High blood pressure, first diagnosed in the ER 4 weeks ago. You have been prescribed hydrochlorothiazide, 12.5mg daily, which you have taken irregularly (see description of current problem).

Prior Illness: You have had no serious illnesses, hospitalizations, or surgeries. You had chicken pox when you were a four years old.

Obstetric History: You do not have children and you have never been pregnant. You aren’t sure why, since you have never actively tried to prevent pregnancy. You and your spouse have not ever felt compelled to have children, and you believe this to be simply the way things are. You are not very concerned about this. (Social history). .You are post-menopausal. You stopped having periods a few years ago.

Medications:

* Hydrochlorothiazide, prescribed as 12.5 mg daily for past 4 weeks (See HPI). (When the student asks about medications, you provide a sheet of paper with the name of the medicine written on it.)

***Contextual Theme #1: Beliefs about treatment***

Herbal/Supplements/Alternative therapies (share only if directly asked, as above):

* + - Traditional Chinese medicine, Dong Quai, for headache, which was recommended by your sister-in-law. You aren’t sure what is in the medicine, but you boil it in water which you then drink, like tea. You drink this at the time you have the headache and once or twice per day for two to three days afterward, “to help make sure it doesn’t come back.”

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Health Maintenance: Your parents did not believe that vaccines were effective, and in fact thought they might be harmful; as a result, you are “pretty sure” they had to talk with the school every year to get permission to waive your immunization requirements. You did not see a physician regularly as a child or in your teenage or college years. Right after college, you took a post teaching English in China, where you met your husband. You have been generally well, and have only consulted various family and friends from time to time for “little illnesses,” such as colds and occasional bug bites. You have not seen a physician since you moved back the U.S. 18 months ago.

**Family History:**

Mother: Living, age 82, diagnosed with diabetes 6 months ago. She does not take any medications.

Father: Died seven years ago at age 70 from cancer of the stomach. The cancer was diagnosed late, after it had already spread to other parts of his body. He underwent chemotherapy, which did not seem to help, and he died about 6 months after he was diagnosed. (You are slightly sad about this, but it is not a major stressor in your life)

Brother: Age 48, healthy; He is married with two school-aged children, and lives in Oklahoma City.

See also Contextual theme 3: headaches, dementia and concern about “Alzheimer’s” in spouse’s aunts and uncles)

No other known family illnesses.

**Social History/Patient Profile:**

Occupation: You worked as an elementary school English teacher in China from age 22-24 as a participant in a cultural exchange program (coordinated through an organization called *Via*, based in San Francisco). While there, you met and then later married your spouse. You continued to work as an English teacher at various elementary schools in your adopted “hometown” in Dalian, China. You have not worked since returning to the United States 18 months ago.

Environment:

* You currently live in your childhood home with your spouse and your mother.
* Your spouse works at a local cleaner’s and shoe repair shop in your neighborhood. You can afford an inexpensive medication like hydrochlorothiazide (your first month’s prescription cost about $5), but a more expensive medicine would present financial challenges.
* In China, your husband was and is a co-owner of a dry-cleaning business with his brother. He is becoming increasingly dissatisfied about living in the United States because he is away from his family and his business.

***Contextual Theme #2: Stressful environment***

* You are stressed by taking care of your mother and helping your spouse continue to adjust to life in the United States.
* You and your spouse moved from China 12 months ago to help care for your elderly mother.

Literacy: You speak English and Chinese fluently.

Family: You have been married for the past 28 years, and you do not have children.

Beliefs: You believe that meditation and simple physical exercises are important practices to keep your spirit and body healthy. You spend about 15-20 minutes 3 or 4 times per week being still and performing simple stretches. You do not associate with any particular faith, and you don’t attend religious gatherings or participate in an organized church.

Alcohol: You do not drink, save rare instances of wine at family celebrations or events.

Tobacco: You have never smoked.

Drugs: You have not tried any other illicit substances.

Diet: You try to be conscientious about your diet. You eat fruits and vegetables several times a day, and you eat pork 2 or 3 times per week. You enjoy some sweets, like hard candies and cookies.

Exercise: You garden for 1-2 hours several times per week, which is active, but not strenuous. You also meditate and stretch as described above.

**Appendix A: Cynthia**

**Activities and Time Required**

10 minute patient encounter followed by 5 minute post-encounter debriefing.

**Materials**

Prior to the encounter, the medical student will receive a folder labeled “Patient Chart” with a Date of Birth and the patient name “Richard Glenshaw” and instructions that the patient is here for an exam required to obtain life insurance (Appendix C). Student will either call the patient in from the hallway or greet the patient after reviewing the chart.

**Chief Complaint**

The patient is visiting the clinician to receive an exam required for obtaining life insurance.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

*Chief Complaint and Social History*

* Patient is at the doctor today for a documented note that has a complete history and exam required to obtain life insurance.
* Patient hasn’t been to the doctor for 5 years due to a number of transphobic interactions with previous doctors. Patient does not like or trust doctors, and does not want to be at the doctor today.
* Patient is in a long-term monogamous relationship with a cisgender man. Patient and her partner recently got married and bought a condo, and the patient’s partner insists that they obtain life insurance.
* Patient does not smoke, drinks the occasional glass of wine, and does not use illicit or recreational drugs.
* Patient has no past medical history, surgical history, nor family history.

*Physician-Patient Introduction*

* The patient prefers the name, “Cynthia”, and the pronouns she/her. The ideal behavior is the student asks the patient what name/pronoun she prefers.
* The patient’s legal name is Richard as per the patient’s door chart for the case.
* If medical student initially uses the wrong name and/or pronouns, SP’s initial demeanor should be one of mild anger and frustration. The SP should become less angry and frustrated as the medical student makes efforts to establish the correct name and preferred pronouns. If the medical student misgenders the SP repeatedly and/or focuses the history-taking on inappropriate questions, the SP should gently refuse to answer questions and eventually ask for a different doctor.

*Medical history taking*

* During medical history, if medical student asks SP if they are on any other medications, the SP should ask what they mean by “medication” (e.g. define it, what drugs qualify as medications including those that are obtained over the counter, herbal, or in this case those purchased on the internet without a prescription). Following the response, then the SP should bring up that they have been using injectable estrogen purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* During medical history, if medical student does not ask SP if they are on any other medications, then the SP should bring up that they have been using injectable estrogen purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* The medical student should then inquire about where the patient obtains the needles and syringes and if she uses anyone else’s or shares hers with other people. The patient endorses purchasing these on-line as well and using new needles and syringes every time she injects.

**Standardized Patient Instructions**

Name:JASON BRODY

Setting: primary care clinic

Dress: clean, casual clothes appropriate for a male in his 20s

Affect: friendly, unconcerned. Open with medical history, including sexual practices

**Background for appointment:** You are Jason Brody, a 26 year-old man presenting for your annual physical with your primary care doctor. You feel well and don't have any active health concerns. As is your custom, you came in last week for blood work in preparation for your physical. At this appointment, you will be told that your screening HIV test has unexpectedly returned positive.

**General guidelines:** For the initial portion of the encounter, you should be casual and carefree, making small talk. You feel well and have no health complaints. Any questions relating to any current symptoms or elements of your past history should be answered in an unconcerned manner.

At some point in the encounter, however, you will be told that your HIV test has returned positive. This is a completely unexpected result, and you are shocked and upset at the news. To demonstrate your emotional reactions, you should display a narrow range of controlled emotions, speechlessness, a sense of being overwhelmed, and then tearfulness. Your first thought is whether you could have contracted HIV from your boyfriend, Alec. Your second thought is whether you might have given it to him.

Purpose for the visit: You are returning for the results of your annual blood work, taken last week. You have no physical complaints.

Past history:

If asked in a general way whether you have any medical problems, say, “Nope, I’m healthy.” If the resident continues to press you for more details, provide some or all of the following details as is relevant: Other than a broken arm in 4th grade, you have never had any medical problems and consider yourself very healthy. You have never had any surgeries.

If asked about medications and allergies, you take a Tylenol rarely if you have a headache, but otherwise you do not take any medications, vitamins or over-the-counter supplements. As far as you know, you don't have any allergies to medications.

Personal History:

You have never been a smoker, and have a few drinks a week. This is mainly on the weekends, and never more than two drinks at a time. You smoke marijuana a couple of times a month. You have never tried any other drugs, including crystal meth, or any injected or nasal drugs. You eat well and exercise several times a week at the gym. You work as a freelance graphic designer and supplement your income painting houses.

Sexual History:

You live with your boyfriend, Alec, whom you've been with for about 6 months. You have been monogamous throughout this relationship, and believe the same about Alec. You usually use condoms with anal intercourse with Alec, but not for oral intercourse. In general, you are usually a "bottom." There have been a few occasions when you didn't use condoms for anal intercourse with Alec. With previous partners, you almost always used condoms for anal intercourse, never for oral sex. Before Alec, you have had a couple of other boyfriends, and had other periods of time when you were single but sexually active with men you met in bars and online. You've had about 20 partners in your life.

Before the test you had done a few days ago, it had been a year since your last negative HIV testing, at your last physical. Alec told you he was HIV-negative when you first met him, but don't know when he was last tested.

You had chlamydia once about a year and a half ago and took some kind of pill for about a week. As far as you know, you have never had syphilis, gonorrhea, or herpes.

Family history: State that your father left your mom when you were a child, but he might have had high blood pressure. Your mom is healthy and you have no siblings.

**Receiving the HIV results**:

At some point the resident should transition to relaying the HIV test results. This may be signaled by a change in tone or body language that suggests that the conversation is about to turn serious.

If the transition does not seem to occur, if the resident seems to be somewhat aimless and vague in the line of questioning, it is appropriate to prompt the resident, “So are we done here? Were my tests okay?” in a carefree way.

After receiving the HIV results

After receiving the positive HIV results, your demeanor will instantly change. You are initially speechless for at least 5 seconds. A rush of emotions and thoughts will enter your mind. You are shocked and distressed. If the resident tries to fill the silence with words in those first few seconds, pretend not to hear them, since you are still processing the news. As you slowly regain your composure, pose some questions in a slow, halting manner, as if in disbelief that this is happening to you. Please intersperse these into the encounter as appropriate, but ask all four questions at some point:

* Could the test be wrong? Do you know for sure?
* Can you tell how long I've had it?
* How did I get it?
* How long do I have to live?

If asked what your understanding of HIV is, answer that you don't know a lot about HIV, but you do have one HIV-positive acquaintance. If asked specifically, you think you could talk to this person. You know HIV is an infection you can get from sex or drugs. If asked what you know about its effect on people’s lives is, say that it killed a lot of people back in the 1980s, but you have heard there are good medicines for it now. You've heard that the medicines have lots of side effects, and once you start, you can never stop them.

If asked about your partner, state that you are very nervous to tell Alec about these results and you aren’t sure how it will change your relationship. Sound initially reluctant to tell Alec, but if the resident encourages you in a gentle way, state that you understand that he needs to know so he can be tested. You think he'll be supportive about it.

**At the end of the visit:**

You will be asked if you have any other questions. If you have not yet asked any of the four questions above, please use this opportunity to do so.

If the resident has not already asked, please ask, “When should I come back to see you?”

If all four questions have been asked, you do not have any other questions right now, but you would like to know what the next steps are.

Pre-Brief Case 1

Author: Jenna Sizemore

Welcome to your discharge simulation!

You will perform a hospital discharge on a patient that has complex medical needs and has had an extended period of time being hospitalized very far away from their home.

You will be escorted to your patient’s hospital room when you arrive to the waiting area of our simulation center. In this scenario, you just started your first day of hospital service, so this will be your first time meeting the patient. A family member will be present that is planning to assist the patient home. The patient has an anticipated discharge date of the day of your simulation encounter.

During this encounter, your goal is to discuss the discharge plan with the patient and their family member. Please review and discuss their medication list, any anticipated follow ups, or other discharge needs that you can anticipate for the patient. Please answer the questions to the best of your ability. It is normal and expected that you may not know an answer that is asked, of which you can respond that you will find the answer for the patient.

After determining a discharge plan of care with the patient, you will leave the room and place discharge orders in the discharge navigator in a playground EMR environment.

A brief hospital summary follows.

Case 1:

Patient Name: Jo Smith, Adult Patient

Hospital Service: Medicine 4

Discharge Diagnosis: CAD, DM II

Admitting diagnosis: DKA, NSTEMI II

Hospital Problem List:

NSTEMI (resolved)

Diabetes Mellitus, Type II

DKA (resolved)

HTN

HLD

Brief Hospital Course: Adult patient admitted to a large academic hospital with an acute non ST elevation myocardial infarction and diabetic ketoacidosis. The patient received a left heart catheterization, with access through the right groin, with deployment of 2 drug eluting stents to the LAD and RCA. Treatment resolved the diabetic ketoacidosis after several days of hospitalization. Overall, the patient feels much improved. The left heart catheterization was tolerated well without the development of any pseudoanuerysm or groin hematoma.

Activity/ambulation: Cleared for full activity without restrictions by Cardiology. No ambulatory restrictions.

DMC: Full capacity

Diet: Diabetic

1. **Emergency Medicine Pre-Code Scenario: Theophylline Overdose**

6. **Case Narrative**
   1. **Scenario Background**
      1. Chief Complaint: A 55 year old patient presents to the ED with the complaint of 4 hours of severe nausea and vomiting accompanied by a new coarse tremor noted in the arms and legs bilaterally. Secondary complaints include palpitations, abdominal pain, and lightheadedness.
      2. History: A medical history of moderate to severe COPD controlled with a multi-drug regimen at home. The patient had some worsening of COPD over the last 48 hours and recognized this as a COPD exacerbation. The patient believed that 10 tablets of prednisone were taken at 8 hours and 1 hour before presentation (20 tablets total). Shortness of breath and wheezing completely resolved, but soon after the patient developed severe nausea, vomiting, and tremor.
      3. Extended History: The true story is that the patient accidentally took 20 theophylline tablets, not prednisone.
      4. Medications: The patient has a medication list in a pocket and will identify the medication that was taken as theophylline when asked by the medical learner.
      5. Allergies: NKDA
      6. Family and Social History: 100 pack year history of smoking cigarettes, quit within the last 5 years. No alcohol or illicit drug use. No family history of cardiac disease.
   2. **Scenario Initial State**
      1. Patient Habitus and Presentation: Sitting up in bed actively vomiting when the medical learner first arrives. Active coarse tremor visualized. No tachypnea is seen and the patient is not wheezing.
   3. **Scenario Branch Points**
      1. **Scenario B:** The patient is experiencing the same symptoms with progression to a seizure about 5 minutes into the simulation.
         1. **Changes in Patient Condition:** The patient’s condition will deteriorate over the course of the scenario. After several minutes the patient will have a tonic-clonic seizure.

**Appendix B**

**Moulage & Standardized Patient / Manikin Support**

**Moulage** in this scenario included simulated sweat and vomit.

The **standardized patient** (SP) is a 55 year old patient with a history of COPD.

When learners enter the room the SP should be sitting up in bed actively vomiting. The SP should be in a patient gown. Sheet should be down covering the SP's feet but not legs.

* **Facial Expressions-** Pained.
* **Physical Movements-** Active process of retching and vomiting. Hands have a coarse tremor at rest and the shaking becomes much more noticeable as the SP tries to reach for the sheet to cover the legs. Make sure learners notice this shaking as it is a symptom.
* **Speech-** Short responses to questions. No full sentences. Speech is broken and labored due to nausea. No filler conversation. Once questions are answered, go back to focusing on nausea and stop focusing on the learners.
* **Key Talking Points to offer with minimal prompting**
  + I’ve been having a lot of trouble with my COPD lately.
  + I took 20 of my steroid pills.
  + The pills improved my breathing dramatically but now I am very nauseated, I have been vomiting for hours, and I have crampy abdominal pain.
  + I have never had this reaction to steroids before.
* **Key Talking Points to offer only when asked specifically**
  + The specific name of the medication that you took 20 tablets of is theophylline, or point to this medication on the medication list.
* **Important notes**
  + Learners may likely try to steer the SP toward a diagnosis of chest pain or a cardiac issue or focus on the pulmonary review of systems first; it is important to redirect the learner that the main concern is the vomiting, tremor, and palpitations.
  + When asked, breathing feels fine at this time.
  + Pain is abdominal, not in the chest.

**Scenario Continues (minutes 2-4)**

* **Facial Expressions-** Increased discomfort. Fatigue and mild confusion are also appropriate to add at this time.
* **Physical Movements-** Lay back slowly on bed in preparation for tonic-clonic seizure. Continue tremor.
* **Speech-** The SP begins to become confused. Continue short responses to questions but start ignoring every few questions and asking, “What?” here and there. No full sentences. Start answering questions with random words.
* **Key Talking Points to offer with minimal prompting**
  + None
* **Key Talking Points to offer only when asked specifically**
  + The SP is becoming more delirious and will only answer questions sporadically. Answers may not make sense.

**Scenario End (Tonic-clonic seizure minutes 4-6)**

* **Facial Expressions-** Eye roll back and look up and to the right.
* **Physical Movements-** Arms and legs straighten gradually over a 2-3 second time period. Limbs then stiffen quickly and the patient starts shaking extensively. Fists clench and toes point. Limbs stay straight and stiff while shaking violently. When the learner orders a benzodiazepine medication as a first line treatment, continue the simulated seizure activity. Once the learner has ordered propofol or phenobarbital, stop all seizure simulation and lay motionless in the bed with minimal breathing if possible.
* **Speech-** Start of seizure can be accompanied by a moan as all muscles tense and air is forced from the abdomen.
* **Important Notes**
  + Seizure will stop only when phenobarbital or propofol is given. The SP will relax, go limp, and become unresponsive. Eyes are closed and there is no further reaction to any stimuli.

**Appendix E**

Medication list

Spiriva one inhalation daily

Advair 500mg/100mg: 2 puffs twice daily

Theophylline 300mg: 1 tab daily

Albuterol / Atrovent nebs: one nebulization every 4 hours as needed

Singular 10mg: 1 tab by mouth daily

# 9. **The Case of** ***Jane Henderson***

## Part III

# 16. **Presenting Problem:** 

Patient is returning for a regularly scheduled follow-up visit with her primary care provider, Dr. Johnson, who she has now met twice.  Her first visit was on November 13/15th to establish care and her follow-up visit was on January 15/17th.  During her last visit, she was having increasing headaches that she attributed to stress.  She was feeling the strain of caring for her grandchildren and felt that the stress of this might be causing the headaches.  Although previously supportive, her husband had become more withdrawn, leaving her with much of the responsibility for raising her grandchildren.  Prior to her second visit with Dr. Johnson, Mrs. Henderson did not get her blood tests drawn and was also having difficulty remembering to take her medications.  At the end of the last visit, she was more motivated to take her blood pressure medications and she had made a plan with her doctor to get her blood work done.

In early April, she experienced an episode of chest pain, SOB and palpitations.  Her husband called 911 and she was rushed to the ED.  In the Emergency Department, she had a full evaluation.  She was reassured by the doctors in the ED; they did not think the episode of chest pain was her heart but thought she might have had a panic attack.  She had been under a lot of stress and recalled that she had similar symptoms in her 20s when she was diagnosed with panic attacks.  After further follow-up, she was reassured that the episode was not due to her heart. You also realize the relationship of stress with your blood pressure management and overall health and have tried to pay closer attention to your own personal needs. You had investigated some summer activities, all of which were way too expensive, and you were beginning to become anxious that you would need to take care of the girls full-time over the summer.
