question_text:
Patient Name: Kelly Wilson

Chief Complaint: “I have pain when I urinate”

Background: 35 year-old female presents to the clinic with complaints of burning on urination. Patient is wearing sunglasses inside the clinic. Patient is in a hurry to go pick up her children from school.
private_patient_context:
**Name and Age:** Kelly Wilson, 35 y.o.

**Props:**

Sunglasses. Bruise surrounding one eye.

**Setting:**

You have come to the clinic today because you are experiencing burning on urination.

**Opening Statement**:

“I have pain when I urinate”

**SP (Standardized Patient) Presentation and Starting Position:**Sitting in chair, wearing sunglasses, poor eye contact and darting gaze all around the room. You give fast / short answers. You want an antibiotic prescription and then promptly leave to pick up your children from school. You appear somewhat anxious and fidgety.

**Bruising makeup:** You will have a “black eye”. See “The bruise” section below.

**Style of talking and answering questions:** You don’t particularly want to talk about what’s going on at home so you will be somewhat hesitant with any information beyond the presenting complaint (urinary tract infection).

**If** the student starts with *open-ended questioning,* e.g. “**How did this start?” Or “Tell me about it?”** Give the following story:

You started having frequent urination 3 days ago and the pain becomes worse when you urinate.

*Student only gets this information if they allow you to “tell your story.”*

**If asked for more details...**You get frequent UTI’s (urinary tract infections). The present symptoms are similar to your last UTI about 2 months ago. You usually get a prescription for 3 days of Bactrim, which takes care of it.

IF ASKED - You do not have any fever, abdominal pain, or vomiting.

IF the learner begins asking direct questions, answer as follows

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| How long have you been having these symptoms? | 3 days |
| Anything make it better | Bactrim (it’s why you are here) |
| Anything make it worse | Hurts more when you urinate. |
| Describe the pain | You feel pressure in the bladder area, a sensation of urinary urgency (gotta go NOW), burning when attempting to urinate. |
| Location | Vaginal to bladder region |
| Severity | …give it a 7 |
|  |  |
| PAST MEDICAL HISTORY |  |
|  | Started treatment for depression a couple of years ago with Zoloft. |
| Hospitalizations/surgeries | Hospital for child birth (5 & 7 years old) |
| Medications | Zoloft 50mg/day (little pale blue torpedo) |
| Allergies | Cipro – gives you a rash |
| FAMILY MEDICAL HISTORY | Both parents living. Mom has high blood pressure. Dad had a stroke a few years ago (doing “okay”). |
| SOCIAL | * You are a stay at home mom, live with your husband *(married for 8 years )* and two children, ages 5 & 7. * Husband worked in a bank (middle manager) but lost his job last year – not surprising there are financial stressors at home. *Currently, you are living off of your savings.* * You drink a glass of wine once or twice per week (to relax) * No drugs no smoking |

Answers to any other medical questions should mirror your own or otherwise be “normal”

**The Bruise**

Your sunglasses hide a bruise around your left eye. Your story is that you got it when you slipped and fell in the bathtub last week. You will not directly admit that your husband “backhanded” you.

Careful, sensitive interviewers will allow you time (and head space) to open up. If you feel comfortable with and *trust* the learner, after a little bit you can begin to open up. If you feel rushed or imposed upon, it will be difficult for them to get very far. Either way, you will not directly admit to any violence in your life. The closest you will get to disclosure is that your husband can ‘lose his temper’.

**Opening the Discussion:**

A Framing Question the student may ask:

* *“Because violence is so common in the patients I see, I ask all my patients this question”* or *“This pattern of injury is often caused by another person, did someone hurt you?”*

Your initial reaction will look something like:

* You will insist the bruise occurred after a slip and fall in the bathtub. You just came here for antibiotics. You have two young children at home you have to take care of. You do not want the any police involved. You are able to manage any conflicts in the home.

**Conditional Statements**

IF the student asks why you are wearing sunglasses.

* Response: Pause – “I’m finding the (sunlight/room lights) bother my eyes today.”

IF the learner asks you to remove your sunglasses.

* Response: *Only take off your sunglasses if student asks in a respectful (compassionate) way.* Gingerly take off the sunglasses, examples of appropriate ways to ask include:
  + “I usually like to look at patients’ eyeswhen I am interviewing them… is there a specific reason for you to keep them on?” or
  + “It would help me in my evaluation if I can look at your eyes, do you mind taking your sunglasses off?”

IF the learner asks about how you got the bruise under your (left) eye.

* You report that you are clumsy – the bruise occurred after you slipped and fell in the bathtub.

IF the learner asks “Do you feel safe going home from here”? “Are you and children safe where you are currently living?”

* Response: “Me and my children are fine where we are”.

IF the learner asks “Do you have any other injuries that you would like me to evaluate today?”

* Response “I’m ok, I just need some antibiotics”.

IF the learner asks “Has your partner ever hit you or physically hurt you in the past?”

* Response: “Sometimes when my husband drinks too much he can lose his temper. When he’s not drinking, he would never harm me or the children”.

question_text:
**Triage Note**

You are a resident working a night shift in the Emergency Department.

A 65-year old patient presents with neck pain.

**General:**  Patient appears the stated age and is in distress.

**Vital signs**: Pulse= 90 bpm, RR=18 bpm, BP=130/80 mmHg,  Temp: 99.0
private_patient_context:
**Case summary**: The patient is a 65-year old man or woman presenting to the emergency department with a history of neck pain over the last several weeks. The pain has become increasingly worse, and is present all day, every day. The patient has also developed weakness of all four extremities, clumsiness, and had an episode of urinary incontinence. Overall, the symptoms are very concerning to the patient. The patient’s past medical history includes colon cancer, which had been treated with surgical resection two years ago. The patient does not know what stage the cancer was and never returned for follow up. The patient is not really concerned about the colon cancer at this time.

**Patient appearance**: The patient should be a 65-year old man or woman. The patient should appear to be in pain, and should be touching the neck and grimacing.

**Patient instructions**: The challenge for the patient is to communicate with the physician as one would naturally, without giving away too much information. If the physician uses technical terminology, ask for clarification.

**Onset**: It is hard to pinpoint exactly when it started. However, the pain seems to have developed gradually over the last several weeks.

**Location:** In the back of the neck – (point to the middle of the neck, over the bones)

**Radiation**: None.

**Quality**: Gnawing pain.

**Severity**: Several weeks ago it was a 5/10, but now it’s a 10/10.

**Course/Progression**: At first it was just an ache that would become bothersome at work. The patient sits at a desk all day. However, the pain has become increasingly worse and it is hard for the patient to get through a day’s work.

**Prior neck pain**: Nothing like this.

**Neck stiffness**: Present, and it hurts to move it.

**Duration**: Currently, it is present all day, every day.

**Factors that alleviate the pain**: The patient tried ibuprofen for the pain. It helped a bit at first, but now it does not help at all.

**Factors that exacerbate the pain:** Moving, bending it forward and back, coughing, and straining.

**Daily fluctuations**: The pain is severe at night and the patient has difficulty sleeping.

**Weakness**: The patient’s hands feel weak, as do the legs. The patient dropped a coffee mug one morning.

**Numbness:** None noted.

**Urinary dysfunction** – The patient has the sensation that his or her bladder doesn’t completely empty. There was one episode during which the patient didn’t make it to the bathroom. The patient thought he or she held it too long.

**Weight loss**: The patient has lost approximately 20 pounds over the last several months. The weight loss was unintentional.

**Fever, chills, or recent infections**: None

**Prior testing for tuberculosis**: The patient gets tested at work, and it has always been negative.

**Trauma or inciting event:** The patient doesn’t remember anything that could have triggered the pain.

**What made the patient come to the hospital now**? The pain is unbearable and it just seems to be getting worse.

**Patient’s thoughts on the cause:** The patient thought the pain might be from sitting at a desk all day or bad posture.

**Emotion**: The patient is very concerned about the pain, because it has worsened and become quite severe.

**Past medical history**: Two years ago, the patient was diagnosed with colon cancer. It was resected.

**Further details about the colon cancer:**  The patient did not follow up after the surgery. The medical bills were too expensive and the patient just wanted to get back to work.

**Medications:** The patient has tried acetaminophen, aspirin, and ibuprofen, without relief.

**Family history**: Positive for colon cancer. There is no other significant family history.

**Social history**: The patient is married, monogamous, and works in medical records.

**Alcohol** – The patient drinks only occasionally.

**Tobacco** – No history of tobacco use.

**Recreational drugs** – No history of drug use.

question_text:
Station 4: Delivering Bad News

Scenario:

You are the third year student on the inpatient wards during your medicine clerkship. You are caring for Larry Brown, a 60-year old man, who was admitted to the hospital four days ago with severe iron deficiency anemia. Mr. Brown was called by his PMD and told to go to the emergency room because his blood test showed that his hemoglobin had fallen significantly from his baseline five months ago. Mr. Brown had also reported several episodes of melena and early satiety over the past month, but no nausea and vomiting. He was admitted to your service for further management and evaluation.

Mr. Brown underwent a procedure during this hospitalization, and the gastroenterologist had told Mr. Brown that a mass had been found and that he would need to wait for the biopsy results. You have now found that the biopsy confirms gastric adenocarcinoma. Your team is going into Mr. Brown’s room to tell him the results of the biopsy, and your attending physician has asked you to initiate the conversation with the patient.
private_patient_context:
**Station 4: Delivering Bad News**

## 1.1. <u>Instructions for Standardized Patient</u>

You are Larry Brown, a 60-year old man. You were admitted to the hospital four days ago after your primary care doctor called you and told you to go the ER because of severe anemia. The day prior to that, you had seen your primary care doctor and reported to him that you had been feeling somewhat more fatigued in the past few weeks. You also noticed two episodes of dark black stools and an early sense of fullness after eating for the past few months. Your primary care doctor ordered blood work and called you the following day to tell you that your red blood cell count was very low and that you needed to go to the emergency room right away. When you arrived, you were told that there was most likely bleeding in your stomach. You received a blood transfusion and had a procedure 2 days ago (EGD) where a camera was placed inside your stomach to identify  the source of bleeding. After the study was done, the gastroenterologist told you that a mass was found inside the stomach and that a biopsy had been taken.

You are waiting in the hospital for the biopsy results. Overall, you feel a little better, with more energy since the blood transfusion. However, you have not heard any information about the biopsy result from your doctors in the past few days and you have not seen the gastroenterologist since the procedure.

**Emotional tone:** 

You have been feeling stronger and overall healthier since you came to the hospital and received blood transfusions, but the doctors told you that you had to wait in the hospital until the biopsy results came in. You are a little concerned about the biopsy results, but you have not thought that you might have cancer. The gastroenterologist said there was a mass, and you thought it was probably an ulcer.

**Your role is to portray a patient who is very shocked to learn that you have cancer. No one has ever said cancer to you before; so when you first hear the news, you are in disbelief. Initially, you feel unprepared to handle the situation, so you are in denial and have a difficult time processing the news**.

**Medical History:**

In your adult years, you have remained mostly healthy. You were diagnosed with hypertension when you were 40 and have been taking medications since then. Your blood pressure is controlled on medications. You have not been hospitalized before.

Medications:

Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily

Lisinopril 10 mg daily

**Social history:**

You started to smoke cigarettes in your 20’s but quit smoking over 15 years ago. You used to drink rather heavily, but have also cut down and now only at parties, and no more than 1-2 drinks. You do not have any history of drug use.

You have been happily married for almost 40 years. Your wife Jean has been worried about your recent hospitalization since you have never been sick before, but you think of her as a strong support for you. You have 2 grown daughters and 3 grandchildren.

<u>Scenario for Standardized Patient:</u>

When the student enters the room, you greet him/her pleasantly. You are sitting up in bed and comfortable appearing. Let the student start the conversation.

“Mr. Brown, I wanted to discuss the results of the biopsy with you today.”

The student should ask you what your thoughts are about the test results.

“What did the gastroenterologist say to you about the procedure and the biopsy?”

**“He said that he saw something inside the stomach that was almost blocking the exit of the stomach. He said that it looked like a mass and that was probably where I was bleeding from. He told me that he took some biopsies and that we’d know what it was soon.”**

You should answer matter-of-factly without showing too much anxiety or concern.

The student should ask,

“What is your understanding of your medical condition? When you first had your symptoms, what did you think it might be?

**“I guess I was a bit worried when I started feeling tired. That was really strange for me because I’ve never felt so tired before. And I was concerned when I saw the dark stools, but that only happened twice and then stopped on its own.”**

	**“I still don’t know what it could be. But I guess that’s why they did the biopsy.”**

If the student asks you whether you want to receive information or how much information you want to know,

“Would you want to know about this condition, even if it were something serious?”

“Some people would prefer that their family be told about the full details of their condition, rather than receiving the information themselves. What do you prefer?”

**“Oh yes, of course I want to know. I need to know about my health, right?”**

The student should then inform you of the biopsy results, but she should first give you a warning shot

“Unfortunately I do not have good news.”

The student should say the results of the biopsy. The student should use very clear and straightforward language to report the bad news. The student should use the word “cancer.” If he/she does not say cancer, but rather uses another word such as “You have a malignancy.” or “The biopsy shows a neoplasm” then you should appear confused, as though you do not understand what he/she means.

If he/she does say cancer, you should respond in a loud and surprised way,

**“What? Cancer?”**

You express disbelief because up until this point you have not strongly thought that you might have cancer. No doctor has told you about this before, so you feel unprepared for the news. You initially deny the results.

**“This can’t be true… The doctors just said it was a mass, they never said it was going to be a cancer.”**

**“Is there another test you can do to make sure it’s cancer? Are you really sure that I have cancer?”**

	**“How could this be happening right now? I feel fine. I don’t feel like I have cancer.”**

After each of your reactions, give the student a chance to respond. The student should acknowledge that it is difficult for you to believe the news, and he/she should express empathy about this. S/He should give you time to react and not rush you through your emotions.

“I can tell that this comes as a real shock to you…”

“I wish the news were different. I can tell that this is very difficult news for you...”

If the student has acknowledged your initial response of denial about the news, then you should move on to asking questions about how to tell your family and what this news will

ultimately mean for you.

 **“What am I going to tell Jean? What am I going to tell my grandkids? What does this mean? Does this mean that I’m not going to be here for my grandkids?”**

**“Is it really advanced? Does this mean I’m going to die?”**

**“Do you know how much time I have left?”** 

The student should not give you many details about your prognosis and treatment course. S/He may state that they are going to ask the oncologists (cancer specialists) and surgeons to see you so that together you and then can move forward in terms of gathering more information and coming up with a plan. The focus of the student should be towards acknowledging your feelings and being supportive.

“I don’t know the answers to all of your questions but I know that this is not easy for you, and I want to know that our priority is to support you and your family right now to help you.”

The student should give you a chance to verbalize your understanding of the bad news to ensure that you and understand. S/He should ask you to repeat the news back to him.

“Sometimes it is overwhelming to receive this kind of news. Can I ask you to repeat back to me what I’ve just told you so that I know you understand the results of the biopsy?”

“It’s important to me that I know you understand the news I’ve just told you. Can you tell the results back to me so that I know you understand?”

	**“Yes. You said that the biopsy shows I have a cancer in my stomach.”**

The student should ask what you are feeling and specifically what you are worried about.

“I understand this may be difficult to process.  Can you tell me how you’re feeling right now?”

“What are your biggest concerns when hearing this news?”

**“I’m worried about my wife.”**

	**“I’m worried that I won’t see my grandchildren grow up.”**

The student should start to close the conversation by asking you if you have any questions. Give him/her an opportunity to close by saying,

“No, I just don’t know what else to ask right now. I think I need a little time by myself.”

The student should talk to you about initial steps and a follow-up plan. S/He should say that he or other doctors will come back shortly to talk to you again, to see what other questions you have. The student should offer support and reassure you that he/she and the doctors are going to help and be actively involved in the next steps with you. S/He should be specific about when the doctors will come back to see you again or what the first steps of the plan will be.

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

# 1. **ADULT CASE SUMMARY**

# **Life-Sustaining Treatment: Ben/Benita Ward**

**Patient Information: Ben/Benita Ward**

**Your Role:**

You are a medicine intern. You are on call and admitted a patient with a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation. While presenting the case to the senior resident, she asks you about the patient’s “code status.” You have not had that conversation with the patient yet, so you have to go back and discuss it with them. It’s been a busy day and you only had about 30 minutes to spend with Mr./Ms. Ward previously.

**Situation:**

Mr./Ms. Ward is a 65-year-old with moderate-severe COPD who was admitted for the 2nd time in nine months with a COPD exacerbation. This is the patient’s fifth admission overall for COPD. He/she developed worsening shortness of breath and increased volume of sputum production over the past four days and is starting to feel better.

Mr./Ms. Ward first developed dyspnea on exertion (DOE) about 10 years ago and was diagnosed with COPD. He/she smoked two packs per day for 45 years but quit two years ago. The patient reports that their DOE has worsened every year. They can walk up a flight of stairs but is very winded at the top and stops to rest and coughs daily. The patient does not require oxygen. They have continued to work, but it is getting harder to do so.

PMH: COPD, hypertension

Home Meds: tiotropium, fluticasone, albuterol, hydrochlorothiazide

Records from the patient’s primary care physician indicate there are no documented advance directives.

Family Hx: both parents died from myocardial infarctions

Social Hx: married, lives with spouse in Arbutus. Has two children and two grandchildren. Works as a delivery person for a linen service that supplies local hospitals and nursing homes. Completed the 11th grade. Quit smoking two years ago.

**Your Task:**

Discuss his/her “code status” or preferences for life sustaining treatment.
private_patient_context:
# EOL I Adult Case Life-Sustaining Treatment: Ben/Benita Ward

# CASE SUMMARY

**STANDARDIZED PATIENT INSTRUCTIONS**

**Ben/Benita Ward**

**The Scenario**

Four days ago, you became more short of breath than usual and started to cough up more phlegm. Yesterday, when you started to feel short of breath when just sitting down, you went to the emergency department. You were told you are having a flare up of your emphysema. You were started on medication and you are feeling better. You have been in the hospital since yesterday. You met the resident yesterday. They are now being asked to follow up with you regarding advance directives.

This whole episode has happened to you before. In fact, this is the second time in nine months you have been in the hospital for the same problem and the fifth time overall since you were first diagnosed with emphysema 10 years ago. Every time this happens, you get some medicine and feel better within a week, so you figure it is not that serious and that it will be treatable every time. You smoked a lot, two-three packs per day for almost 45 years but quit about two years ago.

You know your breathing has not been good, and every year it seems to get worse. You used to play sports with your kids, but in the past year you noticed you have to stop and rest when you get to the top of a flight of steps. You are worried about this happening, but no one has ever told you your emphysema is “severe”, and you figure that there must be other medicines you can take. At the very least you think you could live another 10 years.

Recently your primary care doctor mentioned the emphysema was “getting bad” and that at the next visit you should talk about your “living will”, but you’re not sure why your doctor wants to know about your finances. The resident in the hospital told you they’d “have you out of here in no time”, the nurse told you “take your medicine and everything will be fine” and the pulmonary doctor told you that you might need oxygen all the time from now on. You are very confused and don’t understand why everyone is saying something different.

You want to believe you are going to be fine and live several more years. You tend to believe the people who reassure you and think the pulmonary doctor must not know what he’s talking about. He’s only met you once, so how could he possibly know anything about you? He used a lot of big words and you didn’t understand half of what he said anyway, but you were embarrassed to admit that to him.

You really want to live to see your grandkids grow up and graduate from high school. You worked a lot when your kids were younger, so now you are really enjoying the chance to spend time with their kids.

***Past Medical History***: Emphysema (COPD) for which you have used inhalers for 10 years, and high blood pressure for which you take hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) or “water pills.”

***Family History:*** The doctors always ask you about “diseases that run in your family” so you tell them about your parents who both died from heart attacks. If you are asked about ‘bad’ deaths, your older brother was in a car accident about three years ago and had severe injuries. He was hooked up to life support (on a ventilator) for three weeks before he died. It was very hard for you to see your brother like that and you were very concerned that he was in pain and suffering. After that you are not sure you would ever want to be on a ventilator but at the same time you want to live for a long time.

***Social History:*** You are 65 years old. Married for 30 years, live with your spouse in Arbutus (suburb). You have two children and two grandchildren and work as a delivery person for a linen service that supplies local hospitals and nursing homes. You’ve worked there for 25 years. When your children were younger and living at home, you worked two jobs to support your family, but now are just working for the linen company. You completed the 11th grade. You quit smoking two years ago. You do not drink alcohol. You spend a lot of time with your grandchildren and often babysit them on the weekends when their parents are working. You were raised Methodist, but you don’t have particularly strong religious beliefs.

**The Medical Encounter**

You are very confused by all the different opinions you have been told, and if the student does not gain your trust, you will be skeptical of what they say.

You are scared about what will happen to you because of your emphysema and that fright may translate into some anger if you think the doctors are “giving up” on you.

You only completed the 11th grade and have a somewhat low health literacy level.

Opening statement: Depends on what student says

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ***Introducing topic, describing/defining advance directives, rationale*** | What you do is … |
| If, without establishing trust or explaining, the student starts by saying they want to talk to you about your “code status”, “CPR”, advance directives, or whether you want to be resuscitated … | This will make you confused and scared (which translates into being mildly angry) because it will make you think you must be dying. Abruptly say “Yes, I want everything done.” This will shut you down a bit and the student will have to recognize your emotion and work to regain trust. |
| If the student says above but then qualifies by saying “This is something we talk to everyone about in the hospital.” | Ask “What for?” |
| If the student starts the conversation by being falsely reassuring, “I think you’re going to be fine” or “You’re not going to die any time soon” | Latch on to that and press the student about it. “Oh good, so you think I’m going to be fine. That’s not what that lung doctor said, but I don’t think he really knows anything.” |
| If the student demonstrates respect, empathy, humility, or tries to understand your situation | “I know I have lung problems, but I can still do a lot.” “I think my doctor thinks I’m fine.” “Several people here told me I would be fine.” “I thought I would be okay, but people here keep telling me different things. I don’t know who to believe.” “There must be some medicine that can make me feel better.” “I think I could live for a long time if I take care of myself.” |
| If student contradicts or puts down other health care providers | Depending, you will join in or grow more confused/angry. If the student says something like “Sounds like Dr. X left you feeling very hopeful. I’m sure they really care about you…” you will not get angry if they later contradict Dr X. |
| If the student clearly explains illness and prognosis and asks for your thoughts | You will accept what they have to say. “Thanks for being honest with me, doc” or “I guess everyone has their time.” |
| If the student introduces a term such as advance directives or living will without explanation | “I have a will; I’m leaving everything to my wife/husband.” “Yeah, that’s the thing where you set up your burial ahead of time. I haven’t done that.” |
| If the student asks whether you have a living will, advance directive, or health care proxy after explaining the terms | “No, no one ever talked to me about it” or “My doctor mentioned last visit we should talk about it next time.” |
| If the student launches directly into asking you if you would want CPR, intubation, etc. | “Of course, I want to live” and shut down a bit unless the student explores the options or your feelings about them. |
| If the student asks whether you have known someone who had to go on a ventilator, get CPR, or seen someone who had a “bad death” | Say “Yes, that happened to my brother.” Do not disclose this unless they ask, and do not discuss your feelings about it unless they ask. |
| If they ask you about someone who had a “good death” | “My grandmother died in her sleep at home.” |

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ***Assessing goals*** |  |
| “What is your life outside the hospital like?” “What are the most meaningful or enjoyable parts of your life?” “What makes life worth living for you?” “What do you consider your quality of life to be like now?” “What are your most important hopes?” “What are your biggest fears?” “If you were to die sooner rather than later, what would be left undone?” | Describe life being very involved with grandkids, working although that’s getting much harder. You think your quality of life is “pretty good” although a bit frustrated you can’t physically do everything you used to. Most important thing is seeing grandkids grow up, graduate from school, etc. Biggest fear is being a “burden” and “suffering.” |
| “Are there any circumstances that would make life not worth living for you?” | Wouldn’t want to live like a “vegetable.” |
| If the student asks for clarification about what your general phrases mean | Clarify as below. |
| “Vegetable” | You don’t want your life prolonged if there is little or no chance of having a decent quality of life. This means the ability to talk and carry on a conversation, to interact with your family, to be part of your grandkids’ lives, which means not being in a nursing home and not being “hooked up to machines.” |
| “Burden” | You don’t want your spouse or children to have to provide much in the way of physical care for you and you do not want to place any financial strain on them if they had to pay for a nursing home or hire people to care for you. |
| “Suffering” | Feeling like you can’t catch your breath, having a lot of pain, being “locked up” in a nursing home or on machines, knowing your grandkids were growing up but you couldn’t see them. |
| “Hooked up to machines” | Feeding tubes, ventilators. |

The student may pose scenarios to you or ask generic questions. The goal of the conversation is not necessarily to come to an agreement. After choices are posed to you, it is okay to say you need more time to think about it or discuss it with your spouse.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ***Discuss scenarios, explain risks and benefits of proposed interventions*** |  |
| “Dire consequences scenario” Severe brain damage, massive heart attack, widely metastatic cancer, chance of recovering to your “quality of life” almost none | You would not want CPR, ventilation, or tube feeding in that situation. |
| “Reversible scenario” Needed minor surgery, chance of recovering to your quality of life very good or excellent | You would want everything in that scenario. |
| “Uncertain scenario” Bad pneumonia, stroke, pancreatitis, heart failure, chance of recovering to your “quality of life” hard to predict | You’re not sure. Part of the reason is that you worry if you did not choose intubation, etc., the doctors would “give up” and let you suffer. |
| If the student reassures you that you would still be kept comfortable even without life-sustaining measures, or explores what makes you unsure | You will feel relieved and say that you’re glad to have the discussion and will talk more with your spouse about it. |

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ***Forms, health care proxy*** |  |
| If asked who should make decisions about your healthcare for you if you couldn’t speak for yourself | Your spouse and then your daughter. |
| If asked if you’ve ever discussed this with them before | No. |
| If asked whether it was more important for them to follow your wishes strictly, or make slightly different decisions in your care if they felt it was right | You trust your family to do what is best. |
| If they offer you a form to look at or tell you they will get one for you | Be grateful, but also ask if you can change your mind later about this. |

Again, at the end of the conversation, it is not absolutely necessary for you to have made a decision about your life sustaining treatment.

The bottom line is you previously were afraid your emphysema might be bad but had not had an honest conversation about it.

Right now, you feel like you have a lot to live for and would be willing to try some aggressive treatment if there was chance of benefit.

**SP Instructions on Discussing Life-Sustaining Treatment**

**Flow**

Initially:

Confused as to why discussing now

Confused by conflicting messages

Confusion makes you mildly angry

If student demonstrates repeated negative behaviors, you will either become mildly angry or try to shut down the conversation.

If student demonstrates consistent, positive behaviors, you might disclose some of your fears, for example: “I don’t want to die, but I don’t want to be a burden.”

**Emotional modulation: Moderate** 2-3/10 (0= flat, 2-3=normal; 10=intense):

You are confused by conflicting messages and the timing of the conversation, which makes you either shut down or become mildly angry, but if the student earns your trust, your affect is normal.

John Smith, a male with severe COPD and ongoing nicotine dependence, presents to the clinic for an acute care visit. He is having more difficulty with breathing over the past week, even though he just completed a course of steroids and antibiotics for a COPD exacerbation at the end of last month.

**Smoking Cessation Case**

Information for the Standardized Patient:

History: Feeling difficulty with breathing, especially with any exertion, such as walking up stairs or walking to do errands. Difficult to catch breath, no chest pain or tightness. No fevers or any other symptoms, but you feel similarly to last month when you required a course of steroids and antibiotics. You did feel better after the course of treatment, but feel that the same symptoms are returning again. You are very frustrated as this happens over and over again, and these episodes seem to be happening more frequently.

You have been smoking since age 15 years, at least one pack of cigarettes daily. You are beginning to get serious about smoking cessation because these exacerbations of COPD have been difficult to overcome. However, you have a very stressful job and smoking helps you to relax.

ROS: negative for all systems reviewed

PMH: no other medical problems

Family history: none

Social history: smoking since age 15, 1 pack per day, no alcohol or drug use, living alone, working at a very stressful job as an accountant

No medications or allergies

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* Life goals and values: I’d like to have better health, be able to do my daily activities without getting so tired, not be so stressed out all the time.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? It conflicts with my values, but I really like smoking because it helps me relax.
* What are the good things about smoking: It helps me calm down when I’m stressed out, and it helps me manage my boredom since I live alone.
* What are the bad things about smoking: I’m getting really frustrated with these exacerbations and it is getting harder to do daily activities without getting winded. I’m too young to have COPD and if I get worse I might need to hire someone to help me with my daily activities. It is frustrating to have to keep going to the doctor about this.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? I wouldn’t have these episodes and exacerbations, I wouldn’t feel so winded when I do my daily activities, I’d have more energy and I’d feel better. My health would be better overall.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Patches, Chantix, using a self-help book, calling a smoking cessation hotline, using online resources, going to a stop smoking group. You tried quitting cold turkey 4-5 times but that only lasted a few days or a couple of weeks at best. You really had trouble managing the cravings and ended up relapsing each time.
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 7/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? I’m just so sick and tired of being out of breath and having these episodes!
    - How could you move that number higher? If there were another way for me to deal with my stress and boredom, I think I’d say 10/10.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? I’ve been through some really difficult things in my life, and I know if I stick my mind to it I can do it.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? I think the cold turkey approach didn’t work because my cravings got the better of me. Maybe if I had some help, like a patch and some information, I’d feel more confident.
* Ask for a decision: I’m going to look into different ways to quit, like patches and medication and information.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? I need to find some websites to get information about ways to quit smoking, and I can ask the doctor for recommendations. I will talk with my friends about their advice for dealing with boredom and stress. I would like to set a follow up appointment to meet in a month to discuss quit aids and activities I have decided on trying~~.~~
* What do you intend to do? I will do this in the next month.

**Presenting Complaint:** Patient is encouraged to visit the psychiatry clinic by his/her parents. The patient's chief complaint: "My parents insisted that I come in. They got a call from my office. There are some problems there."

**Patient Name:** Paul/Paula Byers

**Patient Presentation:** Male or female. Young adult, flat affect, guarded in providing verbal responses.

**Necessary equipment, props, makeup, moulage, costume, etc.:** None except for casual dress.

**Standardized Patient Training Summary**

**Opening Statement:** "My parents insisted that I come in. They got a call from my office. There are some problems there."

**Follow up statements (if asked about the problems at work):**

1. "My boss is trying to have me arrested."
2. "Because I have stolen his/her personal secrets"

**Summary of case:**

You are Paul/Paula Byers. You are a 22-25 year old single man/woman who lives alone in an apartment near your parents' home. You work in an office as an administrative assistant. Your latest placement by a new temp agency started 3 months ago at the local museum. However, you have not gone into work for the past week. You have not called your employer, and you have not answered your telephone. Your parents were contacted by the agency about your absence. You have told them that your boss at the office is trying to have you arrested for "stealing his personal secrets". They encouraged you to visit the psychiatric clinic, and you have agreed to an evaluation by a psychiatrist to "put your parent's minds at ease".

Patient Affect and Attitude:

**Physical**: You are ever-ready, feet under your knees flat on the floor ready to get up at a moment's notice. Your hands rest very deliberately and symmetrically on the top of your thighs. You are physically stiff, but not obviously anxious. You are watchful and distant, appearing contained and aloof. You do not have symptoms of mania.

In general, you do not make eye contact with the interviewer. You stare straight ahead or at floor when being asked and/or answering questions. A few times during the interview, you should make extremely direct and strong eye contact with the student. This pattern is intended to be odd or even unsettling for the interviewer.

You appear somewhat hypervigilant, intermittently checking out hidden areas of the room (as if looking for a listening device or camera) but you are not particularly anxious or distressed. You only do this 3 or 4 times during the 20 minute encounter. Some potential items to look at in the exam room are the computer, the telephone, or the notes being taken by the student.

**Verbal**: There is some latency (at least 5 seconds) to all of your answers. Your initial response to questions is slow and guarded. You are not spontaneous with the interviewer and do not reveal information easily. You consider your response carefully and when you speak you deliver it with confidence and your voice is monotone, lacking any intonation at all.

**Recent History:**

You recently moved out of your parents' home with much prodding from them. You don't understand why they had urged you be more independent. In fact, they had presented you with an ultimatum that you seek psychiatric help to "get your life on track" or get a job and start being responsible. You had chosen the latter and had moved out with a great deal of assistance. Your parents rented the apartment and virtually arranged for everything. You got a job in an office as a temporary worker and still rely on your parents for some financial support.

Problems at Work:

You have been working at your current placement for 3 months. You stopped going to work one week ago because you believe that your supervisor (Douglas Dullerman) knows that you have determined some very "personal matters" about him.

* You believe that you can decode typing assignments from the computer and that they contain messages for you.
* You believe everyone in the office knows you are "a faggot/dyke" and that "your days are numbered".
* You are not sure what is expected of you next but you are waiting to interpret all the messages from the television channel (where you can also see the code) you have been watching for the past week.
* You have heard taunting male/female voices (same gender as you) you do not recognize talking about you. These voices are challenging you to "stop the ridicule;" the voices are becoming more derogatory and have been saying, "You are not worthy." They are telling you need to "cast the first stone". You believe this means you need to take action against your supervisor. You have not acted on anything the voices have commanded of you. You have vague thoughts of wanting to harm your boss, but have no specific plans. You are awaiting further instructions.

Other Psychiatric Symptoms: You **do** see and hear things that others do not see and hear.

* NOTE: If asked, "Do you see or hear things that aren't really there", you reply in the negative, because, to you, the code is really there. But if asked, "Do you see or hear things that other people do not?," then you can acknowledge that others don't seem to see the code or hear the voices; only you can.

If you are asked any Mini-Mental Status Examination questions, you are clear and coherent, although your response to certain logic questions is very concrete:

* You know the date, day of the week, where you are, what town, and why you are here.
* You can spell WORLD backwards and count backwards from 100 by 7's
* You can draw a clock accurately, follow written and 3-part commands, and remember 3 words.
* Your interpretation of proverbs or reaction to hypothetical situations is **very concrete**:
  + If asked, "What does the phrase, 'people in glass houses shouldn't throw stones' mean?," you answer, "Glass breaks easily, so don't throw stones."
  + If asked, "What does the phrase, 'don't cry over spilt milk' mean?", you answer, "Milk is cheap and easily replaceable."
  + If asked "What would you do if you saw a stamped addressed envelope next to a mailbox?", you answer "Is it addressed to me?" or "I would pick it up".

Suicidal Ideation: You are not suicidal. You are not depressed.

Alcohol/Tobacco/Drugs: You do not drink alcohol, smoke, or use any illicit drugs.

Sleep: You have not noticed a significant change in your sleeping patters over the past few months. You still get the same 7-8 hours of sleep that you always have.

**Past Psychiatric History:** You have never been treated for any sort of psychiatric illness, although your parents did ask you to either see someone or move out and get a job three months ago and you chose the job. You have never heard voices before the last few months. You have never been in a psychiatric hospital. You have never seen a psychiatrist or other mental health professional before. You have never taken medication for a psychiatric concern before. You have never considered or attempted suicide. You have never threatened or been violent toward another person.

**Past Medical History:** Your physical development was normal and you have been in good health. You do not have any medical problems. You have never had any surgeries or hospitalizations. You do not take any medications.

**Family Psychiatric History:**

There is a family history of psychiatric illness. Your mother's brother lives as a "recluse" and your maternal grandmother died in a state mental institution. This is the extent of your knowledge about their conditions.

**Social and Developmental History:**

You are the only child of Martha and Mark Byers. Your parents are both on the faculty at aa local university and they have always focused on academic achievement and career success. Personal and emotional issues were rarely discussed at home. You were not psychologically, physically or sexually abused as a child.

As a child and early adolescent you were very successful in school and got straight As. Socially, you have always been isolated. You had few friends as a child and none as an adolescent. In high school, you were ostracized for being a "nerd," and to avoid teasing you remained aloof and developed no friendships at all. Your parents thought that your social isolation was the price you paid "for your genius I.Q". You did very well academically in high school (GPA of 3.8) and received a scholarship to the state university's mechanical engineering program.

Beginning in the second semester of your freshman year in college, when you were 19, you began to have difficulty completing assignments on time and your absenteeism increased. You are aware of the change, but you attribute it to faculty bias. You had two particular professors that you were sure didn't like you, and they were teaching your favorite subjects, English and Calculus. After returning home, you started taking classes at a local community college but quickly dropped out in the first semester.

Since dropping out of community college, you enrolled with a few temporary employment agencies near your home and have had several placements. Until three months ago you have been living at home, spending hours alone in your room listening to music, surfing the internet and watching TV. Your parents believe that you need to be more disciplined and that you have a motivation problem. The fact that you had to leave their home was emotionally painful for you. You do not own any guns or other weapons.

**Sexual History:** Your only sexual contact took place one evening with a man/woman (same gender as you) that you met at the community college. You did not really have a relationship, only a physical contact. You aren't really sure whether that makes you a lesbian/gay. You are actually asexual and have really not explored that part of your life much at all, but are not able to verbalize this. When you say that the people at work "...know that I'm a faggot/dyke", you are supposing that they think of you negatively and derogatorily by using this word. You don't think that you are a homosexual, although you did have the single experience.

TIMELINE of Immediate Complaint:

* 3 months ago: Parents gave you an ultimatum to either see a psychiatrist or move out/get a job. You moved out of their house into a small apartment and started your current job at the museum as an administrative assistant.
  + Around the same time you started this new job, you began seeing a code in your typing assignments at work. You also began hearing 2 voices you do not recognize who have grown steadily more derogatory towards you.
* 1 week ago: You stopped going into work or answering your phone. You have been watching a TV channel where you also see the same code from work.
* Today: You agreed to a psychiatric assessment and are here today to "set your parents' mind at ease" after they got a call from your office.

Standardized Patient Training Materials

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting in chair.

**Opening Statement**: "My back hurts."

**Affect**: You want to stay as still/stiff as you can, with low energy, face and voice are strained.

**Current Condition**:

You are M. Sidney and are a 38 year old patient with back-pain. You work as a patient care transfer technician at Skyline Hospital. You help move patients from OR table to mobile stretchers for 8-12 hours per day.

For the past 2 days you have felt increasing back-pain in the right lower back region. Today the pain has worsened significantly, keeping you from being able to perform your duties on the job. When asked where the pain is located, you should place your hand over the right portion of your back. You first noticed it at work about 4 days ago when you took a break at work. If asked a question about what you had been doing prior or if anything unusual happened, you report that you just finished transporting a couple of patients to radiology and didn't notice anything unusual until you sat down. You are concerned because your boss has been upset because you are getting slightly behind in your duties.

Your back hurts if you try to lean over, tie your shoes, and especially if you cough or sneeze. In the standing position, it is tolerable - but if you try to bend or twist your trunk it gets worse. Also, the pain is worse when you laugh and it has been difficult to sleep because your back also hurts when you lie down. You feel the pain in your lower back and, at the same time, you have a dull ache in your right buttock. Sometimes pain also shoots down the back of your right leg. A couple times you have felt some numbness on the outside of your right calf. You haven't noticed any problems with your bladder or bowel function. If asked to describe the pain, you say it's the worst you've ever had before, it's a deep dull ache. If offered a pain scale to describe the pain, you think it's a 6-7 out of 10 at baseline, but when you bend your lower spine it is a 10/10. The pain is constant, but gets worse with certain movements or when you cough or laugh. Keeping your knees bent and not moving gives you the most relief from the pain. You would like something for the pain and maybe a mild muscle relaxer, so you could go back to work and finish what you were working on. You are not taking any medication for this pain. Your job requires some heavy and awkward lifting.

**Past Medical History:**

You get an occasional cold and flu every year or two. You are usually healthy. In high school, during your junior year you hurt your knee working on a school project. You took a prescription painkiller for a couple months. You do not remember what kind of painkiller it was because that was so long ago. Your knee took about a year to heal thoroughly, and you do not have any problems with it now. (IMPORTANT INFO FOR SP: You did NOT develop any kind of dependency on the painkillers.)

No prior history of kidney stones.

You don't know if you are allergic to any medications because you haven't taken many in your life.

**Social History:**

You have been married for 10 years. You have 3 children, ages 7, 5, & 3 years. You are accustomed to working very hard around the house, carrying one or more of the children and doing a lot of physical chores. Your family is quite healthy, except for Susanna, who sees the school's speech therapist because of a lisp. You eat a healthy diet, but it is limited in variety.

You do not drink alcohol now because you had a drinking problem in high school. You hung out with "the wrong crowd" and started to get into a lot of trouble. Your grandmother really started to get more involved with your school and made sure you went to church on Sundays. Your grades improved and you found success in sports. You realize how much your grandmother sacrificed to give you a life with a future. You wish she was around to know your kids.

You do not smoke or use any kind of drugs. Your spouse has been your only sexual partner since you met your spouse 15 years ago.

**Family History:**

You know of no illnesses that run in your family. You are an only child. Your parents died in a car accident when you were about 8. Your maternal grandmother raised you until you were 18. She died from a heart attack a few days after you graduated high school. You never knew your other grandparents. They all died of old age.

**Physical Exam:**

If the student lifts either straightened leg while you are lying on the bed, you should indicate the shooting pain down your right leg when it's lifted at about a 45 degree angle. You are able to walk normally. Pain should be indicated when you move from sitting up to a laying down position. You do not experience pain when the student performs tests to test the strength in your legs and feet, for example asking you to push against their hands. You do not have decreased leg strength, or decreased strength in your right toe and ankle. You can shrug your shoulders with no problem or pain. If student palpates the back it is tender medially from the spine but there is no pain if the spine is pressed directly. You have some difficulty sensing light touch on the outside aspect of your right calf and the top of the right foot/outer ankle, but the difficulty is only to light touch, such as to a cotton swab or monofilament.

If the student wants to get blood pressure check again, say: "The nurse just did that and said it was the same."

**Patient Behaviors:**

Below are some statements that you need to say during the course of the encounter:

"I just want to get some pain medication."

Said in the first 2-3 minutes of the encounter.

"Can you give me something for the pain?"

Said once the student has started the physical examination.

"It is from the middle over to the right side."

Said when asked about location.

**Embedded Concern:**

"A friend of mine had severe pain in his right arm and he was just diagnosed with cancer." You will say this after the second request for pain medicine. You don't have any information about what type of cancer it was as you just heard about it through another friend about a week ago. You are concerned about the connection between severe pain and cancer since you are in pain but you won't ask them if they think it could be cancer. If asked if you are afraid you might have cancer, you can respond, "Maybe a little."

After the "2 minutes remaining" announcement, if the student has not conveyed a diagnosis, you must say "So what's your plan?"

**Appendix B: Student Preparation Information for the ISPE**

Provide students with their scheduled Interprofessional Standardized Patient Experience (ISPE) date and time. The following information is the only student preparation needed and can be shared via email or a Learning Management System. Students are not provided with any case information in advance.

**Interprofessional Standardized Patient Experience (ISPE) Overview**

During the ISPE, health professional students (e.g., nursing, social work, occupational therapy, physical therapy, medical and pharmacy students) collaborate to subjectively assess a client and plan care during a simulated case. The students use interviewing skills to gather subjective data; there is no physical assessment involved (except for general observation).

**Directions for participating in the ISPE**

Professional clinic dress is mandatory. Be prepared to take notes - no stethoscope or other clinical supplies are needed. Further instructions will be given at the start of each session.

**How to prepare for the ISPE**

Students should be prepared to represent their profession and articulate their profession’s contributions to offer a clinical case. Articulating the roles and responsibilities of your profession may be more challenging than anticipated. Consider how to share your professional role with others in advance. Otherwise, you have already acquired the necessary knowledge, skills, and abilities to excel with the ISPE.

**Appendix C: ISPE CHF Case Door Instructions**

**INSTRUCTIONS**: After you have read this scenario and organized your thoughts, you may enter the room.

**BACKGROUND**:

This 71-year-old patient comes to you today for a routine visit for the management of congestive heart failure. The patient has a pocket card with medications listed. The CMA (certified medical assistant) has roomed the patient and took their vital signs, which are as follows:

Temperature: 37.0

Pulse: 88 beats per minute and irregular (chronic)

Respiratory rate: 20 breaths per minute

BP: 130/70 mmHg

O2: sats 97% on room air

**Paul L. Foster School of Medicine** **Standardized Patient Program** # 1. **Case Development Blueprint: \_\_\_** **Amelia de Volvér****\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_**

Presenting Complaint:

Nausea and vomiting

Length of encounter:

20 minutes

Gender and age:

41-year-old woman

Setting:

Ambulatory outpatient clinic.

Case Summary:

Amelia is a 41 year old woman who presents with nausea and vomiting over the last two days.

The symptoms started two days ago at 2 o’clock in the morning with vague abdominal discomfort, fatigue, and nausea. Later that morning Amelia experienced the onset of abdominal pain and started vomiting. This vomiting has continued 2-3 times per hour since that time. She has been able to drink some clear liquids, but has not been able to eat at all. She continues to be lethargic with shivering, flushing, salivation, repeated vomiting and severe abdominal discomfort. She has no appetite at all.

This episode is essentially identical to previous episodes that have been occurring over the last six years. In between episodes, Amelia feels fine and has no symptoms. At first the symptom-free intervals would last 4-5 months, but over the last two years they have decreased to 2-3 months. Amelia’s last vomiting episode was two months ago and lasted 5 days.

Amelia’s doctors are not sure why she has these episodes. She has had a thorough GI workup which was essentially negative. Her primary care doctor calls them her abdominal migraines. Another doctor wants Amelia to see a psychiatrist. Amelia doubts them all, and has become sadly resigned to her condition.

Exam Room Needs:

  • Standard exam room equipment
  • A plastic emesis basin, “ just in case”
**SP Training Notes**

Case Name

Amelia de Volvér, a 41 year old female

Presenting Situation

Nausea and vomiting for two days.

Psychosocial Profile

Amelia is a homemaker and mother of two.

Her mother described her as a “sensitive child” who would sometimes stay home from school because of abdominal pain.

She had migraine headaches as an adolescent that coincided with her menstrual periods, and these headaches have continued into adulthood.

Outlook and Coping Style

Amelia is frustrated about her condition.

She has a great deal of stress in her life.

  • Her two teenage children are difficult, sullen, oppositional, and occasionally get into trouble.
  • In particular, her son has fallen with some bad friends, and has been caught using drugs twice.
  • Her husband is frequently upset, and has become critical and easily frustrated with Amelia.

Amelia has become anxious, depressed, and withdrawn.

  • She has talked with her primary care doctor, and has been prescribed a medication for her anxiety.
  • She hates being sick, and wishes medications worked better.
  • What is particularly bothersome is the abdominal pain that she has each time she vomits, so she has a feeling of dread about the next vomiting episode.
  • In the past, when she was hospitalized during vomiting episodes, anti-emetic medications were not very effective, even at high doses.

She is cooperative with the health care team, and would like help for her condition.

  • She is convinced that there is something that can be done to help her… But what could that be?

Opening Statement

“I’ve been throwing up for the last two days.”

History of Present Illness

You are playing the role of Amelia, a 41-year-old housewife, mother of two.

You were feeling healthy until two days ago.

  • Two days ago, at 2 o’clock in the morning, you awakened with:
    • Nausea
    • Mild, diffuse abdominal discomfort
    • Headache
    • Slight shivering sensation
    • Your husband stated that you appeared to be flushed
    • Salivation
  • About three hours later you felt the onset of severe abdominal pain and you immediately started vomiting.
  • Since then you have continued to vomit about twice each hour
    • This decreases to about once each hour when you are sleeping.
  • The vomiting has been mainly dry retching, as you have no gastric contents to bring up.
  • When not vomiting, you have spent most of your time in the shower with hot water running.
    • When the hot water is exhausted, you have spent the remaining time in bed during curled up under the covers.
  • You want the light turned off in your room and the drapes closed.
  • You have been able to take sips of carbonated beverages (Coke, 7-Up) and keep them down.

    • The nausea seems a little better.
    • Your abdomen still is painful.
    • Your abdominal muscles are also sore from repetitive muscle contractions. You dread each episode of vomiting because it is going to hurt.
    • The shivering has resolved.
    • The salivation has resolved, too.
    • The headache is still there.
  • Urine output is decreased but not absent.
  • You are quite thirsty and still taking sips of fluids continuously when not vomiting.
  • As expected, you are frustrated about your situation.

Previous attacks of vomiting (note: don’t volunteer this information upfront. Instead, wait for the student to ask for this information in some way).

  • You have had identical attacks in the past.
  • Your first attack was at age 34.
    • That attack lasted three days.
    • In your mid-30s, you had attacks every 4-5 months.
      • Each attack lasted about four days.
    • By your late 30s, the attacks were happening every three months.
      • Now the attacks were lasting five days.
    • Your last attack was two months ago.
      • The symptoms of this last attack are almost identical to what you are experiencing right now.
      • In fact, the clinical features of all of the attacks have been basically the same.
  • Early on, you went to the hospital during each attack.
    • The doctors tried anti-emetic medications with little benefit.
    • IV fluids were helpful.
    • You had a complete GI evaluation.
      • CT scans of the abdomen on several occasions
      • Endoscopy several times (with biopsies)
      • Colonoscopy once
      • Ultrasound studies of the abdomen
      • Small bowel capsule endoscopy to look for Crohn’s disease
      • A gastric emptying study
      • Complete blood work including assessments for metabolic disorders, infections, inflammatory conditions
    • All of these studies were essentially negative.
    • One surgeon was convinced that you had “acalculous cholecystitis” and advised cholecystectomy. You agreed to the procedure, but this did not change your symptoms at all.
  • Each attack seems to resolve on its own regardless of treatment.
  • Importantly, when you used to go to the ED at the beginning of an attack, you would ask for pain medication. The ED staff responded by stating that you were merely seeking narcotic pain medications.
    • You were labeled as a “drug seeker”.

Medical

  • Diabetes
  • Hypertension

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • HIV infection
  • Kidney disease
  • Heart or lung disease

Social Hx

  • Married.

P 94

BP 110/72

You are a cooperative but somewhat frustrated 41-year-old woman

You have a headache right now. You like the window blinds closed and the room darkened and quiet.

Special Instructions:

Actual patients with cyclic vomiting syndrome are among the most challenging and complex patients in medical practice. This is likely to be a daunting, even overwhelming case for the first-year medical students. Therefore, it is important to moderate the level of challenge.

  • You are frustrated, but not exasperated about your situation.

question_text:
# Station 1: Model for behavior change: Tobacco Dependence

Scenario:

You are on your inpatient medicine rotation. Last night, your team admitted a patient Charles Thompson, a 55-year old man, with a COPD exacerbation. He presented with worsening of his chronic cough as well as increased dyspnea over one week, and he was admitted for a COPD exacerbation. The patient was hospitalized once previously last year for a similar COPD exacerbation, but he was lost to follow up after that hospitalization. The intern reported on rounds that the patient smoked cigarettes, but did not get any further information about the patient’s smoking history. The attending physician has asked you and your fellow third year medical students to get more information about the patient’s smoking history. You are returning to his room after rounds to discuss this matter with the patient.
private_patient_context:
## **Station 1: Model of behavior change: Tobacco Dependence**

Training Materials

<u>Scenario for Standardized Patient:</u>

You are Charles Thompson, a 55-year old man. You have had a chronic daily cough for many months, usually worse in the morning, with a little bit of productive white phlegm. For the past week however, you developed worsening of your cough with increased frequency. You have been coughing all the time and noticed thick yellow phlegm as well as increased difficulty breathing. You don’t have a specific physician whom you identify as your primary care doctor, so you came to the Emergency room last night to seek treatment. The doctors in the emergency room admitted you to the hospital and told you that you have a “COPD exacerbation” and wanted to keep you in the hospital until your breathing and oxygen levels improved because your oxygen level at the time of your presentation to the ER was very low (87%).

<u>Medical History:</u>

You were hospitalized last year for similar symptoms. During that first hospitalization, you remember that the doctors told you that you had a disease called chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or “chronic bronchitis.” You don’t remember too much about what the disease meant or was caused by, but your understanding is that it is similar to asthma. You remember being sent home from the hospital with some inhalers, but once the medications ran out, you did not get any more refills. Your symptoms never seemed to be as bad as when you were hospitalized, so you did not get any more medications, nor did you follow up with an appointment to see a new primary care doctor, which the doctors in the hospital had arranged for you.

Since that first hospitalization, you have had a daily cough as described above. It was only during this last week that you found your symptoms have gotten so bad that you needed to go see a doctor.

Besides the hospitalization last year and your current hospitalization, you have considered yourself to be in generally good health. You don’t like to see a doctor unless you really feel sick, and you have not had a primary care doctor before. You don’t have any other significant medical problems, nor have you ever been on any chronic medications besides the inhalers that the doctors gave you on the last visit.

# 1. <u>Smoking history</u>

You have been a life-long smoker since the age of 20. First you started in college, socially smoking, but have now been a pack a day smoker for the past 30 years. You enjoy smoking. Your life and work are stressful and you find that smoking helps to relax you. You smoke Camel Lights. You smoke on your way to work, during breaks, and after meals. Your job as a restaurant manager gets very stressful, especially during the rush hours. You find that stepping outside for a quick cigarette break helps you to calm down from the bustle of work.

You are married and your wife also smokes. Neither of you smoked inside the house when your daughter was at home. However, she is grown and doesn’t live at home, so you both smoke at home.

You have never tried to quit smoking before, nor have you seriously thought of quitting smoking. You have been a smoker for most of your adult life. You know that smoking is generally not good for anyone’s health, but you don’t remember talking to a doctor before about smoking or having him/her tell you directly to quit before. Smoking is your habit and you enjoy it. You also feel attached to smoking and know that to a certain extent, your body is probably addicted to it. You know that it would be very hard to quit and are worried about weight gain as you are sure you will replace smoking with eating so you are even less inclined to try.

# 2. <u>Family Smoking history</u>

Your parents were both smokers. Your father died of a heart attack at age 60 and your mother osteoporosis and high blood pressure, but is still alive.

**Your role is to portray a smoker who has very little interest in quitting. You are not aware that your hospitalization is because of an illness (COPD) that is directly caused by cigarette smoking. You enjoy smoking, it relieves stress for you, and you have not thought seriously about quitting before.**

# 3. <u>Emotional Tone</u>

You are generally respectful and eager to get better and be discharged from the hospital. You don’t like being so short of breath as you’ve been for the past week, and you want to get better and return to work. It doesn’t upset you to talk about your smoking, but you get somewhat reluctant when discussing quitting. You want to focus on getting better and you don’t feel ready to discuss quitting.

If the student asks you whether you think your smoking is related to your current illness,

**“I haven’t really thought about it. I know that smoking’s probably not great for my health, but I thought that what I had was something like asthma.”**

The student should explain that your illness and reason for hospitalization is directly related to smoking, and quitting smoking can prevent further worsening of this illness. You are initially skeptical of this.

**“My parents smoked all the time when I was growing up and none of them ever had chronic bronchitis.”**

**“I work near the bus station and I’m exposed to a lot of diesel fumes and pollution all the time at work. Couldn’t that have more to do with my lung condition?”**

If the student warns you of long-term smoking risks (such as heart disease, cancer, worsening of lung disease), say:

**“Well, I’ve been smoking for more than half my life. Isn’t it just too late for me at this point? I mean, aren’t I already sick because of smoking?”**

If the student warns you of short term risks (cost, bad smell, cough)

**“Smoking is something that I do every day to relax. It’s really hard to get out of this habit for me because I think I’d be a stress case without it.”**

If the student directly advises you to quit smoking again, say,

**“I could never do that. It would be impossible to quit. If I go a couple of hours during the day without a cigarette, I feel my body craving it.”**

**“My wife smokes in the house. She’s never going to quit. It would be so hard to quit while she’s still smoking.”**

You should pay attention to the student’s behavior towards you. The student should not “push” you to quit. S/he can advise only, give you information, and help you think of reasons to quit. Things that might help make you think about quitting are: its direct link to your current illness, its cost, its potential future effects on your health. If s/he explains the connection between your current illness and smoking, then you are willing to consider quitting and accept further counseling:

**“I guess if quitting is going to keep me out of this current situation, I’ll think some more about it.”**

If the student gets too pushy or gets into too much blaming, you can get a defensive, then shut down and say:

**“Okay, whatever.”** or **“Well, I know myself and there’s no way that I’m really going to be able to give up smoking right now.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**
