CASE 2
Kevin D’Angelo,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Kevin is a 16 year old high school baseball player who has been experiencing intermittent stomach problems: dyspepsia, diarrhea, nausea and some dizziness. These symptoms have been occurring two or three times a week without any apparent cause. His parents have noticed this and have prompted him to see a physician. Kevin insists that there is nothing wrong and is only going to see the MD to please his parents.

What his parents don’t know is that he has been using chewing tobacco for the last few weeks during baseball games. Right now, he only uses during games and occasionally at practice. His teammates goaded him into trying it. However, their coach forbids the use of <u>any</u> tobacco products and Kevin knows that he will be suspended for five games if he is caught. Several scouts are coming to see the team over the next few weeks, so Kevin wants to be sure to play in every game. However, his friends are putting pressure on him to use the chew, so he doesn’t want to stop. Therefore, he is swallowing all the “spit” rather than expelling it so as not to be detected.

**Your role is to portray a chew tobacco user who has** <u>**very little interest in stopping**</u>**. You have the mistaken belief that chew is safer than smoking, and you do not realize that swallowing the chew is causing your stomach aches. You also believe that chew use will somehow “make you a man” and improve your baseball game.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

You have no interest in being examined by the physician, although you are respectful and cooperative.

When asked why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I don’t know. My parents think there is something wrong with my stomach, but I don’t think it’s a big deal.”**

<u>**Medical History**</u>

Your problems started about three weeks ago after you first tried chew. You became dizzy, began burping a lot, and started to feel nauseous. You are swallowing all the “spit” because you don’t want your coach to know that you are using tobacco. You even vomited a little the first two times you used. Since you play center field you were able to go far enough up field between plays so that no one noticed you vomiting. You didn’t vomit much so you just thought you had a “bug.” You felt better a few hours after the game, so you have not made the connection between using the chew and your stomach problems.

You are in good health otherwise, and have had no other physical problems. You are not on any medications and have had no past hospitalizations.

<u>**Family Smoking History**</u>

No one else in the family uses any form of tobacco.

<u>**Drug/ Alcohol Use**</u>

**“I don’t use anything like that. I’m serious about playing college baseball and don’t want to mess up my chances.”**

<u>**Smoking History**</u>

You are an adamant nonsmoker and have never even tried one puff. You are very serious about playing college ball and you know that smoking limits lung capacity. You don’t want anything to interfere with your ability to play your best. Besides, your grandfather died of lung cancer recently and you know that his smoking caused it.

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

When the student asks you what stomach problems you have been experiencing, explain that you have been

**“Burping, getting a lot of gas and feeling nauseous. I even threw up a little once. But every time I feel fine a few hours later, so what’s the big deal.”**

If the student specifically asks you <u>**when**</u> you have experienced the stomach problems, you can say that you have felt this way only after your baseball games for the last month or so. Otherwise, do not volunteer this information.

If the student asks you *if you smoke*, answer in a very emphatic fashion,

**“I would never smoke. I really want to play college ball and I know that smoking ruins your lungs. I need to be able to breathe well to be on the top of my game. Besides, my grandfather died from lung cancer that he got from smoking. I don’t want that to happen to me.”**

If he or she then questions you further and asks *about tobacco use*, become quiet and look down at the floor. Be somewhat evasive about answering until the student brings up confidentiality. Deny that you have ever smoked but eventually admit that you have “tried” chewing tobacco.

If the student asks you from the start *if you use chewing tobacco,* become quiet and look down at the floor. Be somewhat evasive about answering until the student brings up confidentiality. Then admit that you have “tried” chewing tobacco.

If the student begins to ask for more information about your chew use, respond as follows:

**“I don’t want to talk about this. I know you’ll tell my coach what I tell you and then I’ll get kicked off the team. There are some scouts coming to see our next few games and I need to be there. If they don’t see me playing I’ll never get recruited”**

The student should assure you that everything you say is confidential. If he or she does so, you **may reluctantly reveal that you have been using chew during the last few games and that you have been swallowing all the spit.**

If the student doesn’t say anything about confidentiality, continue to repeat that you don’t want to say anything until he or she addresses this issue.  If the student looks like they are getting frustrated or confused, ask,

**"Who are you going to tell anyway?"**

When the student begins to counsel you on quitting or begins to discuss the problems with using chew, use the following rebuttals:

**“Chew is safer than smoking, isn’t it? You can’t get lung cancer from chew can you?”**

**“My teammates say that there is something in tobacco that helps you play. My buddy, Kevin is playing better than ever since he started to use chew.”**

**“Anyway,** ***all*** **the great baseball players use chew. I want to be just like them.”**

By the end of the interview, the student should clearly and emphatically tell you to stop using the chew immediately.  This should not be done with a judgmental tone, but with an educational or informative tone.  For example, "The best thing you can do for your health is to stop using chew."  (Not, "Stop using chew, that is stupid.")

If the student tells you to stop smoking, and seems to be done with the interview, end the interview by saying,

**“Well, I’ll think about it but I’m not going to do it if it messes up my game.”**

# 1. **Morris**

# 3. <u>**CASE SUMMARY**</u>

You are Morris, a 45 year-old patient with a one week history of mild (3/10) lower abdominal pain.  Initially it seemed to come in waves lasting about 30 minutes, and occurred every 2-3 hours. It sometimes awakens you from sleep and it seems to help if you get up and walk around. You have been able to get some sleep, but not much. Every day it got worse and yesterday, when you woke up in the morning, it became constant, more severe and made worse by movement. You stayed at home from work yesterday and rested in bed all day, staying as still as possible. Last night you felt like you were getting a fever, and checked your temperature which was 101. You took 2 Tylenol and went back to sleep.

You decided it was time to go to the ER. It is now 6:00AM, Currently, the pain is sharp (6/10), steady and is made worse by moving and sneezing (you have Spring allergies). You have had a poor appetite all week and have not eaten any solids since yesterday (not hungry). You have been able to keep down several glasses of ginger ale and a cup of bouillon.

You had a few loose stools when the pain started a week ago, but now feel constipated and **have not had a bowel movement for 2 days**.

Over the past 2 years, you have had several similar episodes (two or three times total) that have lasted a few hours and were much less severe. They seem to subside after a bowel movement.

# 4. <u>**PRESENTATION/EMOTIONAL TONE**</u>

When the student enters the room, you are lying on your back on the exam table with your legs extended.  You are in some discomfort and lie still.  You are not moaning, but you are preoccupied with the pain. You are cooperative, and answer all of the student’s questions with relatively short answers.  You verbally relay your anxieties (if asked) because you are worried about the possibility of having an operation. Only if the student doesn’t seem to be handling your situation well will you become impatient, and less communicative.

# 5. **Opening Statement or CC:** 

**In response to the question**, <u>***(“Why are you here today?”***</u>**) you answer in exactly these words:**

	**“I have this pain in my abdomen that seems to be getting worse.”**

# 6. <u>**MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

# 7. With the next open ended question such as “Can you tell me more about the pain?”

“**It has been going on for about a week; it got a lot worse last night.”**  

# 8. **With specific questions:** 

# 9. **The Pain:**

# 10. **Where:	“It’s kind of in my lower abdomen over here (points to the left lower quadrant)”**

If the student asks where the pain was when it <u>STARTED</u>, the issue being <u>***“Was the pain someplace other than where it is now?”***</u> respond to this question by saying **,“ No,  it has always been in the same place.”**

# 11. If asked  <u>***“Does the pain go anywhere else?”***</u>  respond , **“ NO”** the pain is in the left lower quadrant, and has always been that way.

# 12. **Intensity:**	The pain is moderate.  On a scale of 1 to 10, this pain is a 6.  

**Constant/Intermittent**:	The pain is <u>constant</u> “since last night,” and slowly building. It is worse right now. “**It initially came and went, but now is there all the time”**

**Character:** 	The pain is sharp and concentrated in the left lower quadrant.

**Better or worse:**	The student might ask you if anything makes the pain <u>better</u> or if anything makes the pain <u>worse</u>.

# 13. <u>***“What makes it better?”***</u>  …

# 14. Reply:  “Lying still used to make it better.” 

# 15. If the student asks you if you can do anything to lessen the pain, if there is anything that increases the pain, or if there is any position that relieves the pain, you answer:

# 16. “If I lie on my back, it helps a little. The Tylenol didn’t help at all.”

# 17. <u>***“ Does anything make it worse?”***</u>

# 18. Reply: “If I move it gets worse”

# 19. <u>***“What medications have you tried?”***</u>

“I tried taking 2 Tylenol for my fever, but they didn’t help.”

<u>***“Have you ever experienced pain like this in the past?”***</u>

“I’ve had some discomfort in the past…but not like this”

**With more specific questioning**

**-** Crampy discomfort in lower abdominal area that lasted a few hours but resolved itself after bowel movements. This happened **two or three times over the past 2 years.** Didn’t affect your eating habits, and you had no fevers. You don’t remember more specific information about these occurrences. You did not think it was significant to call the doctor.

***Nausea*****-** Yes**.** You have not felt hungry for more than 24 hours.  Your last meal was dinner last night, a cup of bouillon. You had ginger ale earlier in the day. You complain of thirst and a dry mouth.

# 20. ***Vomiting*****-** No**. (do not volunteer this unless they ask specifically)**

# 21. ***Fever/sweating/chills:***

If asked, you had a fever of 101 last night.

# 22. ***Last bowel movement:***

# 23. You had loose stools last week. No BM for 2 days. You feel constipated. No blood or black stools (if they ask). You are able to pass gas. 

# 24. ***Urination:***

# 25. You urinated when you got up this morning.  The color was yellow, no blood (if they ask).

# 26. ***Gas:***

# 27. You are able to pass gas, but you have not been passing a lot of gas.

# 28. <u>**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

You are in good health, except for as described above. No prior operations.

# 29. <u>**PAST HOSPITALIZATIONS**</u>

None

# 30. <u>**MEDICATIONS**</u>

# 31. **Prescription drugs:**    

# 32. If they ask whether or not you’re on any prescription medicine your answer is **“None”**

# 33. **Over-the-Counter (OTC) drugs:**   

You took 2 Tylenol last night because you were concerned about your fever.

# 34. **Illicit/street drugs:**   

# 35. None

# 36. <u>**SEXUAL HISTORY**</u>

You have a monogamous relationship with your spouse for the past 15 years, and have always enjoyed a good sex life.

# 37. <u>**LIFESTYLE/HABITS**</u>

# 38. **Alcohol:** 

You will not volunteer the following information, but will answer honestly if the student asks you about your drinking.  You consider yourself a “social drinker”, and do not have more than 2-3 drinks per week.   You don’t get drunk and have never been arrested for a DUI (Driving Under the Influence).

You answer “No” to all the CAGE questions:

	**C**	Have you thought about <u>cutting</u> down?

	**A**	Does anyone get <u>angry</u> because of your drinking?

	**G**	Do you ever feel <u>guilty</u> about your drinking?

**E**	Do you ever need an <u>eye-opener</u> to get you started in the morning?

# 39. **Tobacco:**

# 40. You do not smoke. 

# 41. **Caffeine:**  

You drink one cup <u>of coffee per day</u>, in the morning.  You stay away from other caffeinated beverages.

# 42. **Diet:**

You usually have cereal for breakfast, a fast food salad for lunch and pasta or chicken for diner.

# 43. **Exercise:**

You exercise regularly on the treadmill at home, about 30 minutes 3-4 times per week.

# 44. **Suicide Risk:**

# 45. None

# 46. **Activities/Hobbies:**

You are in too much pain to discuss.

# 47. **Education:**

# 48. Finished graduate school in industrial engineering.  

# 49. <u>**ENVIRONMENTAL RISK FACTORS**</u>

You have worked as an industrial engineering professor at CMU for the past 10 years.

# 50. <u>**FAMILY MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

Your parents are alive in their early seventies and are in good health.  Your father had colon cancer at age 60 and was cured with surgery. Four siblings are healthy.

# 51. <u>**PERSONAL/FAMILY HISTORY**</u>

You have been **married** for 15 years.  You have no children.

# 52. <u>**PHYSICAL EXAM : The students are told to watch you carefully during the PX and during their questioning to see how you move . Consistency in your pain portrayal is very important.**</u>

**NO** rectal exam has been done on you yet.  If the student asks about a rectal exam, say **“The nurse told me someone would be in to do that after you spoke with me.”**

**...** <u>**percussed**</u> **my abdomen in at least ONE place.**

**Your response:** 	  

<u>When</u> the student taps on your lower left abdomen, you grimace and wince in pain.

You do not wince if they tap in other quadrants.

If asked, you report according to where they are tapping:

Don’t give the info until touched

<u>This is moderate pain, a 6 on a scale of 1 to 10</u>.

**\*\*** ***Remember*****:**	T<u>he FIRST time</u> the student touches your lower left abdomen (for this item “percussion” OR the next item “palpation” OR even if the student bears down too hard with the stethoscope while “listening” to your abdomen), say:

	**“That hurts!”**

**...** <u>**palpated**</u> **(pressed) my abdomen in all four quadrants.** 	

**Your response:**	Hold your abdominal muscles rigid when they palpate the left lower quadrant.

It is only bad <u>in the left lower quadrant</u>; you grimace and wince in pain.

<u>***Rebound Maneuver***</u>:	Watch for this maneuver.

The student might try it in one of several ways:

1.	Push in on your abdomen (with their hands or stethoscope) <u>and let go quickly (but gently)</u>.

2.  Bump the bed.

3.  Rock your pelvis.

4. Tap on your feet.

**Your response:**	You grimace or moan in pain to all items only in the left lower quadrant.  The student may ask you if it hurts more when they let go than when they push down.

**“When you push down”**

**Other Items you can expect the student to do:**

Punch mid-back (gently) for CVA tenderness- this would cause pain, because of the movement it causes in your body….not because your kidneys hurt

# 55. <u>**QUESTIONS YOU MUST ASK THE STUDENT:**</u>

# 56. **Middle of the encounter:**  

During the physical exam, when the student pushes on your left lower quadrant, you moan in pain and say:

# 57. **“That really hurts!”**

If the student has not already addressed this issue, you ask:

# 58. **“Is there anything that you can do to make this pain go away?”**

# 59. A convenient place to insert this issue is when the student asks if <u>you</u> have any questions.

# 60. **End of the encounter if the student has not told you what they think is going on:** 

# 61.    **“What do you think is wrong with me?”** 

If the student mentions surgery, you may react with concern, and ask questions about the process mentioned.

You fear the shame of getting caught living in your car by the police and therefore move around a lot. You and Fiona fight often, and because of this she sometimes stays either in a shelter or with a friend. You would like Viagra, because this is the only way you can think of to rekindle your relationship. You are awaiting housing options, which are not readily forthcoming. Generally, you consider yourself to be in fairly good health. After your diagnosis of diabetes 7 years ago, your prior doctors scheduled you for visits every 3-4 months, but you would come in maybe every 8-9 months. With all the chaos and stress of the past 6 months, you missed your last appointment, so it has been more like 11 months since you were last seen. You made the current appointment by using the services at a Project Homeless Connect - Veterans Connect event yesterday. You had a bad experience at the last clinic visit with a doctor that threatened heart attacks and losing your eyesight and legs if your diabetes were to continue like that, and you didn’t want to hear that. **Diabetes** You were diagnosed with diabetes 7 years ago. You had some abdominal pain and came into the Emergency Department. You got some antibiotics, but then the doctors went on about having diabetes or sugar or something like that, and initially you thought that the abdominal pain was causing the diabetes, so you didn’t really pay much attention to it. No one has really explained diabetes to you that well. You only check your blood sugars when your wife Fiona insists. You don’t like to prick yourself; you have no idea what targets are for blood levels of glucose or hemoglobin A1C. The trainee will tell you that your A1C is high at 11.7, with a desirable level at 7. Unless this is particularly stressed, you don’t think 7 is too far from 11, and they’re all kind of lucky numbers to you anyway. If the trainee asks if you have any difficulty with eyesight, chest pain, lightheadedness, breathing, snoring, increased thirst, urination, weight changes, or numbness/tingling in your feet, you will respond no to each question. You are doing the best that you can. You know you should eat better, but you don’t really feel you can make choices on a very limited budget - and you’re not that excited about changing your diet anyway. You cannot think of changing anything toward a more healthy lifestyle; there’s too much going on right now. So if a trainee asks, “What will it take for you to start taking care of yourself (checking blood sugars, exercise, proper diet, etc.),” you should just shrug. Say, **“I don’t know, . . . I’m doing the best I can. I’m just trying to survive right now.”** You will say that you are “willing to try whatever, if I can do it pretty easily” (given your “current circumstances”). But if the trainee tries to get you to commit to improving your adherence, you will negotiate and ultimately only agree to try to improve one area in which you are having difficulty (or two, if the trainee can make it seem simple), but too many (more than 2) suggestions will make you feel pressured and overwhelmed. **You do not want to go on insulin (you hate needles). If the trainee wants to start insulin therapy, let the trainee know that you’d rather not resort to insulin: “I really hate needles and want to stay away from insulin.” And you also state that you’d “have no place to keep it anyway.”** **High triglyceride levels & high cholesterol** You don’t remember when your doctor discovered high triglycerides and high cholesterol in you, but it was shortly after your diabetes was discovered. You do not have any symptoms, but you do know that you were prescribed a cholesterol medication for it. You’re not great at numbers, and you don’t really keep track of them. **Diet** You have received some information from a dietitian about the things you should eat, but since you have so little cash, you eat when you are hungry and what you can afford. Mainly you go to Chinese food places for lunch and fast food burger or burrito places for dinner. Sometimes you go to the Project Homeless Connect - Veterans Connect events, but struggle with a lot of shame around needing to use such services. You also go to the grocery store sometimes to stock up on bread, cookies, and chips. You vaguely remember that someone told you that you should record your eating habits but you do not do this; you barely keep track of what you eat, since you basically live day to day. Because of your disorganized living situation, the idea of losing weight is nowhere near a priority for you. **Exercise** When you are not in the library surfing the web, you spend time sitting and walking in the park; it gives you solace and peace. **Nursing Note – Admission**

Patient presented to the ED with right-sided weakness. Patient was at home when suddenly became weak and started to fall to the right. Spouse was at home and was able to get the patient to the couch and call 911. Spouse reported that the patient could answer questions but speech sounded slurred. EMS brought patient to the hospital.

**Standardized Patient Team Experience (SPTE) Facilitator Guide – Admission**

Students will work with the team to develop an admission plan for a patient that reflects the contributions of each team member.

***Standardized Patient Case Description****:*

Middle-aged patient with history of high blood pressure suddenly became weak and started to fall to the right at home earlier today. Spouse called 911. Spouse reported patient could answer questions, but speech sounded slurred. EMS brought patient to hospital where code stroke protocol was activated and IV thrombolytic therapy (tenecteplase) was administered. Weakness started improving after thrombolytic administration. Team will be interacting with patient on arrival to step-down unit to develop an admission plan. Patient chart provided to students has more information.

Case Summary: The patient is a 22-year old woman with a history of occasional headaches. Recently, she has been experiencing headaches that are different from her usual headaches. Patient appearance: The patient should be a 20-something year-old overweight woman. If she is not overweight, she should wear a big shirt stuffed with a pillow, in order to appear obese. The patient should be well-groomed. Preferably, she should be wearing a hospital gown. However, conservative dress would also be acceptable.

Patient instructions: The challenge for the patient is to communicate with the “physician” as one would naturally, without giving away too much information. Location: whole head and neck and behind the eyes

**CASE 3C**
Robert Goodman,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Robert Goodman is a 60 year old laborer who works for a moving company (oversees moving crew). Over the last month he has experienced some vague, minor chest pains on exertion, especially while at work when he is lifting. One of Robert’s coworkers recently had cardiac problems and was a smoker. His physician recommended that he quit smoking and he did so. He discussed the issue with Robert several times.

Robert is now concerned that there may be some connection between his current symptoms and his smoking. He approached this friend, who gave Robert his leftover patches. Robert tried them a month ago for a few days but used them incorrectly.

Robert is now blaming his inability to quit on the patch. However, Robert smokes about two or three packs a day but started on the lowest level of the patch. That’s what his friend gave him. In addition, Robert took the patch off two or three times a day to smoke. He kept a pack of cigarettes in the moving van, “just in case.” Robert never read the package instructions and did not make any behavioral changes.

The chest pains persisted for about a week, so Robert is now in the office for a follow up visit after having the usual battery of cardiac diagnostic tests (all of which are negative). The subsequent visit revealed that the chest pains were a result of gastritis and reflux which have responded to antacids (Zantac). However, Robert does not like taking medicines, and this incident has brought the concept of quitting to the forefront of Robert’s thinking. He is now motivated to quit, but this prior “attempt” has left him somewhat disheartened. He does not understand why the patches worked for his friend and not for him.

**Your role is to play a smoker who is** <u>**definitely interested in quitting**</u>**. However, he has come to believe that his recent failure to do so is the fault of the patches he used. He does not understand that he used them incorrectly. He also does not understand that the quitter must actively participate in the quit (make behavioral changes) to be successful. He is mistakenly waiting for the patches to “cure” him.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

Robert is scared that he is going to have a heart attack at any moment even though all the tests came back negative. There is a long history of cardiac problems in Robert’s family, all of whom were smokers. His father reminded him of this in a recent conversation.

During the office visit he is anxious, stating many times that he really wants to quit now. However, in spite of his anxiety, he is motivated to quit smoking, but not at all confident that he will be able to do so.

When the student asks why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work.”**

**“What do I do now?”**

<u>**Your Smoking History**</u>

You began smoking while in the service at age 18. You have been smoking ever since and now smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy you are at work. On slow days you smoke more since you have a lot of time on your hands. You have never tried to quit before, other than the attempt last month.

During that attempt you experienced significant withdrawal in spite of wearing the patch.  You were very irritable, anxious, restless, and impatient. After three days you returned to your regular pattern of smoking.

<u>**Family Smoking/Medical History**</u>

Both sets of grandparents smoked, as well as both parents. Father has quit, but mother still smokes about a pack a day.

Paternal grandmother had two heart attacks at age 67 and died at 68 as a result.

Maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 55. He was bedridden for eight years as a result and died at age 63.

Father had triple bypass at age 64.

Mother has had a long history of angina starting in her mid-eighties.

<u>**Drug/Alcohol use**</u>

You drink a few beers a week on Friday or Saturday night. You have cut back considerably on your drinking in recent years. **“I just can’t do it anymore!”**

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

If the student asks you about family cardiac history, review the above information with him or her. Otherwise, don’t bring this up.

If the student asks you what you did the last time you tried to quit, just say,

**“I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work.”**

If the student questions you further as in, **“Which patch did you use?”** or “**Describe to me how you used the patch,”** you may explain exactly what you did:

**“I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me.”**

**“I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”**

**“They didn’t work at all. I still wanted to smoke even though I had the patch on.”**

**“But I want you to know I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.”**

As you explain all this become increasingly anxious. Ask the student,

**“Why can’t you cure me? Can’t you just give me a pill or something?”**

If the student asks you to set a quit date,

**"It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday."**

**"Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready."**

If the student asks you what kind of changes you made in your routines or

behavior, ask,

**“What do you mean? Don’t you just put the patch on and forget about it?”**

If the student asks you when you most need a cigarette,

**"In the morning when I wake up, during breaks at work, and after meals."**

If the student asks you what you could do besides smoking at those times,

**“What do you mean?”**

If they give examples of other behaviors (chewing gum, etc.),

**"That's interesting.  My buddy who quit is always carrying around those pretzel sticks.  I never really asked him about them, but that would probably help.  I also like gum."**

**"I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals."**

If the student suggests that you go to a group cessation program, say,

**“I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do?”**

If the student <u>**does not**</u> ask you any questions about how you used the patch or what you did, just continue with the “What am I supposed to do? I really want to quit” line of questioning until he or she does.

**Overview of Case**

- Jane Henderson is coming in for a follow-up with her primary care physician, Dr. Johnson, who she met for the first time at her last visit.  She comes in today for a regularly scheduled appointment to follow-up on her blood pressure and cholesterol control.  She has noticed a recent increase in headaches that she attributes to stress and brings this up in the visit. She is feeling the strain of caring for her grandchildren and feels that the stress of this may be causing the headaches.  Although previously supportive, her husband has become more withdrawn, leaving her with much of the responsibility for raising her grandchildren. This has caused a strain in their relationship.

#### 8.1.1.1. **Part 2 - Follow-up Interview**

**Your Profile**

You are Mrs. Henderson, a 60-year-old retired schoolteacher who is being seen in follow-up for management of your blood pressure and cholesterol. You have had 2 appointments to date at this practice, one with the medical student/primary care physician for your initial history and physical exam and a second with the nurse for a blood pressure check 2 weeks after your initial appointment.

You present today at a regularly scheduled follow-up appointment with several concerns.  One of your main concerns is that you have had increasing headaches over the past month or so that you attribute to stress, but also wonder if your blood pressure could be too high. You are feeling the strain of caring for your grandchildren.  You are also interested to see if your blood pressure is better.

**Presentation/Emotional Tone**

You are worried about your husband’s ongoing health issues (emphysema) and somewhat frustrated by the fact that George has become increasingly withdrawn, leaving you to shoulder the majority of the childcare responsibilities.  You are also worried about your own health issues, specifically increasing headaches, which you think could be related to stress or to your high blood pressure.  You have tried to be more consistent about taking your medications and have been successful for the most part, but are still struggling with issues of diet and exercise.  You feel somewhat guilty that you haven’t been able to make the lifestyle changes you know you should.  You continue to feel overwhelmed, but you are a stoic individual who does not complain.

The holidays came and went and were more difficult than you expected.  You thought the girls were finally settling in with you and George, but the holidays brought out how much they miss their mother and their home.  Katie (the 5-year old) demanded to go home so that Santa would know where to find her.  When she didn’t get exactly what she wanted, she was upset with you for several days saying that it was because Santa got confused about where she was and must have delivered the wrong presents.

On top of all that, both the girls were sick in December.  Katie had a bad fever for a while – there was a very serious form of croup going around some of the younger kids in Sunday school, and you were very worried that she might catch it – but she got better with repeated doses of Tylenol.  When ill, Katie became very emotionally needy and clingy and would not let you out of her sight.  She acted out with tantrums several times and had nightmares at night.  Because of the nightmares, she started crawling into bed with you.  You weren’t able to sleep well with her in your bed, especially with the nighttime awakenings and Katie getting up at 5:30 every morning.  Tiffany had a bout of diarrhea that lasted about two or three days.  She never vomited, thank goodness, and overall she seemed like she was doing fairly well emotionally, but with both of them ill one right after the other, there was no way you could get much rest.  You weren’t able to send them to school, Sunday school, or regular play dates with their friends.

Your daughter Michelle came home over the holidays (from Florida), and she was a great help and support, but the change in routine sort of threw the girls off a bit.  You were really hoping that your son Bob would come to California for the holidays with your other two grandchildren – he wanted to, but his wife’s father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the beginning of December, and he felt he needed to stay with her family in Virginia. At the same time, you are somewhat relieved about not having to deal with extra children in the house and Bob’s wife Ellen.  You’re not sure what you would have done if Katie and Tiffany did not respond well to Bob’s family, with whom they have never spent any time. You don’t dislike Ellen, but your relationship has been distant and somewhat strained due to disagreements with her in the past about sending your grandsons to private school, even though they may not be able to afford it (Ellen is a stay-at-home mom, and Bob’s real estate business is not doing very well with the mortgage lending crisis).  This ambivalence you feel towards Bob’s family is a source of guilt for you.

**INTERVIEW CONTENT:**

**Medical History – Mrs. Henderson**

**(Note:** Students will be expected to practice a technique of interviewing today for follow-up patients in which they should elicit the full spectrum of patient concerns at the outset of the interview, followed by a brief collaborative agenda-setting period.)

##### 8.1.1.1.1. **How have you been since you last came in?**

*Oh, the holidays were very stressful, but Michelle, my daughter in Florida, came home for a couple of weeks, which was a great help.*

(If the student appears particularly empathic or asks specifically about how the holidays were stressful, feel free to reveal parts of your holiday story.)

*I’m really happy to see you again – I’ve been worried about several things.*

##### 8.1.1.1.2. What concerns do you have today?

(**Note:** If the student asks for “headlines” or a couple of words that describe the topics you would like to raise today, please oblige willingly.)

For example:

I’d like to get a sense of the range of topics you’d like to cover at this visit.  What headlines do you have for us today?

*I definitely want to talk about my blood pressure.*

##### 8.1.1.1.3. OK, blood pressure – anything else worrying you?

*I’ve been having headaches.  They’re very bothersome.*

##### 8.1.1.1.4. Sounds like we’ll need to make time for that.  Something else?

*Oh, I know I was supposed to get a lab test to check my cholesterol, but with everything going on, I just couldn’t do it before today.  I’m really sorry.  I absolutely promise to do it before next time.*

##### 8.1.1.1.5. Anything else?

*Oh, I think that’s about it.*

**Note:** The highly skilled and attentive student will then say something like: “Sounds like two very important issues for you: the blood pressure, and headache.  Obviously the blood tests are something that we will need to work on, so let’s talk about that next time.  We should be able to cover those things in the time we have today.”

Otherwise, with a very open-ended non-directive question, please respond immediately with the appropriate paragraphs below.)

Tell me about your concerns about blood pressure.

##### 8.1.1.1.6. *Well, I’d like to see how my blood pressure is doing.  I have been trying to keep up with the medicines, and I came in to see the nurse like you asked at the last visit. I’ve been checking my blood pressure every few weeks at the Safeway when I remember to.  It seems better than it was at my last visit with you…the top number is usually between 140 and 150 and the bottom number is usually around 90 to 100. I’m wondering if it is still too high because I’ve been having more headaches lately.*  

##### 8.1.1.1.7. What are you most worried about with your blood pressure?

*Well, I think my doctor at Kaiser told me that high blood pressure can cause a heart blockage like the kind I had.  I can’t afford to be sick, not with George’s health the way it is, and having the kids around.  And Michelle, particularly, asks me a lot about my blood pressure.*

##### 8.1.1.1.8. What are your goals for controlling your blood pressure?

*Well, it’s been so hard.  I want to have my blood pressure good so I don’t have to worry about my health.  And I can take the medications every morning – the girls take their vitamins, and George and I take our pills – that’s actually worked out ok.  But I’ll forget the evening pills sometimes.*

##### 8.1.1.1.9. What ways can you think of that might help you remember to take your evening medicines?

*Michelle wants to buy me a blood pressure cuff so I can keep better track of my blood pressure. I’m not sure it is worth the cost, especially on her teacher’s salary. Do you think that would be a good idea?* 

##### 8.1.1.1.10. Any other ideas?

*Well, I might have the girls help me remember – like maybe when they are brushing their teeth, I can take the evening pills?*

**Note:** If the student brings up the idea of using a pill box as a strategy for remembering to take your pills, you agree that it would be helpful, but you’ve been afraid of having a pillbox at your bedside that the girls can easily get into.

##### 8.1.1.1.11. Could you tell me more about the headaches?

*I have headaches 2-3 times per week.  They aren’t severe, but I definitely notice them more often than I used to have them. In the past, they’d be once or twice a month at most, but now they’re more frequent.  It’s hard to attend to the girls with these headaches; I try not to snap at them, and I’ll say, ‘sorry kids, Grandma has a headache,’ but it just gets to me sometimes, and I think I’ve gotten curt with them a couple of times.*

**Note:** If student doesn’t inquire about what might cause the headaches, the patient should specifically ask the student:

*Do you think the headaches I’m having are due to the high blood pressure or to stress?*

Students may ask for additional details about your headaches:

- *They are a 3-4 out of 10 in severity*
- *They are throbbing, dull headaches*
- *They are located across your forehead*
- *They last 2-3 hours and are relieved by rest*
- *They seem worse when you are stressed*
- *You haven’t taken any medications for them because you were worried about potential interactions with the other pills you are taking*

Students may ask about associated symptoms:

- *You have had no nausea or vomiting*
- *You have not had blurry vision*
- *You have not had any numbness or weakness in your arms or legs*

What do you think is causing your headaches?

*I guess it could be my blood pressure, but I am trying to be better about taking my medications and my last blood pressure check was better.  I’m also worried about my husband, George, and feeling overwhelmed with all my responsibilities with the kids, so maybe stress is causing my headaches.  George’s health hasn’t been the greatest because of his emphysema and recently he seems even more withdrawn.  I know he loves the girls, but he doesn’t pay much attention to them.  He’s always reading the newspaper, doing his crosswords or watching TV.  I don’t think he knows what to do with them.  George likes his routines and the girls upset his routine.  The more they act out or are difficult, the more he withdraws.  That means most of the responsibility falls on me.*    

Students may ask about other symptoms related to your heart/high blood pressure:

- *You haven’t had any shortness of breath*
- *You haven’t felt dizzy or palpitations (heart racing)*
- *You don’t have any chest pain, jaw pain or arm pain*
- *You never actually had a heart attack*
- *You can’t walk too far because of your arthritis*
- *No recent blurry vision*

**Medications:**

*I have my list with me today.  I’ve tried to be better about taking my medicines consistently.  Sometimes I forget to take the pills I am supposed to take in the evening for my blood pressure and cholesterol.  It’s just hard to remember them at the end of the day.  But, overall I’ve been pretty good.*

**Lipitor 40 mg at night (cholesterol medicine)**

**Metoprolol 50 mg twice daily (blood pressure medicine)**

**Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily (blood pressure medicine)**

**Lotensin 20 mg daily (blood pressure medicine)**

**Aspirin (to protect heart)**

If student doesn’t ask about medications, the patient can initiate this discussion by saying:

*I brought my list of medications with me today like you asked. I’ve tried to be better about taking my medicines consistently.  Sometimes I forget to take the pills I am supposed to take in the evening for my blood pressure and cholesterol.  It’s just hard to remember them at the end of the day.  But, overall I’ve been pretty good.*

##### 8.1.1.1.12. Any herbs, vitamins or complementary medicine?

*I’m taking my calcium every morning.*

###### 8.1.1.1.12.1. <u>**Social History**</u> 

##### 8.1.1.1.13. How are things going at home?

*Okay, I guess.  Things have just been really busy.  I worry about George’s health and I also worry about the kids.  George is usually quiet, but lately he has kept even more to himself.  Sometimes he is short-tempered with me and the girls, most of the time he just wants to be left alone.  I feel guilty because I know the kids can be really loud sometimes and I should be able to control them, but it’s a lot harder when they’re your grandkids, not someone else’s, especially when they are used to doing what they want with their mom.  I’m trying to use techniques that worked so well in the classroom when I was a teacher, but they just aren’t used to the discipline.  If I push too hard about instituting house rules, they just rebel and act out even more.  One of my granddaughter’s teachers mentioned that I should consider asking for help from the social worker at the clinic where I take the girls for their check-ups or maybe the Sunday school program at church.  I’m not one to ask for charity…I’m used to helping others, but I’m starting to think that I could use some help.*

Have you been able to get any more help from your friends at church?

*No, that’s about the same.  There’s no way I could tell Lorraine about … (you become somewhat tearful as you think about Kathy – it is all so overwhelming – but you also don’t completely lose it – you are really strong and can hold it together)*

**Note:**  You are open to exploring ideas for how to reach out to church friends for support and help if the student brings it up.  You are mostly embarrassed about having to divulge information about Kathy being in jail.  If there was a way to ask for help and advice about caring for the children or dealing with George without revealing Kathy’s predicament, you would most likely be willing to try it.  You are also open to the idea of respite care and exploring options in the community or at the church where someone or an activities program could take the girls off your hands for a few hours a week.

##### 8.1.1.1.14. Are there others at church who can help you?  The pastor, maybe?

*I’ve thought about talking to Father Cavanaugh, but then I think he’s got enough to think about with a large congregation.  I wouldn’t want to bother him too much.*

**Note:**  you would be willing to approach Father Cavanaugh if you have a conversation with the student about it.  You hadn’t thought of approaching one of the younger associate pastors, but if you get into a conversation about other available clergy with the student, you begin to think that one of the younger ones might be better in terms of coming up with tips about Kathy and the kids.

###### 8.1.1.1.14.1. <u>**Health-related Behaviors**</u>

**Diet** 

##### 8.1.1.1.15. Have you made any changes in your diet?

*I know we talked about it, but I’ve just been too busy, especially over the holidays. I tried to follow a healthier diet, but over the holidays it was tough, especially with the girls getting sick.  The kids are so picky about food and are used to eating all sorts of unhealthy food and snacks. George can be picky as well – he’s used to his meat and potatoes (he grew up in the Midwest) – and is having a hard time adjusting to having to eat differently.   I either eat with them or I just end up having to make 4 different dinners for 4 different people.  I don’t have the energy left at the end of the day to do that.* 

**Exercise**

##### 8.1.1.1.16. Are you exercising more regularly?

*After we met last time, I did look into an exercise class for seniors that meets twice a week and is at a time when the girls are in school.  I haven’t had a chance to go yet, especially with the girls having to stay home sick from school so much in December, but maybe when things calm down…But the only time I have for George and to get things done around the house and run errands is when the girls are at school, so I’m not sure about giving up that time.  Also, with my arthritis, I worry that I won’t be able to keep up, or that I’ll have more pain in my knees and then will have to stop.*

If the student doesn’t ask about diet or exercise during the encounter, the patient can ask the student about them.

*I know we talked last time about my diet and exercise.  I haven’t been as good as I’d hoped to be after the last appointment.  I tried to follow a healthier diet, but over the holidays it was tough.*  

**Physical Examination**

There will be no physical exam.  The interview ends at the point where it would naturally lead to an examination and/or lab tests.

question_text:
Station 2 – Difficult Doctor-Patient Encounter

Scenario:

You are rotating at the adult medicine general medicine clinic. You have just seen and examined Natalie Smith, a 27-year old woman, who presents with 3 days of cough, runny nose, and sore throat. She has had no sick contacts, and denies any fevers, nausea, vomiting, or trouble breathing. She came to clinic as a walk-in patient today because the Nyquil she took for congestion was making her too drowsy at her job as an attorney, and she needs to get better as soon as possible. She had a similar illness last year, and she remembers getting a “Z-pack” from a doctor which improved her symptoms quickly; so she has specifically requested antibiotics again. She has no past medical history, and she is not on any medications except for birth control pills. She is not allergic to any medications.

You stepped out of the room to present the case to the attending preceptor. You are returning to the exam room to discuss the situation with Ms. Smith. The attending physician asks you to talk to Ms. Smith first while he finishes his paperwork, then he will come into the room to examine her and confirm your findings.
private_patient_context:
**Station 2 – Difficult Doctor-Patient Encounter**

Training Materials

<u>Scenario for Standardized Patient:</u>

You are Natalie Smith, a 27-year old woman. You are a generally healthy woman with no medical problems. However, for the past three days you have had symptoms of runny nose, sore throat with as scratchy voice, and a dry cough. You don’t have a fever, but you’ve felt very congested throughout your head and chest, and a little bit run down in the past few days.  You have tried drinking tea with lemon and honey. You don’t usually take any medications, but the symptoms got so bad that you bought Nyquil. However, the medicine made you feel extremely drowsy, so you stopped it because it was interfering with your job as an attorney.

Last year you had similar symptoms, so you know that you have a bad cold and probably bronchitis now. You went to a doctor last year and got antibiotics called a “Z-pack” and that cleared up your symptoms within 1-2 days. You have come to the walk-in clinic today to get a prescription of Z-pack again.

<u>Medical History</u>

You have no significant medical problems. You have never been hospitalized, and your only daily medications are birth control pills. You haven’t needed to take too many medications, except for occasional antibiotics for a urinary tract infection and the Z-pack last year.

<u>Social History</u>

You work as an intellectual property attorney in a busy law firm. You are a junior associate, and you have an extremely demanding job with long hours. You have been very busy preparing a big case, so despite feeling ill, you’ve been going in to work every day. You are not thinking of taking time off from work – missing work except for major emergencies is unthinkable in your office. It was enough of a hassle to take a little time in the morning to come to the clinic, but you are still trying to get down to your office as soon as you are finished with your doctor’s appointment. You are frustrated because even though you came to the clinic at 8:30 in the morning, you had to wait for an hour just to be seen. A medical student talked to you and examined you and just stepped out to talk to his/her attending supervisor. You have now been waiting another 10 minutes for the student to return, and you are stressed because it is already late morning.

You don’t smoke cigarettes or use drugs. You drink alcohol just on occasion – a glass of wine with dinner, or 1 or 2 cocktails on weekends when you go out with friends. You take your health and fitness rather seriously and like to exercise at the gym before work and go on longer jogs on weekends. You have felt too ill to exercise this week.

**Your role is to portray a patient who has come to the doctor’s office expecting to receive a prescription for antibiotics for your symptoms. You have an extremely hectic work life, and you want to get over your symptoms as soon as possible. You are also stressed out by being ill during this busy work time and by having to miss several hours of work today just to go to the doctor’s office. You are also frustrated by the long wait this morning and you are hoping to just get your prescription and return to work as quickly as possible. You are not expecting to be told that you don’t need antibiotics.**

<u>Emotional Tone:</u>

You are dressed in formal work clothes (pantsuit or blouse/skirt)

When the student enters the room, you are on your cell phone speaking with your assistant at work telling her that you are running late at the doctor’s office, but that you are coming in as soon as you can and will make it to your afternoon meeting.

You finish your conversation and hang up the phone when the student arrives.

Your demeanor is rushed, a little frustrated by the need to get back to work. You are eager to wrap things up. At the same time, you are a little run down from your cold; and you are here because you just want to get better as soon as possible.

The student will discuss the plan with you. “I think that you have a viral upper respiratory infection or cold. The best treatment for this is rest and fluids because your symptoms will most likely get better on their own. There are some medications that we can give you for your symptoms, but you don’t need antibiotics at this time.”

You are truly surprised when the student states that you don’t need antibiotics. You should express this surprise and initially challenge the student when he/she states that you don’t need antibiotics.

**“What do you mean I don’t need antibiotics? It’s what I got last year when I had the same exact symptoms, and I know that they worked right away.”**

	**“How do you know I don’t need antibiotics? Isn’t this bronchitis or sinusitis? I have horrible nasal congestion and a constant cough. It’s so disruptive for me at work. At work, people stare at me like I’m going to get them all sick and I feel like nobody wants to be around me. Don’t you give antibiotics for this?** 

As the student explains why he doesn’t think that antibiotics are necessary or even why they might be harmful, you get more frustrated. You start to express anger because you feel like you are not getting treatment for illness, and you feel that you have wasted time in coming to the doctor’s office. You can respond with more questions, to defend yourself and keep your guard up. Your tone is angrier.

**“These symptoms are horrible. I have to get better right away. The Nyquil doesn’t do anything for me. I know that I need something stronger. Isn’t there something strong that you could give me?”**

**“I had to wait an hour and a half just to see a doctor and now you are telling me that I don’t need antibiotics. I feel like I just wasted my entire morning.”**

	**“I don’t feel like you are really doing anything to help me. Isn’t that the point of coming to the doctor’s office?”**

You are angry, mostly out of frustration. You feel like there has been no point for you to come to the doctor’s office only to be told that you don’t need antibiotics. You speak quickly and somewhat angrily because you feel that the student doesn’t understand your symptoms and your need to get better right away.

**“I don’t think you know the kind of stress I’m going through right now. I can’t be sick right now.”**

The student must make a connection with Natalie Smith and show empathy towards her. S/He must acknowledge her frustration and the stress that she is feeling towards missing work and let her feel safe in expressing this anger.  If the student acknowledges the reason for Natalie’s anger and frustration and validates her emotions:

“You seem to be under a lot of stress at work. It must be difficult to be sick during this time.”

“I’m sorry that you feel as though you wasted your time. It must be very hard for you to miss work even to go to a doctor’s appointment. We can talk about medications besides antibiotics that might relieve some of your symptoms.”

“I’m sorry that you had to wait such a long time. I know that it’s hard when you are trying to get back to work.”

Then Natalie’s attitude changes and you gradually become more cooperative.

**“I just want to feel better now. Are there any medications that might help me now?”**

	**“I know that I probably just need to rest, but the problem is that I feel like I can’t do that right now.”**

The student may also try to explain why antibiotics are not helpful and may be harmful when used to treat viral infections, such as the upper respiratory infection that you have.

“Using antibiotics will not help viral infections in any way and will not shorten the duration of symptoms.”

“Using antibiotics can give you unwanted side effects such as diarrhea or increasing your risk for developing a yeast infection.”

“Overusing antibiotics may make the antibiotics less effective against actual bacterial infections.”

Natalie may ultimately accept the student’s reasons for stating that antibiotics are not an appropriate treatment right now. However, it is more important that the student acknowledges Natalie’s anger and tries to relieve her frustration and concerns.

If the student is defensive and does not acknowledge Natalie’s frustration, then she will ultimately accept the treatment plan, but she will continue to express doubts that it will work.

**“Fine. Just give me whatever you think I need to get rid of my symptoms. I have to leave now anyway. If I still feel lousy I’m probably going to have to go to another doctor’s office and lose another morning of work for this.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

private_patient_context:
**Patient Complaint(s):** Patient feels their behavior is misunderstood by family members. The patient's chief complaint: "My spouse and my brother insisted that I come in. They think I need help, but it's just some stress I'm having with work."

**Patient Name:** John/Joan Marriot

**Patient Presentation:** Middle-age. Physically healthy-appearing. Loquacious with rapid speech. Difficulty sitting still. Elated affect.

**Necessary equipment, props, makeup, moulage, costume, etc.:** Religious/New Age reading material (can be a journal with flyers), crystal/pendant, all-white or very colorful attire.

Standardized Patient Training Summary

Opening Statement: "My spouse and my brother insisted that I come in. They think I need help but it's just some stress I'm having with work."

**Summary of case:**

You are a middle-aged (35 to 50-year old) married adult who is employed as a budget analyst for a military contractor. Your spouse recommended that you see a psychiatrist because they were concerned with your erratic behavior recently. Particularly concerning to them are your personality changes, that you are now very excitable and talking about a "soulmate" who is not your spouse, and your new-found religiosity. They also say that your boss has expressed concern about your work performance. You agreed to the evaluation, but think they are "concerned over nothing."

Patient Affect and Attitude:

**Physical:** You stand, and remain standing, acting very animated and excited for about 20 seconds when the medical student enters the room, and you introduce yourself using your full name: John/Joan Fitzgerald Marriott ("My mother had a thing for the Kennedys!!"). You are extremely excited about your new spiritual group and feel it is your duty and privilege to impart your feelings upon whoever will listen. You are also fidgeting a lot, and frequently stand up to pace around. You are generally cooperative with the interview, but get distracted and have a hard time staying sitting still or on topic.

**Verbal:** You speak clearly but very rapidly. You are friendly, and your tone is exceedingly upbeat. You smile and even chuckle at times during the interview. You go off on some verbal tangents during the interview.

*** At some point in the interview, you ask the student if it would be okay to hold their hands to release "negative energy" as this is something you were taught in the religious group. Many students will decline, which you accept after asking, "Are you sure? I think it will be very helpful to you." If your offer is accepted, you should proceed to lightly squeeze both hands for ten seconds while closing your eyes, then releasing them with the comment, "There's a lot of energy there."

**Recent History:**

For the last 2 months, you have been spending a lot of time with a spiritual group of people and report that you are now a "New Age Believer". You have joined a group called "The Third Mind". You do not see the group as a "religion in the traditional sense of the word" but as "my spiritual anchor." The leader of the group is referred to as "The Ella". Her real name is Alice Clark. With this group of people, you feel appreciated and loved, and it was at one of these meetings where you met your "soulmate." The group is located in a store front in a strip mall near your house. You were walking by an open door and made eye contact with someone inside, and "were drawn in, like there was some sort of immediate connection." When asked to provide details about this group, you are unable to be too specific about the group or its beliefs. For the last couple of months, you have spent all of your free time reading about spirituality, new age philosophy, and mysticism.

Other Recent Behaviors:

* You just charged $500 worth of books on these topics on a credit card, which is now past the credit limit. You also report a need to buy some more appropriate new clothes that are more fitting for a "New Age Believer". You withdrew $700 from your savings account last week to buy some clothes that reflect your "new spiritual wisdom."
* You have found that you no longer need much sleep, and are sleeping 2 to 4 hours each night, waking up energetic and either reading or entering New Age chat rooms on your computer. "It's great. It's amazing how much I can get done."
* You have also started weight lifting for the first time in 10 years, and spend 2 hours per day at the gym. "My body is a temple."
* Your appetite has been normal.
* You feel like you might be the Archangel Michael, but you aren't sure. You don't believe you have any special powers, and you aren't hearing voices.
* You have been having a lot of insight lately into spirituality and are keeping a journal with you to jot down all of these thoughts. You think that this book might be a future "Bible-like" text for others.
* If asked about your relationship with your spouse, you note that your spouse is never interested in your beliefs, and that over the past 4 days you have concluded your spouse is not a good match for you.
* You met another adult a few months ago who you feel is your "soulmate," and you are thinking of leaving your spouse. You had sex with this person, a 22-year-old adult, once about 2 months ago. Shortly after that you talked with your spouse about opening the marriage to include this person "in every way." You haven't had sex with either your spouse or this person since then. Your sex drive is high. However, all of your energy is going to your new activities and acquaintances. You are "ecstatic" about the changes in your life. You describe your interest in this person as "beyond sex".

Other Psychiatric Symptoms:

* You do NOT see things or hear things that others do not see or hear.
* Your mood is "wonderful." You are NOT depressed. You are NOT anxious.
* You are NOT suicidal: "Don't be silly. Why would I do that? Life is a wonderful journey."
* You are NOT homicidal or having thoughts of harming others.
* You normally drank about one beer per night, but since you joined the spiritual group you have stopped drinking any alcohol, believing that it will "harm my spirit". You don't use any illicit or over the counter drugs. You do consume about 2 cups of coffee per day. You quit smoking 10 years ago.

**Past Psychiatric History:**

* If asked whether you have ever felt like this before, you indicate that 5 years ago you got very involved in a Protestant Church for a month. You started attending church twice a day and volunteered for activities which conflicted with your job. You missed work during this time period, and your supervisors insisted that you commit to your job or you would be disciplined. You forced yourself to stop participating in all these activities, and after a week or two, you lost interest in this church. You almost had an affair during this time period, but you refrained. You also only slept a few hours per night, but gradually returned to your normal 7 hours. Your spouse insisted you needed help, but you never sought any medical or mental health care.
* You have never been psychiatrically hospitalized, taken psychiatric medications or attended any therapy.
* You have never attempted suicide.

**Past Medical History:** Your physical development was normal and you have been in good health. You do not have any medical problems. You have never had any surgeries or hospitalizations. You do not take any medications.

**Family Psychiatric History:** You are not sure if you have a family history of mental illness, although you remember your mother as having lots of energy followed by periods of moodiness and sadness. She never sought help for this as far as you know.

**Social and Developmental History:**

You are the older of 2 children who were raised by both parents in Baltimore. You describe having a "good" childhood, and were never abused in any way. You were raised as a Roman Catholic, and your family attended church once a week. Your mother was a sales clerk at Sears Roebuck, and your father was an accountant. You describe your mother as "very giving, but I wasn't in tune with that sort of love". You describe your father as "extremely harsh". You have never been close to him, even as an adult. Your parents are both retired and still live together in Baltimore. Your brother, Paul, is 2 years younger, lives nearby, and works as a Dominican priest. You and your brother are on friendly terms, and he is usually a good source of support to you. However, at times you worry about his motivations, and feel he is jealous of your brains, skills, looks, family and, most recently, your spiritual insights.

You did well in school and report that you could have graduated early, but you chose not to. You had some good friends in high school, and you almost got expelled senior year for lighting a firecracker in a pipe in a water fountain. Although you were suspended for that, you never had any troubles with the law. You attended college, got a BA in liberal arts, worked for a while at a local community college before becoming a government contractor. You met your spouse, a nurse, while in college, and you have been married since shortly after college. You have 3 children, ages 20, 19, and 15, and you get along alright with each of them. Your kids will appreciate you later, through your "writings".

You work as a budget analyst and oversee a large government contract for computer services provided to the military. The contract involves about 200 employees located in 3 states that are overseen by 5 or 6 program managers. The program managers are your primary contacts. You describe being bored with your job, particularly with the lack of challenge. You are angry about being passed over for promotion twice, and feel that your company has not appreciated your skills. When asked about problems at work, you describe being "talked to a couple of times" for missing work to attend the religious meetings and working on your book. You say that coworkers comment about you "having a lot of energy but get nothing done," and "talk too much about this religious group." Your retort is that "They just don't understand." You have no history of marital problems, legal problems, or previous thoughts of divorce.

**NOTES on BEHAVIOR/RESPONSES, ATTITUDE TOWARD STUDENT:** In general, you are familiar and very friendly with the student. If the student suggests a plan of treatment, you remain pleasant, but secure in your conviction that you don't need help. You might react to a request to come back in or to talk to the student's attending physician by saying, "If it'll make you feel better, knock yourself out," or, if the student suggests medication, "My body is a temple; I don't take medications." If the student brings up a "manic" diagnosis, you laugh that off. You might ask if there is some sort of conspiracy between your spouse, your brother, and the student, but you remain pleasant.

question_text:
**Not getting infected tooth pulled**

Presentation to Student:

A 40 year old patient you are seeing back in the emergency department for the second visit in a week for tooth pain. On last visit, you diagnosed them with an infected tooth and referred them to the dentist for tooth extraction. The patient is back with worse pain and a fever, after failing to schedule a dental appointment. You are concerned that if the tooth doesn’t get extracted the patient might get a serious infection and need surgery.
private_patient_context:
**Not getting infected tooth pulled**

Information for the Standardized Patient:

40 years old

History: You have returned for a second visit to the ER with complaints of progressive achy tooth pain, as high as 7/10, currently 3/10, and have now had fever to 101 at home. Your tooth hurts on your right lower jaw, and you haven’t been able to eat much because of the pain. You acknowledge that the doctor referred you to a dentist, but you were too scared of the dentist to make the appointment. You’ve had bad experiences with dentists in the past and figured the pain would go away, which it hasn’t. It’s been about 15 years since you last saw a dentist, and that was for a cavity. You are worried that if you tooth gets worse, you’ll get a serious infection and need surgery, which you heard happening to one of your friends’ coworkers.

ROS: fever to 101 last night, decreased oral intake due to pain

PMH: no other medical problems

Family history: none

Social history: no tobacco, alcohol or illegal drug use

No medications or allergies

MI Information

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? Patient’s goal is to avoid surgery, which would be even worse than seeing a dentist.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Not seeing a dentist to get the infected tooth pulled puts you at risk for a more serious infection and need for surgery.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? Avoiding the dentist allows negative reinforcement of patient’s fear of dentists.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? Patient is afraid of needing a surgery.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Being healthy and being able to avoid surgery.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past). Asking for laughing gas, taking a trusted friend with you to the dentist for emotional support, etc.
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 5
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? Not lower because patient really doesn’t want surgery.
    - How could you move that number higher? Thinking about how getting a surgery would be worse than going to a dentist.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 6
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You are also afraid of the doctor but you are able to push yourself to go by taking a trusted friend with you to the appointment.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Getting a friend to accompany you to the appointment.
* Ask for a decision. Patient will call a friend and ask them to go to the dentist appointment with them.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? Call the friend, make another dentist appointment.
* What do you intend to do? Make another dentist appointment and call a friend for help.

**A Covert Standardized Patient with Medication-Induced QT Prolongation**

**Part B**

**Identifying Case Factors**

**Presenting Complaint**: "I have fainted twice in the past few days."

Case Summary/SP Training Notes

**SP demographics**: Patrick Smith is a 65 year old male who is visiting family/friends in the area.

**Setting**: Patrick Smith is visiting the area from out-of-town. (Props include paper-based intake forms because there is no record of the patient in the electronic health system.) Patrick recently retired and decided to drive across country to visit various friends and family members along the way. During the trip across the country, Patrick experienced a "respiratory bug" and stopped at an urgent care clinic where he was given a prescription for an antibiotic to treat a sinus infection and bronchitis. Patrick is still taking the antibiotic and has almost a week's worth of medications remaining.

Since arriving to town, Patrick has experienced two episodes of fainting - both of which were witnessed by friends/family. Patrick's family/friends suggested that Patrick make an appointment to come to the Family Medicine practice today because of these episodes - the most recent of which occurred last night. The physician that Patrick is seeing today is a friend of the family and graciously agreed to see Patrick.

The first time Patrick fainted was immediately after arrival when straining to pick up his suitcase to carry it into the house. Last night, Patrick and friends were coming home from dinner when a car in the neighborhood backfired; the sudden loud noise caused another fainting incident. Fortunately, Patrick did not get injured either time, and Patrick was not unconscious for long. Patrick feels fine at the moment. Patrick has noticed a fluttery sensation in his chest a few times during the past few days, but other than that, Patrick believes that he has always been relatively healthy. Patrick has not experienced any chest pain with these episodes.

Patrick expresses concern about a heart attack. He has recently lost a close friend from a heart attack.

**History of present complaint**: Patrick has fainted twice since arriving in town.

**Past medical history**: Patrick's health overall has been good compared to many other friends of the same age. Prior to the recent respiratory infection, the only medical conditions that Patrick has had include: high blood pressure that's been controlled with a simple "water" pill, long-standing asthma, and a recent diagnosis of a toenail fungal infection. Patrick has a list of medications that include:

* **Hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg** daily for blood pressure
* **Fluticasone/salmeterol diskus 500/50** to be used twice daily for asthma. If the students do not ask specifically how the medications are being used, Patrick should volunteer that he has been using the diskus several times a day for the last week or so - since the respiratory infection has been causing his chest to feel tight with more coughing/wheezing.
* **Itraconazole 200 mg** daily. This is to be used for 12 weeks for the nail fungus. Patrick has used it for 2 months thus far.
* **Clarithromycin XL 500 mg** to be taken as 2 tablets daily in the morning for 2 weeks for a respiratory infection. Patrick has used one week of the tablets thus far.
* **Note:** if asked, Patrick does NOT currently have a short-acting "rescue" inhaler (e.g. no albuterol) and has not had one for several years. He uses the fluticasone/salmeterol diskus extra times when needed for chest tightness/coughing/wheezing.

**Social history**:

Occupation: retired; Patrick had owned his own photography business and was fortunate to be able to retire earlier this year at 65

Marital status: divorced

Life details: 2 adult daughters

Health Insurance: Blue Cross and Blue Shield Plan

Alcohol: Not daily, but sometimes has an occasional glass of wine or cocktail probably 5 times a week

Tobacco: never smoked

Caffeine: 3 cups per day

Drugs (illicit): no illicit drug use

Exercise: no formal program. Patrick intends to begin walking more.

**Physical examination** (This information is to be shared with the student during the review of systems and physical examination - even if the student does not explicitly ask):

Cardiovascular: Patrick has not experienced any chest pain -- only noticed a "fluttering" sensation in the chest occasionally. BP is 122/82 mm Hg and is controlled only by hydrochlorothiazide.

Pulmonary: Patrick has a history of asthma. Patrick feels that in general, his asthma is reasonably well-controlled. He just uses extra inhalations of the diskus whenever he has symptoms. Since developing the recent respiratory infection, Patrick has been using the diskus more than twice a day. No wheezing currently.

Ears/Eyes/Nose/Throat: Patrick has noticed that his voice sounds lower and more raspy than it used to be and wonders what could be causing that change in the sound of his voice?

Neurological: Patrick has noticed that he has been having trouble sleeping - feels "wired" and "jittery" and has trouble "getting my brain to turn off". Patrick is currently alert and oriented.

Gastrointestinal: no significant findings

If the student does not suggest an electrocardiogram, Patrick should ask, "Isn't there a test you can do to look at my heart to make sure it is okay? I am so worried about having a heart attack since my friend died of one recently."

**Patient's response to special interviewing techniques**:

The SP should wait to be asked questions by the student and not volunteer information except where noted. Patrick should be poised and self-assured, though clearly concerned about his health condition - since he has a long drive home and does not want to faint while driving. Patrick should seek clarification from the student if the student uses medical jargon. Patrick should ask for clarification if any information is unclear, e.g. "What does that mean?"

Patrick is given additional information about the use of the diskus if students ask additional questions. For example, if the student asks how the diskus is used, Patrick should respond, "I use it whenever I feel like I need it - sometimes several times a day. Sometimes, I'm not sure if I actually get any medicine when I breathe in, so I make sure by using it again." If the student asks if Patrick takes a drink after using the diskus, Patrick should respond that "No one ever told me to do that."

**Special Considerations**:

* **Specific body type/physical requirements**: Patrick should wear closed-toed shoes so the medical student cannot see the toenail fungus for which he is taking itraconazole.
* **Props**: a medication list can be provided if it is difficult to remember the names and dose of medications; paper copies of the initial patient intake form used by the outpatient practice should be completed.

  • No fever
  • No nausea or vomiting

Social Hx

  • You are in an executive position
  • No smoking
  • You like having a beer almost every evening, and you rarely would have more than one
  • You are divorced and live alone
  • You have never used illicit drugs
  • Your sexual life is “sporadic”
  • Your two sons live in Texas with their families
  • You have good insurance (Blue Cross and Blue Shield)
  • You love Mexican food and you believe that cooking with lard makes it tastier

Family Medical Hx

  • Both your parents had hypertension
  • Your father is living with your brother in El Paso, Texas, on the border with Mexico; your mother is deceased – she died of complications of diabetes last year

Physical Exam Findings:

  • BP 220/125; HR 105 bpm; RR 18 /min; T 37˚C (98.6 F)
