  • Your R hand is held close to your abdomen, with fingers in a relaxed fist and elbow slightly flexed (so it is not overly noticeable to the student)
  • Your R leg is somewhat “stiff” and held extended when you walk; you try to quickly transfer the weight from your R leg to your L, because the R is “clumsy” (only if the student asks you to walk)
  • You walk without fully bending right knee and your right foot/ toes point down – “circumduction gait” (only if the student asks you to walk)
  • You speak with slight difficulty – see “special instructions” below
  • On the right side, your tendon reflexes are stronger than normal – you will be trained
  • You are oriented for self, date, time but you have difficulty speaking
  • Your tongue deviates to the left when asked to show it
  • When asked to move against resistance, on the right side, your extremities are weak
  • Babinski (+) R foot

Special Instructions:

  • You will be trained for the physical exam findings
  • You are collaborative, answer all questions
  • You act worried about your bad headache and do not mention the weakness in your right body (R arm and R leg) – these should come out during physical exam, and if the student asks you to walk. You pretend you have not really noticed this weakness and changed gait; you have attributed how you feel to “being very tired”
  • You should be sitting on the examination table, so you do not have to move from the chair and reveal early the problem with walking and R side weakness
  • From time to time you use word description instead of the correct word (example: “that thing you write with” instead of “pen”) or you use the wrong word (“clock” instead of “watch”)
  • You pronounce the words correctly, but your speech is in short phrases and monotonous (you play that you do not notice that!)
  • Your comprehension is intact – you understand everything you are told/asked
  • You called your son this morning to drive you to the doctor’s office because you did not feel well; you felt somewhat tired and weak
  • You are worried about the headache but not about your blood pressure because “high BP runs in your family”
  • If the student asks where you got the Lasix from, you will explain that your brother (as well as the rest of your family members living in El Paso, Texas) often go across the border and buy medications in Mexico, where you do not need a prescription and the prices are much cheaper. Your brother helps you get from Mexico any medication you need.
  • Again: you pretend you have not really noticed the weakness in your R. body, and if asked during physical exam/walking, you act surprised

question_text:
**PTSD STANDARDIZED PATIENT**

MEDICAL STUDENT INSTRUCTIONS

(to be read prior to the interview)

You are a first year medical student tasked with conducting a medical interview. Your primary goal is to take a patient history using open-ended questions and listening skills, in order to facilitate responses which encourage and clarify the patient’s story. Mr. “Bob” Roberts is today’s patient and this is his first time being seen in this office. Mr. Roberts is married, currently employed, and a veteran. His wife made this appointment for him due to his problems with sleep and the impact that it is having on his life and their relationship. Difficulties with sleep has been a persistent problem which has led to a general feeling of fatigue and lack of energy.
private_patient_context:
**PTSD STANDARDIZED PATIENT: “BOB ROBERTS”**

1. **Chief Complaint**
   * Bob is concerned about the trouble he has had with falling and staying asleep. This has been a persistent problem and the patient believes it has led to a general feeling of fatigue and lack of energy.

1. **Detailed Description of the Case**

* **Type of Encounter –** New patient / Office Visit
* **Location –** Doctor’s office located in the community
* **Description of the Patient –** Bob is a 45 year old Veteran of the United States Navy. He has been healthy for the most part but has been struggling with issues regarding his sleep (i.e. falling asleep, staying asleep, wakes easily). He graduated high school and attended college for two years on the G.I. Bill earning enough credits to receive an associate’s degree. He currently works as a mechanic but has had several jobs over the past 10 years and would be listed in the middle to lower class income range.
* **Patient Behavior, Affect, Mannerisms –** Bob is not very talkative and answers somewhat brusquely, but he is not hostile nor is he disrespectful. He does not offer information unless it is asked for by the physician. Bob’s demeanor is fidgety as he does not sit still very well and constantly looks around the room. He appears uncomfortable while waiting in the office. He also appears to be startled by the sound of the office paging system.
* **Patient’s Agenda –** Bob has decided to come for a physical because his wife, Jane, has been extremely frustrated by his inability to sleep. She has been pushing him to see a doctor and his reluctance to this point has caused arguing at home. It should also be noted that because Bob has had several job changes over the years, there were often periods of time when he and his wife lacked health insurance. Bob has attempted to use sleep aids but abandoned the effort because of how they made him feel the following day. Jane has been insistent on this appointment as she has become frustrated from Bob’s tossing and turning and constant wandering of the house during the night, as well as his waking up screaming from bad dreams.

1. **Patient History**

* **HPI -** Bob will eventually report that he has had trouble with both falling and staying asleep for the past 24 years. Over the years his trouble sleeping has caused problems with his marriage as well as at work. Bob has been received written warnings at work for falling asleep during his shift. Shortly after being discharged from the Navy, Bob sought the guidance of a physician for his “insomnia” and was prescribed Ambien. After 6 months of use, Bob stopped taking the prescription because he reported feeling drowsy during the day. Bob believes the medication caused him to fall asleep at work resulting in some of his problems.
* Additionally, Bob has struggled with persistent headaches and becomes irritable easily. This has caused interpersonal problems with co-workers and supervisors over the years. He was recently reprimanded at work for a verbal altercation with his supervisor and received a written warning for his language and behavior.
* **Current Prescribed Medications –** Lisinopril for hypertension, which he has been taking for 5 years.
* **Relevant Past Medical History –** Bob was involved in a fire aboard a naval vessel during his service receiving burns over 20% of his body. Scarring is visible on the forearms and hands which Bob received while attempting to pull victims from the fire. Bob was treated in a naval hospital and was discharged following several weeks of care. He completed his service with no other injuries or medical treatment.

Other than his time in the Navy, Bob has not been admitted or treated for any major injury or illness.

**Fire/Injury –** Bob will eventually report the following story regarding the accident and subsequent injury received. This will be a difficult story for him to tell. (**SP** **Note\* - When asked by the medical student, the Standard Patient should become visibly nervous and uncomfortable. The SP should take his time and give the impression that he was caught off guard by having to tell the story**).

According to Bob, he was stationed aboard a guided-missile destroyer (USS Conyngham). He was a mechanic working on a problem identified in an area adjacent to the engine room. Bob had just come on duty for his tour when the explosion happened. The explosion was deafening and knocked Bob and several of his co-workers to the ground. Because the shifts were changing, there were more sailors in the area than normal. Bob was knocked unconscious momentarily. When he regained consciousness, he heard screaming and smelled smoke as much of the area was on fire. (**SP** **Note\* - When asked by the medical student, Bob will mention the sounds, the shaking of the boat, and the smell of burning flesh.)**

Because Bob was in the process of picking up the tools he needed, he was further away from the explosion and was not immediately injured. His forearms and hands were burned while he was pulling two sailors from the fire.

It was later determined that the accident was caused by an overworked generator that Bob had serviced one month prior to the accident. Although he was not blamed for the accident, Bob felt some responsibility for the explosion and fire. Several months later, Bob and several other sailors were awarded the Navy Commendation Medal for their bravery and heroism during the rescue attempt. (**SP** **Note\* Because Bob feels that he is somewhat responsible for the accident, he has feelings of guilt. He should become irritated when asked if he received a medal for his actions).**

**Relevant Social History**

* **Marital Status/Family Status** – Bob has been married to his wife Jane for 6 years. This is his second marriage as his first lasted 16 years ending in a divorce. Although Bob and Jane have been married for 6 years, they have had periods of separation with the longest time frame approximately 5 months.
* **Military History:** Bob was in the US Navy for 4 years. During the latter part of his enlistment, he served on the guided-missile destroyer USS Conyngham out of Norfolk, Virginia. He was discharged honorably at the rank of E-4, Petty Officer 3rd Class.
* **Living Environment** – Bob currently lives with his second wife and son in a home that is rented.
* **Drug Use** – Experimented with Marijuana, with last use approximately 24 years ago when in the Navy.
* **Alcohol Use** – Drinks 2-3 beers a day and 2 six-packs on the weekend. Bob will report that he drinks to help him sleep at night. (Bob – “I only drink to fall asleep”)
* **Tobacco Use** – Currently does not smoke.
* **Work Environment** – Bob does not socialize with his co-workers. Since he has shown agitation on a number of occasions, many of his co-workers stay clear of Bob and often don’t invite him to any type of non-work related gathering. Bob’s supervisor is unaware of his military history and therefore has little tolerance for Bob’s behavior. This has led to several verbal warnings and at least one written.
* **Sexual History** – heterosexual

**Relevant Vocational History**

* **How does their job affect their health? –** Bob is currently working as a mechanic but has had several jobs over the past 10 years. Although he works well alone, he has had interpersonal problems consistently over the years. Work can sometimes be difficult for Bob because load noises can cause him to startle. Unfortunately some of his co-workers have noticed this and attempt to startle him purposely to see his reaction.

**Relevant Family History**

* Bob has two children (Steven 20 and Emily 18). Although Bob’s first wife was granted custody of the children, Steven chose to move in with his father when he turned 18.
* Parents – Deceased (Father passed away from a heart attack, Mother passed from complications due to diabetes)
* Siblings - None
* Does not socialize with friends

**Review of Systems**

* GI distress – routinely has problems with digestion, stomach cramping and diarrhea
* Headaches
* Hypertension

1. **Prop List**

* Clothing worn should be coveralls (grease stains if possible)
* Burn scars on hands and forearms
* US Navy Veteran hat

1. **Instructions for Standard Patient**

**(Entry points and specific triggers causing minor irritation)**

**Entry Points** – Since this scenario was designed for a first year medical student, several “entry points” were written into the scenario to give the learner cues as to the patient’s history. Examples of these entry points include the burn scars on the forearm and hands of the patient as well as the hat clearly identifying “US Navy Veteran”. Another entry point would be the clothing worn by the standard patient (grease stained coveralls). These visual cues give the learner clear starting points for questions that can be asked in the process of capturing the patient’s medical and social history.

**Behavioral Cues -** The Standard Patient should become visibly agitated, uncomfortable, or fidgety at specific times during the interview. Examples of visible agitation displayed by the Standard Patient could be:

* Shifting in the chair
* Getting up from the chair and pacing
* Sighing heavily
* Intense eye contact or staring at the learner
* Throwing arms and hands in the air with a disgusted look
* Looking away from the learner (taking long periods of time looking around the room)

**Student Instructions**

You are a primary care physician. You are seeing Robert McInnis, a veteran who has just been discharged from the hospital after a new heart failure diagnosis. He was advised to see his primary care provider for follow-up after his discharge.

You are expected to:

1. **Perform a FOCUSED assessment** to evaluate Mr. McInnis’ current medication-related needs.
2. **Develop** an appropriate medication-related plan
3. **Communicate** the medication plan to Mr. McInnis in a way that satisfies his concerns about taking more medications, whether they are the “right” medications, what should be “watched out for”, and how he will know if the medications are working

**CHART NOTES**

Temperature: 37.4 degrees C

Pulse: 84/minute

Respirations: 17/minute

Blood pressure: 168/94 mmHg
private_patient_context:
Heart Failure

STATION NAME: Heart Failure

PATIENT NAME: Robert McInnis

PRESENTING SITUTION: Robert McInnis is a 70 year old man who was just discharged from the Veterans Affairs (VA) Medical Center recently due to an admission for heart failure. He is here to see you, his primary care provider in private practice, today as a follow-up to that admission. Although as a veteran he is able to get free care with the VA health system, he harbors a great deal of distrust of the government and maintains you as his PCP.

ACTIVITIES: Assessing the situation (10 min)

Leave room and develop a plan (10 minutes)

Return to room and provide patient with information to satisfy his concerns (10 minutes)

**STANDARDIZED PATIENT INSTRUCTIONS**

**CASE SYNOPSIS**

You are Robert McInnis, a retired, lifetime military man.

**WHY YOU ARE SEEING THE DOCTOR TODAY**

You were discharged from the local VA Medical Center recently. Last week, your son and his family had come to visit. They noticed how winded you were just walking around the house. You could barely make it up the stairs. They also pointed out to you how **swollen your feet and ankles were**. You didn’t admit it to them at the time, but you had also noticed that you recently started waking up in the middle of the night because you were **short of breath**.

In the hospital, the doctors told you that you have heart failure. They hooked you up to a bunch of machines and gave you all sorts of drugs. After four or five days, you came home. **They sent you home with a bunch of new prescriptions** which you have with you and you have not filled. **You hate taking medicines and you already put enough “poison” in your body with the other pills that your PCP (the doctor that you are currently seeing) had prescribed previously.**

You are here today at the insistence of your wife and son because the VA doctors told you to follow up with your PCP. You think all of this concern about your health and all of the new medications that they gave you are “hogwash”. You are **grumpy and a little tired since they don’t let you get “any sleep at all in the hospital –always someone poking or prodding at all hours of the night**”.

Opening Statement

Your initial statement should relate to only being here because my family is making me. For example:

The student may ask: “Why did you come to the clinic today?”

* You could respond: “**My family made me**.”

The student may say something like: “Good morning. How are you feeling?”

* You could respond: “**Well, I’ve been better**.”

**HOW YOU APPEAR DURING THE ENCOUNTER**

**Physical description**

* You should be reasonably neat and well groomed
* You should wear comfortable clothes that a retired man would wear when visiting his primary care provider

**Description of affect and behavior**

* You are gruff around the edges, but receptive to at least listen to your doctor.
* You view the VA system and the current government with distrust.
* You are tired, but otherwise feel fine.
* You are able to sit up, stand, and walk just fine.
* You are intelligent
* You have a “tough” exterior disposition & dislike appearing vulnerable
* **You are open to the doctor explaining what heart failure is**
* **You are open to the doctor explaining the new medications you were prescribed – why they are necessary and how they work**
* **You are open to the doctor explaining how you can be actively involved with monitoring your symptoms**
* **You are open to the doctor explaining how s/he will monitor you for side effects of the medications**

**Review of Systems**

**Cardiovascular:** You have a hard time describing it, but you have experienced a sensation where it feels like your heart is beating extra hard (palpitations) sometimes. You have not had chest pain. You haven’t exercised regularly since you retired 12 years ago.

**Pulmonary**: You have noticed that you had trouble catching your breath before your hospitalization. You were “getting winded” just walking across the room. Walking up stairs had become increasingly difficult. You were beginning to think that all those year of smoking when you were in your 20s, 30s, and 40s had caught up with you. In fact, you were starting to wonder if this was an early sign of lung cancer; you were “in denial” about “being winded” and had not mentioned it to anyone.

**Musculoskeletal**: You know your feet and ankles were swelling. Before your hospitalization, you were finding that your shoes were harder to put on than normal.

**Medications:**

The VA hospital physicians and your primary care provider have prescribed the following medications for your heart, your asthma, and your BPH over the last couple of years:

**Patient can have a list of these medications in his wallet if it is too difficult to remember.**

* You were prescribed diltiazem 360 mg daily by a VA hospital physician about 5 years ago at an annual physical. You were told something about high blood pressure. But you felt fine. You took the medication sometimes, but you admit to skipping a number of doses because you didn’t feel any different whether you took it or not.
* You use Advair twice daily for asthma.
* You use albuterol. Historically, you had rarely used it, but during the last couple of months, you’ve been using 2 puffs about four times a day – sometimes even more. You were using it often because you were feeling short of breath, but you don’t think that it had really helped.
* You use Proscar 5 mg daily for BPH (benign prostatic hypertrophy)
* You use Terazosin 10 mg daily for BPH

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Drug** | **Dosage** | **Notes** |
| Diltiazem | 360 mg daily | Blood pressure |
| Advair puffer disk | 500/50 2x/day | Asthma |
| Albuterol inhaler | 2 puffs 4x/day and whenever needed | Asthma |
| Proscar | 5 mg daily | Prostate |
| Terazosin | 10 mg daily | Prostate |

**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY**

**Overall Health:**

Until the past few months, you had been feeling fine. During the past couple of months, you had noticed that you became “winded” pretty easily. You were afraid that it was lung cancer – from all those years of smoking when you were younger. You weren’t ready to accept that this “might be the end” so you ignored the problems you were having until your family took you to the hospital.

Since you were waking up more during the night during the past couple of months because of difficulties breathing, you also recognized that you were getting up several times during the night to use the bathroom –which also had made you concerned about having more serious “prostate problems”.

While you use your inhalers and take your prostate medications every morning, you were never very good at taking that other pill they gave you for the blood pressure --primarily because you didn’t feel like you had any problems – so why take a pill for something that doesn’t even cause any problems since the drug would probably just cause side effects and you felt fine.

Until this recent hospitalization, you had never been hospitalized. In addition to the high blood pressure, you have asthma and prostate troubles.

**FAMILY HISTORY**

**Parents:** died in their 80s. Father had been a pastor; had a heart attack. Mother was a home-maker; died following complications associated with a broken hip.

**Grandparents:** never knew them; died before he was born

**Brothers/sisters:** two brothers, ages 75 and 73. Typical “old people problems” like cataracts, high blood pressure, blood thinners

**Children:** one son, age 42; he is married and has 2 kids

**PRESENT LIFE**

**Age**: 70

**Marital status**: married for 37 years; spouse, age 65, is in good health

**Life details**: you have one son who lives 2 hours away. You have a good relationship with your spouse. You fought in Vietnam and served at Fort Indiantown Gap until you retired from the military at age 55.

**Health Insurance**: Blue Cross

**Personal habits**:

**Alcohol**: 1-2 beers per day; occasionally more on the weekends

**Tobacco**: smoked for 30 years, but quit about 20 years ago

**Caffeine**: about 2 cups of coffee each morning

**Drugs (illicit)**: None

**Vitamin and dietary supplements**: none

**Exercise**: no formal program. You always intended to be more physically active once you retired, but it just hasn’t happened.

**HOW YOU WILL RESPOND TO DIFFERENT INTERVIEWING STYLES**

You are gruff and skeptical of the VA health system. You are not even entirely sure how you feel about the medical system in general, but you feel as if your primary care provider will “tell you like it is”. You expect that the student is a competent, concerned, and straight-forward physician. You do not try to dominate the encounter. You wait for the student to take the lead.

If the student uses medical jargon, e.g. “workload of the heart”, “systolic dysfunction”, “diastolic dysfunction”, “edema”, “jugular distension”, etc. you should request clarification, e.g. “What does that mean?”

1. You will give the physician a stack of new prescriptions that you received from the VA hospital when you were discharged. You haven’t filled them yet because you want to know if it is really necessary for you to take them. You tell the doctor, “**You know, I think all these medications are ridiculous. I don’t want to take them unless you really think they are necessary and they will really help me**.” Then, ask the following questions (NOTE: these questions are the primary goals of the case. Keep re-directing the student back to these because this is what you want to know):
2. “Are all of these pills – the **old ones and the new ones** -- **really necessary**?”
3. My wife read on the internet that **some pills actually CAUSE heart failure. Are you sure that the pills I am already taking haven’t caused this to happen to my heart**?
4. “Are these the **right prescriptions** for me or did the VA just give these to me because the government has a special contract with the drug company for these pills?”
5. “What **side effects** are they going to cause for me?”
6. “How are we going to **know if they are even working** or if they are **causing me to have other problems**?”

**ENDING THE ENCOUNTER**

Ordinarily, the student will end the encounter with a statement such as: “Do you have any questions?” You can reiterate your **concerns about all the new medications – are they are needed, are they the “right ones” for you, how will you know if they are working or causing more problems, what should you “watch out for”, etc. You can ask, “What do I need to know about all these prescriptions and do you think it is really necessary for me to fill them?”**

**Physical Exam Cards**

**Neck**

(+) JVD distension sitting (5 cm); no lymphadenopathy or thyromegaly

**Lungs**

Crakles bilaterally 1/3 of way up; no expiratory wheezing

**Heart**

Irregularly irregular; (+) S3; displaced PMI

**Abdomen**

Soft, mildly tender, non-distended; (-) hepatojugular reflex; no masses, no hepatosplenomegaly; normal bowel sounds

**Genital/Rectal Exam**

Not performed; declined

**Musculoskeletal/External**

1+ pitting edema bilaterally; radial pulses and pedal pulses are intact

question_text:
**Pre-diabetic Who Needs to Lower Carbs**

Presentation to the student
private_patient_context:
**Pre-diabetic Who Needs to Lower Carbs**

Information for the SP:

You are a patient returning to the clinic for a yearly follow up visit. You do not have any medical problems at this time, but your mother is a diabetic with multiple diabetic complications. Your blood sugar is high on your fasting lab work done prior to coming in. You do not have a special diet at this time, you eat a variety of foods, including candy occasionally, and you love to eat Italian food like pasta. After learning that you may have diabetes or prediabetes and further testing is necessary, you are open to making lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise due to your mother’s complications resulting from diabetes.

PMH: none, no medications or allergies.

Family history: mother with type II insulin dependent diabetes with complications of amputation and kidney damage requiring dialysis three times per week.

Social history: you do not smoke, no alcohol intake, no drug use. You are a school teacher.   You don’t exercise regularly.  You have a partner you hope to marry soon.

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health?  Family? Work?  Finances?  You don’t want to end up like your mother, with her amputations and dialysis.  You want to get married to your partner and hopefully have kids soon (you’d like to be active with your kids).
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals?  Continuing to eat pasta and candy, and not exercising, will raise your blood sugar and could get you diabetes, but you need the doctor to explain this to you.  You don’t understand the connection between your eating, lack of exercise, blood sugar, and mother’s health until the doctor explains it to you.
* What are the good things about the target behavior?  How does it benefit you?  You love to cook and you feel comfortable eating pasta because it reminds you of your homeland.  You eat candy with your school kids often and you feel your shared love of candy makes you popular with your kids.  You don’t exercise because it is so hard to find the time.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior?  What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior?  You don’t want to gain weight and you don’t want to develop diabetes or have complications of diabetes.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change?  What are the best reasons to change?  Not ending up like your mother.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): You could get sugar-free candy, you could explore other cuisines with fewer carbohydrates, you could restrict your carbs, you could get your partner on board with helping you change, you could pair up with your mother in eating a diabetic diet.  To begin exercising you could identify another teacher as an exercise buddy and walk the track at lunch, or you could organize an exercise club with the kids and work out with them (before or after school, or at lunch).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 4/10 (low because you really love pasta and candy, and you don’t understand the connection with diabetes and your mom’s complications)
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You want to be healthy, you want to get married and have kids
    - How could you move that number higher? Understanding the connections between your eating and diabetes.  Perhaps making some lifestyle changes with your mother (you would do it for your mother even if you struggled to do it for yourself).
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? Because you really love your mother, and you really don’t want the complications she has had from diabetes.
* What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the connections between eating/exercise and diabetes, understanding the complications that can arise from uncontrolled sugars, exploring diabetic diets, working on your dietary goals with your mother.
* Ask for a decision: You will consider changing your diet and starting to exercise.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals.  What are the first steps? You will talk with your mom about making dietary changes together, you will buy and try sugar free candy, you will learn about healthy eating for diabetics, and you will ask a colleague at work to walk with you at lunch.

question_text:
# Case 1

# Carrie Edwards, Urinary Incontinence

# URINARY INCONTINANCE PATIENT: CARRIE EDWARDS

LEARNER INFORMATION (to be shared with learner prior to role–play)

Patient’s Name: Carrie Edwards

Chief complaint: Unable to keep from leaking urine

Location: VA Primary Care Physician’s Office

Learner Skill Set: Eliciting data in an objective and non-judgmental manner; accurate recording of symptoms; sensitivity; motivational interviewing (MI) skills; self-awareness
private_patient_context:
# CARRIE EDWARDS URINARY INCONTINENCE STANDARDIZED PATIENT TRAINING MATERIALS

# CASE SUMMARY

Carrie Edwards is a married 51-year-old female. She presents to the office at this time because of involuntary urine loss, which has become worse over the past 1-2 years. This has significantly influenced her social life and her ability to maintain normal activities. She thought that her symptoms were normal for a woman her age who had kids. Her girlfriends convinced her that her symptoms were not the norm and that she should be evaluated by her personal physician. Her husband thinks it’s a menopause “thing” and wants her to ask about hormone therapy.

She has not been to the doctor for years as she has been very healthy and has seen no need. She is very independent and “tough,” thinking that it is weak to get sick. She would express the opinion that preventative care is unnecessary. She is horrified at this loss of control over her body.

During the day her urine loss is mostly related to involuntary urine loss on the way to the bathroom, but is occasionally also associated with coughing, sneezing, or laughing. The amount that leaks out when laughing has increased.

Recently she and her husband are now noticing involuntary urine loss with sexual activity. She has noticed an ammonia-like odor. This is what tipped the scale and caused her to make the appointment.

# PAST MEDICAL HISTORY

General health: Good.

Have there been any recent changes in the patient’s health? Just the urinary incontinence.

Any previous Hx of diabetes or hypertension? None. (This is important as worsening disease states can worsen symptoms, especially if patient were on a water pill, which she is not on.)

Any new medications that could potentially worsen her urinary symptoms? None.

Ask open ended or specific questions:

High blood pressure: Not that I know of.

High cholesterol: I don’t think so.

She has not been to the doctor since the birth of her youngest child. She has had no pap smears, no mammograms, and no checkups. She has not seen the need for it since she has been so healthy.

Since the delivery of her last pregnancy over 18 years ago she has had increasing difficulty with involuntary urine loss. Her symptoms began right around then, but have significantly increased over the past 1 to 2 years. Initially it was only associated with rare loss on the way to the bathroom and occasionally having to get out of bed to urinate in the middle of the night.

Over the past 2 years she has noted increasing need to void at night. Initially she was getting up about once a night but that has increased to 3-4 times nightly. She is having increasing difficulty not losing urine on the way to the bathroom to void and is now also experiencing urine loss with coughing, sneezing, or laughing. She generally needs to wear either a maxi pad or an adult diaper to not soil her clothing.

She does not lose gas during sexual activity.

V. Simulators

A. Roles – standardized participant, patient care assistant/nurse, operator and voice of SimMan3G or other high fidelity simulator   
B. Who may play them – standardized participants trained to portray the spouse (age range 22-40), simulation staff member well acquainted with the operation of the high fidelity simulator   
C. Participant Role – what role do they serve in the scenario – the standardized participant serves as the main informant since the high fidelity simulator is short of breath and receiving breathing treatments; the patient care assistant serves a nursing function role and carries out treatment orders for applying oxygen, giving nebulizer treatment, and IV steroid to the SimMan3G; the simulation staff member is the voice of the SimMan3G patient and adjusts the monitor controls based on the intervention rendered.

VI. Case Narrative (describes what the learner will experience)

This simulated clinical encounter takes place in an emergency room setting. The SimMan3G is the patient, Sam Brown. He is accompanied by his significant other, Kelly Walsh. Note that this could be portrayed as a same sex couple if desired. The patient care assistant will also be in the room, ready to perform duties as assigned. The student is expected to initiate the history taking while taking note of monitor settings and the patient’s condition. The student may start examining and treating the patient while obtaining further history from the family member. The student will instruct the patient care assistant to administer treatment rather than directly give the treatment himself. The student will then evaluate the SM3G’s response to the treatment via repeat chest auscultation and review of vital signs. This will aid decision making regarding further actions. Once the student feels that the patient has stabilized, the student will verbalize a disposition, which could be hospitalization or discharge to home with medication and close outpatient follow up.

Case development notes:

The case was designed to give an opportunity to incorporate the functionality of the high fidelity simulator into a SP clinical skills case dealing with asthma exacerbation. All student examinees had reported some level of experience with asthma management based on review of student log data.

The case was conceived and written by Valerie Hearns, MD, Director of OSCE for the University of South Dakota/Sanford School of Medicine. Further development was completed with input from faculty and staff members which included then Director of the Parry Center for Clinical Skills and Simulation, Jeremy Hall MD; Jill Tyler, PhD. Department of Communication Studies, Brian Wallenburg, Simulations specialist and Kimberly Bertsch, Training Specialist both from the Parry Center.

A. Scenario Background Given to Participants (specify if given freely or must be asked for)

After reading the instructions posted outside the room, students become aware that the setting for the case is in the emergency room. The instructions also make it clear that they are working in a team of two students with the help of a patient care assistant. SimMan3G has limited verbal interaction and initially asks the student to speak with Kelly. If asked later he states that he feels a little better after treatment. Kelly provides most of the history when asked for specifics by the student. The patient care assistant does not volunteer any information, but may ask for clarification of orders given if necessary and as the scenario winds down may ask about disposition.

**HIV medication compliance**

Information for the SP:

You are a 55 year old patient with HIV. You were diagnosed about 10 years ago and you have had times when you have taken your medications as directed, and times when you stop taking them. You love your work at a local bookstore and when you are feeling well, it is tough to remember the daily medication. When asked about your hospitalizations, you have had pneumonia multiple times, always when you stopped your HIV medications, and the recovery process is difficult to regain your strength. You have had the discussion with your provider that when your CD4 count is low and viral load is high, you are at risk for more infections. You are agreeable to finding ways to improve remembering your daily medicine, even when you are feeling well. Your boss is frustrated by your frequent use of sick leave and you are now out of sick leave. Your boss has threatened to fire you if you need any more time off work. If you lose your job you will also lose your insurance, and you can’t afford to do that.

PMH: You do not have any additional medical history

Medication: Atripla 1 tablet daily

No allergies, surgeries or family history

Social history: nonsmoker, no alcohol intake, no drug use, work in a bookstore, monogamous relationship with partner for the past 15 years

MI Information

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You love your job at the bookstore and need to continue to work so you can keep your insurance.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? If you don’t take your HIV meds you might need to be hospitalized again, which would threaten your job and insurance.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? Taking HIV meds is a reminder that you are sick, and not taking them allows you to avoid remembering you are sick even when you aren’t feeling sick.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid of another hospitalization, which would threaten your job and insurance.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Staying out of the hospital, being able to continue working, keeping your much needed insurance.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past). You could put reminders in your phone, or download an app that sends you reminders, use pill boxes, pair pill-taking with other well-established behaviors like brushing teeth, etc., put reminders all over the place, enlist your partner’s support to help you remember to take your pills, etc.
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 7
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You really love your job and you really hate the hospital.
    - How could you move that number higher? Take that horrible picture of yourself from your last hospitalization and put it next to your medications.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You remember to take your meds when you are ill, so you know you can do it.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Employing some of the strategies for remembering to take your meds, like apps or text reminders on your phone.
* Ask for a decision. You will look for a reminder app.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will find and download an app in the next week, and you will ask your partner for support.
* What do you intend to do? Look for an app and talk with your partner.

**A Covert Standardized Patient with Medication-Induced QT Prolongation**

**Part B**

**Identifying Case Factors**

**Presenting Complaint**: "I have fainted twice in the past few days."

Case Summary/SP Training Notes

**SP demographics**: Patricia Smith is a 65 year old female who is visiting family/friends in the area.

**Setting**: Patricia Smith is visiting the area from out-of-town. (Props include paper-based intake forms because there is no record of the patient in the electronic health system.) Patricia recently retired and decided to drive across country to visit various friends and family members along the way. During the trip across the country, Patricia experienced a "respiratory bug" and stopped at an urgent care clinic where she was given a prescription for an antibiotic to treat a sinus infection and bronchitis. Patricia is still taking the antibiotic and has almost a week's worth of medications remaining.

Since arriving to town, Patricia has experienced two episodes of fainting - both of which were witnessed by friends/family. Patricia's family/friends suggested that Patricia make an appointment to come to the Family Medicine practice today because of these episodes - the most recent of which occurred last night. The physician that Patricia is seeing today is a friend of the family and graciously agreed to see Patricia.

The first time Patricia fainted was immediately after arrival when straining to pick up her suitcase to carry it into the house. Last night, Patricia and friends were coming home from dinner when a car in the neighborhood backfired; the sudden loud noise caused another fainting incident. Fortunately, Patricia did not get injured either time, and Patricia was not unconscious for long. Patricia feels fine at the moment. Patricia has noticed a fluttery sensation in her chest a few times during the past few days, but other than that, Patricia believes that she has always been relatively healthy. Patricia has not experienced any chest pain with these episodes.

Patricia expresses concern about a heart attack. She has recently lost a close friend from a heart attack.

**History of present complaint**: Patricia has fainted twice since arriving in town.

**Past medical history**: Patricia's health overall has been good compared to many other friends of the same age. Prior to the recent respiratory infection, the only medical conditions that Patricia has had include: high blood pressure that's been controlled with a simple "water" pill, long-standing asthma, and a recent diagnosis of a toenail fungal infection. Patricia has a list of medications that include:

* **Hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg** daily for blood pressure
* **Fluticasone/salmeterol diskus 500/50** to be used twice daily for asthma. If the students do not ask specifically how the medications are being used, Patricia should volunteer that she has been using the diskus several times a day for the last week or so - since the respiratory infection has been causing her chest to feel tight with more coughing/wheezing.
* **Itraconazole 200 mg** daily. This is to be used for 12 weeks for the nail fungus. Patricia has used it for 2 months thus far.
* **Clarithromycin XL 500 mg** to be taken as 2 tablets daily in the morning for 2 weeks for a respiratory infection. Patricia has used one week of the tablets thus far.
* **Note:** if asked, Patricia does NOT currently have a short-acting "rescue" inhaler (e.g. no albuterol) and has not had one for several years. She uses the fluticasone/salmeterol diskus extra times when needed for chest tightness/coughing/wheezing.

**Social history**:

Occupation: retired; Patricia had owned her own photography business and was fortunate to be able to retire earlier this year at 65

Marital status: divorced

Life details: 2 adult daughters

Health Insurance: Blue Cross and Blue Shield Plan

Alcohol: Not daily, but sometimes has an occasional glass of wine or cocktail probably 5 times a week

Tobacco: never smoked

Caffeine: 3 cups per day

Drugs (illicit): no illicit drug use

Exercise: no formal program. Patricia intends to begin walking more.

**Physical examination** (This information is to be shared with the student during the review of systems and physical examination - even if the student does not explicitly ask):

Cardiovascular: Patricia has not experienced any chest pain -- only noticed a "fluttering" sensation in the chest occasionally. BP is 122/82 mm Hg and is controlled only by hydrochlorothiazide.

Pulmonary: Patricia has a history of asthma. Patricia feels that in general, her asthma is reasonably well-controlled. She just uses extra inhalations of the diskus whenever she has symptoms. Since developing the recent respiratory infection, Patricia has been using the diskus more than twice a day. No wheezing currently.

Ears/Eyes/Nose/Throat: Patricia has noticed that her voice sounds lower and more raspy than it used to be and wonders what could be causing that change in the sound of her voice?

Neurological: Patricia has noticed that she has been having trouble sleeping - feels "wired" and "jittery" and has trouble "getting my brain to turn off". Patricia is currently alert and oriented.

Gastrointestinal: no significant findings

If the student does not suggest an electrocardiogram, Patricia should ask, "Isn't there a test you can do to look at my heart to make sure it is okay? I am so worried about having a heart attack since my friend died of one recently."

**Patient's response to special interviewing techniques**:

The SP should wait to be asked questions by the student and not volunteer information except where noted. Patricia should be poised and self-assured, though clearly concerned about her health condition - since she has a long drive home and does not want to faint while driving. Patricia should seek clarification from the student if the student uses medical jargon. Patricia should ask for clarification if any information is unclear, e.g. "What does that mean?"

Patricia is given additional information about the use of the diskus if students ask additional questions. For example, if the student asks how the diskus is used, Patricia should respond, "I use it whenever I feel like I need it - sometimes several times a day. Sometimes, I'm not sure if I actually get any medicine when I breathe in, so I make sure by using it again." If the student asks if Patricia takes a drink after using the diskus, Patricia should respond that "No one ever told me to do that."

**Special Considerations**:

* **Specific body type/physical requirements**: Patricia should wear closed-toed shoes so the medical student cannot see the toenail fungus for which she is taking itraconazole.
* **Props**: a medication list can be provided if it is difficult to remember the names and dose of medications; paper copies of the initial patient intake form used by the outpatient practice should be completed.

question_text:
**Noncompliance with Medication Regimen Case**

Presentation for the Student:

Roberta Stanley is a 67-year-old female presenting to the clinic today for a new patient visit. She has prior history of hypertension, but has not seen a physician in about 2 years. Her very close friend recently had a large stroke at the age of 68 years old, and remains in a rehab facility.
private_patient_context:
**Noncompliance with Medication Regimen Case**

Information for the SP:

You are a 67-year-old patient and are coming to the clinic for follow-up. You have not seen a doctor in a couple of years and have not been taking any blood pressure medications. You were taking Lisinopril (40 mg daily) previously for your blood pressure control, but you were feeling well and stopped taking the medicine when life “became busy.” You still work, helping a friend in an office setting. You do not have any other known medical problems, and you do not have any issues today during clinic (no headaches, chest pain, fevers, etc). When asked, you are a bit concerned because your friend of 30 years just had a large stroke and though she is in a rehab facility, she has quite severe deficits. You are willing to consider taking Blood pressure medications regularly, even though you feel no symptoms without the medications, when you learn that high blood pressure is a risk factor for stroke.

PMH: high blood pressure, previously prescribed Lisinopril 40 mg daily, not taking

Family history: unknown, adopted

Social history: you have never smoked, no alcohol intake, live with spouse, working in office setting

Allergies, none

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? Patient wants to avoid having a stroke like her friend. She wants to control her blood pressure and continue to work and enjoy her family.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with blood pressure medications will put you at risk for having a stroke.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? Not taking meds for hypertension allows you to believe that you are healthy and don’t need to take medications (taking the medicine is a reminder that you have HTN), you are “busy” and find it hard to fit taking medications into your schedule.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are very afraid of ending up like your friend with the stroke. You do not want to have the severe deficits that have resulted from your friend’s stroke.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? You can manage your hypertension and avoid having a stroke. You can be around for your spouse/family and be able to continue working.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): You could try a pill box, setting a reminder on your phone, putting up reminder notes, pairing pill taking with another regular behavior like brushing your teeth, taking your blood pressure regularly to remind you of your HTN, etc.
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 9/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You really don’t want to have a stroke like your friend.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe keep a picture of your friend by my pill bottle, to remind you of what could happen if you don’t take my medications.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? I think the strategies we discussed will help.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Maybe get your husband involved in reminding you? Get a blood pressure cuff at home to take your own pressures regularly.
* Ask for a decision: You will try a pill box with calendar reminders and getting your husband to help remind you.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will leave the office and buy a pill box and home cuff, you will set calendar reminders in your phone, and ask your husband to help you remember.
* What do you intend to do? Take the above steps.

**Alcohol Abuse Case**

Presentation to the Student:

Elle Frank is a 50-year-old female, presenting to your clinic for a routine follow-up visit. She has been continuing to consume alcohol on a daily basis..
private_patient_context:
**Alcohol Abuse Case**

For the SP:

History: You are a 50-year-old patient. You have been drinking about a six-pack of beer on a daily basis. On days when you are feeling more stress, you are also consuming about 2 or 3 mixed drinks in addition, happening about 1-2 times per week. You do not have history of drug use and you quit smoking 10 years ago. You are currently unemployed after losing your job for having alcohol on your breath repeatedly, have one DUI from last New Year’s Eve, and you notice mild withdrawal symptoms (trembling, headaches) when you stop drinking alcohol. You started to drink heavily because that is what everyone did together after work, but now you drink to deal with your boredom and depression. You have a support network of family members and friends, who are reminding you and urging you to stop drinking alcohol also. You feel that drinking alcohol has become an important part of your day, and following discussion with your doctor, you would like to find the motivation to stop drinking to be able to find work again. You are becoming concerned about your “liver tests” that have been worsening since your last visit 2 months ago.

PMH: high blood pressure, taking a blood pressure medication (amlodipine) daily at home, no allergies

Family history: Father died of alcoholic cirrhosis

Social history (see above)

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You are concerned about your liver tests and what that might mean for your health, you don’t want to turn out like your alcoholic father, you don’t want to get a second DUI because that would mean a mandatory 30 days in jail, and you really want to return to work.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Continuing to drink conflicts with all of these goals.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It used to help you socialize after work, manage the stress of the day, and fit in with friends when you were working. Now it helps you to manage your boredom and depression since you are out of work.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You really don’t want to turn out like your alcoholic father and die of cirrhosis, you don’t want another DUI and end up in jail, and you don’t want to lose another job because of your drinking. You also realize that drinking makes your depression worse in the long run, even though it helps you in the short run.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? You would have a better chance at getting and keeping a job, which would help with your boredom and depression, you wouldn’t have to worry about getting another DUI, your health would improve, and you would be less likely to turn out like your dad.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): You went to one AA meeting ~~but you were unsure about the whole “God” part of AA,~~  and you might be willing to try it again. You can’t afford therapy or medications to help curb cravings. Once when you had a non-drinking girlfriend (or boyfriend) you quit drinking through her (his) support and spending time with her (him).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You’re so tired of feeing this way, you really want to work because that would make so much of your problems better, and you don’t want to further damage your liver.
    - How could you move that number higher? If you better understood what effect alcohol is having on your liver and moods.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 4/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You were able to quit drinking before when you were with a nice partner, so you know you can do it.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? If you had better support, friends who don’t drink, had medications for your depression, had help finding work, and tried AA again.
* Ask for a decision: You agree to try an antidepressant and to go to several different AA meetings.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will go to 5 different AA meetings in the next week and try socializing with AA members who do not drink. You will start a trial of antidepressants and follow up with your doctor in 3 weeks.
* What do you intend to do? Try AA and antidepressants.

**Medication Allergy Case: PHYSICIAN**

Background: Patient Nancy Roberts, 92 y.o. female patient with moderate dementia and moderate, controlled hypertension, arrived at the UC Davis ED from a local assisted living residence at 2000. Before admission, she became increasing SOB, with yellow-greenish sputum, and febrile to 38.5 with pulse oximetry = 88. The assisted living residence staff were concerned Mrs. Roberts had developed pneumonia and, after receiving permission from the patient's son/daughter, called an ambulance for transport to the ED.

Admission Status: You were involved in the aftermath of a difficult and unsuccessful resuscitation attempt when Mrs. Roberts arrived, so an intern working in the department did the initial physical exam and initial workup. At 2100, you picked up the case and reviewed the results, reexamining Mrs. Roberts to confirm the diagnosis of pneumonia. She received IV antibiotics at 2200. Because of continued oxygen requirement, dehydration, and poor po intake, you contact the Hospitalist Service to admit the patient. You continue to see other ED patients.

At 2230, you are called to urgently evaluate Mrs. Roberts. She is experiencing an anaphylactic reaction involving flushing, itching, difficulty swallowing, coughing, wheezing, hypotension and difficulty breathing. You directed her emergency management. She is stabilized and transferred to the MICU.

Current: An ED nurse informs you that Mrs. Roberts had a cephalosporin allergy documented in the medical records that accompanied her from the assisted living residence. The cephalosporin allergy was noted on a face page but you never saw these records. Based on the assisted living residence records, Mrs. Roberts developed hives, pruritis and shortness of breath with ceftriaxone she received for a UTI 1 year ago at UC Davis ED. The allergy was not noted in allergy banner in EMR, but was noted in the ED progress note from that visit.

Situation: Mrs. Robert’s son/daughter has arrived at the ED. You are going to talk with the family about the events of the evening and why his/her mother is going to the ICU.

<u>**Case Summary/Standardized Patient Training Notes**</u>

# **Communicating a Critical Incident with a Family Member**

# **Presenting situation for the Standardized “Patient” in the role as the daughter of the patient**

# 1. SP arrives in the Emergency Department (ED) to see her mother who was taken here from assisted living residence in Sacramento for shortness of breath and fever

# **Demographics and psychosocial profile for the Standardized “Patient”**

# 2. 55-64 year old, non-Hispanic woman (Peggy Jones) who is the only daughter of the patient, Nancy Roberts

# 3. Librarian at Sacramento State University

# 4. Lives Grass Valley, CA with husband, 2 adult children live in San Francisco bay area

# 5. Mother, **Nancy Roberts**, lived in home of SP for 3 years before entering an assisted living residence in Sacramento 6 months ago due to progressive dementia

# 6. SP visits her mother at assisted living residence 1-2 times a month

# 7. Father of SP and husband of patient died of severe sepsis 5 years ago while receiving treatment in an intensive care unit (ICU)

# 8. **Background for the Standardized “Patient”**

# 9. Serves as her mother’s health care proxy

# 10. Actively involved in her mother’s health care for last 10 years including attending all medical visits

# 11. Well familiar with her mother’s medical history, current medications, past surgeries, allergies

# **Patient (SP’s mother, Nancy Roberts) background**

# 13. 92 year old non-Hispanic woman with moderate dementia and moderate, controlled hypertension.

# 14. Needs assistance with activities of daily living, medications, ambulatory with walker.

# 15. Rarely requires unscheduled health care visits—last ED visit was 1 year ago at this ED for an uncomplicated urinary tract infection. She was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and developed hives, itching and throat “tightness” that resolved with diphenhydramine treatment. She was subsequently discharged from the ED with a different antibiotic. She had no further medication reactions.

# 16. For last few days, her caretakers at the assisted living residence note increasing shortness of breath, cough, and fever.

# 17. The assisted living staff calls the SP with this information, and the SP provides permission to transport her mother to this ED by ambulance

# **Patient (your mother) Past Medical History**

# 18. Current illnesses: Moderate, controlled hypertension since 1996, progressive dementia.

# 19. Surgeries: appendectomy at age 6

# 20. Medications: water pill (chlorothiazide) twice a day, aspirin every morning

# 21. Allergies: an antibiotic she received last year for a urine infection

# 22. Family medical history: SP’s maternal grandfather died of coronary artery disease at age 77 and maternal grandmother died of breast cancer at age 84

# 23. Social history: Mother of 1 daughter (Peggy Jones), retired elementary school teacher, husband of 42 years died of sepsis 5 years ago, lived in daughter’s home for 3 years before entering an assisted living residence in Sacramento 6 months ago

# 24. Advanced directives: not completed

# 25. **Diagnosis**

# 26. Pneumonia complicated by anaphylaxis to medication

# 28. **Communication Case: Standardized “Patient” Role Guidelines**

# **In this case, the standardized “patient” (SP) is the patient’s daughter. Emotions begin on a moderate level, escalate somewhat but remained controlled, then de-escalate to acceptance. Examples of statement and questions that could be used by the SP during the conversation are provided below. These are only examples, and not a script.**

# **Participants:** SP as the patient’s adult daughter, ED resident and nurse or pharmacist as confederate actors. Other clinical students can be substituted in the role of the ED resident.

# **Setting:** ED examination room, 3 chairs, SP arrives in the ED as her mother is being wheeled to the ICU. The SP has given her mother a kiss as she rolled by, and the ED team asks the SP to stay behind to get an update on her mother’s condition.

# **Initial contact with clinical team:** SP’s feelings include anxiety, disappointment, and controlled anger. **Emotional range 4-5** (1=flat response, 10=out-of-control).

# 29. SP arrives at the ED to find her mother on a ventilator and being moved to an ICU. The SP is surprised to see her on a ventilator and the SP’s level of concern rises.

# 30. SP’s initial comment to the ED resident is *“why is my mother going to the ICU? She didn’t seem that sick.”*

# 31. ED resident should tell the SP her mother has pneumonia and received an antibiotic called cefepime as treatment. SP’s mother had a severe allergic reaction. A breathing tube was placed and she will be monitored in the ICU.

# 32. SP could say something like, *“Mom didn’t want to ever be in an ICU after watching Dad die there.”*

# 33. The resident should ask SP about her experience with her father’s illness, ICU stay, and subsequent death

# 34. **Emotional de-escalation. SP’s emotion level should be 3 out of 10 and you listen attentively to the ED resident’s comments and explanation**

# 35. ED resident should explain the significance of the allergic reaction and next steps in treating the patient**. SP will focus attention on her mother’s condition** by asking questions such as *“how long will it take Mom to recover? Will she be aware she is in the ICU? How bad is her pneumonia?”*

# 36. The ED resident should reveal the patient’s record indicated she is allergic to the type of antibiotic she received.

# 37. If not revealed, ask *“I remember she was allergic to the antibiotic she received last year for a urine infection but I don’t remember the name. I think if was “cef - something…” Is it in her chart?”*

# 38. If the medication allergy was known to the ED providers, ask “why did she get a drug she is allergic to?”

# **Emotional escalation**

# 39. **SP‘s emotional level rises to 4-5** while asking probing questions to find out what happened. *“I can’t believe this. How come you didn’t know she was allergic to this type of antibiotics?“ “How could you miss something like this?*

# 40. If the ED resident responds openly, disclosing details, answering questions directly and appearing empathetic, the SP shows an attitude of acceptance.

# 41. If ED resident appears to be evading the questions, the SP reacts with increasing frustration and **emotional level rises to 6 or 7.** “*Don't you understand why this is so upsetting/disappointing to me?*

# 42. If SP’s anger/anxiety is acknowledged, the SP responds appropriately.

# 43. If SP’s anger/anxiety was not acknowledged, the SP continues to appear sad/anxious and detached. i.e. break eye contact, deep breaths etc…

# 45. SP should help learners get closure on conversation after about 8 minutes by suggesting you want to get on with the exam so *“we can move on.”* **Sigh and reduce emotional level to 3**

# 46. End neutrally. **Resist the urge to make the learner feel good.** Possible closing statements could be something like *“I appreciate your honesty. I think we just need to move forward from here and I need you to tell me when things haven’t gone right.” or “I’m not happy about my mother’s care but we need to focus on getting her back home.”*

question_text:
**Mitochondrial Disorder Case: Copy for Resident**

You are the overnight resident for the general floor team and are taking care of a 2-year-old girl with a mitochondrial disorder who was admitted earlier that day for fever and diarrhea. At 9 pm her nurse calls to say that her mother is here and upset that her daughter has not received her home (non-formulary) medication of Ubiquinone (an oxidized form of Coenzyme Q-10). The mother states that the staff nutritionist had assured her that it would be given with her evening meal. The medication is a white powder in an unmarked bottle at the child’s bedside. It is against hospital policy to give medication that is unlabeled.

You must now respond to the mother’s concerns and make a plan for next steps.

I. Rehab Emergencies for Post-Graduate Year 2 (PGY-2) Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) Residents: Autonomic Dysreflexia (AD)

II. Target Audience: PGY-2 PM&R Residents

IV. Environment

1. Station signs

2. Hospital bed

3. Blood pressure cuff

4. Stethoscope

5. Foley catheter with leg bag

6. Adhesive or means to fasten foley to thigh/groin

7. Bed sheets

8. Hospital gown and socks

9. Note cards

V. Actors

1.Standardized patient, male, 27 years of age, in good physical health, dressed in hospital gown in bed

VI. Case Narrative (describes what the learner will experience)

Opening Line: "Please stop my headache, doc, I beg you."

* 1. **Encounter:**
     1. When the resident knocks and enters the room, you are laying supine, flat, in bed moaning in pain and grabbing at your head in the dark. You are upset, and ask if the resident “can help with the pain. I’ve been waiting here for 15 minutes in excruciating pain and no one has done anything.” You are testy and demand something be done about the pain.

**Describe the overall purpose of the resource**

This rehabilitation related emergency situation in a spinal cord injured patient is a resource that was designed for medical residents beginning their rehabilitation residency.

**Describe the conceptual background (i.e., why and how it was created)**

This pilot program was designed to expose the rehabilitation resident to potential emergencies that might be encountered in the clinical setting of a rehabilitation facility, particularly when on call.

The scenario was based on characteristics of our associated free standing rehabilitation facility, with a hospital bed, bedside blood pressure cuff, 24 hour nursing staff, etc. Finally, the timing of the scenario was specific to reflect a nighttime challenge to the resident to simulate an "on-call" scenario.

V. Actors

1.Standardized patient, male, 27 years of age, in good physical health, dressed in hospital gown in bed

VI. Case Narrative (describes what the learner will experience)

Opening Line: "Please stop my headache, doc, I beg you."

Standardized patient HPI: Your name is Steve Spiner, age 27. You were in good health, working construction, and had a young daughter named Hannah at home, who just turned 1 years old. You have a wife, whom you’ve been married to for 2 years. You were fixing a burst pipe in your home and were trying to access the a ceiling panel in your basement on a ladder. Unfortunately, you pulled a ceiling panel a little too hard and fell backwards, landing on your back, which resulted in a fracture of your 4th thoracic (T4) vertebra. You were taken to the hospital, where you underwent surgery by Dr. X to stabilize the spine and were fused from T2-6.

After a brief recovery at a large teaching hospital, you were transferred to a free standing Rehabilitation Hospital, where you have spent the past 3 weeks learning to function independently with your disability. You are an American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) A, meaning that you have a complete injury, no volitional movement of your lower extremities, and some difficulty with trunk stability. Additionally, you are working toward intermittent catheterization, but still have a foley catheter due to some difficulty with void trials.

Aside from the voiding difficulty, you are doing well. You did not have any blood clots during your acute care stay, and you did not develop any pneumonias. The one issue that is worth mentioning is that you had a urinary tract infection several weeks ago, but you were successfully treated with Cipro.

This evening you went to bed at a normal time, and had a good day of therapy. You were able to fall asleep quickly, and did not have a headache at that time. Your shoulders are a bit sore from transfer training, but otherwise you had felt well prior to sleep. You were awoken from sleep about 15 minutes ago with a headache. This headache is pounding and located in the front of your head on both sides. It feels like someone is squeezing your head together, you rate the pain as 10/10. There is no numbness, tingling, or sensory changes in your hands or anywhere else in the body. You do not have any flashes, floaters or see halos around lights. You do not feel nauseous, and have not vomited. The light in the room is not making your headache worse. Additionally, you feel sweaty and flushed in the face, and your vision is somewhat blurred, but you attribute this to the intense pain you are having. You have goosebumps on your legs and nasal congestion. You think that perhaps this is a really bad “head cold.” You are now upset that the nurse has not given you anything for pain and you want something done about the pain.

* 1. **Life situation**: You are newly married with a young child at home. Your wife was out of work to care for the child, and you worked in construction to pay the bills.
  2. **Character description**:
     1. Objective: To alleviate this headache
     2. Obstacles: You are upset that no one has adequately addressed the headache yet
     3. Tactics:
        1. You are initially confrontational and impatient, wanting something to be done. If the resident is sympathetic, then you calm down a little. If not, then you continue to be angry.
        2. If the resident does not sit you up and take your vital signs within 3 minutes of the encounter, you feign that the pain is worsening, and start to pass out. You then will direct them to a simulator to run a code.
  3. **Personality**: You are a risk taker and tend to be a little hot-headed. In this scenario, since you are in quite a bit of pain, you are impatient and demanding of the physician.
  4. **Past medical history**: Aside from the recent spinal cord injury 5 weeks ago, you are in good health.
  5. **Family history**: Your mother is alive and well, with high blood pressure. Your father suffered a heart attack at age 50, but is currently doing well after heart surgery. There is no family history of headache.
  6. **Medications**: Docusate, senna, bisacodyl suppository, lioresal, tizanidine, diazepam at night, oxycodone immediate release every 4 hours as needed (PRN), acetaminophen PRN
  7. **Allergies:** None
  8. **Encounter:**
     1. When the resident knocks and enters the room, you are laying supine, flat, in bed moaning in pain and grabbing at your head in the dark. You are upset, and ask if the resident “can help with the pain. I’ve been waiting here for 15 minutes in excruciating pain and no one has done anything.” You are testy and demand something be done about the pain.
     2. The resident should turn on the lights and sit you up. While asking you questions, he/she should take vitals. If he/she does not do this within a few minutes, then you will degrade clinically and pass out, causing a code, whereby you direct them to a simulator.
     3. If the resident does at least sit you up, you can continue to answer questions about the headache. He/she should be asking questions relevant to onset, provocation/palliation, radiation, quality of the pain, etc. With respect to your current state:
        1. Pain- “10/10”
        2. Quality- “Throbbing, intense”
        3. Location- “both sides in the front above the eyes”
        4. Radiation- “No”
        5. Palliation/provocation- “I haven’t gotten anything for the pain yet, Doc, give me something and stop asking these questions.”
        6. Visual disturbances (flashes, floaters, halos around light) - “No.”
        7. Blurred vision- “Yes.”
     4. Associated symptoms: Offer the fact that you are feeling really warm, and are sweating an awful lot, and you feel like your face is flushed. You feel like this all might be related to a head cold, because your nose is runny too, and you feel congested.
     5. The resident may ask you when you moved your bowels last. If this is the case, then you had your bowel routine around 7PM with a good amount of stool evacuated. The resident may also ask about skin breakdown. If this is the case, you can tell him/her that you do not have a pressure ulcer, and that the nurses faithfully turn you, and that you perform weight shifts in the wheelchair every 30 minutes.
     6. At some point during the physical exam, the resident should get your vitals. If he/she does not do this and finishes his/her assessment,, say “Doc my head feels like it’s going to explode!” Subsequently you will pass out and direct them to a simulator to run a code.
     7. If they do not attempt to look at the feet, legs, and groin, and continue to examine the head/neck/ or eyes, then you say “Doc my head feels like it’s going to explode!” If they start to test your muscles or sensation, pass out and direct them to a simulator to run a code.
     8. If the resident recognizes that the foley catheter is the problem, and unkinks it, then you should ask him/her about why this happened. He/she should explain to you about AD.
  9. **Timing:** There are a lot of places where the Standardized Patient (SP) can decompensate. If the resident acts appropriately during the encounter, and the SP “survives” without decompensation, then the SP may ask about prevention with any time left over, or what to do if you can’t find a reason for the dysreflexia.
