Clinical Education & Assessment Center

Standardized Patient Lab

# 1. Mary Smith (GERIATRICS OSCE)

STANDARDIZED PATIENT SIMULATION GUIDELINES

GERIATRICS OSCE – MARY SMITH

  1. Case Overview
    • You are Mary Smith, a woman who presents to the outpatient office for overdue follow-up of your diabetes and hypertension. In addition, you are not compliant with the self-care regimen established for you.
    • The examinee’s task is to obtain a focused history and counsel you regarding your situation. Following the encounter, the examinee will then document the encounter in a patient note.
  1. ENCOUNTER SETTING
  • University Health Services: exam room of an ambulatory (outpatient) medical practice.
  1. SP RELATIONSHIPS

All participants in this encounter are strangers to one another. You are NOT expected to have already made the acquaintance of the examinee, so you do NOT have to pretend any familiarity.

  1. WHAT GOES ON IN THIS ENCOUNTER

A chart is provided to the examinee before the encounter, which contains information about your medical history and lab work.

The onus is on the examinee to question you about your medical history and how you take care of yourself and then to counsel you accordingly. There is no physical examination required or expected in this encounter.

  1. PATIENT CHARACTER PRESENTATION

Presentation

Body Language/ Symptom Presentation

  • Feeling a bit tired and weak

Affect

  • Pleasant, cooperative, good eye contact
  • You are not someone who is particularly knowledgeable about diabetes or any health issues and try to avoid doctors as much as you can. You feel that it’s all way over your head, too complex for you to bother with.
  • This encounter is an exercise in the examinee’s pursuing and delving into your self-care habits and then counseling you to change the behaviors that need adjustment for optimal diabetes control. Listen carefully to the questions and answer only what’s asked. You are not trying to withhold information; Mary Smith, an otherwise intelligent, well educated and worldly woman, is pretty much clueless when it comes to her disease, so you are not portraying someone who is hiding information. Rather, someone who genuinely doesn’t have the knowledge or skills to manage herself.

Appearance/ Costuming

  • Street clothes

Starting Position

Sitting in the chair.

**Towards the end of the encounter, if not already covered by the student’s own questioning, make sure to broach the following two topics:** 1. **Why should I take the prescriptions? They don’t make me feel any different.** 2. **Do I really have to check my blood at home?**
  1. MARY SMITH’S STORY
    • Opening line: To be honest, I really didn’t want to come here today, but my daughter insisted that I make an appointment. She says I’m way overdue.

Depending on the examinee’s follow-up comments or questions (an open-ended question inviting you to tell your story), you can add the following:

My daughter is worried about me because I haven’t been seen for about a year. I’m diabetic.

She thinks I haven’t been taking my medicine the way I’m supposed to.

I haven’t really been sick, except a bad case of flu a few months ago, but I got over that.

  • Your current situation:
    • You take your medicines sometimes, but you haven’t been taking them recently because they don't make you feel better and you don’t feel differently whether or not you take them.

I might as well be eating candy instead of taking those pills. They don’t do a blessed thing for me.

    • You are, however, willing to take them again (if you are advised to). It’s not like you have a bias against taking medicine.
    • You have NOT been checking your blood sugars at home. It hurts too darn much, and you can’t see the numbers on the blood sugar monitor anyway.
    • You urinate every couple of hours and about 3 times every night. In the last 2 months, you’ve been urinating even more than usual. NO pain or burning with urination.
    • Your mouth feels dry sometimes and you are occasionally thirsty.
    • Your eyes feel dry and your vision seems blurry.
    • Your feet burn and tingle, but you wouldn’t actually describe the situation as painful.
    • You’ve lost a little weight, perhaps a couple of pounds.
    • You do NOT need assistance with eating, grooming, dressing, walking or going to the bathroom. However, sometimes, you need someone to run errands for you because you are too tired and don't feel good.
    • Come to think of it, you’ve been feeling tired all the time of late.
    • You try not to eat sweets.
    • You do NOT exercise regularly.
  • Medications:

When I was here before, the doctor gave me 2 or 3 medications for diabetes and something for blood pressure.

I don’t exactly remember their names anymore.

Don’t you know what they are? Didn’t the doctor write them down?

  • Past Medical History:
    • Surgeries: Had your tonsils and appendix out as a child.
    • Illnesses: Had the flu a few months ago. Recovered just fine. Otherwise, nothing else.
    • Routine care: Haven’t been to the gynecologist since you went through menopause.
  • Family History
    • Mother had diabetes. Died at age 80 from pneumonia
    • Father: died of heart attack at age 58
    • Older sister died last year of a heart attack at age 72
  • Home Life
    • Live alone in a small one-floor home.

It’s paid for!

    • Husband was a smoker, died a long time ago from lung cancer.
    • Used to enjoy going out, but you haven’t so much in the last few months because you feel so tired and have to go to the bathroom all the time. You watch a lot of TV these days.
    • Habits: Never smoked but husband smoked during your entire 30 year marriage. No alcohol. Drink 3-4 cups of tea/day (no coffee). No alcohol. Don’t exercise and not very physically active
  • Education/Vocation: College degree in Education. Retired (about 10 years ago) elementary school teacher.

After that, I volunteered at a senior center, and I’ve worked for political candidates and at the polls.

But, I haven’t felt like doing any of that for the last few months.

Towards the end of the encounter, if not already covered by the student’s own questioning, make sure to broach the following two topics:

Why should I take the prescriptions? They don’t make me feel any different.

Do I really have to check my blood at home?

(none)

**Depression in the LGBT Patient:**

**A Standardized Patient Encounter**

**Standardized Patient Training Materials**

Benjamin H. Huang, David A. Milling, Sarah Dimiduk, Harsha K. Nair, Karen H. Zinnerstrom

**Case:** Michael Carlson

**Patient Complaint:** “I feel tired all the time.”

**Case Synopsis:** A 17-year-old man’s parents make him an appointment at the physician’s office after noticing recent changes in his behavior. He has been feeling fatigued lately, and cannot seem to get enough sleep. He has recently engaged in risky sexual behavior and is concerned about the possibility of HIV infection.

**SP Recruitment Profile:** 17-year-old male

Last Revision: February 17, 2014

**CASE OVERVIEW**

You are 17-year-old Michael Carlson, and have come to the clinic today because you have been feeling tired and have had difficulty sleeping for the last 2 months. Your parents have told the doctor that they made the appointment because you have been more despondent lately, and that you are spending much more time alone in your room with the door closed, avoiding friends and family. They are concerned for your well-being. Before the encounter, a nurse came in the room to take your vitals and offered routine HIV screening, to which you consented.

**OPENING STATEMENT**

**“I feel tired all the time.”**

If asked another follow-up or open ended question, you will reply:

**“I just don’t feel like I can ever get enough sleep.”**

**APPEARANCE AND BEHAVIOR**

Appearance

* Sitting on the exam table dressed in a gown.
* Patient looks like a healthy young man.
* Patient does not need to be of any particular ethnicity.

Initial Behavior

* Patient responds in a monotonous voice.
* Patient avoids excessive direct eye contact.
* Patient is not forthcoming.

Case Props

* Cell phone in hand.
  + Many teenage patients often cannot be separated from their handhelds, so this is simply a part of the costume. You do not need to pretend to text or answer calls, and your phone should be turned off.

**PATIENT BACKGROUND**

You are a young man who identifies as gay, or homosexual, and is experiencing symptoms of fatigue.

Foremost amongst your concerns is the extreme lack of energy, which you’ve been experiencing for about 2 months. You have difficulty falling asleep, and the result is poor energy and concentration which has impacted nearly every aspect of your life, including your grades.

You also have a fear of HIV infection. You had a sexual encounter 3 weeks ago with someone you met on the internet to try and get over breaking up with your boyfriend. You did not use a condom or any other form of protection. You regret your decision and worry about the consequences.

Your boyfriend broke up with you 2 months ago after a 6 month relationship. You don’t wish to talk about the details at this time. Initially, you tried to remain friends, but things always got awkward between the two of you, and he has recently started dating someone else. When he left, you felt angry and miserable. Even though you were very upset at the time, you had to try to pretend that nothing was wrong at home so that no one would suspect what was happening.

Things you used to enjoy no longer make you happy. You used to play soccer on the weekends and spend a lot of time hanging out with friends, but no longer find yourself interested or motivated to do either. You shared many friends with your ex-boyfriend, and have avoided them since you broke up.

You feel like there is no one to talk to about your problems, and don’t feel ready to come out to your parents yet. You have been thinking about telling your sister, but it seems like you start to argue every time you try to talk. You are scared to tell any of your professors because you are worried it might impact your academic career. You don’t know of any resources in the community.

**THE ENCOUNTER**

Before coming in to talk to you, the examinee will be informed on your door chart that you have agreed to routine HIV screening. If they do not mention this, or otherwise elicit this fear through other dialogue, by the end of the encounter find somewhere to interject:

**“Do you think I could have an HIV infection?”**

(Answer follow-up questions as detailed in section A below, under ‘I have a lot on my mind. Do you think I could have HIV?’)

Examinees are typically taught to start with some ice-breakers, followed by a couple open-ended questions about what brought you in to the office. This is followed by a more thorough history, including a review of systems, past medical history, family history, and social history. Afterwards, the examinee should perform a quick physical exam, summarize a plan, and positively reinforce your decision to come to the office today.

**A. CHIEF COMPLAINT / HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS**

The following few sections are presented as several, short, answer-response dialogues in roughly the order that many examinees will approach history-taking in this patient. Different examinees may ask the same questions in several different manners, so several examples are given where appropriate. Examinee dialogue is marked with •, and patient response is marked with ⇒. Attempt to stick as closely to the script as is reasonable, especially for bolded dialogue. Because questions can be unpredictable, some patient responses do not contain specific dialogue, but will have bullets with general information that will help you respond to the question at hand.

• Examinee opens with an ‘ice-breaker’: “Wonderful/horrible weather we’re having”, “I hope the drive over was okay”, “It’s very nice to meet you.”

⇒ Acknowledge the examinee and respond appropriately, but maintain minimal eye contact.

⇒ Your gaze should mostly be directed downwards, such as at your own feet.

⇒ You can briefly give a weak smile to attempts at humor, but try to avoid prolonged smiling or outright laughter.

• Examinee elicits chief complaint: “What brings you in today?”, “What can I help you with?”, “How are you feeling?”, “What is bothering you?”

⇒ Respond **“I feel tired all the time.”**

• Examinee asks a follow up question to the chief complaint: “Why do you think that is so?”, “Are you getting enough sleep?”, “What is making you tired?”

⇒ Respond **“I just don’t feel like I can ever get enough sleep.”**

• Examinee investigates sleep hygiene: “Can you describe your sleep pattern?”, “How much sleep do you get?”, “When do you go to bed at night?”, “Are you having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?”

⇒ You go to bed around midnight every night, but fail to fall asleep until 3 or 4 AM. You have to be up for classes by 7 AM, so you barely get any sleep.

⇒ Even on weekends, you can’t seem to sleep in and find yourself lying in bed with a lot on your mind.

• Examinee probes into sleep complaint: “Why has sleeping been a problem?”, “What is making sleep difficult?”, “What is keeping you up?”

⇒ Respond **“I can’t get to sleep because I have a lot on my mind. Do you think I could have HIV?”**

⇒ You ‘hooked up’ with a male partner 3 weeks ago. You did not use a condom. This was your first time having unprotected anal sex. You engaged in oral and anal sex with that partner. You were the insertive “top” participant.

⇒ Your only other sexual partner was your ex-boyfriend, who broke up with you 2 months ago. You do not wish to talk about the details of the breakup at this time. Your relationship had lasted 6 months before that. You always used a condom with your boyfriend, and were always the insertive “top” participant.

⇒ You have never better the receptive “bottom” participant during anal sexual intercourse.

• Examinee elicits onset: “When did this start?”, “How long ago did you notice these symptoms?”, “How long has this been going on?”

⇒ The symptoms started 2 months ago, and came on gradually, rather than suddenly.

**B. SCREENING FOR DEPRESSION**

If the examinee believes that you may be depressed, they may begin a screening for depression.

* Mood: “Do you think you might be depressed?”, “Do you feel hopeless?”, “How are you feeling?”
* Respond **“I’m just feeling really down right now.”**
* If the examinee tells you that your worries about school and friends could be making you feel depressed, gently nod your head in agreement.
* Sleep: “Have you had troubles sleeping?”, “Do you get enough sleep?”, “How much rest do you get at night?”
* Respond **“I just don’t feel like I can ever get enough sleep.”** (See section A, above)
* Interest: “Have you lost interest in activities?”, “Do things you used to enjoy no longer interest you?”, “Are hobbies no longer making you happy?”
* Respond **“Nothing seems to make me happy anymore.”**
* You used to play soccer on the weekends, but no longer find yourself interested.
* You used to enjoy hanging out with friends, but since many of them are mutual friends with your ex-boyfriend, you have been avoiding them.
* Guilt: “Do you ever feel guilty or worthless?”, “Do you feel like you’ve let yourself or your family down?”
* You do not feel guilty or worthless.
* Energy: “Do you feel tired?”, “How much energy have you had lately?”, “Is it hard to get through the day?”
* Respond **“I just feel tired all the time.”**(See section A, above)
* Concentration: “Has it been difficult to concentrate?”, “Are your grades slipping?”, “Is it affecting your schoolwork?”
* You used to be an ‘A’ student, and now your grades are slipping.
* If the examinee asks if you have spoken to teachers/faculty about it, respond **“I don’t feel like I can talk to them about this.”**
* Several of your professors and classmates are politically conservative and you worry that coming out may negatively impact your academic career.
* Appetite: “Are you eating more or less than you used to?”, “How is your appetite?”, “Do you feel like you’ve been losing weight?”
* Respond **“I’ve been eating less, but I haven’t lost any weight.”**
* You haven’t been hungry lately, and have found yourself eating less than you used to.
* Psychomotor Slowness/Agitation: “Has anyone told you that you’ve been moving really slowly?”, “Do you feel more sluggish than usual?”, “Are you feeling more restless than before?”
* You have not noticed any of these symptoms.
* Suicidal Thoughts: “Have you ever thought about hurting yourself?”, “Do you feel like committing suicide?”, “Are you thinking about killing yourself?”
* Respond **“I could never do that to my family.”**
* You would never commit suicide.
* You do not have access to firearms at home.

**C. STRESS**

* Examinee probes for life stressors: “Has anything been causing you stress?”, “Something seems to be worrying you; would you like to talk about it?”, “What do you think is behind all this?” (Note: The following stressors are presented in order of importance. Skip the ones that the examinee has already addressed, but otherwise present the first item in the list. If the examinee probes for additional stressors, then present the next item in the list.)

⇒ 1) If the examinee has not yet elicited your fear of HIV, use this opportunity to respond:**“Do you think I could have HIV?”**

2) If the examinee has not yet elicited your concern about slipping grades, you should respond **“I’m concerned because my grades are slipping”** (see section C, above).

3) If the examinee has not yet elicited that you broke up with your boyfriend, you should respond **“I was dumped by my boyfriend 2 months ago.”**

4) Otherwise, respond **“I don’t feel like I have anyone I can talk to.”**

* You are not ready to come out to your parents. You have been thinking about telling your sister, but you are scared as to what she might think.
* You feel that talking to your professors about it may negatively impact your academic career.
* You shared most of your school friends with your boyfriend, and they still hang out with him, so you have been avoiding them.
* You are not aware of any community resources.

At this point, the examinee may have concluded that you are depressed and continue to a review of systems. Examinees are typically taught to perform this in a head to toe fashion, and may ask you these questions during the physical exam. Only give out these answers to direct questions from the examinee, and do not give out more information than they are asking for.

**D. REVIEW OF SYSTEMS**

* + General Health
    - You are fatigued.
    - You think you had a couple fevers earlier this week, but did not take a temperature.
    - You had swollen glands earlier this week, but they have gotten better.

**Postoperative Patient Not Following Postoperative Instructions**

Presentation to the Student:

The patient is a 42-year-old patient presenting to postoperative 2-week follow up appointment for recent surgery. He is a weightlifter and was lifting weights this past weekend with friends, as part of his exercise routine. The postoperative instructions specified no lifting over 15 pounds for 6 weeks duration.
private_patient_context:
**Postoperative Patient Not Following Postoperative Instructions**

Information for the SP:

You are a 42-year-old patient with recent surgery. You were told not to lift any objects over 15 pounds, but your friends invited you to work out and you lifted weights with them last weekend. Now, you are concerned about the surgical area during your postoperative visit. When the surgeon talks with you about the importance of the lifting restriction to protect your fresh surgical area, you are very motivated to comply with the postoperative instructions, as you would not like to have a second operation.

Medical history: none

Medications/Allergies: none

Family history: none

Social history: you quit smoking 10 years ago, you don’t drink alcohol or use drugs. You work as a sales representative and you can’t wait to return to this job once your wounds heal.

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to continue working at the job you love, heal well from your surgery, and be healthy. You really want to avoid a second surgery.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Once you are educated by the doctor about the dangers of lifting so early after your surgery, you realize that lifting weights is in conflict with your goals of healing well, being healthy, and returning to work.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? You think of yourself as strong and healthy, and you really like to work out with your friends because you are a social person.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You don’t want to damage the surgical area and/or have a second surgery, and you don’t want to jeopardize your return to work or your general health.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Advantages are proper healing after your surgery and more assurance that you can avoid another surgery and return to work.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): You can learn to say no to lifting weights with friends in the next five weeks and you can find other ways to be social with friends.
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 9/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You don’t want a second surgery and you want to return to work.
    - How could you move that number higher? You could learn more about complications of lifting.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 7/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You really like to be social with your friends, but you also realize there are other ways to be social (like by going for a walk or out to dinner with friends).
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? You were able to quit smoking 10 years ago; you feel that you could find other ways to be social with your friends.
* Ask for a decision: you will not do any heavy lifting for the next 5 weeks.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will tell your friends that you cannot lift heavy objects for the next 5 weeks.

# 2. **Case #1: Student Reference Guide**

Patient Information:

Diane Peterson is a 40 year old woman who is here to see you for back pain. She is a new patient to this clinic.

Brief Summary:

The patient is here today at the urgent care clinic to see you for a work related injury.

# 3. **Case #1: Student Assignment Form**

Interviewer:

You are charged with obtaining a complete problem history from the patient, Ms. Peterson.
private_patient_context:
## **Case #1: Standardized Patient (SP) Case Instructions** ## **Diane Peterson -- Work-Related Back Injury**

Patient Name

Diane Peterson

Gender/Race/Age (age range)

Female, Age 40 yrs old

Presenting Situation

Diane Peterson, age 40 presents to the clinic today with back pain.

Opening Statement

“I have this sharp pain in my back that is just killing me”

Elaboration of Complaint

You work as a nursing assistant at a local nursing home. While lifting a heavy paralyzed patient who had slumped in bed, you felt a sudden onset of low back pain. The human resources department at the nursing home said you should come to this clinic for your on-the-job injury.

Clinical Content*

Present illness/symptoms:

  • Sudden onset of back pain. When the injury “happened” it felt sharp and sudden. You describe the pain as DEEP and AWFUL. Your pain and stiffness has gotten worse over the last few hours and you had to leave work and come here. If asked to rate the pain your having now on a 0-10 scale, you would answer an 8.
  • Pain is shooting down your right leg to the ankle. It is difficult to walk – partly because moving increases your pain and partly because your right leg feels weak. You shift uncomfortably in your chair, often wincing and grimacing in your discomfort.
  • You took 2 Advil about 30 minutes after the pain started. This had no effect.

Pertinent Past Medical History:

  • You have never had any prior back pain or difficulties with your back.
  • Other than this injury, you have been in good health. You smoke 1 pack/day and drink alcohol – 6 beers on the weekend. You do not use any other drugs and take no medications. You do not exercise on a regular basis though you do get quite a bit of exercise on the job.

Family Medical History:

  • Your parents are both alive and well, living in Florida.
  • You had one brother who died several years ago of a drug overdose.

Physical Exam

No physical exam will be performed.

Psychosocial Profile

You have only been working at St. Camillas nursing home for short time. (Bluemound Rd. near the zoo). Your supervisor at work was not at all sympathetic to your injury. You are at the end of your probation period at work and do not have any accrued time off. You are quite worried about how this injury might affect your job status and financial picture. You need a form filled out because of leaving work early today and a doctor’s note to take any time off.

You are married with 2 children in high school. Your husband is laid off. You will get health insurance though your job if you are there for over 90 days. Right now your family is insured under COBRA and it’s very expensive. You are also responsible for caring for your elderly mother-in-law, visiting her most evenings to clean and do laundry.

Scenario Development

You should be sitting, uncomfortably, in a chair when the student(s) start the scenario. In general, let the student(s) set the pace and scope of the interview. You are to remain slightly anxious about work and in quite a lot of pain during the entire session.

If the scenario/ communication should come to a stall (more than a necessary pregnant pause). You can use one of the following questions to “jump start” the conversation:

  • Is this what a slipped disc feels like?
  • Don’t I need a MRI or something?
  • Can I get something for the pain that won’t make me sleepy? I really can’t afford to miss any work.
  • This should all be covered by worker’s comp, right?

**PRESENTING SITUATION & INSTRUCTIONS TO THE STUDENT**

# 1. **Travis**

You are in the Emergency Room at 4am.  Your patient is Travis , a 60-year-old patient with abdominal pain.

The patient’s vital signs are:

# 2. 	**Pulse:**	110

	**BP:**	100/60

	**Resp:**	24

	**Temp:**	101.4 orally

You are to:

**--	Take a relevant history.**

**--	Perform an appropriate physical exam.**

	**--	Tell the patient what you believe is going on with the patient and what you want to do next.**
private_patient_context:
# 1. **Travis**

# 3. <u>**CASE SUMMARY**</u>

You are Travis, a 60 year-old patient with a 6 hour history of severe mid-epigastric abdominal pain.  You were in your usual state of health until 10pm last night when you noticed the sudden onset of sharp upper abdominal pain. Thinking it was indigestion you took several antacids and went to bed. The pain was unrelenting and at midnight you vomited. It became so severe during the middle of the night that you and your wife came to the Emergency room, it is now 4:00AM. The pain is constant and radiates to the mid back. You work as a truck driver and returned home last night from a three day route.

# 4. <u>**PRESENTATION/EMOTIONAL TONE**</u>

When the student enters the room, you are lying **very still** on your back on the exam table with your knees bent.  You are in obvious pain that shows on your face; you are very still and quiet….not wanting to move at all.  You are not moaning, but you are preoccupied with the pain. On the way over you could feel the car hit every bump.  It hurts if your stretcher is bumped.

You are cooperative, because you want help with this terrible pain….you want to help the student to figure it out.  You would answer all of the student’s questions with relatively short answers; you cannot be drawn into a lengthy conversation because of the severity of the pain.  You verbally relay your anxieties (if asked) because you are worried about the possibility of having an operation. Only if the student doesn’t seem to be handling your situation well will you become impatient, and less communicative.

You don’t have the energy to be angry or aggressive….you would just become less communicative.

# 5. **Opening Statement or CC:** 

**In response to the question**, <u>***(“Why are you here today?”***</u>**) you answer in exactly these words:**

	**“I have this horrible pain in my stomach.”**

# 6. <u>**MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

# 7. With the next open ended question such as “Can you tell me more about the pain?”

“**It started around 10 last night.  I took some antacids but they didn’t help. It got so bad I threw up.  I couldn’t sleep. I finally told my wife I couldn’t stand it any longer and we came here.”**

# 8. **With specific questions:** 

# 9. **The Pain:**

# 10. **Where:	“It’s mostly right here (slowly points to mid-epigastrium), but now it hurts all over.” (With further questioning, it hurts all over your abdomen, but it is worse at the center just below sternum)**

If the student asks where the pain was when it <u>STARTED</u>, the issue being <u>***“Was the pain someplace other than where it is now?”***</u> respond to this question by saying “**It was always just right here...”**

# 11. If asked  <u>***“Does the pain go anywhere else?”***</u>  respond that the pain is the worst in the mid-epigastrium but that it also goes to the mid-back, **“like a knife in my gut”**

# 12. **Intensity:**	The pain is severe.  On a scale of 1 to 10, this pain is a 10.  

**Constant/Intermittent**:	The pain is <u>constant</u>:  **“It never goes away...”**

**Character:** 	The pain is stabbing and concentrated in mid-epigastrium but radiates to the mid back.

**Better or worse:**	The student might ask you if anything makes the pain <u>better</u> or if anything makes the pain <u>worse</u>.

# 13. <u>***“What makes it better?”***</u>  …

# 14. Reply:  **“Nothing makes it better.”** 

# 15. If the student asks you if you can do anything to lessen the pain, if there is anything that increases the pain, or if there is any position that relieves the pain, you answer:

# 16. **“If I don’t move at all, it helps a little. The antacids didn’t help at all.”**

# 17. <u>***“ Does anything make it worse?”***</u>

# 18. Reply: **“If I move or take a deep breath it gets worse.”**

# 19. <u>***“What medications have you tried?”***</u>

**“I tried taking 2 TUMS last night, but they didn’t help.”** 

***Nausea*****-** Yes**.** You have been in such pain that you haven’t been able to eat.  It makes you sick to your stomach to smell, or even think about food. Your last meal was dinner last night, right after you came home from work around 6pm. You had some leftover pork chops, spicy cabbage and iced tea.

# 20. ***Vomiting*****-** Yes**. (do not volunteer the vomiting unless they ask specifically)**

You vomited once in the middle of the night.

# 21. ***What color was the vomitus*** 

The vomitus was last night’s dinner and greenish yellow. No blood or “coffee grounds” (if they ask).  Also, there was not a lot of food in the vomit.

***Appetite***

You have no appetite (you can’t even think about eating/drinking). You have had nothing to drink since the episode started.

# 22. ***Fever/sweating/chills:***

If asked, you don’t know if you had a fever but you feel cold and sweaty right now.

# 23. ***Last bowel movement:***

# 24. You had a normal bowel movement yesterday morning. No blood or black stools (if they ask).

# 25. ***Urination:***

# 26. You urinated last night before bed.  The color was yellow, no blood (if they ask).

# 27. <u>**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

You have never had abdominal pain like this before. You are treated for high blood pressure and high cholesterol with three different medications. You see your Family Physician every year for a checkup and she often tells you to quit smoking but it has been very hard.

# 28. <u>**PAST HOSPITALIZATIONS**</u>

You were hospitalized for a tonsillectomy when you were 10.

# 29. <u>**MEDICATIONS**</u>

# 30. **Prescription drugs:**    

# 31. If they ask whether or not you’re on any prescription medicine your answer is **“Yes, I take three different pills for my blood pressure and cholesterol: metoprolol, Benicar and simvastatin.”** 

# 32. **Over-the-Counter (OTC) drugs:**   

You took 2 TUMS last night because of your stomach pain that you thought might be indigestion. You take Motrin or aspirin occasionally for headaches, most recently you took 3 Motrin 2 days ago.

# 33. **Illicit/street drugs:**   

# 34. None

# 35. <u>**SEXUAL HISTORY**</u>

You have a monogamous relationship with your spouse for the past 35 years, and have always enjoyed a good sex life.

# 38. <u>**LIFESTYLE/HABITS**</u>

# 39. **Alcohol:** 

You will not volunteer the following information, but will answer honestly if the student asks you about your drinking.  You consider yourself a “social drinker”, even though you usually have one or two beers everyday; sometimes you drink more, depending on the social occasion.  You don’t get drunk and have never been arrested for a DUI (Driving Under the Influence).

You answer “No” to all the CAGE questions:

	**C**	Have you thought about <u>cutting</u> down?

	**A**	Does anyone get <u>angry</u> because of your drinking?

	**G**	Do you ever feel <u>guilty</u> about your drinking?

**E**	Do you ever need an <u>eye-opener</u> to get you started in the morning?

# 40. **Tobacco:**

# 41. You smoke 1 PPD of Marlboros for the past 45 years. You know you should quit but have not been able to using the patch. 

# 42. **Caffeine:**  

You drink at least <u>two cups of coffee per day</u>, one in the morning and one about 10am.  You also drink at least two diet Cokes, one at lunch and another one at about 3pm.

# 43. **Diet:**

You usually skip breakfast, have a sandwich for lunch, and have “meat and potatoes” for dinner.

# 44. **Exercise:**

You do not exercise regularly.

# 45. **Suicide Risk:**

# 46. None

# 47. **Activities/Hobbies:**

You are in too much pain to discuss.

# 48. **Education:**

# 49. Finished high school.  

# 50. <u>**ENVIRONMENTAL RISK FACTORS**</u>

You have worked for one trucking company for the past 30 years. You are thinking about retiring in the next few years.

# 51. <u>**FAMILY MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

Your father died of a heart attack at age 55. Your mother died recently at 82 from a stroke.

# 52. Your **brother** is 62 and has coronary artery disease.

# 53. <u>**PERSONAL/FAMILY HISTORY**</u>

You have been **married** for 35 years to \_\_\_\_\_, who works at Wall Mart.  You have three children, all grown, and in good health.

# 54. <u>**PHYSICAL EXAM : The students are told to watch you carefully during the PX and during their questioning to see how you move . Consistency in your pain portrayal is very important.**</u>

**NO** rectal exam has been done on you yet.  If the student asks about a rectal exam, say **“The nurse told me someone would be in to do that after you spoke with me.”**

**...** <u>**percussed**</u> **my abdomen in at least ONE place.**

**Your response: 	Hold your abdominal muscles rigid and firm.** Think TOTAL Abdominal protection. You would not push them away, because you don’t have the energy to “fight”

<u>When</u> the student taps on your abdomen, you grimace and wince in pain.

If asked, you report according to where they are tapping:

Don’t give the info until touched

<u>This is severe pain, a 10 on a scale of 1 to 10</u>.

**...** <u>**palpated**</u> **(pressed) my abdomen in all four quadrants.** 	

**Your response:**	Hold your abdominal muscles rigid.  Lie very still.

It is especially bad <u>in the mid-epigastrium (upper third, in the center)</u>; you grimace and wince in pain with the whole exam, but it is excruciating in the mid-epigastrium.

<u>***Rebound Maneuver***</u>:	Watch for this maneuver.

The student might try it in one of several ways:

1.	Push in on your abdomen (with their hands or stethoscope) <u>and let go quickly (but gently)</u>.

2.  Bump the bed.

3.  Rock your pelvis.

4. Tap on your feet

**Your response:**	You grimace or moan in pain with any of these manoevers.  The student may ask you if it hurts more when they let go than when they push down.

**“I don’t know – every time you touch me it hurts!!”**

**Other Items you can expect the student to do:**

Punch mid-back (gently) for CVA tenderness- this would cause pain, because of the movement it causes in your body….not because your kidneys hurt.

If they ask you to sit up, you would say, “I don’t think I can.”

If the student insists, it would be very difficult and slow…you would ask “I think I need help.” **Lying back down would be equally as difficult.**

# 57. <u>**QUESTIONS YOU MUST ASK THE STUDENT:**</u>

# 58. **Middle of the encounter:**  

During the physical exam, when the student pushes on your mid-epigastrium, you moan in pain and say:

# 59. **“Do you have to do that?  That really hurts!”**

If the student has not already addressed this issue, you ask:

# 60. **“Is there anything that you can do to make this pain go away?”**

# 61. A convenient place to insert this issue is when the student asks if <u>you</u> have any questions.

# 62. **End of the encounter if the student has not told you what they think is going on:** 

# 63.    **“What do you think is wrong with me?”** 

If the student mentions surgery or additional tests, you may react with concern, and ask questions about the process mentioned.

private_patient_context:
**CASE 3A**
Robert Goodman,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Robert Goodman is a 25 year old laborer who works for a moving company. Over the last month he has experienced some vague, minor chest pains on exertion, especially while at work when he is lifting. One of Robert’s coworkers (age 45) recently had cardiac problems and was a smoker. His physician recommended that he quit smoking and he did so. He discussed the issue with Robert several times, saying, "Don't wait until you are my age to quit."

Robert is now concerned that there may be some connection between his current symptoms and his smoking. He approached this friend, who gave Robert his leftover patches. Robert tried them a month ago for a few days but used them incorrectly.

Robert is now blaming his inability to quit on the patch. However, Robert smokes about two or three packs a day but started on the lowest level of the patch. That’s what his friend gave him. In addition, Robert took the patch off two or three times a day to smoke. He kept a pack of cigarettes in the moving van, “just in case”. Robert never read the package instructions and did not make any behavioral changes.

The chest pains persisted for about a week, so Robert is now in the office for a follow up visit after starting a medication for gastritis and reflux (Zantac). The symptoms have been relieved by the medication, however, Robert does not like taking pills, and this incident has brought the concept of quitting to the forefront of Robert’s thinking. He is now motivated to quit but this prior “attempt” has left him somewhat disheartened. He does not understand why the patches worked for his friend and not for him.

**Your role is to play a smoker who is** <u>**definitely interested in quitting**</u>**. However, he has come to believe that his recent failure to do so is the fault of the patches he used. He does not understand that he used them incorrectly. He also does not understand that the quitter must actively participate in the quit (make behavioral changes) to be successful. He is mistakenly waiting for the patches to “cure” him.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

Robert is scared that he is going to have a heart attack at any moment, even though his doctor said his heart was fine. There is a long history of cardiac problems in Robert’s family, all of whom were smokers. His father reminded him of this in a recent conversation.

During the office visit he is anxious, stating many times that he really wants to quit now. However, in spite of his anxiety, he is motivated to quit smoking, but not at all confident that he will be able to do so.

When the student asks why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the doctor says that it isn't my heart, but the whole incident made me really think about my smoking.  I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work.”**

**“What do I do now?”**

<u>**Your Smoking History**</u>

You began smoking while in the service at age 18. You have been smoking ever since and now smoke anywhere from one to two packs a day depending on how busy you are at work. On slow days you smoke more since you have a lot of time on your hands. You have never tried to quit before, other than the attempt last month.

During that attempt you experienced significant withdrawal in spite of wearing the patch. You were very irritable, anxious, restless and impatient. After three days you returned to your regular pattern of smoking.

<u>**Family Smoking/Medical History**</u>

Both sets of grandparents smoked as well as both parents. Father has quit, but mother still smokes about a pack a day.

Paternal grandmother had two heart attacks at age 57 and died at 58 as a result.

Maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 55. He was bedridden for eight years as a result and died at age 63.

Father had triple bypass at age 54.

Mother has had a long history of angina starting in her mid-forties.

<u>**Drug/Alcohol use**</u>

You drink a few beers a week on Friday or Saturday night. You have cut back considerably in the last couple years, for no particular reason.

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

If the student asks you about family cardiac history, review the above information with him or her. Otherwise, don’t bring this up.

If the student asks you what you did the last time you tried to quit,  just say,

**“I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work.”**

If the student questions you further as in, **“Which patch did you use?”** or “**Describe to me how you used the patch,”** you may explain exactly what you did:

**“I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me.”**

**“I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”**

**“They didn’t work at all. I still wanted to smoke even though I had the patch on.”**

**“But I want you to know I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.”**

As you explain all this become increasingly anxious. Ask the student,

**“Why can’t you cure me? Can’t you just give me a pill or something?”**

If the student asks you what kind of changes you made in your routines or behavior, ask,

**“What do you mean? Don’t you just put the patch on and forget about it?”**

If the student asks you when you most need a cigarette,

**"In the morning when I wake up, during breaks at work, and after meals."**

If the student asks you what you could do besides smoking at those times,

**“What do you mean?”**

If they give examples of other behaviors (chewing gum, etc.),

**"That's interesting. My buddy who quit is always carrying around those pretzel sticks. I never really asked him about them, but that would probably help.  I also like gum."**

**"I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals."**

If the student asks you to set a quit date,

**"It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday."**

**"Two weeks from Saturday is a good time, that should give me enough time to get ready."**

If the student suggests that you go to a group cessation program, say,

**“I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do?”**

If the student <u>**does not**</u> ask you any questions about how you used the patch or what you did, just continue with the “What am I supposed to do? I really want to quit” line of questioning until he or she does.

**PRESENTING SITUATION & INSTRUCTIONS TO THE STUDENT**

# 1. **Graham**

You are in the Emergency Room at 9 pm.  Your patient is Graham, a 55-year-old patient with abdominal pain.

The patient’s vital signs are:

# 2. 	**Pulse:**	118

	**BP:**	90/65

private_patient_context:
# 1. **Graham**

# 3. <u>**CASE SUMMARY**</u>

You are Graham, a 55 year-old patient with a 1 day history of right sided abdominal pain.  You were in your usual state of health until 8 pm the night before when you noticed the gradual onset of right upper abdominal pain. You ate takeout Chinese food at around 6 pm. The pain was dull but constant and lasted several hours before you finally fell asleep. This morning you initially felt a little better and had some toast for breakfast and then went to work. The pain recurred around mid-morning and has become worse throughout the day, leading you to come in to the Emergency Room tonight. It is now 9:00PM, you have not eaten since breakfast. You had an attack of shaking chills in the waiting room and now feel like you have a fever (you would emphasize this). You have not wanted to eat anything since breakfast but have not vomited. Your last bowel movement was yesterday and was normal.  The pain is constant and located in the right upper quadrant. You also have pain in the right shoulder blade. You work as schoolteacher in a local middle school.

# 4. <u>**PRESENTATION/EMOTIONAL TONE**</u>

When the student enters the room, you are lying on your right side on the exam table with your knees bent.  You are in obvious pain that shows on your face.  You are not moaning, but you are preoccupied with the pain. You are cooperative, and answer all of the student’s questions with relatively short answers; you cannot be drawn into a lengthy conversation because of the severity of the pain.  You verbally relay your anxieties (if asked) because you are worried about the possibility of having an operation. Only if the student doesn’t seem to be handling your situation well will you become impatient, and less communicative.

# 5. **Opening Statement or CC:** 

**In response to the question**, <u>***(“Why are you here today?”***</u>**) you answer in exactly these words:**

	**“I have a terrible pain in my stomach that seems to be getting worse.”**

# 6. <u>**MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

# 7. With the next open ended question such as “Can you tell me more about the pain?”

“**It started around 8pm last night.  It lasted a few hours and then seemed to get better. This morning it came back and it is now so bad I can hardly walk. I also feel like I am getting a fever.”**

# 8. **With specific questions:** 

# 9. **The Pain:**

# 10. **Where:	“It’s right here (points to right upper quadrant).”**

If the student asks where the pain was when it <u>STARTED</u>, the issue being <u>***“Was the pain someplace other than where it is now?”***</u> respond to this question by saying “**It was always right here...”**

# 11. If asked  <u>***“Does the pain go anywhere else?”***</u>  respond that the pain is the worst in right upper quadrant but also seems to go to the right upper back **“Where my shoulder blade is”.** 

# 12. **Intensity:**	On a scale of 1 to 10, this pain is an 8.  

**Constant/Intermittent**:	The pain is <u>constant</u>:  **“It never goes away...”**

**Character:** 	The pain is concentrated in the right upper quadrant but radiates to the right shoulder blade. It is intense and constant.

**Better or worse:**	The student might ask you if anything makes the pain <u>better</u> or if anything makes the pain <u>worse</u>.

# 13. <u>***“What makes it better?”***</u>  …

# 14. Reply:  **“Nothing seems to make it better. I feel like it is getting worse.”** 

# 15. If the student asks you if you can do anything to lessen the pain, if there is anything that increases the pain, or if there is any position that relieves the pain, you answer:

# 16. **“If I lie still, it helps.”**

# 17. <u>***“ Does anything make it worse?”***</u>

# 18. Reply**: “Not really, it hurts all the time.”**

# 19. <u>***“What medications have you tried?”***</u>

**“I am not a big medicine taker.”** 

***Nausea*****-** Yes**.** You have been in such pain that you haven’t been able to eat.  It makes you sick to your stomach to smell, or even think about food. Your last meal was dinner last night, right after you came home from work, around 6pm. You had Chinese takeout (Kung Pao chicken, egg roll, wonton soup). This morning you had some toast and coffee.

***Vomiting*****-** No.

# 20. ***Fever/sweating/chills:***

If asked, feel like you are getting a fever right now. In the waiting room of the ER you had an episode of shaking chills **“I just couldn’t stop shaking”.** 

# 21. ***Last bowel movement:***

# 22. You had a normal bowel movement yesterday morning. No blood or black stools (if they ask about changes to your stool).  You have noticed that your stools are a lighter color (if they ask about changes to your stool).

# 23. ***Urination:***

# 24. You last urinated this afternoon.  The color was dark, “almost like tea” (if they ask).

# 25. If they do not ask, you would mention this as it is a concern of yours. 

# 28. <u>**PAST MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

You have had two episodes of abdominal pain in the recent past. The first was about 6 months ago and occurred at night after dinner. It lasted 3 hours and went away. You thought it might have been food poisoning but didn’t throw up or have diarrhea. The second episode occurred about 2 weeks ago after a lunch birthday party at work. You went to bed early and it seemed to go away by the next day. Both episodes were constant pain in the mid-epigastrium, maybe slightly on the right. You did not have a fever with either episode.

You are treated for asthma with two different inhalers (flovent and albuterol) and hypothyroidism with Synthroid. You see your Family Physician every year for a checkup and have otherwise been healthy.

# 30. <u>**MEDICATIONS**</u>

# 31. **Prescription drugs:**    

# 32. If they ask whether or not you’re on any prescription medicine your answer is **“Yes, I take two inhalers (flovent and albuterol) for asthma and Synthroid for hypothyroidism.”** 

# 33. **Over-the-Counter (OTC) drugs:**   

None.

# 34. **Illicit/street drugs:**   

# 35. None

# 36. <u>**SEXUAL HISTORY**</u>

You are single and not in a sexual relationship at present.

# 37. <u>**LIFESTYLE/HABITS**</u>

# 38. **Alcohol:** 

You will not volunteer the following information, but will answer honestly if the student asks you about your drinking.  You consider yourself a “social drinker”, and have 2-3 drinks per month; sometimes you drink more, depending on the social occasion.  You don’t get drunk and have never been arrested for a DUI (Driving Under the Influence).

You answer “No” to all the CAGE questions:

	**C**	Have you thought about <u>cutting</u> down?

	**A**	Does anyone get <u>angry</u> because of your drinking?

	**G**	Do you ever feel <u>guilty</u> about your drinking?

**E**	Do you ever need an <u>eye-opener</u> to get you started in the morning?

# 39. **Tobacco:**

# 40. You do not smoke. 

# 41. **Caffeine:**  

You drink <u>one cup of coffee per day</u>, in the morning.  You do not drink other caffeinated beverages.

# 42. **Diet:**

You usually have toast for breakfast, a salad for lunch, and “some kind of take out” or frozen meal for dinner.

# 43. **Exercise:**

You walk 30 minutes a day with the dog.

# 44. **Suicide Risk:**

# 45. None

# 46. **Activities/Hobbies:**

You are in too much pain to discuss.

# 47. **Education:**

# 48. Finished high school and college with a degree in education.  

# 49. <u>**ENVIRONMENTAL RISK FACTORS**</u>

You have worked as a middle school teacher for 30 years and enjoy your work.

# 50. <u>**FAMILY MEDICAL HISTORY**</u>

Your father is alive with high blood pressure at 77. Your mother is alive and healthy at 76.

# 51. You have no siblings.

# 52. <u>**PERSONAL/FAMILY HISTORY**</u>

You were married for 20 years, divorced for 10. You have two children aged 15 and 19 who are healthy.

# 53. <u>**PHYSICAL EXAM : The students are told to watch you carefully during the PX and during their questioning to see how you move . Consistency in your pain portrayal is very important.**</u>

**NO** rectal or pelvic exam has been done on you yet.  If the student asks about a rectal or pelvic exam, say **“The nurse told me someone would be in to do that after you spoke with me.”**

**...** <u>**percussed**</u> **my abdomen in at least ONE place.**

**Your response:** 	Hold your abdominal muscles rigid only when they touch the right upper quadrant.

<u>When</u> the student taps on your abdomen in the right upper quadrant, you grimace and wince in pain.

If asked, you report according to where they are tapping:

Don’t give the info until touched

<u>This is moderate to severe pain, an 8 on a scale of 1 to 10</u>.

**...** <u>**palpated**</u> **(pressed) my abdomen in all four quadrants.** 	

**Your response:**	Hold your abdominal muscles rigid only when they touch the right upper quadrant.

It is especially bad <u>in the right upper quadrant</u>; you grimace and with the whole exam, but it is really bad in the right upper quadrant.

<u>***Rebound Maneuver***</u>:	Watch for this maneuver.

The student might try it in one of several ways:

1.	Push in on your abdomen (with their hands or stethoscope) <u>and let go quickly (but gently)</u>.

2.  Bump the bed.

3. Rock your pelvis.

4. Tap on your feet.

	**Your response:**	You grimace or moan in pain in the right upper quadrant only.  The student may ask you if it hurts more when they let go than when they push down.

**“It hurts more when you push down!”**

<u>***Murphy’s Sign:***</u> 	Watch for this maneuver.

The student will push in your right upper quadrant and ask you to take a deep breath.

**Your response:** 	You wince as you breathe in, then abruptly stop breathing in due to pain.

**Other Items you can expect the student to do:**

Punch mid-back (gently) for CVA tenderness- this would cause pain on the right.

# 56. <u>**QUESTIONS YOU MUST ASK THE STUDENT:**</u>

# 57. **Middle of the encounter:**  

During the physical exam, when the student pushes in your right upper quadrant, you moan in pain and say:

# 58. **“Do you have to do that?  That really hurts!”**

If the student has not already addressed this issue, you ask:

# 59. **“Is there anything that you can do to make this pain go away?”**

# 60. A convenient place to insert this issue is when the student asks if <u>you</u> have any questions.

# 61. **End of the encounter if the student has not told you what they think is going on:** 

# 62.    **“What do you think is wrong with me?”** 

If the student mentions surgery or additional tests, you may react with concern, and ask questions about the process mentioned.

**Recurrent STD with Continued Unprotected Sex**

Introduction for the Student:

Bridget Cooper is a 50-year-old heterosexual female presenting to the gynecologist for STD screening. She has had prior sexually transmitted infection screenings in the past and despite being counseled about safe sex practices, has not been using condoms with her partners. She has had 2 partners in the past year and denies any symptoms. She had a partial hysterectomy due to fibroids 12 years ago and is up to date on her PAP smear, colonoscopy and mammogram (all normal). Vital signs are normal. Additionally, she recently had a friend diagnosed with HIV, and therefore would like to have an HIV test also.
private_patient_context:
**Recurrent STD with Continued Unprotected Sex**

Information for the Standardized Patient:

You are a healthy female patient, presenting to the gynecologist for sexually transmitted infection testing. You have had a hysterectomy because of “fibroids” (no cancer) about 12 years ago, so you have not had a menstrual period since that time. You are up to date on your PAP smears and other health screenings, such as mammograms and colonoscopies. You and your gynecologist have had multiple discussions about safe sex practices, but at this time you continue to not use condoms for protection. You do not have any symptoms and have had 2 sexual partners in the past year since your last screening. Prior to that, you cannot remember the number of sexual partners you have had exactly. You are especially concerned today because your friend was diagnosed this year with HIV. You would like to have an HIV test also. Once you have a discussion with your provider about the importance of safe sex practices to prevent STIs and HIV, you are welcoming the change to your lifestyle.

Medical history: none

Medications/Allergies none

Family history: none

Social history: you do not smoke, no alcohol use, no drug use, sexually active with one partner now, male, and one partner prior to that for approximately 6 months. You cannot remember how many partners you have had exactly and your last STI screening was approx. one year ago.

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You do not want to get HIV like your friend, and you didn’t think you could get it since you are heterosexual.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Unprotected sex could lead to STI’s like HIV.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? You love the spontaneity of sex, and you worry that using a condom would ruin the moment for you and your partner. You also worry that your partner will not want to continue having sex with you if you talk about using condoms. You don’t worry so much about SDI’s that can be treated easily like chlamydia, but you really don’t want HIV.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? For the past 12 years, pregnancy has not been a concern, but you worry about HIV and other STIs.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? You would avoid STI’s like HIV.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): You could have a discussion with your partner about using condoms to prevent STIs and how to incorporate this into your sexual activity.
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 9/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You don’t want HIV, and you now realize that you still need to worry about getting it even though you are heterosexual.
    - How could you move that number higher? Watching your friend go through treatment for his HIV will motivate you further, you believe.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 7/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You have used condoms in the past.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Changing your beliefs/attitudes about condom use, incorporating it into foreplay, finding other ways to have spontaneity in sex.
* Ask for a decision: you will use condoms now.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will buy condoms and have them available to use.

# 1. GINA BABKINS  (GERIATRICS OSCE)

# 2. STAGING

**Scenario**

An elderly female patient presents to an outpatient clinic with lightheadedness and is unsteady on her feet.

Complete feedback form.

**STANDARDIZED PATIENT SIMULATION GUIDELINES**

GERIATRICS OSCE – GINA BABKINS

1. Case Overview

- You are Gina Babkins, a 75 year old woman who presents to the outpatient office with a complaint of lightheadedness. You have an appointment in 2 weeks but asked to be seen now because you don’t think you can wait.
- The examinee’s task is to obtain a focused history, perform a focused physical examination and counsel you regarding your situation. Following the encounter, the examinee will then document the encounter in a patient note.

2. ENCOUNTER SETTING

- University Health Services: exam room of an ambulatory (outpatient) medical practice.

3. SP RELATIONSHIPS (Relationship between patient and student doctor)

All participants in this encounter are strangers to one another. You are NOT expected to have already made the acquaintance of the examinee, so you do NOT have to pretend any familiarity.

4. WHAT GOES ON IN THIS ENCOUNTER

A chart is provided to the examinee before the encounter, which contains information about your chief complaint and your vital signs.

Guided by the examinee’s questions and actions, you present with a complaint of lightheadedness and brief medical history to back it up.

A physical examination is expected.

5. PATIENT CHARACTER PRESENTATION

**Age Range**

75

**Presentation**

- Body Language/ Symptom Presentation: Wobbly on your feet when you are asked to move from the chair to the exam table.
- Affect: Good eye contact, alert.
- Appearance/ Costuming: Hospital gown; otherwise well groomed.

**Starting Position**

Sitting in the chair.

6. GINA BABKINS’ STORY

- Opening line: “I have an appointment in two weeks, but I didn’t think I could wait. I hope you don’t mind. I’ve just been so lightheaded lately.”

[The examinee must get the following information out of you by asking you the right questions to elicit this information. Do not volunteer any of this.]

- (Onset) You think the lightheadedness started about a week ago.
  *I have felt this way for about a week*
- (Description) You describe it as a “fuzzy” feeling. It’s not dizziness and the room does not spin. You have not fallen, but you do feel unsteady. Sometimes you feel like you are going to pass out.
  *I feel fuzz or unsteady. I have not fallen and it’s not dizziness, but sometimes I do feel like I could pass out.*
- (Duration) You feel lightheaded a lot (of the waking day).
  *I feel like this most of the time I am awake,*
- (Progression) It’s getting worse this week.
  *This past week it has gotten worse*
- (Additional symptoms) You feel tired, too, and have less of an appetite.

- You aren’t urinating as much as you had been before even though your fluid intake hasn’t really changed (you drink water with your meals). There is no burning or pain with urination, no incontinence. You attribute this problem to your medication not working.
  *I don’t think the water pill is working anymore because I’m not urinating a lot, like I was before.*
- You have been a bit constipated, but the prunes you are eating seem to be helping.
  *I have had a little trouble moving my bowels, but I have been eating prunes and they have seemed to help.*
- (Changes in weight)
  *They weighed me today and it seems like I may have lost weight.*
- (Mitigating factors) The lightheadedness is worse when you stand.
  *When I got up from bed this morning, I got really lightheaded. I had to hold on to the bed.*
- (Prior experience with this/similar problem)
  *I had this problem once before, last year sometime, but it went away.*
- Medications:
  - The “Name” card lists only the names of the medications that you take and should be handed over to the examinee IF AND ONLY IF the examinee asks you if you take any medications.
  - The medications that you are taking are as follows:

ASA (aspirin) 325 mg po daily

Amlodipine 10 mg po daily – (Note: you have been taking this medication for 10 years)

Furosemide 40 mg po daily – (Note: you have been taking this medication for 1 year)

Lisinopril 40 mg po daily – (Note: you have been taking this medication for 10 years)

Atorvastatin 40 mg po at bedtime – (Note: you have been taking this medication for 5 years)

- You take all of the medications exactly as prescribed EXCEPT the furosemide (“water pill”). You sometimes take an extra dose if you feel bloated or your shoes/clothes feel tight. However, there has been no change in your medication dosing by your doctor since you were first prescribed these medications.
  *I check the labels on the bottles every day to be sure I’m taking them correctly.*
  *I do take an extra water pill (furosemide) occasionally when I feel bloated or my clothes or shoes feel too tight.*
- Medical History
  - High blood pressure/cardiac risk – you are on 3 different medications to control your blood pressure, and on one medication (atorvistatin – Lipitor) to control cholesterol. You were first diagnosed with hypertension (high blood pressure) 10 years ago and high cholesterol 5 years ago. You have been experiencing swelling (edema) in your legs for the past year.
  - No surgeries, no illnesses, no allergies
  - If asked: up to date on your flu vaccine and had a “pneumonia shot” about a year ago.
- Family History
  - Father: Deceased at 90 from old age.
  - Mother: Deceased at 87 from breast cancer.
  - Brother: Alive and well at age 87. *He has high blood pressure like me.*
  - Sister: Older sister, age 79. Had a stroke a year ago and lives in assisted living. *She’s close, but I’m not able to get out to see her much.*
- Home Life
  - Live alone. Widowed 10 years. A son and a daughter, both of whom live far away out of state and are not involved in your daily living.
  *My husband had a fall coming out of church and he died in the hospital. He was a sick man and had lots of troubles*
  - Homemaker
  *I’m retired. I took care of my husband when he was alive.*
  - Still drive but haven’t been going out much lately. Nephew brought you to doctor today.
  - Enjoy reading, church bingo
  *...when I’m able to get out.*
  - No alcohol, tobacco or street drugs ever. Don’t drink much coffee. Don’t exercise.
  - Live in one-story ranch house. Helpful nephew lives nearby. Lots of church friends who are supportive.
  - Functioning (if asked): You can get dressed and toilet yourself independently.
  *If I take my time, I can get past that lightheaded feeling.*
  - You take your medication without assistance or reminders from anyone.
  - You drive and do your own shopping, although you haven’t been getting out much.
  - You can cook, but you haven’t felt like it much.
  *...because I’m only cooking for myself.*

7. PHYSICAL EXAM SIMULATION

The examinee is expected to do the following assessments. Except where indicated, allow your body to respond normally.

- Examine the mucous membranes of your mouth for dryness. (Note: If asked, this does not mean that your mouth feels dry or that you are thirsty.)
- Listen to your heart.
- Check your lower extremities for swelling.
- Palpate your abdomen in all 4 quadrants. When the examinee presses on your right or left upper quadrant, express discomfort.
  *When you press there I feel a little uneasy, a little sore.*
- Evaluate your balance, probably by making you stand with your eyes open and closed and walk.

8. DIALOGUE

- Use the wording shown in *italics*, or similar wording of your own, to respond to the examinee.
- If wording in *italics* is also **bolded**, please use the exact phrase provided or as close as possible.
- If you are asked questions not addressed here, please respond “*No*” or create a reasonable response that would not affect the substance of the dialogue or misdirect the examinee.
- Any information that you supply should be consistent from examinee to examinee.
- Allow examinee to probe for information. Do not provide examinee with every fact and detail provided.

**Key Dramatic Points & Response Guides**

**Opening Line**

If Examinee asks: What brings you in today?

SP Responds something like:

*I have an appointment in two weeks, but I didn’t think I could wait.*

*I hope you don’t mind. I’m just not feeling myself.*

*I’ve been feeling lightheaded and tired lately. I don’t know what’s wrong.*

If Examinee asks: WHEN DID THE LIGHTHEADEDNESS START?

*It started about a week ago, but it's been getting worse, this week in particular.*

If Examinee asks: DESCRIBE THE LIGHTHEADEDNESS. HOW DO YOU FEEL?

*I feel lightheaded a lot.*

*My head just seems fuzzy.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU PASSED OUT OR FAINTED?

*No, but sometimes I feel like I’m going to pass out*

If Examinee asks: WHEN DO YOU FEEL LIGHTHEADED? DOES ANYTHING MAKE IT WORSE?

*It's worse when I stand.*

*When I got out of bed this morning, I got really lightheaded.*

*I had to hold onto the bed.*

*I even had it when I was getting out of my nephew’s car today.*

If Examinee asks: DO OBJECTS SPIN AROUND YOU WHEN YOU FEEL LIGHTHEADED? DO YOU FEEL LIKE THE ROOM IS SPINNING?

*No. I don’t really feel dizzy and the room doesn't spin.*

If Examinee asks: DOES MOVING YOUR HEAD SIDE TO SIDE OR CHANGING YOUR POSITION MAKE YOU FEEL LIGHTHEADED?

*No*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU FALLEN?

*No, I haven’t fallen, but I feel unsteady and at times like I might faint.*

If Examinee asks: HOW’S YOUR BALANCE?

*I feel wobbly sometimes*

If Examinee asks: HAS THIS EVER HAPPENED BEFORE?

*Yes, I had this problem once before, last year sometime, but it went away.*

If Examinee asks: DO YOU URINATE FREQUENTLY?

*I don’t think that water pill is working anymore because I’m not urinating a lot, like I was before.*

If Examinee asks: DO YOU HAVE PAIN OR BURNING WHEN YOU URINATE?

*No*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU HAD ANY INCONTINENCE?

*No.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU HAD ANY CONSTIPATION?

*I’ve been a little constipated. Usually, I go every other day.*

*I’ve been taking prunes this week to keep me regular.*

If Examinee asks: HOW ARE YOU SLEEPING?

*Pretty well, thank goodness.*

If Examinee asks: HOW IS YOUR APPETITE? WHAT DO YOU EAT ON A REGULAR DAY?

*Okay.*

*I don’t eat as much as I used to. I just don't feel hungry.*

*I have some toast in the morning. If I feel like eating during the day, I have a little something. TV dinner at night*

If Examinee asks: HOW MUCH FLUID DO YOU DRINK EACH DAY?

*I never did really drink that much.*

*I drink a little water when I eat my meals and to take my medicines – you know, enough to wash it down.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU HAVE ANY CHEST PAIN OR CHEST DISCOMFORT?

*No*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU HAD ANY PALPITATIONS?

*No*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU HAD A COUGH, SHORTNESS OF BREATH? HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY WHEEZING?

*No.*

If Examinee asks: ANY NAUSEA OR VOMITING?

*No.*

If Examinee asks: ARE YOU TAKING ALL OF YOUR MEDICATIONS?

*Yes, I check the bottles every day to be sure I take them correctly.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE THERE BEEN ANY CHANGES IN YOUR MEDICATION?

*No, but I do take an extra water pill when I feel bloated.*

*Otherwise, though, I wouldn’t change my medication without my doctor telling me to do so.*

If Examinee asks: HOW MUCH EXTRA FUROSEMIDE/LASIX DO YOU TAKE?

*Oh, I would only take one extra pill a day.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU TAKEN EXTRA FUROSEMIDE/LASIX RECENTLY?

*A couple of times recently. My shoes felt tight and I was bloated, so I took a little extra.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU EXPERIENCED ANY HEARING LOSS?

*Not that I’ve noticed.*

If Examinee asks: HAVE YOU HAD ANY CHANGES IN YOUR VISION?

*No*

If Examinee asks: DO YOU HAVE ANY CHILDREN?

*I have a daughter in California and a son in Michigan.*

*My nephew brought me here today, but then he went to work. He’s going to pick me up during his hour break.*

If Examinee asks: DO YOU LIVE WITH ANYONE?

*No.*

*My nephew lives about 30 minutes away from my house, but I do live near his work and he visits me every week.*

*He picks up medications, if I need refills, but I can’t depend on him for everything.*

If Examinee asks: HOW ARE YOU FUNCTIONING AT HOME? ARE YOU ABLE TO TAKE CARE OF YOURSELF? DO YOU TAKE CARE OF YOUR OWN SHOPPING?

*I can get dressed and go to the bathroom myself. If I take my time, I don't get lightheaded.*

*I take my medications also.*

*I can drive and do my own shopping, but I haven’t been getting out much.*

*Lately, I don’t feel like cooking either because I’m only cooking for myself.*

If Examinee asks: WHAT DO YOU THINK YOUR LIGHTHEADEDNESS IS DUE TO?

*I don't know.*

9. WHAT TO DO WHEN THE EXAMINEE LEAVES THE ROOM

- Paperwork: For each examinee, complete *Geriatrics OSCE Patient Perception Scale*.
- Re-establish the room to its initial set-up: exam table flat, exam stool under table, side chair by table.
- Assume your starting position.

**Simulated Patient (SP) Training: Cases Information Provided to SPs**

# Case 2: Diabetes Checkup + Certified Deaf interpreter

You have come to the clinic for a routine diabetes management checkup. You have had diabetes for several years and feel like you’re generally managing it ok but haven’t been seen in about a year. You take your medications as prescribed and try to follow a healthy diet. Sometimes you forget to monitor your blood sugar regularly. At times, you notice some numbness or burning in both feet. You have access to an ASL interpreter and a CDI.

**Simulation Setup:**

• Family Medicine Clinic

• ASL Interpreter & CDI present for communication.

**Instructions for the Patient Actor**

**Patient Background:**

• **Name**: You may use your own name or create one

• **Age**: 45

• **Job:** You work at a library and care for your kids.

• **Living Situation:** Middle-income housing in a city of your choice.

**Your Condition & Concerns:**

You have had type 2 diabetes for several years. You take your medications, monitor your blood sugar, and try to follow a healthy diet. However, you have a few questions and concerns:

• Are new diabetes medications better than what you’re taking?

• Could your children develop diabetes, and what can you do to prevent it?

• Is your diet plan effective for managing blood sugar?

• Will your diabetes get worse over time?

• You walk daily—should you try other exercises?

• You feel confident in your routine but want reassurance that you’re doing everything right.

**How to Act During the Simulation:**

• You are calm and cooperative but want clear answers.

• **Facial expressions:** Nod/smile when you understand, frown if confused, look concerned if unsure.

• Ask clarifying questions (listed below)

• There is no physical exam required for this scenario.

• Examples of scripts that you may use below:

*• “Five years ago, my doctor told me I had type 2 diabetes. At first, I was overwhelmed, with all these new rules about food, needles, and numbers. I learned to take my metformin and insulin every morning, though sometimes I forget when life gets busy. Lately, I’ve noticed my feet tingle or feel numb, especially at night. It scares me because my father lost his toes to diabetes. I try to walk daily and eat veggies, but carbs are my weakness. Those Ozempic ads make me wonder, am I doing enough? Could my kids end up like me?”*

*• “Meal planning takes hours. Birthday cakes feel like landmines. My kids ask why I prick my finger, and I don’t want them to fear food or their genes. That’s why I’m here today to learn how to protect my family.”*

**Health Information**

**Diabetes Management:**

• **Medications:** Metformin and insulin, but you sometimes forget to take insulin.

• **Diet:** Balanced but struggle with portion control, especially carbs.

• **Glucose Monitoring:** Regular, but you sometimes forget to log results.

• **Exercise:** Walk daily but want to know if other exercises are better.

**Understanding & Beliefs:**

• You know diabetes is chronic and requires careful management.

• You sometimes feel overwhelmed by all the details.

**Impact on Your Life:**

• Managing diabetes is part of your routine, but it feels burdensome at times.

• You worry about long-term complications.

• You want to feel confident and in control of your health.

**Symptoms & Medical History:**

• Diagnosed with type 2 diabetes five years ago.

• Occasionally fatigued when blood sugar is high.

• No recent low blood sugar episodes (no dizziness, sweating, shaking, irritability)

• No major medical conditions, no tobacco or drug use, occasional alcohol use.

• Family history of diabetes, managed with lifestyle changes.

**Key Questions You Might Ask the Doctor:**

• “Are my current medications still the best option for me?” You’ve seen commercials for new diabetes medications (Ozempic)

• “Is my diet plan working for blood sugar control?”

• “How can I improve my glucose monitoring routine?”

• “What happens if I forget my insulin?”

• “Are there any new diabetes treatments I should know about?”

• “How can I stay motivated to manage my diabetes?”
